Mansa Musa is best remembered for a long journey he made to Mecca, a holy city far to the east. He did not travel quietly. According to accounts from the time, he set out with a huge group of followers and a great supply of gold. As he passed through cities along the way, he gave away and spent so much gold that prices in some places were thrown out of balance for years afterward.

The journey did more than display his riches. It put Mali on the maps that distant scholars drew, and it drew attention to the empire's wealth and learning. Mansa Musa also brought back scholars and builders, and he supported the growth of cities such as Timbuktu, which became known as a center of study. His reign showed how a powerful African empire could shape trade and knowledge across a wide region.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the word 'mansa' means what?
choices: Gold
City
Ruler
Journey
questions.explanation: The passage directly states that the word mansa means ruler.

questions.stem: Why did prices fall out of balance in some cities he passed through?
choices: He took gold from those cities
He gave away and spent so much gold that it upset local prices
He closed the markets
He raised taxes
questions.explanation: The text says he spent and gave away so much gold that prices were thrown out of balance.

questions.stem: Which city is named as a center of study that grew under his support?
choices: Mecca
Mali
Timbuktu
Cairo
questions.explanation: The passage says he supported the growth of Timbuktu, known as a center of study.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How gold is mined in West Africa
How maps were drawn by distant scholars
The founding of the city of Timbuktu
A wealthy ruler of Mali whose famous journey spread his empire's wealth and fame
questions.explanation: The passage centers on Mansa Musa: his gold-rich empire, his journey to Mecca, and how that journey drew the world's attention to Mali's wealth and learning. Timbuktu and the maps are details serving that larger story.

lesson.strategy: A biography in three beats: who Mansa Musa was (gold, salt, "enormously wealthy"), the act he is "best remembered for" (the journey to Mecca), then why it mattered. At "did more than display his riches," the passage turns from spectacle to legacy. Read for the last line's claim.

signals.means: The writer names the single act the rest of the passage will explain and weigh.

signals.phrase: did more than display his riches
signals.means: The turn: from showing off wealth to lasting effects on maps, scholars, and cities.

signals.phrase: thrown out of balance for years afterward
signals.means: A concrete consequence that stands in for scale: he spent so much gold it disrupted whole economies.
The legacy claim: the journey's real result was fame and knowledge, not just show.

vocab.inContext: A ruler or king; the text glosses it directly: "The word mansa means ruler."
The period of his rule as king, summed up in the passage's final sentence.
Learned people who study and write, both the distant mapmakers and the ones he brought back.

skillTips.main-idea: Don't stop at "he was rich." It builds to its last line: his reign "showed how a powerful African empire could shape trade and knowledge." Wealth is the setup; influence is the point.
skillTips.inference: No gold amount is given. Infer scale from effect: if prices were "thrown out of balance for years," he must have spent a staggering quantity. Read the consequence to size the cause.
skillTips.vocabulary: "mansa" is defined inside the text: "The word mansa means ruler." When a biography introduces a foreign title, look for the author's own gloss nearby before guessing.
skillTips.detail: After the pivot, track the journey's results separately: it put Mali on scholars' maps, he brought back "scholars and builders," and he supported Timbuktu as "a center of study."

passages.title: Before and After Jenner’s Vaccine
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Long before vaccination, communities in parts of Asia and Africa practiced forms of variolation: introducing material from a person with smallpox in hopes of causing a milder infection and later protection. The method carried serious risks, but knowledge of it traveled to other regions. Edward Jenner’s work therefore began within a longer, international history of preventing smallpox.

In England, Jenner also learned from rural observations that people who had caught cowpox seemed protected from smallpox. In 1796, he used material linked to cowpox from Sarah Nelmes in an experiment on James Phipps, his gardener’s eight-year-old son. Jenner later deliberately exposed Phipps to smallpox, and the boy did not develop the disease.

That experiment helped demonstrate a path toward vaccination, but it also presents an ethical wrong. An eight-year-old could not provide modern informed consent, and exposing a child to such danger would violate current research protections. Naming that problem is part of telling the history accurately, not a denial that vaccination became valuable.

Jenner did not end smallpox alone. Researchers, vaccine producers, governments, the World Health Organization, and local health workers built later campaigns. Vaccination was combined with case finding, surveillance, and rapid containment across many countries. In 1980, the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated. The achievement joined earlier knowledge, scientific testing, public-health organization, and sustained work by many people.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
choices: Earlier knowledge and Jenner’s unethical experiment advanced smallpox vaccination; eradication required collective work.
Jenner alone invented smallpox prevention, ran an ethical child experiment, and immediately achieved global eradication.
Variolation and vaccination were identical, equally safe practices developed entirely by Jenner.
Smallpox disappeared after one English experiment, before organized international campaigns began.
questions.explanation: The passage joins earlier variolation, Jenner’s contribution and ethical failure, and the later international eradication campaign.

questions.stem: What practice existed before Jenner’s vaccination experiment?
choices: Modern informed-consent review
Worldwide laboratory surveillance
Variolation in parts of Asia and Africa
The World Health Assembly’s eradication declaration
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph describes forms of variolation practiced before vaccination.

questions.stem: Why does the passage discuss informed consent?
choices: To show that useful results erase concerns about how research is conducted
To evaluate the experiment’s method as well as its later importance
To explain why Phipps designed Jenner’s experiment
To argue that all historical medicine should be ignored
questions.explanation: The passage says ethical criticism belongs in an accurate account even when the later medical contribution mattered.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, “eradicated” means
choices: made more difficult to observe
eliminated worldwide
renamed by an international group
treated in one English village
questions.explanation: The declaration followed coordinated work across many countries, so “eradicated” means eliminated worldwide.

lesson.strategy: Read this as a layered history, not a lone-inventor story. Paragraph one establishes earlier practice; paragraphs two and three separate a result from the ethics of the experiment; paragraph four distributes credit for eradication across a public-health network.

signals.means: Places earlier prevention knowledge before Jenner’s experiment.
Turns from the result to the treatment of the child participant.
Rejects lone-person credit for global eradication.
Introduces the other public-health methods needed in the campaign.

vocab.inContext: an older, risky method intended to produce protection from smallpox
an informed and voluntary agreement to take part
eliminated worldwide through sustained public-health work

skillTips.main-idea: A complete summary includes earlier knowledge, Jenner and Phipps, the ethical problem, and collective eradication.
skillTips.detail: The first paragraph names the preventive practice that came before vaccination.
skillTips.inference: Historical importance and ethical acceptability are separate questions; the passage evaluates both.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the worldwide campaign and 1980 declaration to distinguish eradication from local control.

passages.title: The Brothers Who Learned to Fly
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Orville and Wilbur Wright were two brothers in the United States who ran a shop that built and repaired bicycles. In their free time, they shared a big dream. They wanted to build a machine that could fly.

Many people had tried to fly before and failed. The brothers studied birds and tested small models. They built a flying machine with wings and an engine, and they practiced controlling it. They also used a wind tunnel to learn how air pushed against different shapes.

In 1903, near a windy beach in North Carolina, their machine lifted off the ground and flew for a short time. It was one of the first flights by a powered airplane. Their patient work helped open the age of flying.

questions.stem: What kind of shop did the Wright brothers run?
choices: A bakery
A bicycle shop
A bookstore
A clothing store
questions.explanation: The passage says they ran a shop that built and repaired bicycles.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest helped the brothers succeed?
choices: They were lucky on the first try with no practice
They studied, tested, and practiced patiently
They copied a finished airplane
They flew without any planning
questions.explanation: The text describes them studying birds, testing models, using a wind tunnel, and practicing.

questions.stem: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: How to fix a bicycle
Two brothers whose careful work led to one of the first powered flights
A trip to the beach
How birds build nests
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on the brothers' effort to build a flying machine and their early flight.

questions.stem: In the passage, "patient" work means work that is:
choices: done in a hospital
quick and careless
slow, careful, and not giving up
loud and exciting
questions.explanation: The brothers studied birds, tested models, and practiced for years before their short flight. "Patient" work is steady, careful effort that keeps going without giving up.

lesson.strategy: This tells how two brothers built the first flying machine. Read it as a how-they-did-it story: follow the steps in order, then the date it worked, then the last line that says why it mattered.

signals.means: Flying was not their job. They fixed bikes for money and chased the dream on the side.

signals.phrase: Many people had tried to fly before and failed
signals.means: Sets up the stakes: the brothers were trying to do what others could not.
The turning point. All the studying and testing before this leads to the one moment it worked.

signals.phrase: Their patient work helped open the age of flying
signals.means: The closing line says why the story matters: slow, careful work changed the world.

vocab.inContext: a box that blows air, used to test how air pushes on different wing shapes
run by an engine, not just floating or gliding on the wind
willing to work slowly for a long time without giving up

skillTips.main-idea: One question drives it: how did two bike-shop brothers build the first flying machine? Do not stop at the flight; the last line "helped open the age of flying" says why it mattered.
skillTips.inference: The text never calls the brothers clever or hard-working. You see it in what they did: they "studied birds," "tested small models," and "used a wind tunnel." Name the trait these show.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words come with a nearby clue. "Wind tunnel" is explained right after: "to learn how air pushed against different shapes." Read the next few words before you guess.
skillTips.detail: The when and where sit in the last paragraph. To find a fact, go there: "In 1903, near a windy beach in North Carolina." The date and place are stated, not hinted.

passages.title: The Quiet Power of Compounding
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine planting a single coin that grows a little each year, and that the growth itself starts to grow. This is the heart of compound interest. In the first year, you earn a small amount on what you saved. In the second year, you earn money not only on your original savings but also on the interest from the first year. Each round builds on the last.

The surprise is how slow it feels at the start and how fast it becomes later. For a long time the pile barely seems to move. Then, almost without warning, it climbs steeply. People who begin saving early often end up far ahead of those who save more but begin late, because they give the process more time to fold gains upon gains.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Saving money is impossible for most people
Compound interest makes savings grow on earlier gains, rewarding time
Coins are a poor way to store money
Interest rates change every year
questions.explanation: The passage explains that interest is earned on both original savings and prior interest, and that time is the key advantage.

questions.stem: Why might an early saver beat a later saver who saves more?
choices: Early savers earn higher interest rates
More time lets gains keep building on gains
Later savers always lose money
Banks favor younger customers
questions.explanation: The text says beginning early gives 'the process more time to fold gains upon gains.'

questions.stem: In the passage, 'steeply' most nearly means
choices: slowly and evenly
sharply and quickly upward
downward toward zero
in a flat line
questions.explanation: The pile 'climbs steeply' after a slow start, meaning a sharp, fast rise.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do you earn money on in the second year?
choices: Only your original savings
Only the first year's interest
Both your original savings and the first year's interest
Nothing until the third year
questions.explanation: The passage says that in the second year "you earn money not only on your original savings but also on the interest from the first year." Each round builds on the last.

lesson.strategy: This explainer teaches one idea with a picture. Hold the coin in mind, then follow the year-by-year steps that unpack it. Track the contrast between "slow at the start" and "fast later," and notice the passage ends on a point about time.

signals.phrase: the growth itself starts to grow
signals.means: The one idea the whole passage explains: gains earn their own gains, not just the savings.

signals.phrase: Each round builds on the last
signals.means: Marks the step-by-step mechanism: each year uses last year's total as its new base.

signals.phrase: how slow it feels at the start
signals.means: The turn. The main surprise is the shape of the change over time, not the size of it.

signals.phrase: begin saving early often end up far ahead
signals.means: The takeaway. After the mechanism, the point lands on time, not on the amount saved.

vocab.inContext: interest that grows on both your savings and the interest already earned
rising fast and sharply, like a steep hill
to keep stacking new gains on top of old gains, layer over layer

skillTips.main-idea: The passage names its point: "This is the heart of compound interest." The main idea is that line, growth that grows on itself. Don't pick a detail instead.
skillTips.inference: No plain rule says why early savers win. Join two clues: they "begin saving early" and "give the process more time." Time, not the amount, does the work.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words are unpacked by nearby sentences. For "compound," read the year-one and year-two example right after it; that story shows the meaning.
skillTips.detail: The two years are exact steps. Year one: you earn "on what you saved." Year two: also "on the interest." For "earn on what?" reread those two sentences.

passages.title: Seeing What We Expect
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Once we form a belief, the mind quietly begins to defend it. We notice facts that fit what we already think and skim past those that do not. This habit is called confirmation bias, and it operates below our awareness, which is what makes it so stubborn.

Consider someone convinced that a certain food cures colds. When they recover after eating it, they count that as proof. When they stay sick, they decide they simply did not eat enough, or they forget the case entirely. Every outcome is bent to support the belief.

The danger is not that we hold opinions but that we stop testing them. A more careful thinker deliberately searches for evidence that could prove the belief wrong. If the belief survives that honest search, it has earned more trust. Confirmation bias is not a sign of stupidity; even brilliant people fall into it. It is simply the path of least mental effort, and resisting it takes practice.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
choices: why certain foods cure colds
how we favor evidence that supports beliefs we already hold
why brilliant people make fewer mistakes
the importance of holding strong opinions
questions.explanation: The whole passage defines and illustrates confirmation bias, the tendency to favor confirming evidence.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what makes a belief more trustworthy?
choices: Holding it confidently
Finding many people who agree
Surviving an honest search for evidence against it
Repeating it often
questions.explanation: The text says if a belief survives a search for disproving evidence, it 'has earned more trust.'

questions.stem: As used here, 'stubborn' most nearly means
choices: easy to remove
hard to change or overcome
loud and obvious
rarely noticed by anyone
questions.explanation: The bias is called stubborn because it operates below awareness, making it hard to change.

questions.stem: In the passage's example, what does the believer do when they stay sick after eating the food?
choices: They give up the belief right away
They test the food on someone else
They decide they did not eat enough, or forget the case entirely
They warn others that the cure fails
questions.explanation: The passage says that when the food fails, "they decide they simply did not eat enough, or they forget the case entirely": every outcome is bent to support the belief.

lesson.strategy: This essay defines a mind-trap, then argues against it. Get the definition ("confirmation bias"), watch the food example show it, then find the turn at "The danger is not..." where the fix appears: search for evidence that could prove you wrong.

signals.means: The named idea the whole essay explains; everything after it is example or argument about this one thing.

signals.phrase: Every outcome is bent to support the belief
signals.means: The food story's point: recovering and staying sick both get read as proof, so nothing can disprove it.
The thesis turn. The real argument sits here, not in the opening definition: the danger is not testing beliefs.

signals.phrase: It is simply the path of least mental effort
signals.means: The reframe: the bias is laziness, not stupidity, so anyone can fall in and must resist on purpose.

vocab.inContext: Hard to get rid of, because the bias works below our awareness where we can't see it.
Twisted or forced by us so any result ends up looking like proof of the belief.
On purpose, by choice; the careful thinker searches for disproof on purpose, not by accident.

skillTips.main-idea: The main point is not the paragraph-one definition. It is the claim at "The danger is not... that we stop testing them." The bias is defined only to argue we should test our beliefs.
skillTips.inference: The food example is proof by design: recovering counts as "proof," staying sick they "forget the case entirely." If both outcomes support the belief, it can never be disproven: the trap.
skillTips.vocabulary: "bent" is figurative, not physical. Read "Every outcome is bent to support the belief" as: the person twists each result until it fits. Recovering and staying sick both show the twisting.
skillTips.detail: See paragraph three for the careful thinker: they "deliberately" search for evidence that could "prove the belief wrong," and only if it survives has it "earned more trust".

passages.title: The Shared Field
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Picture a meadow open to every herder in a village. Each may graze as many animals as they like, free of charge. For any single herder, the logic is simple: adding one more cow brings a clear private gain, while the cost of slightly overgrazed grass is spread across the whole village. So each herder, acting reasonably, keeps adding animals.

The trouble is that everyone reasons the same way. The grass, which could have fed the herds for generations, is stripped bare within a few seasons. What was rational for each person turns out to be ruinous for all. This pattern is known as the tragedy of the commons, and it appears wherever a shared resource has no limits on its use: fisheries emptied of fish, air thickened with smoke, roads choked with traffic.

The lesson is not that people are wicked. The herders are not villains; they are responding sensibly to the incentives in front of them. The failure lies in the structure. When the benefits of use are private but the costs are shared, individual good sense produces collective harm. Solutions usually require changing that structure, by assigning ownership, setting enforceable limits, or charging for use, so that the cost of taking more lands on the one who takes it.

questions.stem: What is the central point of the passage?
choices: Herders are greedy and should be punished
Shared resources with no limits get overused because costs are spread while gains are private
Meadows are the best place to raise cattle
People always act against their own interests
questions.explanation: The passage defines the tragedy of the commons: private gains plus shared costs lead to overuse and collective harm.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, why do the proposed solutions focus on structure rather than character?
choices: Because changing laws is cheaper than educating people
Because the harm comes from incentives, not from people being wicked
Because herders cannot understand the problem
Because shared resources can never be saved
questions.explanation: The text stresses that herders are not villains; the failure is in the structure of incentives, so fixes target structure.

questions.stem: Which example of the tragedy does the passage give?
choices: Banks running out of money
Fisheries emptied of fish
Forests planted too densely
Crowds at a concert
questions.explanation: The passage lists 'fisheries emptied of fish' as an example of a shared resource being overused.

questions.stem: In the passage, "ruinous" most nearly means:
choices: profitable
reasonable
destructive
temporary
questions.explanation: Each herder's rational choice left the meadow "stripped bare within a few seasons," so what was "ruinous for all" was destructive to everyone.

lesson.strategy: Read this as an argument, not a story. The meadow just sets it up; the real claim lands at "The failure lies in the structure." Track how "private" gain and "shared" cost drive each herder, then see every fix change that structure.

signals.means: The turn: reasonable individual logic becomes collective disaster once everyone reasons the same way.
The writer blocks a wrong reading (people are wicked) before naming the real cause.

signals.phrase: The failure lies in the structure
signals.means: The thesis: blame the incentive setup, not the herders. Everything else supports this line.
Shift to the fix; each remedy works by changing the private-benefit, shared-cost structure.

vocab.inContext: a resource open to everyone with no limits on use, like the "free of charge" meadow
the rewards and costs "in front of" a person that steer their choices
destructive; grazing sensible for one "turns out to be ruinous for all"

skillTips.main-idea: Don't stop at the meadow. Find where it names the cause: "The failure lies in the structure" and "individual good sense produces collective harm." The point is structure, not grass.
skillTips.inference: Herders are "not villains," so the setup causes overgrazing. Each herder gets "clear private gain" while the cost is "spread across the whole village": gains fully, pays a sliver.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Commons" is never defined directly. The opening line, "a meadow open to every herder... free of charge," shows it means a resource anyone can use with no limits.
skillTips.detail: The pattern isn't only grass. For concrete cases, scan the list: "fisheries emptied of fish, air thickened with smoke, roads choked with traffic."

passages.title: The Loop Behind a Habit
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A habit is a behavior the brain has learned to run on autopilot. It usually forms around a simple loop with three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. The cue is a trigger, such as a time of day or a feeling. The routine is the action itself. The reward is the payoff that tells the brain the loop is worth remembering.

When the same loop repeats often enough, the brain stops deliberating and lets the cue pull the routine along almost automatically. This saves effort, which is the whole point: habits free attention for harder tasks. But the same machinery that builds helpful habits also builds harmful ones, because the brain does not judge whether a reward is good for you, only whether it feels rewarding.

This is why willpower alone rarely changes a habit. A more effective approach keeps the cue and the reward but swaps the routine in between for a better one. The trigger still fires, the payoff still arrives, but the action that connects them is replaced.

questions.stem: The passage mainly explains
choices: why willpower always works
how habits form through a cue, routine, and reward loop
which rewards are good for health
how the brain rests during sleep
questions.explanation: The passage centers on the three-part habit loop and how it operates.

questions.stem: Why does the passage suggest keeping the cue and reward while changing the routine?
choices: Because cues and rewards cannot be removed
Because the loop still triggers and pays off, but with a better action between
Because routines are the easiest part to ignore
Because rewards are always harmful
questions.explanation: The text says the trigger still fires and the payoff still arrives, but the routine in between is replaced.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the reward do?
choices: It creates the cue
It signals to the brain that the loop is worth remembering
It cancels the routine
It replaces willpower
questions.explanation: The text states the reward is 'the payoff that tells the brain the loop is worth remembering.'

questions.stem: In this passage, "deliberating" most nearly means:
choices: resting between tasks
repeating an action
thinking a choice over carefully
seeking a reward
questions.explanation: The text says the brain "stops deliberating" once a loop is learned, meaning it stops thinking the choice over and lets the cue pull the routine along automatically.

lesson.strategy: A psychology explainer built on one model: the three-part habit loop. Pin down cue, routine, and reward first, then follow the two turns: "But the same machinery" (the same process builds bad habits too) and "This is why willpower alone rarely" (so swap the routine, keep the other two).

signals.phrase: a cue, a routine, and a reward
signals.means: The three parts of the loop; the next three sentences define each one in order; this is the backbone.
The turn: the same process that builds helpful habits also builds harmful ones.

signals.phrase: This is why willpower alone rarely
signals.means: The payoff line: it uses the loop to explain why willpower fails and points to the real fix.

signals.phrase: keeps the cue and the reward but swaps the routine
signals.means: The solution stated exactly: change the routine, keep the other two parts.

vocab.inContext: a trigger that starts the loop, such as a time of day or a feeling
thinking a choice over; the brain stops doing this once a loop repeats enough
the brain's habit-building process, pictured as a machine that runs good or bad the same way

skillTips.main-idea: The first sentence defines a habit; the last paragraph says what to do about one. The passage circles one model: the cue-routine-reward loop and how to change it.
skillTips.inference: The brain "does not judge whether a reward is good for you, only whether it feels rewarding." Chain that to the loop: a bad routine that feels rewarding still gets remembered.
skillTips.vocabulary: For cue, routine, and reward, read the sentence right after each is named: "The cue is a trigger...", "The routine is the action...", "The reward is the payoff...".
skillTips.detail: Details come in threes and in what-stays-vs-what-changes. Track which two the fix keeps (cue, reward) and which one it swaps (routine). Match a question to the exact part it names.

passages.title: Where Price Comes From
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Prices are not set by a single person. They emerge from a tug-of-war between two forces: how much of a thing is available and how much people want it. These forces are called supply and demand.

When many people want a product but little of it exists, the price rises. Buyers compete, and sellers can ask for more. When a product is everywhere but few people want it, the price falls, because sellers must lower it to attract anyone at all. Most of the time the two forces pull toward a balance, a price where the amount offered roughly matches the amount wanted.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How to start a business
How supply and demand together shape prices
Why oranges are expensive
How buyers can avoid paying
questions.explanation: The passage explains that price emerges from the interaction of supply and demand.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what would likely happen to the price of umbrellas during a long drought?
choices: It would rise sharply
It would likely fall, since fewer people want them
It would stay exactly the same
It would be set by the government
questions.explanation: Lower demand pushes price down, as the passage says sellers must lower prices when few people want a product.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'emerge' most nearly means
choices: disappear
come into being from something
stay fixed
be commanded
questions.explanation: Prices 'emerge from a tug-of-war,' meaning they arise out of those forces.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens when many people want a product but little of it exists?
choices: The price rises
The price falls
Sellers give it away
The product disappears
questions.explanation: The text states that when many want a product but little exists, "the price rises": buyers compete, and sellers can ask for more.

lesson.strategy: This explains where a price comes from. The first two sentences give the answer: two forces, supply and demand. The middle two are mirror cases: price rises, then falls. The last sentence lands on balance. Read it as answer, two examples, then the middle point.

signals.means: The core image: price is a pull between what's available (supply) and what people want (demand).
Case one: lots of want, little supply. Buyers compete, so sellers can charge more.
Case two: lots of supply, little want. Sellers drop the price to attract buyers. Mirror of case one.
The landing point: the two forces usually settle where amount offered matches amount wanted.

vocab.inContext: come out on their own; prices are not set by one person, they come from the two forces
pull buyers in; sellers lower the price to attract anyone at all
an even middle point where the amount offered roughly matches the amount wanted

skillTips.main-idea: The answer is in the first two sentences: two forces, supply and demand. To state the main idea, join those forces to the ending 'balance', not just one example.
skillTips.inference: The two 'When...' sentences show a pattern, not one fact. Much want + little supply pushes price up; much supply + little want pushes it down. Infer the rule from both cases.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words sit next to their own clue. 'emerge from a tug-of-war' means come out of it; 'lower it to attract anyone' means pull buyers in. Read the words around the hard word.
skillTips.detail: The passage gives two opposite cases. For a detail question, match the exact condition first: 'few people want it' goes with 'the price falls', not rises. Pick the case that fits.

passages.title: The Price of Your Attention
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Many of the apps and sites people use every day cost nothing to open. This generosity has a hidden logic. The companies behind them do not sell a product to you; they sell you, or rather your attention, to advertisers. The longer you stay and the more often you return, the more there is to sell.

This arrangement quietly reshapes the design of the things we use. A tool built mainly to be useful would help you finish a task and leave. A tool built to capture attention does the opposite: it is engineered to keep you scrolling. Endless feeds, autoplaying videos, and notifications timed to pull you back are not accidents. They are the natural result of measuring success by time spent rather than tasks completed.

None of this requires bad intentions. Designers are simply responding to what they are rewarded for. If a small change makes people linger a few seconds longer, it spreads, while a change that helps people leave satisfied may be quietly discarded. Over millions of users, those tiny choices accumulate into systems that are very good at holding us and not always good for us. Understanding the incentive does not switch it off, but it does let you watch the machinery work and decide, more deliberately, how much of yourself to feed it.

questions.stem: The central idea of the passage is that
choices: free apps are a gift to users with no catch
when attention is the product, apps are designed to hold us rather than help us finish
advertisers dislike apps that are free
designers intend to harm their users
questions.explanation: The passage argues that selling attention to advertisers shapes design toward holding users, not serving them.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say a feature that helps people 'leave satisfied' might be discarded?
choices: It is too expensive to build
Users complain about it
Success is measured by time spent, so features that reduce time spread less
It violates advertising laws
questions.explanation: Because success is measured by time spent, changes that make people linger spread, while ones that help people leave are discarded.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'accumulate' most nearly means
choices: disappear over time
build up into a larger whole
stay separate forever
cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Tiny choices 'accumulate into systems,' meaning they build up into something larger.

questions.stem: Which design features does the passage name as engineered to keep you scrolling?
choices: Passwords, settings, and search bars
Subscriptions, receipts, and login screens
Endless feeds, autoplaying videos, and timed notifications
Maps, calendars, and reminders
questions.explanation: The passage names them directly: "Endless feeds, autoplaying videos, and notifications timed to pull you back are not accidents." They follow naturally from measuring success by time spent.

lesson.strategy: This is an argument. The first sentence is bait, not the thesis. Find the real claim about who the product is, then track how design follows the money. Watch the turn at 'None of this requires bad intentions': blame shifts from people to the reward system. End on what you can actually do.

signals.phrase: sell you, or rather your attention, to advertisers
signals.means: The thesis: you are the product being sold, not the buyer. Everything after explains this.
Feeds and notifications are deliberate results of the incentive, not sloppy or accidental design.

signals.phrase: None of this requires bad intentions
signals.means: The pivot. Blame shifts from villains to a reward system that produces the outcome on its own.
The qualified conclusion: awareness cannot stop the machinery, only let you choose how much to feed it.

vocab.inContext: The reward driving design: keeping you longer, since that is what advertisers pay for.
Tiny per-user choices build up over millions into powerful attention-holding systems.
Making a conscious choice about your attention instead of being pulled in automatically.

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea is not the first sentence. Combine 'they sell you... your attention, to advertisers' with the ending: free apps are shaped by what advertisers reward, not what helps you.
skillTips.inference: The text calls features 'not accidents' and says designers respond 'to what they are rewarded for.' Infer the stance: no villain is needed; the reward system produces the harm by itself.
skillTips.vocabulary: For 'incentive,' read the sentence around it: 'responding to what they are rewarded for' defines it. Let the cause-and-effect language nearby pin the word's meaning.
skillTips.detail: Separate claim from example. 'Endless feeds, autoplaying videos, and notifications' are concrete cases of the claim that tools are 'engineered to keep you scrolling.' Tie each to its claim.

passages.title: Why the Crowd Attracts a Crowd
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Some products become more valuable the more people use them. A single telephone is useless; there is no one to call. A million telephones form a system worth far more than the sum of its parts. This pattern is called a network effect.

The pull is powerful. Once a service has many users, newcomers join because that is where everyone already is, and each new member makes it more attractive to the next. The same force can trap people, too. A product may keep its lead not because it is best but because everyone is already there, and no one wants to be first to leave. This is why strong networks are hard to challenge: a rival must offer not just a better tool, but a reason for the whole crowd to move at once.

questions.stem: What is the main idea?
choices: Telephones are outdated technology
Some products grow more valuable as more people use them, which both attracts and traps users
The best product always wins the market
People dislike joining large networks
questions.explanation: The passage defines network effects and shows how they attract newcomers and lock users in.

questions.stem: Why is the strongest network hard for a rival to defeat?
choices: Rivals lack money
A rival must convince the whole crowd to move at once, not just build a better tool
Networks are protected by law
Users never try new products
questions.explanation: The text says a rival must offer a reason for the whole crowd to move together, not merely a better tool.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why is a single telephone useless?
choices: It is too expensive
There is no one to call
It breaks easily
It cannot connect to the internet
questions.explanation: The passage states 'A single telephone is useless; there is no one to call.'

questions.stem: In the passage, "rival" most nearly means:
choices: a loyal user
a competing product trying to win users
a telephone engineer
a network's founder
questions.explanation: The rival is the challenger that "must offer not just a better tool, but a reason for the whole crowd to move at once," that is, a competing product trying to take the users.

lesson.strategy: An explainer that defines one idea, then complicates it. Read the telephone example to grab the core claim, then watch the turn at 'The same force can trap people, too': the same pull that helps also locks people in. Hold both sides together.

signals.phrase: This pattern is called a network effect.
signals.means: The passage names its central idea. Everything before is the example; everything after explores this term.

signals.phrase: The same force can trap people, too.
signals.means: The turn. The writer flips from the good side (pull) to the bad side (lock-in) using the same cause.
The key contrast: a product can lead on crowd size, not quality. Watch the 'not X but Y' shape here.
A short line that shifts the passage from defining the effect to showing what it does to people.

vocab.inContext: When a product gets more valuable as more people use it, like phones needing others to call.
To keep people stuck in a product because everyone else is there, not because it is best.
A competing product trying to win users away from the one already in the lead.

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea is not the telephone; the phones are proof. Ask what they prove: a product can gain value from having many users. Add the twist: that same pull can also trap people.
skillTips.inference: Why are strong networks 'hard to challenge'? Link two lines: people stay 'because everyone is already there,' and a rival needs 'the whole crowd to move at once.' The crowd is the wall.
skillTips.vocabulary: For 'network effect,' don't guess from the words 'network' and 'effect.' The passage defines it right after the telephone example: value that grows as more people use the product.
skillTips.detail: Details here come in pairs. 'A single telephone is useless' sits against 'A million telephones form a system.' When asked about a number or example, find its matching opposite nearby.

passages.title: Does Choosing Wear Us Down?
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
After many difficult choices, people sometimes feel tired or reach for an easy option. One explanation is called decision fatigue: the hypothesis that making repeated decisions reduces the quality of later choices.

Some studies have found patterns that fit the hypothesis. A person may accept a default, delay a decision, or use a shortcut later in a sequence. Yet a pattern over time has other possible causes. The later cases may be harder. People may become hungry, bored, rushed, or more experienced. Researchers may also choose one of many ways to define a “worse” decision.

Stronger tests try to separate these explanations. In one large preregistered study of healthcare calls, researchers predicted specific changes as workers handled repeated cases. They did not find the predicted decision-fatigue effects in that setting. This result does not prove that repeated choices never matter. It does challenge the idea of one general effect that reliably drains a fixed store of mental energy.

Reducing needless choices can still be useful. A routine may save time, lower stress, or prevent distraction. Those benefits do not prove a fuel-tank theory of the mind. The careful conclusion is narrower: mental work can feel tiring, but when and how repeated decisions alter judgment remains an active research question.

questions.stem: The passage mainly argues that
choices: decision fatigue is a debated hypothesis whose effects and mechanism are not settled
every repeated choice empties the same fixed mental fuel tank
routines are harmful because they remove all useful choices
healthcare workers never feel tired during repeated work
questions.explanation: The passage presents the hypothesis, alternative explanations, a null result, and a cautious conclusion.

questions.stem: Why does using a routine not prove that the mind has a fixed fuel tank?
choices: A routine always creates more decisions than it removes
A routine can help for reasons such as time, stress, or distraction
People cannot feel tired while following a routine
Researchers define every routine in the same way
questions.explanation: The final paragraph gives several benefits that do not require the fixed-energy explanation.

questions.stem: In this passage, a “hypothesis” is
choices: a result that no evidence could ever change
a shortcut used to avoid every decision
a possible explanation that can be tested
a list of cases in the order they arrived
questions.explanation: Decision fatigue is introduced as an explanation to test, not as an established fact.

questions.stem: What did the large preregistered healthcare study find?
choices: Every later call received the same answer
Workers stopped making decisions after one hour
Hunger explained every change in judgment
The predicted decision-fatigue effects did not appear in that setting
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the researchers did not find the predicted effects in that setting.

lesson.strategy: Track claim, alternatives, test, and conclusion. The passage does not replace “decision fatigue is true” with “fatigue never exists.” It narrows what the evidence supports and separates a useful routine from proof of a mechanism.

signals.means: Marks decision fatigue as a testable explanation, not a settled fact.
Introduces rival explanations for the same pattern.
Reports the preregistered study’s result with its setting attached.
Signals the qualified final claim.

vocab.inContext: a possible explanation that researchers can test
planned and recorded before researchers saw the results
an option selected when a person makes no active change

skillTips.main-idea: Keep the uncertainty: neither an absolute fuel theory nor “choices never matter” matches the passage.
skillTips.inference: A helpful routine can have several explanations, so usefulness alone does not identify a mechanism.
skillTips.vocabulary: The colon after “decision fatigue” introduces the hypothesis in plain language.
skillTips.detail: Attach the null result to its healthcare-call setting; do not turn one study into a universal proof.

passages.title: Memory as Rebuilding
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
We tend to imagine memory as a recording, a faithful video stored away and replayed on demand. The truth is stranger. Each time we remember something, we are not pressing play; we are rebuilding the event from scattered fragments, filling the gaps with assumptions about how things usually go.

This reconstruction is useful. It lets us recall the gist of an experience without storing every detail, which would be impossibly costly. But it also means memory is editable. A leading question, a later conversation, even our own retelling can slip new details into the rebuilt scene, and we cannot feel the seam where invention meets fact. The altered memory seems just as vivid and certain as a true one.

This has unsettling consequences. Eyewitnesses can sincerely describe events that never happened, not because they lie but because their minds rebuilt the past around suggestions planted afterward. Confidence, it turns out, is a poor measure of accuracy. What feels like replay is really a fresh act of construction, shaped by everything we have learned since.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: Memory works like a perfect video recording
Remembering is an act of rebuilding that can introduce errors we cannot detect
Eyewitnesses always lie about what they saw
Memory should be completely distrusted
questions.explanation: The passage argues memory is reconstructed each time, making it editable and sometimes inaccurate without our awareness.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say confidence is 'a poor measure of accuracy'?
choices: People are usually lying when confident
Reconstructed false memories can feel just as vivid and certain as true ones
Confident people remember less
Accuracy cannot be measured at all
questions.explanation: The text notes altered memories seem as vivid and certain as true ones, so feeling sure does not prove correctness.

questions.stem: As used here, 'seam' most nearly refers to
choices: a type of fabric
the join where invented details meet real ones
a strong emotion
a recording device
questions.explanation: We cannot feel 'the seam where invention meets fact,' meaning the join between false and true details.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what can slip new details into a rebuilt memory?
choices: A good night's sleep
Storing every detail of an event
A leading question or a later conversation
Watching a video recording
questions.explanation: The text says "a leading question, a later conversation, even our own retelling can slip new details into the rebuilt scene," and we cannot feel the seam.

lesson.strategy: Read this as an argument that flips a common belief. Sentence one states the belief (memory as a recording); "The truth is stranger" flips it. Follow one idea (reconstruction) as it turns from "useful" to "editable" to its eyewitness cost. The thesis lands last, not first.

signals.means: Signals a flip: the everyday belief just stated is wrong; the author's real claim comes next.

signals.phrase: But it also means memory is editable
signals.means: The turn. The same trait that helps (recall the gist) is what makes memory changeable. Track both sides.

signals.phrase: we cannot feel the seam where invention meets fact
signals.means: The mechanism: an invented detail feels identical to a true one, which is why we trust false memories.

signals.phrase: Confidence, it turns out, is a poor measure
signals.means: The payoff claim the whole piece builds toward. This is the point, not the opening line.

vocab.inContext: Rebuilding a memory from scattered fragments each time, not replaying a stored copy.
Able to be changed after the fact; new details can slip into a remembered scene.
The join line between real memory and invented detail, which we cannot sense.

skillTips.main-idea: The main claim is the flipped belief, not the opening one. The author rejects memory as "a faithful video" and lands the real point last: confidence "is a poor measure of accuracy."
skillTips.inference: Ask what follows if memory is rebuilt each time. Eyewitnesses describe false events "sincerely," not by lying; the cause the author names is suggestions "planted afterward."
skillTips.vocabulary: For abstract words, use the nearby image. "where invention meets fact" tells you a "seam" is the join between made-up and real; "editable" shows as details that "slip" in.
skillTips.detail: See which details back which claim. The "leading question," "later conversation," and "own retelling" are three examples of one point (memory is editable), not separate facts.

passages.title: The Pull of a Favor
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Across nearly every culture, people feel an urge to return a favor. When someone gives us something, even something small and unrequested, a quiet pressure builds to give something back. This rule of reciprocity helped early communities cooperate and share, and it runs so deep that we often obey it without noticing.

Because the urge is automatic, it can be used as a tool of persuasion. A free sample, an unexpected gift, a small concession in an argument: each can plant a sense of debt that makes us more willing to say yes afterward. The favor need not be large, and we need not even have wanted it. The discomfort of feeling indebted is enough to nudge our behavior.

Knowing this does not make the urge vanish, but it offers a defense. When a gift seems designed to obligate you, you are free to receive it as what it is, a sales tactic rather than a true kindness, and to feel no debt at all.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
choices: why people enjoy giving gifts
how the urge to return favors shapes behavior and can be used to persuade
the history of early communities
why free samples taste better
questions.explanation: The passage explains reciprocity and how it can be used as a persuasion tool.

questions.stem: What defense against this tactic does the passage suggest?
choices: Refusing to speak to salespeople
Recognizing a manipulative gift as a tactic and feeling no debt
Always returning every favor immediately
Never accepting anything from anyone
questions.explanation: The text says you can receive such a gift as a sales tactic rather than kindness and feel no debt.

questions.stem: According to the passage, must a favor be large to create a sense of debt?
choices: Yes, only large gifts work
No, even a small, unwanted favor can create the feeling
Only gifts of money count
Only favors we asked for count
questions.explanation: The passage says the favor need not be large and we need not even have wanted it.

questions.stem: In this passage, "indebted" most nearly means:
choices: proud
wealthy
generous
owing something in return
questions.explanation: The "discomfort of feeling indebted" is the sense of owing something back after receiving a favor, which is what nudges us to say yes.

lesson.strategy: This essay runs in three moves: it names a rule ("rule of reciprocity"), shows how that rule becomes "a tool of persuasion," then hands you "a defense." Read for the turns, not the opening. The payoff is the last line, where relabeling the favor cancels the debt.

signals.means: The essay's core claim: a deep, automatic urge to return a favor. Every later point builds on this one idea.
The first turn. The essay pivots from describing the rule to showing how persuaders exploit it against you.
The second turn and the payoff. Knowing the trick won't kill the urge, but it lets you refuse the debt.

signals.phrase: a sales tactic rather than a true kindness
signals.means: The move that frees you: relabel the gift, and the pressure to give something back disappears.

vocab.inContext: the social rule that a favor received creates a pull to give something back
feeling you owe someone because they gave you something first
a point you give up in an argument, used here as a small favor that plants debt

skillTips.main-idea: Don't lock the main idea to paragraph one's rule. The essay finishes its point only at the end: reciprocity is automatic, persuaders use it, but naming the gift 'a sales tactic' frees you.
skillTips.inference: The passage never says 'distrust free samples.' Read the loaded words: 'a gift seems designed to obligate you' implies some gifts are strategic. The clue is that word 'designed.'
skillTips.vocabulary: This essay defines its hard words in place. 'Reciprocity' follows 'an urge to return a favor'; 'indebted' is glossed by 'a sense of debt.' Read the neighboring sentence, don't guess.
skillTips.detail: Separate the claim from its examples. The claim: reciprocity runs deep, automatic. Its proof is 'A free sample, an unexpected gift, a small concession.' On a detail question, find that list.

passages.title: The Cost You Cannot See
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every choice quietly closes a door. When you spend an afternoon on one activity, you give up everything else you might have done with that time. When you spend a dollar on one thing, you forgo whatever else that dollar could have bought. Economists call this hidden price the opportunity cost: the value of the best option you did not take.

What makes opportunity cost slippery is that it never appears on a receipt. The money you paid is visible and easy to count. The trip you did not take, the skill you did not learn, the rest you did not get, leave no trace, so the mind tends to ignore them. Yet they are the true measure of what a decision costs. A purchase that seems cheap may be expensive once you account for the better use of the same resources, and a free activity is never truly free if it consumes time you valued more elsewhere.

Thinking in terms of opportunity cost changes the question we ask. Instead of wondering whether something is worth its sticker price, we ask whether it is worth more than the next best thing we could do instead. This is a harder question, because it forces us to name what we are giving up. But it is also a more honest one. Resources are limited, and the real cost of having anything is the most valuable thing we surrender to get it. Decisions made without this lens often feel like bargains while quietly draining what matters most: our time, our energy, and our attention.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Most purchases are bargains
The true cost of a choice is the best alternative you give up, which is easy to overlook
Money is the only real cost worth counting
Free activities have no cost at all
questions.explanation: The passage defines opportunity cost as the value of the best forgone option and stresses that it is hidden but real.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say opportunity cost is 'slippery'?
choices: It changes every day
It never appears on a receipt, so the mind tends to ignore it
It only applies to money
It is illegal to calculate
questions.explanation: The text explains the cost leaves no trace and never appears on a receipt, so people overlook it.

questions.stem: How does opportunity cost change the question we should ask about a choice?
choices: Whether it costs less than last year
Whether it is worth more than the next best alternative
Whether other people approve of it
Whether it is the cheapest option available
questions.explanation: The passage says we should ask whether something is worth more than the next best thing we could do instead.

questions.stem: In this passage, "forgo" most nearly means:
choices: give up
purchase
remember
increase
questions.explanation: The text says you "forgo whatever else that dollar could have bought," meaning you give up the alternatives.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does the money paid for a purchase differ from its opportunity cost?
choices: It can always be recovered later
It is visible and easy to count
It matters less than the time spent
It is always smaller than the hidden cost
questions.explanation: The passage states "the money you paid is visible and easy to count," while the trip, the skill, and the rest you gave up "leave no trace."

lesson.strategy: This essay defines one idea, opportunity cost, then defends it. Read in three beats: the definition ("the value of the best option you did not take"), why it hides ("never appears on a receipt"), and the reframe it forces ("changes the question we ask"). Track each "yet" or "but" turn.

signals.means: Names the term being defined; the definition follows the colon, and the whole essay rests on it.
The turn from defining the idea to explaining why it stays hidden from us.

signals.phrase: Yet they are the true measure
signals.means: 'Yet' flips the invisible costs from ignorable to the real point of a decision.
The pivot: from 'worth its price?' to 'worth more than the next best thing?,' the payoff.

vocab.inContext: to give up something else you could have had instead
hard to pin down or keep in mind; easy to overlook
to give up something valued in order to get another thing

skillTips.main-idea: Stated twice. Combine the definition, 'the value of the best option you did not take,' with the close, 'the real cost of having anything is the most valuable thing we surrender.'
skillTips.inference: Apply the rule to a case not named. The essay says 'a free activity is never truly free if it consumes time you valued more elsewhere.' What about a 'bargain' that drains your time?
skillTips.vocabulary: For hard words, use the nearby restatement. 'forgo' sits beside 'give up everything else you might have done'; 'slippery' is explained by the next line, 'it never appears on a receipt.'
skillTips.detail: The invisible costs are listed as examples: 'The trip you did not take, the skill you did not learn, the rest you did not get.' They share one form: things NOT done. That is the point.

passages.title: The First Number Wins
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When we judge an unknown quantity, the mind reaches for a starting point and adjusts from there. The trouble is that the starting point need not be relevant, and the adjustment is usually too small. The first figure we encounter, even an arbitrary one, tugs our estimate toward itself. Psychologists call this the anchoring effect.

The pull is surprisingly strong. In studies, people asked whether a quantity is higher or lower than some random number, perhaps drawn from a spin of a wheel, will later give estimates that drift toward that meaningless number. They do not believe the wheel knows anything, and yet their guesses bend toward it. The anchor works even when we are told to ignore it.

This quietly shapes the marketplace. A high original price printed beside a sale price makes the sale feel generous, because the original anchors our sense of what the item is worth. A first offer in a negotiation frames every counteroffer that follows. Even an absurd opening demand can drag the final agreement in its direction, which is why the person who names the first number often holds an unseen advantage.

The defense is not to feel immune, since no one is. It is to notice when a number has been handed to you and to ask, deliberately, what the thing would be worth if you had never seen that figure at all. Generating your own estimate first, before any anchor appears, is one of the few reliable ways to keep the anchor from setting the terms of your judgment.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
choices: how to win every negotiation
how an initial number, even an irrelevant one, biases our later estimates
why sale prices are always fair
how wheels are used in psychology labs
questions.explanation: The passage defines and illustrates the anchoring effect: a first number pulls our estimates toward it.

questions.stem: Why does naming the first number give a negotiator an advantage?
choices: It ends the negotiation immediately
It sets an anchor that drags later counteroffers toward it
It proves the negotiator is honest
It lowers the final price for everyone
questions.explanation: The text says a first offer frames every counteroffer and even an absurd demand drags the final agreement toward it.

questions.stem: What does the passage recommend as a defense against anchoring?
choices: Believing you are immune to it
Forming your own estimate before any anchor appears
Always accepting the first offer
Ignoring all prices entirely
questions.explanation: The passage says generating your own estimate first, before an anchor appears, is a reliable defense.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, "arbitrary" most nearly means:
choices: carefully calculated
chosen without meaningful reason
secretly accurate
unusually large
questions.explanation: The passage's example is a number "drawn from a spin of a wheel": random, connected to nothing. An arbitrary starting point is one with no real basis, yet it still tugs our estimate toward itself.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens when people are told to ignore an anchor?
choices: The effect disappears completely
They overcorrect away from the anchor
They refuse to give an estimate
The anchor still influences their estimates
questions.explanation: The passage is blunt: "The anchor works even when we are told to ignore it."

lesson.strategy: A four-move psychology essay: para 1 defines the anchoring effect, para 2 proves the pull is real, para 3 shows it in the marketplace, para 4 gives the defense. Read for the mechanism ("tugs our estimate toward itself"), not the examples.

signals.means: Flags the flaw in how the mind estimates: the starting point may be irrelevant and the adjustment too small.

signals.phrase: even when we are told to ignore it
signals.means: The strongest proof of the effect. Knowing about the anchor does not free you from its pull.

signals.phrase: which is why the person who names the first number
signals.means: A causal payoff. The marketplace lesson drawn from the studies: naming the first number is quiet power.

signals.phrase: The defense is not to feel immune
signals.means: The turn from problem to remedy. The rest of the paragraph tells you what to do instead.

vocab.inContext: chosen at random, with no real link to the true answer; still it tugs the estimate
protected, unaffected; here, the false belief that you cannot be swayed by an anchor
on purpose, as a careful conscious step, not by reflex or instinct

skillTips.main-idea: The whole claim sits in para 1: the mind grabs a first number and adjusts too little. Studies, prices, and negotiation all apply that one idea. Name the mechanism, not an example.
skillTips.inference: The passage never says 'let the other side open first.' Combine 'the person who names the first number often holds an unseen advantage' with the defense to infer the smart move.
skillTips.vocabulary: For 'anchor,' skip the boat meaning. The passage defines it by action, the first figure 'tugs our estimate toward itself.' Let the verbs (tugs, drift, bend, drag) fix the sense.
skillTips.detail: The study detail is the point: a quantity judged against 'some random number' from 'a spin of a wheel.' Random and meaningless, yet it still moves the guess. Note that, not the numbers.

passages.title: Why the Sea Rises and Falls
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At many coasts, the sea rises and falls twice during a tidal day. At some places it rises and falls once, and at others the two daily tides have different heights. These patterns are tides, caused mainly by the Moon’s gravity and also by the Sun.

The Moon’s pull is stronger on the side of Earth nearer the Moon than on the far side. In a simple picture, this difference produces two broad tidal bulges. As Earth turns, a coast moves through the pattern.

Real oceans do not cover a smooth, round Earth. Continents block the water, and the shapes of coasts and the seafloor change how it moves. That is why local tides may be semidiurnal, with two similar highs; diurnal, with one; or mixed, with two unequal highs.

The Sun changes tidal range too. Near new and full moons, the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up, so their effects combine to make larger spring tides. Near quarter moons, their directions differ and the range is usually smaller. A tide table uses local measurements and predictions because the Moon supplies the main rhythm, but each coast reshapes it.

questions.stem: What is this passage mainly about?
choices: Why every coast has two tides of exactly equal height
How fish cause the sea to rise near the shore
Why continents move around Earth each day
How the Moon and Sun create a tidal rhythm that local geography reshapes
questions.explanation: The passage combines astronomical causes with the local effects of continents, coasts, and seafloor.

questions.stem: Which local features can change a coast’s tidal pattern?
choices: The shapes of continents, coasts, and the seafloor
The color of clouds above the beach
The number of fish near the surface
The kind of sand in a child’s bucket
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names continents, coast shape, and seafloor shape.

questions.stem: A “diurnal” tidal pattern has
choices: two equal high tides every hour
one high and one low tide during a tidal day
no change in water level
only a full-moon tide
questions.explanation: The passage defines diurnal as a pattern with one daily high, paired with one low.

questions.stem: When are tidal ranges usually smaller than at new or full moon?
choices: Whenever a coast has a tide table
Only when Earth stops turning
Near quarter moons, when the Sun and Moon pull in different directions
Whenever the Moon is visible during the day
questions.explanation: The final paragraph contrasts the combined alignment with the different directions near quarter moons.

lesson.strategy: Read the simple model, then its correction. The Moon and Sun provide the broad rhythm; continents and basin shape change what a coast experiences. Do not turn a useful two-bulge picture into a promise of two equal tides everywhere.

signals.means: Scopes the opening pattern instead of claiming it for every place.
Marks the two-bulge model as a first explanation.

signals.phrase: Real oceans do not cover a smooth, round Earth
signals.means: Introduces the geography that changes local tides.

signals.phrase: because the Moon supplies the main rhythm
signals.means: Balances the astronomical cause with local reshaping.

vocab.inContext: repeated rises and falls of sea level
having one high and one low tide in a tidal day
the vertical difference between high and low water

skillTips.main-idea: Join the source of the rhythm to the local geography that changes it.
skillTips.inference: Compare the line-up at new/full moon with the different directions near quarter moon.
skillTips.vocabulary: The passage defines each tidal pattern immediately after naming it.
skillTips.detail: Local variation comes from physical geography, not from whether the Moon is visible.

passages.title: The Dance of the Honeybee
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When a honeybee discovers a rich patch of flowers, it does not simply fly home and rest. Instead, it returns to the hive and performs a curious movement that scientists call the waggle dance. The bee walks in a straight line while shaking its body, then loops back to repeat the pattern.

The direction of the straight run, measured against the position of the Sun, tells the other bees which way to fly. The length of the waggle hints at how far away the food lies. Nearby flowers earn a short, quick dance, while distant ones produce a long, vigorous one.

Through this silent language, a single scout can send dozens of workers straight to a meal they have never seen.

questions.stem: The passage is mostly about how honeybees
choices: build their hives
make honey from nectar
communicate the location of food
defend against predators
questions.explanation: The whole passage describes the waggle dance as a way bees tell others where food is.

questions.stem: What does the length of the waggle indicate?
choices: The type of flower
How far away the food is
The time of day
The number of bees needed
questions.explanation: The text states the length of the waggle 'hints at how far away the food lies.'

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a very long, vigorous dance most likely means the flowers are
choices: right next to the hive
far from the hive
out of nectar
dangerous to visit
questions.explanation: The text contrasts short dances for nearby flowers with long, vigorous dances for distant ones.

questions.stem: In this passage, "vigorous" most nearly means:
choices: lazy and slow
silent and still
short and gentle
energetic and lively
questions.explanation: Distant flowers produce "a long, vigorous" dance, set against the "short, quick" dance for nearby ones, so vigorous means energetic and lively.

lesson.strategy: This explains one thing: how a honeybee's "waggle dance" tells other bees where food is. Read it as a code with two parts: the direction of the straight run maps to a real direction, and the length of the waggle maps to distance. Watch the "Instead" and "while" turns.

signals.means: The named term the whole passage exists to explain. Every later detail describes a piece of this dance.

signals.phrase: The direction of the straight run
signals.means: One coded variable: which way to fly. Pair it with 'The length of the waggle': two signals, two meanings.

signals.phrase: Nearby flowers earn a short, quick dance
signals.means: A 'while' contrast: near = short dance, far = long dance. The comparison is the point, not either half alone.
The author's label for the dance. When a science text names its subject like this, it states the main idea.

vocab.inContext: the fast side-to-side body shake the bee makes during the straight run
strong and full of energy; here, a long forceful dance meaning the food is far
the single bee that finds the flowers and returns to report their location

skillTips.main-idea: The passage answers one question: how does a bee tell others where food is? To state the main idea, say what the waggle dance does, not just that bees dance.
skillTips.inference: The text never says bees 'talk,' yet a scout can send workers 'straight to a meal they have never seen.' Infer the dance carries exact information, not a vague signal.
skillTips.vocabulary: 'Vigorous' sits beside 'long' and opposite 'short, quick,' so it means strong and energetic. Use the near/far contrast to unlock words you don't know here.
skillTips.detail: The dance codes two facts: the direction ('measured against the position of the Sun') and the distance ('how far away the food lies'). Ask which one a question wants.

passages.title: How Rock Becomes Rock Again
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Rock may look permanent, but over long stretches of time it changes from one form into another. Deep below the surface, intense heat melts rock into a glowing liquid called magma. When magma cools, either underground or after erupting from a volcano, it hardens into igneous rock.

Wind and water then break that rock into tiny grains. The grains settle in layers at the bottom of lakes and seas, and over millions of years the weight above presses them into sedimentary rock.

If sedimentary rock is buried deeper still, heat and pressure can squeeze and bake it into metamorphic rock without fully melting it. Should that rock sink far enough to melt, it becomes magma again. Geologists call this endless loop the rock cycle, and it has been turning for billions of years.

Because each step takes so long, a single grain of sand may carry the history of several different rocks within it, a record patient observers can learn to read.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'magma' refers to rock that is
choices: frozen solid
melted into liquid
broken into grains
pressed into layers
questions.explanation: The text defines magma as rock that intense heat 'melts ... into a glowing liquid.'

questions.stem: According to the text, sedimentary rock forms when
choices: magma cools quickly
grains settle and are pressed in layers
rock melts underground
volcanoes erupt
questions.explanation: The passage says grains settle in layers and the weight above presses them into sedimentary rock.

questions.stem: The best title for the central idea of this passage is
choices: Volcanoes Around the World
How Rocks Constantly Change Form
Why Lakes Form Layers
The Work of Geologists
questions.explanation: The passage describes the rock cycle, the endless loop in which rock changes form.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what would have to happen for a metamorphic rock to become igneous rock?
choices: It would need to melt into magma and then cool
It would need to break into grains and settle in layers
It would need more heat and pressure without melting
It could never become igneous rock
questions.explanation: Igneous rock forms when magma cools, and the passage says rock that sinks far enough to melt "becomes magma again," so the metamorphic rock must melt first and then harden.

lesson.strategy: This traces one loop: magma to igneous to sedimentary to metamorphic and back to magma. Read it as a chain, not a list. At each rock name, ask what force made it (heat, wind, weight, pressure) and what comes next. The "then / over millions of years / again" words carry the sequence.

signals.phrase: it changes from one form into another
signals.means: The whole passage's claim: rock is not fixed. Every detail after this shows one step of that change.

signals.phrase: Wind and water then break that rock
signals.means: "then" marks a step in the cycle. Track each "then/when/should" to keep the order of rock types straight.
Names the structure: the steps form a circle, not a line. That is why it ends back at magma, where it began.

signals.phrase: Because each step takes so long
signals.means: A cause-effect turn. It explains why one grain of sand can hold several rocks' history.

vocab.inContext: Rock melted into a glowing liquid by intense heat deep below the surface.
Rock made when tiny grains settle in layers and weight presses them together.
Rock made when heat and pressure bake buried rock without fully melting it.

skillTips.main-idea: The first sentence states it: rock "changes from one form into another." Everything after is proof. The passage is about rock changing shape over time, not about volcanoes.
skillTips.inference: A grain of sand "may carry the history of several different rocks." To infer why, connect that to "each step takes so long" and the loop that keeps turning. Chain the stated facts.
skillTips.vocabulary: Each rock name is defined by the sentence around it. "igneous" follows "When magma cools... it hardens into." Read the how-it-forms clause next to the word.
skillTips.detail: Details here are ordered steps. To find what makes sedimentary rock, locate the name, then read its force clause: grains "settle in layers," "weight above presses them."

passages.title: The Toughest Animal You Can't See
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Among the most resilient creatures on Earth is one barely visible to the naked eye. The tardigrade, sometimes called a water bear, is a chubby, eight-legged animal smaller than a grain of sand. It lives in mossy patches, ocean sediments, and the films of water that cling to soil.

What makes the tardigrade remarkable is its response to harsh conditions. When its surroundings dry out, the animal expels nearly all the water from its body and pulls in its legs, shriveling into a dormant ball called a tun. In this suspended state its metabolism almost halts, and it can endure temperatures near absolute zero, the vacuum of space, and doses of radiation that would kill most life many times over. Years later, a single drop of water can revive it, and the tiny animal lumbers off as though nothing had happened.

Scientists study tardigrades to understand how life might survive on other worlds, and how delicate biological structures can be preserved through extreme stress.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'dormant' most nearly means
choices: growing rapidly
inactive or resting
brightly colored
newly hatched
questions.explanation: The tun is a state where 'metabolism almost halts,' so dormant means inactive or resting.

questions.stem: Why do scientists study tardigrades in connection with other worlds?
choices: Tardigrades come from space
Their survival hints at how life might endure harsh, alien conditions
They can only live in vacuums
They glow in the dark
questions.explanation: The passage says scientists study them to understand how life might survive on other worlds because they endure extreme conditions.

questions.stem: What does a tardigrade do when its surroundings dry out?
choices: It lays eggs
It expels water and curls into a tun
It swims to deeper water
It grows extra legs
