questions.explanation: The text states it 'expels nearly all the water from its body and pulls in its legs,' forming a tun.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about:
choices: why water bears are dangerous to humans
how moss patches form in the ocean
why space travel is impossible for living things
how a nearly invisible animal survives extremes by entering a dormant state
questions.explanation: The passage describes how the tiny tardigrade endures drying, cold, vacuum, and radiation by shriveling into a dormant tun, then revives years later with a single drop of water.

lesson.strategy: A science profile built on one claim: the tardigrade survives almost anything. Read the opening as the claim, follow the drying-out steps in order (dry out → tun → revive), and treat the extremes it endures as proof. The last sentence says why it matters.

signals.means: The thesis marker: the sentence right after it states the whole point everything else backs up.
Starts the survival process in time order; the tun forms only in response to this trigger.
Signals a result: the extremes it endures come from the tun, not as separate facts.
The so-what close; read on for why the survival matters, not just what happens.

vocab.inContext: able to survive and bounce back from harsh conditions that would kill most life
in a paused, inactive state; alive but with body processes nearly stopped
the shriveled dormant ball a tardigrade becomes when it expels its water

skillTips.main-idea: The claim sits right after "What makes the tardigrade remarkable": its response to harsh conditions. The tun, the extremes, and the revival are all evidence for that one idea.
skillTips.inference: The passage never says outright why this is useful. The last sentence gives the purpose: to learn how life might survive on other worlds. Infer the value from that.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words are defined beside them. "a dormant ball called a tun" names the tun; "suspended state" restates dormant. When a word is new, check the same sentence.
skillTips.detail: For "what can it survive," find the list after "endure": absolute zero, the vacuum of space, radiation. For "how," track the order: expels water → pulls in legs → tun → revives.

passages.title: Eating Sunlight
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Animals must find food to get energy, but green plants make their own. Inside their leaves are tiny green parts that capture sunlight. The plant uses that light energy to combine water from the soil with a gas called carbon dioxide from the air.

This process turns those simple ingredients into sugar, which feeds the plant and helps it grow. The process is called photosynthesis.

As a bonus, the plant releases oxygen, the gas that people and animals need to breathe. So when you stand near a leafy tree on a sunny day, the tree is quietly building food and freshening the air at the same time.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of this passage?
choices: Animals eat plants for energy
Plants use sunlight to make their own food
Trees grow best in soil
Oxygen is a kind of sugar
questions.explanation: The passage centers on photosynthesis, how plants use sunlight to make food.

questions.stem: According to the text, what gas do plants release during photosynthesis?
choices: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Steam
questions.explanation: The text says the plant 'releases oxygen' as a bonus.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'capture' most nearly means
choices: take in or catch
reflect away
burn up
hide from
questions.explanation: The green parts 'capture sunlight,' meaning they take it in to use its energy.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what would most likely happen to a green plant kept in a dark room?
choices: It would grow faster
It would struggle to make its food
It would make more oxygen
It would need less water
questions.explanation: Plants use light energy to combine water and carbon dioxide into sugar, so a plant with no sunlight could not build the food it needs to grow.

lesson.strategy: This explains how a plant makes its own food. Read it like a recipe: track what goes in (sunlight, water, carbon dioxide) and what comes out (sugar, oxygen). The "but" in line one splits animals from plants. The whole process gets one name: photosynthesis.

signals.phrase: but green plants make their own
signals.means: The 'but' splits the passage in two: animals must hunt for food, plants make it. This contrast is the setup.
The ingredients going in. Mark water, carbon dioxide, and sunlight as what the plant uses to make food.

signals.phrase: This process turns those simple ingredients into sugar
signals.means: The result. 'turns...into' is a cause word: ingredients in, sugar out. Sugar is the food the plant makes.

signals.phrase: As a bonus, the plant releases oxygen
signals.means: 'As a bonus' flags an extra result: the plant feeds itself and gives off oxygen we breathe.

vocab.inContext: The name for the whole process: using sunlight to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar.
A gas in the air the plant takes in and uses to make sugar.
The gas the plant gives off, which people and animals need to breathe.

skillTips.main-idea: The passage answers one question: how do plants feed themselves? 'The process is called photosynthesis' names the answer. Hold the question and that name together for the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Link 'releases oxygen, the gas that people and animals need to breathe' with 'freshening the air' to infer why a leafy tree matters to you, not just to itself.
skillTips.vocabulary: This passage defines hard words right beside them: 'a gas called carbon dioxide' and 'oxygen, the gas that people and animals need to breathe'. Read the words just after a term.
skillTips.detail: Read the middle like a recipe. To answer what the plant uses or makes, scan 'combine water from the soil' and 'turns those simple ingredients into sugar' for the exact ins and outs.

passages.title: Messages in the Brain
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every thought, memory, and movement begins as a tiny electrical signal traveling through the brain. The brain contains roughly eighty-six billion cells called neurons, each one shaped like a tree with many branching arms. A neuron receives signals through its branches, and when enough of them arrive, the cell fires a pulse of electricity down a long fiber toward its neighbors.

But neurons do not actually touch. Between them lies a microscopic gap called a synapse. To cross it, the electrical signal triggers the release of chemical messengers that drift across the gap and pass the message along.

This blend of electricity and chemistry lets billions of neurons coordinate in fractions of a second. What we experience as a single smooth thought is really a vast storm of these signals racing through an intricate web of connections, many of them strengthened or weakened by what we learn.

questions.stem: What is the small gap between two neurons called?
choices: A synapse
A fiber
A pulse
A branch
questions.explanation: The text says 'Between them lies a microscopic gap called a synapse.'

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a single thought is
choices: produced by one neuron alone
the result of many neurons signaling together
purely chemical with no electricity
slower than a heartbeat
questions.explanation: The text says a smooth thought is 'really a vast storm of these signals' across billions of neurons.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'intricate' most nearly means
choices: simple and plain
complex and detailed
empty
fast
questions.explanation: An 'intricate web of connections' refers to a complex, detailed network.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea of the passage?
choices: Neurons touch each other directly to pass signals
The brain uses both electrical and chemical signals to pass messages between billions of neurons
Chemical messengers slow the brain down
Each thought comes from a single neuron
questions.explanation: The passage describes electrical pulses traveling inside neurons and chemical messengers crossing the synapse between them: a "blend of electricity and chemistry" that lets billions of cells coordinate.

lesson.strategy: Read this as a process with a twist. It opens with a claim, then walks a signal through a neuron step by step, then turns at "But neurons do not actually touch." Track the sequence and the switch from electricity to chemistry; the last sentence reframes it all.

signals.means: The 'called X' pattern is the author naming a key term right where it first appears.

signals.phrase: But neurons do not actually touch.
signals.means: The turn: a surprising fact that sets up the gap-and-chemistry mechanism the rest explains.

signals.phrase: To cross it, the electrical signal triggers
signals.means: Cause-and-effect: how the signal jumps the gap, switching from electricity to chemistry.

signals.phrase: a single smooth thought is really
signals.means: Appearance-vs-reality reframe: the passage's main point landing at the end.

vocab.inContext: The microscopic gap between two neurons that the signal must cross.
Brain cells shaped like branching trees that receive and fire signals.
Complex and finely detailed, with countless connected parts.

skillTips.main-idea: Read the first and last sentences together: 'begins as a tiny electrical signal' and 'really a vast storm of these signals' - one smooth thought is really many signals.
skillTips.inference: Follow the causal chain to what is unstated. From 'strengthened or weakened by what we learn,' infer that learning physically changes the connections, though the text never says so.
skillTips.vocabulary: This author names its hard words with 'called': 'cells called neurons', 'a gap called a synapse.' When a term is new, look right before or after it for that naming phrase.
skillTips.detail: It is an ordered process: a neuron receives, then fires, then chemical messengers cross the synapse. Use the order words ('when', 'To cross it', 'along') to keep each step in place.

passages.title: Cities Beneath the Waves
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A shallow tropical coral reef looks like a colorful rocky garden, but living animals build it. A coral colony contains tiny soft-bodied polyps. Many reef-building polyps make hard calcium-carbonate skeletons. As generations grow on older skeletons, the reef structure rises.

Inside many shallow reef-building corals live microscopic algae. The algae use sunlight to make food and share some products with the coral. In return, they receive shelter and materials they need. This partnership helps explain why these corals thrive in clear, sunlit water.

Not all corals live this way. Deep-sea corals grow far beyond sunlight and lack the same photosynthetic algae. They capture food carried by currents. Some form large habitats, although their shapes and growth differ from familiar tropical reefs.

When shallow tropical water stays too warm, a coral may expel its algae and turn pale, an event called bleaching. A bleached coral is alive, but it has lost an important energy source and may starve if stressful conditions continue. By naming which corals depend on sunlight, scientists avoid turning one important partnership into a rule for every coral in the sea.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
choices: why every coral in the ocean requires bright sunlight
how tropical fish construct calcium-carbonate skeletons
how shallow reef-building corals depend on algae while deep-sea corals live differently
why bleaching means a coral is already dead
questions.explanation: The passage explains the shallow partnership, contrasts deep-sea corals, and returns to bleaching.

questions.stem: What do algae provide to many shallow reef-building corals?
choices: Deep-sea currents
A hard shell made from steel
Colder water during bleaching
Products of food made using sunlight
questions.explanation: The algae use sunlight to make food and share some of those products with the coral.

questions.stem: Why can deep-sea corals live without sunlight?
choices: They capture food carried by currents instead of relying on photosynthetic algae
They produce sunlight inside their skeletons
They rise to the surface every day to feed
They are not living animals
questions.explanation: The third paragraph contrasts their current-borne food with the shallow algae partnership.

questions.stem: In this passage, “expel” means
choices: feed
push out
copy
cool
questions.explanation: During bleaching a shallow coral expels, or pushes out, its algae.

lesson.strategy: Watch the scope. Paragraphs one and two concern many shallow tropical reef builders; paragraph three gives the deep-sea contrast. The final paragraph uses that distinction to explain bleaching without claiming all corals need sunlight.

signals.means: Sets the scope before the algae partnership is explained.

signals.phrase: Not all corals live this way
signals.means: Introduces the counterexample that limits the sunlight rule.
Shows that deep-sea corals use a different feeding strategy.
Restates why a precise category matters.

vocab.inContext: tiny soft-bodied animals that make up a coral colony
using light to make food
the pale state after a coral loses its algae

skillTips.main-idea: A correct summary includes both the shallow partnership and the deep-sea exception.
skillTips.inference: Use the feeding contrast: current-borne food lets deep-sea corals live without photosynthetic algae.
skillTips.vocabulary: The bleaching sentence shows that expel means push the algae out.
skillTips.detail: Keep builders and partners separate: polyps build skeletons; algae make food products using light.

passages.title: The Endless Journey of Water
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The water in a puddle today may have floated in a cloud last week and rushed down a river last year. Water travels through the world in a repeating path called the water cycle.

The Sun heats oceans, lakes, and rivers, turning some of the water into an invisible gas called vapor that rises into the sky. High up, where the air is cooler, the vapor turns back into tiny droplets that gather to form clouds. When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow. That water flows back into rivers and seas, and the journey starts over.

No new water is made and none is lost; the same water has been moving in this circle for a very long time.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'vapor' is best described as
choices: frozen ice
water in the form of gas
muddy water
a heavy cloud
questions.explanation: The text calls vapor 'an invisible gas' that water turns into when heated.

questions.stem: According to the text, what makes water rise into the sky?
choices: The wind
Heat from the Sun
Falling snow
Cold air
questions.explanation: The passage says 'The Sun heats oceans, lakes, and rivers,' turning water into vapor that rises.

questions.stem: The passage mainly explains that water
choices: is always being newly created
moves in a repeating cycle
only exists in clouds
disappears forever as vapor
questions.explanation: The whole passage describes the water cycle as a repeating path, and notes no water is made or lost.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which statement about the water you drink today is most likely true?
choices: It was newly made in a cloud last week
It has likely traveled the water cycle many times
It will vanish once you drink it
It has never touched the ocean
questions.explanation: The text says "no new water is made and none is lost," and the same water has been moving in this circle for a very long time, so today's water has gone around many times.

lesson.strategy: This traces water through one loop. Read it as a chain where each step causes the next: watch the change-verbs "heats," "rises," "turns back," "gather," "grow heavy," "fall," "flows back." Save the last line for the real point.

signals.means: Names the one repeating path the whole passage follows. Expect a loop that ends where it began.
The cause that starts every round. Heat is what turns liquid water into vapor and lifts it up.
The reverse step: cool air changes vapor back to water. This is where clouds get made.

signals.phrase: No new water is made and none is lost
signals.means: The main claim. All the steps before it prove the same water just keeps circling.

vocab.inContext: The invisible gas water becomes when the Sun heats it; it rises into the sky.
Tiny bits of water that form high up and gather together to make clouds.
A path that repeats over and over, so the journey keeps starting again.

skillTips.main-idea: The last sentence is the point: "No new water is made and none is lost." The Sun-to-rain steps are proof for it. Read the ending, then see how the steps support it.
skillTips.inference: One puddle's water sits in a cloud last week and a river last year. The text never says it moved in that order, but the cycle lets you conclude the same water traveled the whole path.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words are defined right in the sentence. "an invisible gas called vapor" tells you vapor is that gas. Look for the word "called" to grab the meaning without guessing.
skillTips.detail: Facts sit inside the order of steps. To find what happens where, follow the chain: Sun heats, vapor rises, turns to droplets, form clouds, fall as rain or snow, flows back.

passages.title: Glowing in the Dark Ocean
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Sunlight reaches only the upper layers of the ocean. Below about a thousand meters lies a realm of permanent darkness, crushing pressure, and frigid cold. Yet this seemingly empty zone teems with life, and much of it makes its own light. The ability of an organism to produce light through a chemical reaction is called bioluminescence, and in the deep sea it is the rule rather than the exception.

Animals there use their glow for many purposes. Some anglerfish dangle a luminous lure to draw curious prey within reach of their jaws. Certain squid release a cloud of glowing fluid to confuse a predator, much as a shallow-water octopus releases ink. Others flash patterns to find a mate in the vast blackness. Because the deep ocean offers almost no places to hide, light has become both a weapon and a language.

A sudden burst can startle an attacker, while a steady glow can betray the swimmer that produces it, so each animal must balance the risk of being seen against the benefit of being noticed. Some species even tune the color and timing of their flashes so precisely that they amount to private codes, recognized only by their own kind.

Studying these creatures is difficult, since the delicate animals often die when hauled up through warmer, lower-pressure water, so researchers increasingly send cameras and robotic vehicles down to observe them where they live. Each expedition tends to return with footage of species no one has ever catalogued, a reminder of how much of our own planet remains genuinely unexplored.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'bioluminescence' is
choices: the pressure of deep water
an organism producing light by a chemical reaction
a kind of cold ocean current
the lack of sunlight in the deep
questions.explanation: The text defines it as 'the ability of an organism to produce light through a chemical reaction.'

questions.stem: How does an anglerfish use its light, according to the passage?
choices: To warm itself
To dangle a lure that attracts prey
To scare away larger fish
To find its way to the surface
questions.explanation: The text says anglerfish 'dangle a luminous lure to draw curious prey within reach of their jaws.'

questions.stem: The central idea of this passage is that
choices: the deep sea is completely lifeless
many deep-sea animals make and use light to survive
sunlight reaches the entire ocean
anglerfish are the only glowing animals
questions.explanation: The passage describes how bioluminescence is widespread in the deep sea and serves many survival purposes.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, why might a deep-sea animal sometimes keep its light dark?
choices: Its glow could give away its position to a predator
Producing light freezes its body
Darkness helps it swim faster
Its light only works near the surface
questions.explanation: The text notes that "a steady glow can betray the swimmer that produces it," so each animal must weigh the risk of being seen against the benefit of being noticed.

lesson.strategy: A nature explainer built on one claim. Read the first three sentences for the claim: glow is normal down deep. Then treat each animal as evidence for it. Track the frame 'weapon and a language' and the cause words 'because' and 'so.' End on the zoom-out about what stays unexplored.

signals.phrase: Yet this seemingly empty zone teems
signals.means: The turn word Yet flips the setup: the dark, cold, crushing deep is not dead but full of life.

signals.phrase: the rule rather than the exception
signals.means: The thesis. Glow in the deep sea is normal, not rare, so read the animal examples as proof of it.

signals.phrase: both a weapon and a language
signals.means: The organizing frame. Sort each example into attack/defense or communication.
The so marks a cause-effect conclusion: being seen is both a risk and a benefit, a tradeoff.

vocab.inContext: an organism making its own light through a chemical reaction; the sentence defines it
glowing, giving off light, like the anglerfish lure that draws prey within reach
to give away or expose; a steady glow reveals where the swimmer is to a predator

skillTips.main-idea: One idea holds the passage: deep-sea glow is 'the rule rather than the exception.' The anglerfish, squid, and mate-flashers support it. Name the shared claim, not one fish.
skillTips.inference: The passage only hints the ocean is barely known. Combine 'species no one has ever catalogued' with 'genuinely unexplored' to infer discovery is still ongoing.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words are explained nearby. 'bioluminescence' is defined by the clause before 'is called'; 'luminous' sits by 'lure.' Read the surrounding sentence first.
skillTips.detail: Each example pairs one animal with one use: anglerfish lure prey, squid release a glowing cloud to confuse, others flash to find a mate. Match the exact animal to its exact purpose.

passages.title: The Blanket of Air
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Earth stays warm enough for life partly because of gases in its atmosphere. Energy arrives from the Sun mostly as visible light and warms the surface. The surface sends energy upward as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor, absorb and re-radiate some infrared energy, slowing its escape to space. Without this natural greenhouse effect, Earth would be much colder.

Human activities have strengthened the effect. Burning fossil fuels raises atmospheric carbon dioxide, while other activities add methane and nitrous oxide. More heat-trapping gas changes the planet’s energy balance. Oceans absorb most of the excess heat, and land, air, ice, and living systems respond at different speeds.

“Stopping emissions” needs a precise meaning. Cutting annual carbon dioxide emissions slows the rate at which more carbon accumulates, but temperatures do not stabilize while net emissions remain above zero. At sustained global net-zero carbon dioxide (when human removals balance remaining human emissions), carbon-dioxide-caused warming is expected to approximately stabilize, not climb forever. The result also depends on other greenhouse gases and aerosols.

Stabilized temperature does not mean a return to the former climate. Carbon dioxide and stored ocean heat persist, ice sheets respond slowly, and sea level can keep changing for centuries. Reaching net zero therefore prevents additional carbon-dioxide-driven warming while leaving a long task of adaptation. The important lag is not a reason to think action has no prompt effect; it is a reason to distinguish halting further warming from reversing changes already made.

questions.stem: Why would sustained global net-zero carbon dioxide not restore the former climate immediately?
choices: The Sun would suddenly produce more visible light
Net zero means human emissions continue rising each year
Stored heat, long-lived carbon dioxide, ice, and sea level respond over long periods
Greenhouse gases stop interacting with infrared radiation
questions.explanation: The final paragraph distinguishes stabilizing additional CO2 warming from reversing persistent changes.

questions.stem: In this passage, “net zero” carbon dioxide means
choices: all natural carbon dioxide disappears from the atmosphere
every machine in the world stops at the same moment
the oceans release all of their stored heat
human removals balance the remaining human carbon dioxide emissions
questions.explanation: Paragraph three defines net zero as human removals balancing remaining human emissions.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
choices: how the greenhouse effect works and what emissions cuts and net zero do to warming
why the Sun has become hotter during the last century
how oceans remove every greenhouse gas from the air
why climate changes reverse as soon as one factory closes
questions.explanation: The passage explains the mechanism, human intensification, stabilization at net zero, and persistent effects.

questions.stem: What role do oceans play as the climate warms?
choices: They prevent infrared radiation from reaching the air
They absorb most of the excess heat
They eliminate the need to reduce emissions
They return sea level to its earlier position
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that oceans absorb most of the excess heat.

lesson.strategy: Keep three states separate: positive net emissions add warming, net-zero CO2 approximately stabilizes CO2-driven warming, and net-negative CO2 can help reverse it. The final paragraph separates temperature stabilization from slower impacts.

signals.phrase: Human activities have strengthened the effect
signals.means: Turns from the natural process to the added human influence.
Warns that “stopping” can refer to very different emissions paths.
States the expected CO2-warming response at sustained net zero.
Separates stabilization from immediate reversal.

vocab.inContext: the form of energy emitted upward by the warmed surface
small airborne particles that also affect the planet’s energy balance
adjusting to climate effects that already exist or persist

skillTips.main-idea: Follow the mechanism into the policy distinction; the passage is not only a definition of greenhouse gases.
skillTips.inference: Use the final paragraph to distinguish “no more warming” from “back to the old climate.”
skillTips.vocabulary: Net zero is defined in parentheses in paragraph three; use that definition exactly.
skillTips.detail: Do not confuse heat storage with gas removal: the passage says oceans absorb excess heat.

passages.title: The Strength of Spider Silk
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For its weight, spider silk is one of the strongest materials known. A strand far thinner than a human hair can stretch without snapping and absorb the impact of a flying insect many times the spider's size. Engineers admire silk because it combines two qualities that usually oppose each other: it is both strong and stretchy. Steel is strong but brittle, while rubber stretches but tears easily. Silk manages both, which is why a web can catch prey without shattering.

A single spider can produce several kinds of silk from different glands, each tuned for a task. One sort forms the sturdy frame of the web, another the sticky spiral that traps insects, and yet another wraps eggs in a protective case.

Scientists have long hoped to manufacture silk in factories for uses from medical stitches to lightweight armor, but reproducing the spider's recipe has proven stubbornly hard.

questions.stem: Why do engineers find spider silk especially impressive?
choices: It is heavier than steel
It is both strong and stretchy, qualities that usually oppose each other
It dissolves quickly in water
It glows in the dark
questions.explanation: The text says silk combines strength and stretchiness, two qualities that 'usually oppose each other.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is one kind of silk used for?
choices: Building the web's frame
Digesting food
Helping the spider see
Producing venom
questions.explanation: The text says one sort of silk 'forms the sturdy frame of the web.'

questions.stem: In this passage, 'brittle' most nearly means
choices: easily stretched
likely to snap or break
very soft
extremely heavy
questions.explanation: Steel is called 'strong but brittle,' contrasted with stretchy, so brittle means likely to break.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: Spider silk combines strength and stretch in a way scientists have not managed to copy
Spiders make only one kind of silk
Steel is better than silk for building webs
Silk is mainly used to wrap eggs
questions.explanation: The passage centers on silk being both strong and stretchy, describes the several kinds a spider makes, and closes by noting that "reproducing the spider's recipe has proven stubbornly hard."

lesson.strategy: This science explainer turns on one paradox: silk is "both strong and stretchy," traits that "usually oppose each other." Track the opening claim, the steel-and-rubber contrast, the "which is why" payoff, and the closing "but" for what humans still can't do.

signals.means: A qualifier scoping the claim: silk is strongest for its weight, not in raw terms.
Names the paradox the passage exists to explain: strong plus stretchy in one material.
A causation link: strong-and-stretchy is the reason a web catches prey without shattering.
The closing turn: admiration flips to the unsolved problem of copying silk in factories.

vocab.inContext: Strong but breaks or snaps easily instead of bending; the opposite of stretchy.
Organs inside the spider that produce silk, each making a different kind.
In a way that resists all effort; the recipe stays hard however hard they try.

skillTips.main-idea: The point is not "silk is strong" alone. It is the paradox: silk joins strong and stretchy, traits that "usually oppose each other," and copying it is "stubbornly hard." Hold both halves.
skillTips.inference: The steel-and-rubber sentence is never called the lesson, but it proves silk is special: each rival has one trait only, so "Silk manages both" is what makes it rare.
skillTips.vocabulary: Let the built-in contrasts define hard words. "Strong but brittle" pairs brittle against strong; "stretches but tears easily" pairs with stretchy. Read the opposite word beside it.
skillTips.detail: For the kinds of silk, anchor on "each tuned for a task" and count the three: the "sturdy frame," the "sticky spiral," and the wrap that protects eggs. Match each silk to its job.

passages.title: The Lives of Stars
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A star is not eternal; it is born, lives, and dies over spans that dwarf human history. Stars begin within vast clouds of gas and dust drifting through space. Gravity slowly pulls a clump of this material inward, and as the clump shrinks it grows denser and hotter. When the core becomes hot enough, hydrogen atoms begin fusing into helium, releasing enormous energy and igniting the star.

For most of its life a star maintains a steady balance: the outward push of this fusion energy resists the inward crush of gravity. When the hydrogen fuel runs low, that balance breaks, and the star's fate depends on its mass.

A modest star like the Sun swells into a red giant, sheds its outer layers, and settles into a slowly cooling ember. A far more massive star ends violently, collapsing and then exploding as a supernova that briefly outshines an entire galaxy. The debris of such explosions scatters heavy elements across space. Gathered by gravity over billions of years, that scattered debris becomes the raw material for new clouds, new stars, and the planets that circle them.

Remarkably, the carbon in living bodies and the iron in blood were forged inside ancient stars, making every person, in a literal sense, the remnant of stellar death. The very atoms that let you read this sentence were once at the searing heart of a sun that perished long before the Earth existed, a continuity that links the smallest cell to the grandest events in the sky.

questions.stem: Which factor decides whether a star ends as a cooling ember or a supernova?
choices: Its color
Its mass
Its distance from Earth
Its age in human years
questions.explanation: The text states that when hydrogen runs low, 'the star's fate depends on its mass.'

questions.stem: What keeps a star in a steady balance for most of its life?
choices: The pull of nearby planets
Fusion energy pushing out against gravity pulling in
The cold of surrounding space
The light of other stars
questions.explanation: The passage says the 'outward push of this fusion energy resists the inward crush of gravity.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'forged' most nearly means
choices: destroyed
created or formed
cooled down
copied falsely
questions.explanation: Heavy elements like carbon and iron were 'forged inside ancient stars,' meaning created or formed there.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Stars burn hydrogen forever without changing
Only massive stars matter to life on Earth
Stars are born, die, and scatter the elements that build new stars, planets, and living things
The Sun will soon explode as a supernova
questions.explanation: The passage traces a star's birth, life, and death, then shows how the scattered debris becomes new stars, planets, and even the carbon and iron in our bodies.

lesson.strategy: Read this as a life story with a physics engine. Follow "born, lives, and dies," and watch the force-balance (fusion pushing out, gravity crushing in) hold a star steady until "the hydrogen fuel runs low." At "depends on its mass" the path forks; the last lines turn it personal.

signals.means: Frames the passage as a life cycle. Read the stages in order; each paragraph moves one step along it.

signals.phrase: outward push of this fusion energy
signals.means: The core mechanism: this push resists gravity's inward crush. The plot is that balance holding, then breaking.

signals.phrase: the star's fate depends on its mass
signals.means: The fork. Two endings branch from here: Sun-sized vs. massive. Read the next sentences as a contrast pair.
Flags that 'you are made of dead stars' is a factual claim, not a poetic metaphor. Take it at face value.

vocab.inContext: atoms joining into a heavier atom (hydrogen into helium), releasing energy that lights the star
the violent exploding death of a massive star, briefly brighter than a whole galaxy
made or created under heat: here, carbon and iron built inside ancient stars

skillTips.main-idea: The point is bigger than how stars work. It pulls to 'the carbon in living bodies... were forged inside ancient stars.' Ask why the author ends on your body, not the supernova.
skillTips.inference: The text never says the Sun will die, but it files it under 'a modest star like the Sun.' Treat the two mass-paths as a sorting rule, then place the Sun in its branch to infer its ending.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard science words are defined by nearby words. 'fusing into helium, releasing enormous energy' tells you fusing means joining atoms plus energy. Read the nearby clause instead of guessing.
skillTips.detail: Time and cause words are the spine: 'When the core becomes hot enough,' 'then exploding.' For order or cause questions, find the when/then word for that step, not a keyword match.

passages.title: The First Day
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Nadia arrived at the bakery an hour before it opened. Her hands were cold and her stomach felt tight. It was her first day, and she did not know where anything was.

The baker, a tall man named Cole, handed her an apron. "Ask me anything," he said. "Everyone was new once." Nadia felt a little better.

She watched how Cole shaped the dough. She wrote down each step in a small notebook. When she made a mistake and dropped a tray, no one shouted. Cole just showed her how to hold it.

By noon, the shelves were full of warm bread. Nadia was tired, but she was proud. She had asked many questions, and now she knew a hundred small things she had not known that morning. Tomorrow would be easier.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A woman's first day at a new job, and how asking questions helped her learn
How to bake many kinds of bread
A fight between two workers at a bakery
Why the bakery opened an hour late
questions.explanation: The passage follows Nadia through her first day and shows her learning by asking and watching.

questions.stem: What did Nadia write in her small notebook?
choices: Cole's phone number
Each step for shaping the dough
A recipe from her home
The price of the bread
questions.explanation: The text says she watched how Cole shaped the dough and wrote down each step.

questions.stem: Why did Nadia feel "a little better" after Cole spoke?
choices: The bakery was very warm
His kind words told her it was okay to be new and to ask
She had finished all her work
She was about to go home
questions.explanation: Cole said "Ask me anything" and "Everyone was new once," which reassured her.

questions.stem: In this passage, her stomach felt "tight" most nearly means
choices: full after eating
nervous and tense
relaxed and calm
hurt and sick
questions.explanation: On her first day, with cold hands and not knowing anything, "tight" points to nervous, not full or calm.

lesson.strategy: This is a short story about a first day at work. Track Nadia's feelings, not the bread. She starts cold and nervous, hears one kind line from Cole, and ends tired but proud. Watch how each small win changes her mood.

signals.means: Sets the situation. Everything that follows is Nadia learning something new for the first time.
Cole's kind offer. It tells you the bakery is a safe place to be new and to ask for help.
The mistake is not a disaster. This calm reaction shows she is allowed to get things wrong while learning.
The turn in her mood. The hard morning ends in a good feeling, and that is the point.

vocab.inContext: a cloth you tie on to keep your clothes clean while you cook or bake
the soft mix of flour and water that becomes bread when baked
the good feeling you get after doing something hard well

skillTips.main-idea: The story is not about bread. Follow Nadia from "her first day" to "tired, but she was proud." The main idea is what she learned by asking, not how a bakery works.
skillTips.inference: The text never says Nadia is brave. You see it: she asks many questions and writes each step down. Judge her by what she does.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "tight," use the clues around it: cold hands, a first day, not knowing where things are. These point to nervous, not full or calm.
skillTips.detail: Small facts sit in order. Who gave the apron, what she wrote, what she dropped. Reread the middle to find the exact thing asked.

passages.title: Pack Light
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A heavy bag makes a trip harder. You carry it through stations, up stairs, and onto buses. So many travelers learn one simple rule: pack light.

Start by laying out everything you think you need. Then take away half of it. Most people bring more clothes than they will ever wear. Choose a few items in colors that match, so you can mix them. Wear your heaviest shoes on the plane instead of packing them. Roll your clothes to save space. Keep what is important close: your papers, your money, and your phone.

A light bag is easy to carry and quick to pack. You spend less time waiting and more time seeing the place you came to see. The best trips often fit in one small bag.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why and how to travel with a lighter bag
How to choose a good hotel
Which shoes are best for flying
How to save money on flights
questions.explanation: The whole passage gives reasons and steps for packing a lighter bag.

questions.stem: What does the passage say to do after laying out everything you need?
choices: Buy a bigger bag
Take away half of it
Pack the shoes first
Fold the clothes flat
questions.explanation: The text says: "Then take away half of it."

questions.stem: Why does the passage say to wear your heaviest shoes on the plane?
choices: Because planes are cold
So they do not take up weight and space in the bag
Because shoes are not allowed in bags
Because new shoes hurt your feet
questions.explanation: Wearing the shoes keeps them out of the bag, which fits the goal of a light bag.

questions.stem: In this passage, "items" most nearly means
choices: prices
things or objects
problems
people
questions.explanation: "A few items in colors that match" refers to things like clothes; "items" means objects.

lesson.strategy: This gives advice on how to travel with less. Read it as a list of steps: lay out, cut in half, match colors, wear heavy shoes, roll clothes, keep valuables close. The last lines say why a light bag is worth it.

signals.means: The main advice, named early. Every step after this serves the same goal: carry less.
The strongest tip. It tells you most of what you plan to bring is not needed.

signals.phrase: Roll your clothes to save space
signals.means: A concrete how-to. Rolling, not folding, fits more into a small bag.

signals.phrase: The best trips often fit in one small bag
signals.means: The closing point. Less to carry means more time to enjoy the trip.

vocab.inContext: people who take trips from one place to another
single things, like a shirt, a book, or a pair of shoes
go well together, so clothes can be worn in different pairs

skillTips.main-idea: The point is not any single tip. Tie the steps together under "pack light" and the closing line about a small bag.
skillTips.inference: The passage never says a heavy bag ruins a trip in plain words. Infer it from "You spend less time waiting and more time seeing."
skillTips.vocabulary: For "items," look at the examples near it: clothes, shoes, papers, money, phone. "Items" is the general word for all these things.
skillTips.detail: The steps come in order. To answer a "what to do" question, find the matching step: after laying out, you "take away half of it."

passages.title: A Cheap, Good Meal
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Dried beans cost little and keep for a long time. A bag of them can sit in your cupboard for months without going bad. When you are ready, you soak the beans in water overnight. The next day they are soft enough to cook.

Beans and rice together make a full meal. Beans give your body protein, the same thing that meat gives. Rice fills you up and costs very little. People all over the world eat this pair, from Mexico to India to West Africa. You can change the taste each time with different spices, so you never grow tired of it.

A large pot feeds a whole family and costs less than a single fast-food lunch. Simple food, made at home, can be both cheap and good for you.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Beans and rice make a cheap, healthy, and filling meal
Meat is always better than beans
Rice is very hard to cook well
Spices are too expensive for most people
questions.explanation: The passage gives reason after reason that beans and rice are cheap and good for you.

questions.stem: According to the text, what do you do to dried beans before cooking?
choices: Freeze them for a week
Soak them in water overnight
Fry them in hot oil
Mix them with meat
questions.explanation: The text says: "you soak the beans in water overnight."

questions.stem: Why does the passage mention Mexico, India, and West Africa?
choices: To show that people in many places rely on this cheap, healthy pair
To prove beans grow only in those places
To say those foods all taste the same
To explain how rice is farmed
questions.explanation: Naming many far-apart places supports the idea that this meal works well for people everywhere.

questions.stem: In this passage, "protein" is best understood as
choices: a kind of spice
a part of food your body needs, also found in meat
a type of rice
a cooking pot
questions.explanation: The text explains protein as "the same thing that meat gives" to your body.

lesson.strategy: This explains why beans and rice make a smart meal. Read for the reasons: cheap, keeps a long time, full of protein, eaten worldwide. Each sentence adds one more reason to the same claim in the last line.

signals.phrase: cost little and keep for a long time
signals.means: Two early reasons beans are smart: they are cheap and they do not go bad fast.
The core claim. Together, beans and rice give you what one meal needs.

signals.phrase: People all over the world eat this pair
signals.means: Support by example. If many places rely on it, the meal must work well.

signals.phrase: both cheap and good for you
signals.means: The point, stated at the end. Cheap and healthy do not have to be opposites.

vocab.inContext: a closed shelf in a kitchen where you store food
leave in water for a long time so the beans grow soft
a part of food the body needs to grow and stay strong, also in meat

skillTips.main-idea: Do not stop at one fact like cost. Collect all the reasons and match them to the last line: the meal is "both cheap and good for you."
skillTips.inference: The list of countries is not just decoration. Ask why the writer names them. It hints the meal is trusted in many places, not just one.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "protein," read the clue beside it: "the same thing that meat gives." That tells you what protein does without a hard science word.
skillTips.detail: Steps and facts are spread across the passage. To find what you do before cooking, scan for the action: you "soak the beans in water overnight."

passages.title: A Little at a Time
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Saving money feels hard when you do not earn much. But you do not need a large amount to start. You need a habit.

Put away a small sum each week, even if it is only a few dollars. Keep it in a place you cannot easily reach, like a separate account. Do not wait until the end of the month to see what is left, because often nothing is left. Instead, save first, then spend the rest.

Over a year, small weekly savings add up to a real sum. More important, you build the habit of saving. Once saving feels normal, you keep doing it as you earn more. A person who saves a little for many years often ends up safer than one who earns a lot and saves nothing.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How saving a small amount often, as a habit, builds up over time
How to earn a bigger salary
Why banks pay interest on savings
How to make a monthly food budget
questions.explanation: The passage centers on saving small amounts regularly and building the habit.

questions.stem: According to the text, when should you save?
choices: At the end of the month
First, before you spend the rest
Only when you earn a lot
After paying every bill
questions.explanation: The text says: "save first, then spend the rest."

questions.stem: Why does the passage say to keep savings "in a place you cannot easily reach"?
choices: Because banks are far away
So you are not tempted to spend the money you set aside
Because cash is not safe at home
Because the money grows faster there
questions.explanation: Money that is hard to reach is harder to spend on a whim, which protects your savings.

questions.stem: In this passage, "habit" most nearly means
choices: a large amount of money
something you do again and again until it feels normal
a single lucky choice
a strict rule from a bank
questions.explanation: The text ties "habit" to saving each week until it "feels normal."

lesson.strategy: This gives advice on saving money. Read for the one main move: save a small amount first, and do it every week. The passage repeats that the habit matters more than the size. The last line compares two people to prove the point.

signals.means: The real message. Not a big sum, but a repeated action is what makes saving work.

signals.phrase: save first, then spend the rest
signals.means: The key rule. Set money aside before spending, or nothing will be left.

signals.phrase: small weekly savings add up to a real sum
signals.means: The payoff. Tiny amounts, repeated over a year, grow into something that matters.
The closing claim. Steady saving beats high earning with no saving.

vocab.inContext: an amount of money, small or large
a place at a bank where you keep money apart from your cash
an action you repeat so often it becomes automatic

skillTips.main-idea: The point is the habit, not the dollars. Connect "You need a habit" with the last line about who ends up "safer."
skillTips.inference: The text says keep savings where you "cannot easily reach." Ask why. The reason is left unsaid: hard-to-reach money is harder to spend.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "habit," use the words around it: "each week," "keep doing it," "feels normal." These show a habit is a repeated action.
skillTips.detail: The advice is exact. On when to save, the text says "save first, then spend the rest," not at the end of the month.

passages.title: The Simple Walk
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
You do not need a gym or special gear to care for your body. You only need to walk. A walk each day is one of the easiest ways to stay well. It costs nothing.

When you walk, your heart beats faster and grows stronger. Your legs and back feel less stiff. Many people also notice that a walk clears the mind. A worry that felt heavy at your desk can feel lighter after twenty minutes outside.

You do not have to walk fast or far. A slow walk still helps. Try to make it a daily habit: after lunch, or before bed, or on the way to the store. Leave the car and use your feet when you can. Small, steady movement, done often, keeps the body and mind in better shape.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A daily walk is a simple, free way to help both body and mind
Gyms are a waste of money
Walking fast is the only good exercise
You should never drive a car
questions.explanation: The passage praises a daily walk as an easy, free help for both body and mind.

questions.stem: According to the text, what happens to your heart when you walk?
choices: It beats slower and rests
It beats faster and grows stronger
It stops feeling stiff
It clears the mind
questions.explanation: The text says: "your heart beats faster and grows stronger."

questions.stem: Why does the passage say a heavy worry can "feel lighter after twenty minutes outside"?
choices: Because problems solve themselves in time
Because walking can calm the mind, not only exercise the body
Because walking makes you forget on purpose
Because fresh air removes all stress fully
questions.explanation: The line about a worry feeling lighter shows walking helps the mind, not just the body.

questions.stem: In this passage, "stiff" most nearly means
choices: warm and soft
hard to bend or move easily
fast and strong
light and free
questions.explanation: Legs and back "feel less stiff" after walking; stiff means hard to bend or move.

lesson.strategy: This is health advice with one clear message: walk every day. Read for the two kinds of good it names, body and mind, and the reasons under each. The end tells you how to fit walking into normal days.

signals.means: The whole message in one line. No gym, no gear, just walking.

signals.phrase: your heart beats faster and grows stronger
signals.means: The body benefit. This is the physical reason walking helps.
The second benefit, for the mind. Walking helps how you feel, not just your body.
The practical step. The good comes from doing it often, not once.

vocab.inContext: special equipment or tools, like the kind used in a gym
hard to bend; a body that has not moved feels this way
even and regular, done again and again without stopping

skillTips.main-idea: The passage praises two gains: body and mind. Join "heart... grows stronger" and "clears the mind" to state the full main idea.
skillTips.inference: The line about a worry feeling "lighter" is not about the body. Infer that walking helps the mind, since the writer moves from muscles to worries.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "stiff," use the body clue: legs and back that "feel less stiff" after walking. Stiff means hard to move, the opposite of loose.
skillTips.detail: The body facts are stated plainly. On the heart, the text says it "beats faster and grows stronger." Find the exact line first.

passages.title: The Dawn Chorus
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before the sun is fully up, many birds begin to sing. If you wake early, you can hear them: one call, then another, then many at once. People call this the dawn chorus. But why do birds sing so much at dawn?

In the early morning, the air is often still and cool. Sound travels farther when the air is calm, so a bird's song can reach much farther than it would at noon. It is also too dark to hunt for food, so the birds use the time to call instead. A male bird sings to say two things: this is my space, and I am strong and healthy. Females listen and choose.

By the time the sun is high, the singing slows down. The birds go quiet and get to work finding food.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why many birds sing loudly at dawn
How birds build their nests
Which birds sing the best songs
Why birds fly south in winter
questions.explanation: The passage asks and answers why birds sing so much at dawn.

questions.stem: According to the text, why does sound travel farther at dawn?
choices: The birds sing much louder then
The air is often still and cool
There are more birds awake
The sun makes sound move faster
questions.explanation: The text says "the air is often still and cool" and "Sound travels farther when the air is calm."

questions.stem: Why do birds sing at dawn instead of hunting?
choices: They are not hungry in the morning
It is too dark to find food, so they use the time to call
They hunt only at night
Singing gives them energy to hunt
questions.explanation: The text says it is "too dark to hunt for food, so the birds use the time to call instead."

questions.stem: In this passage, "chorus" most nearly means
choices: a single quiet call
many voices singing together at once
a place where birds sleep
the first light of day
questions.explanation: The opening picture, "one call, then another, then many at once," shows a chorus is many voices together.

lesson.strategy: This asks and answers one question: why do birds sing at dawn? Read for the question mark in the middle, then collect the reasons that follow. Each reason is a separate cause of the same behavior.

signals.means: Names the thing the passage explains: the wave of bird song at sunrise.

signals.phrase: why do birds sing so much at dawn?
signals.means: The question the whole passage answers. Every line after this is a reason.

signals.phrase: Sound travels farther when the air is calm
signals.means: Reason one. Still morning air carries a song a long way.

signals.phrase: this is my space, and I am strong and healthy
signals.means: The message in the song. Birds sing to claim ground and attract a mate.

vocab.inContext: the time when the sun first begins to rise
many voices or songs heard together at the same time
still and quiet, with little or no wind

skillTips.main-idea: The middle question, "why do birds sing so much at dawn?", is your guide. The main idea is the set of answers, not the sound itself.
skillTips.inference: The text says it is "too dark to hunt." You infer why that matters: with no hunting to do, the birds have free time to sing.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "chorus," use the picture in the first lines: "one call, then another, then many at once." A chorus is many voices together.
skillTips.detail: Reasons are listed one by one. On why sound carries, the text says the air is "still and cool." Point to that line, not a guess.

passages.title: The Food Cart
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every day at noon, a line forms at Sami's food cart. He parks it on the same corner, near the tall office buildings. He sells warm rice bowls, and he knows many of his buyers by name. "The usual?" he asks a woman in a gray coat. She nods and smiles.

Sami works fast, but he never rushes a person who is not sure. He lets them look and ask. His prices are fair, and the food is fresh, cooked that morning. Some days it rains, and the line is short. Sami still comes. He says the people who show up in the rain are his best customers, and he wants them to find him there.

Over the years, the corner has become a small meeting place. People wait, they talk, and they leave full.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A food cart owner who builds a loyal following through fair prices and care
How to cook rice bowls at home
Why office jobs are so stressful
The best corner in town to park a cart
questions.explanation: The passage shows how Sami treats people, which builds a loyal following.

questions.stem: Where does Sami park his cart?
choices: Inside an office building
On the same corner, near the tall office buildings
Near the train station
In a different spot each day
questions.explanation: The text says he "parks it on the same corner, near the tall office buildings."

questions.stem: Why does Sami come even when it rains and the line is short?
choices: He has nowhere else to sell
He values the loyal customers who still show up
Rice sells better in the rain
He does not notice the weather
questions.explanation: He calls the rainy-day crowd "his best customers" and wants them to find him there.

questions.stem: In this passage, "customers" most nearly means
choices: the other food carts
the people who buy from him
the office workers' bosses
the cooks who help him
questions.explanation: The customers are the buyers who "wait, they talk, and they leave full."

lesson.strategy: Short fiction about a food seller. Do not read it as a menu. Track how Sami treats people: he learns names, he does not rush, he shows up in the rain. Those choices, not the food, are the point.

signals.phrase: he knows many of his buyers by name

passages.title: Asking the Way
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Marcus stood on a busy street in a city he did not know. His map made no sense. The street signs were in a language he could not read. He needed to find the train station, and his train left in an hour. For a while he was too shy to ask anyone.

Then he stopped an older woman with kind eyes. He did not share her language, so he simply said the word "station" and held up his ticket. The woman understood at once. She pointed down the street, held up two fingers, and made a left turn with her hand. Marcus thanked her and followed her signs.

Two streets later, he turned left, and there it was: the station. He had almost missed his train because he was afraid to ask. A few simple words and a kind stranger had saved him.

questions.explanation: He was "too shy to ask anyone" "for a while," and that delay nearly cost him the train.

a person you do not know
a close friend
a seller of maps
questions.explanation: The woman is someone Marcus has never met, so "stranger" means a person you do not know.

lesson.strategy: Short fiction about being lost in a strange city. Follow Marcus's problem and how he solves it: a map he cannot read, a fear of asking, then one brave choice. The last line names the lesson.

signals.means: Marcus's block. His fear, not the map, is the real problem to overcome.

skillTips.inference: The text says he was "too shy to ask anyone" "for a while." Infer that this delay is why he "almost missed his train."
skillTips.vocabulary: For "stranger," use the story: the woman is someone Marcus has never met. A stranger is a person you do not know.
skillTips.detail: The steps are exact. How he asked (one word, his ticket), what the woman did (pointed, two fingers, left turn). Reread to match.

passages.title: A Free Place to Learn
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In almost every town there is a place where you can sit, read, and learn without paying a cent. It is the public library. With a library card, which is free, you can borrow books and take them home. You can read the news, use a computer, or find a quiet corner to study.

Many people do not know how much a library offers. Some hold classes to help adults learn to read or use a computer. Some lend tools, games, or even musical instruments. A library is warm in winter and cool in summer, open to anyone who walks in.

You do not have to buy anything. You do not have to be rich or young. For a person who wants to learn but has little money, the library may be the most useful place in the whole town.

questions.explanation: The library's services are free, so a person with little money gains the most from them.

skillTips.main-idea: The passage is one long list of free services. Sum them under the idea that a library gives learning "without paying a cent."
skillTips.inference: The last line calls the library "most useful" for people with little money. Infer why: it gives learning and tools that others must pay for.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "borrow," note you "take them home" and, by a library's nature, return them. Borrow means take for a while, then give back.

passages.title: Rest Your Eyes
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Many people now spend hours looking at a screen. After a long day of it, the eyes can feel dry, tired, and sore. This happens partly because we blink less when we stare at a screen. We also hold our eyes at one short distance for too long.

There is a simple way to help, sometimes called the 20-20-20 rule. Every twenty minutes, look at something far away, about twenty feet, for twenty seconds. This lets the eye relax and change its focus. Blinking on purpose also helps, since it wets the eye again.

It helps to sit a little farther from the screen and to keep the room softly lit, not too bright or too dark. Your eyes were made to look near and far all day. A few short breaks give them the change they need.

questions.stem: What does the 20-20-20 rule tell you to do every twenty minutes?
choices: Close your eyes for twenty minutes
Look at something far away for twenty seconds
Walk twenty steps away from the desk
Blink twenty times as fast as you can
questions.explanation: The rule is: every twenty minutes, look far away, about twenty feet, for twenty seconds.

questions.stem: Why do the eyes feel dry after staring at a screen?
choices: Because screens give off water
Because we blink less when we stare
Because the room is too dark
Because the eyes grow too strong
questions.explanation: The text ties dry eyes to the fact that "we blink less when we stare at a screen."

questions.stem: In this passage, "focus" most nearly means
choices: the brightness of a screen
how the eye sets itself to see clearly at a distance
a kind of eye drop
the center of a room
questions.explanation: The eye must "change its focus" from near to far, so focus is how it sets itself to see clearly.

lesson.strategy: This explains why screens tire the eyes and how to help. Read for two parts: the causes of tired eyes, then the fixes. The 20-20-20 rule is the main tip, so hold its three numbers clearly.

signals.phrase: we blink less when we stare at a screen
signals.means: A cause of tired eyes. Less blinking means a drier eye.
The main fix, given a name so it is easy to remember.

signals.phrase: A few short breaks give them the change they need
signals.means: The closing point. Small pauses, not big changes, do the job.

vocab.inContext: aching or painful in a dull way

skillTips.main-idea: The passage has causes and fixes, but its message is hopeful: simple breaks help. Tie the fixes to "the change they need."
skillTips.inference: The text pairs "dry" eyes with "we blink less." Infer the link: less blinking leaves the eye dry, so blinking on purpose helps.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "focus," use the action near it: the eye must "change its focus" from near to far. Focus is how the eye sets itself to see clearly.
skillTips.detail: The rule has exact numbers. Every twenty minutes, look about twenty feet away for twenty seconds. Match all three before choosing.

passages.title: The Night Shift
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
While the city sleeps, Priya is already at work. She is a baker, and her day begins at two in the morning, long before the sun. The streets are empty and quiet as she walks to the shop. Inside, the ovens are cold, and she must bring them to life.

She mixes the dough she prepared the night before and shapes each loaf by hand. The work is steady and warm, and she likes the peace of these dark hours. There is no one to serve yet, only bread to make. By the time the first customers arrive at six, the shelves are full and the whole shop smells of fresh bread.

Priya rarely sees the busy afternoon; by then she is home and asleep. Most people would find her hours strange. But she has come to love the quiet start, when the city is still and the day belongs only to her.

choices: A night baker who finds quiet joy in working while the city sleeps

choices: fast and rushed

loud and busy

questions.explanation: "The work is steady and warm" is tied to peace and calm, so steady means even and calm.

lesson.strategy: Short fiction about an unusual work life. Notice the contrast: the city sleeps while Priya works. Track her feelings about the strange hours. Most would dislike them, but the last lines show she loves the quiet.

signals.phrase: the day belongs only to her
signals.means: The closing image. The lonely hours feel like a gift, not a burden.

skillTips.main-idea: Two feelings could fit: hardship or peace. The writer lands on peace. Read past "strange" to "the day belongs only to her."
skillTips.inference: The text says she is "home and asleep" by afternoon. Infer why she misses the busy hours: her body follows a night schedule.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "steady," use the pair beside it: "steady and warm," tied to peace and calm. Steady means even, not rushed or unsure.
skillTips.detail: Times are exact. Her day begins "at two in the morning"; customers come "at six." Match the exact time the question names.

passages.title: The Long Train
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The train would take nine hours to cross the country, and Elena was glad of it. She had chosen the train over the plane on purpose. A plane would have been faster, but from a plane you see nothing but clouds. From the train window, the whole land unrolled before her.

First came the flat farms, green and wide, split into neat squares. Then low hills rose, dotted with sheep. In the afternoon the train climbed into mountains, and the air grew thin and cold.

Elena did not read her book. She simply watched, as one town after another slid past, each with its own small station and its own name. She thought about the people who lived in these places she would never visit.

By the time the lights of the far city appeared, she felt she had truly traveled, not just arrived. The slow way, she decided, had shown her more.

signals.means: The point. The journey itself, not the ending, was the value.

skillTips.main-idea: The changing scenery is support, not the point. The main idea is Elena's belief that "the slow way... had shown her more."
skillTips.inference: She never says she dislikes planes. Infer her reason from "from a plane you see nothing but clouds" set against the rich train view.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "unrolled," picture the land opening like a mat: "the whole land unrolled before her." It means spread out into view.
skillTips.detail: The trip has exact steps: nine hours, flat farms, low hills, then mountains. Follow that order to place any detail the question asks.

passages.title: Why We Sleep
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
We spend about a third of our lives asleep, yet many people treat sleep as wasted time. In truth, the body and brain are hard at work while we rest.

During sleep, the body repairs muscles and heals small hurts from the day. The brain does something just as important: it sorts through what we learned and stores the parts worth keeping. This is one reason students who sleep well remember more than those who stay up all night to study. Sleep also clears waste from the brain that builds up while we are awake.

When we do not get enough, we feel it. We think slowly, forget easily, and grow short of temper. A single bad night is not serious, but weeks of poor sleep harm both health and mood. Sleep is not lost time. It is the quiet work that makes the waking hours possible.

questions.explanation: The passage argues that sleep is not wasted time but active, useful work.

questions.explanation: The text says the brain "sorts through what we learned and stores the parts worth keeping."

choices: Staying awake erases memory on purpose

questions.explanation: Since sleep "stores the parts worth keeping," missing sleep loses some of what was learned.

choices: throws away
fixes what was damaged
grows larger
keeps awake
questions.explanation: The body "repairs muscles" and "heals small hurts," so repairs means fixes what was damaged.

lesson.strategy: This argues against a common idea: that sleep is wasted time. Read for the jobs sleep does, one for the body and one for the brain, then what happens when we miss it. The last line answers the false idea.

signals.phrase: many people treat sleep as wasted time
signals.means: The wrong idea the passage sets out to correct.

signals.means: The main claim. Sleep is active, not idle.

skillTips.main-idea: The passage opens with a wrong idea and closes by fixing it. Tie "wasted time" to "Sleep is not lost time" for the main idea.
skillTips.inference: The text does not spell out why sleepy students forget. Infer it from the brain's job: sleep "stores" learning, so missing sleep loses it.
skillTips.vocabulary: For "repairs," note what it acts on: "muscles" and "small hurts." To repair is to fix what was damaged.
skillTips.detail: Two systems do two jobs. The body "repairs muscles"; the brain "sorts" and "stores." Match the job to the right one.

passages.title: Money for a Rainy Day
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Life brings surprises, and many of them cost money. A car breaks down. A tooth needs fixing. A job ends without warning. People who have no savings must borrow when these things happen, often at a high cost.

That is why many advisers suggest keeping an emergency fund. This is a pot of money set aside for hard times and nothing else. A common goal is to save enough to cover three months of basic costs, such as rent and food. That amount is not easy to reach, and it may take years.

The trick is to build it slowly and to leave it alone. It is not for a holiday or a new phone. It is only for a true emergency.

People with such a fund sleep better, because a sudden bill does not become a crisis. The fund turns a disaster into a mere problem.

skillTips.main-idea: The examples of car and tooth are support. The main idea is the fund itself: money "set aside for hard times and nothing else."

skillTips.vocabulary: For "emergency," use the examples: a broken car, a lost job, a sudden bill. An emergency is a sudden serious event, not a want.
skillTips.detail: The size goal is exact: "three months of basic costs, such as rent and food." Match that figure, not a rounder guess.

passages.title: Otters at Play
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
River otters seem to treat life as a game. Along quiet rivers and lakes, they slide down muddy or snowy banks again and again, one after another, as if for the pure fun of it. But this play has a purpose. Through it, young otters build the strength and skill they will need to hunt.

An otter's body is made for water. Its fur is thick and traps a layer of air that keeps the skin dry and warm, even in cold rivers. Webbed feet and a strong tail push it through the water with ease. Otters hunt fish, frogs, and other small animals, diving and turning faster than their prey can flee.

They live in family groups and seem to enjoy each other's company. To watch an otter is to see an animal that is very good at staying alive and, at the same time, appears to be having a wonderful time.

skillTips.vocabulary: For "prey," look at what the otter does: it hunts "fish, frogs, and other small animals." Those hunted animals are its prey.
skillTips.detail: Body facts are specific. Warmth comes from fur that "traps a layer of air," not from fat. Match the exact cause the text gives.

passages.title: A World of Tea
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
After water, tea is the most common drink in the world. It is made in a simple way: pour hot water over the dried leaves of the tea plant, and wait. Yet from this one plant, people have built countless customs.

In Japan, a tea ceremony can last for hours and follows careful, quiet steps. In England, tea often comes with milk in the afternoon. In Morocco, green tea is poured with mint and plenty of sugar, from high above the glass to make a foam on top. In many places, offering tea to a guest is a sign of welcome, and to refuse it can seem rude.

The tea plant grows best on cool, wet hillsides, and its leaves are still picked by hand in many countries. One plant, one hot pot of water, and yet a thousand ways to share a warm drink with another person.

passages.title: The Case for Used
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A new phone, a new car, a new sofa: the moment you buy them, they lose value. Drive a new car off the lot, and it may be worth thousands less the same day. This is why buying used can be a wise choice. Someone else has already paid for that first drop in price. A used item, checked with care, can serve you just as well for far less money.

The key is to check with care. Look closely, ask questions, and test the thing before you pay. For a car, a trusted mechanic can spot hidden trouble. For furniture, look for strong joints and clean lines.

Not everything should be bought used; some items, like a mattress or safety gear, are better new. But for many things, used is not a step down. It is a way to get what you need and keep more of your money.

passages.title: How the Cactus Survives
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A desert can go months, even years, without rain. Under a burning sun, most plants would dry out and die. Yet the cactus not only survives there, it thrives. Over long ages, the cactus has changed its very shape to hold on to water.

Its thick, rounded stem works like a tank. When rain finally comes, the stem swells and fills, storing water for the dry months ahead. A waxy skin covers the plant and seals that water in, so little escapes into the hot air.

Most plants have wide, flat leaves, but wide leaves lose water fast. The cactus has traded its leaves for sharp spines. The spines lose almost no water, and they guard the juicy stem from thirsty animals.

Shallow roots spread out wide, just under the surface, ready to drink in any rain before it sinks away. Every part of the cactus is built for one task: to save water.

passages.title: The Home Office
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For many jobs today, the office is wherever a laptop opens. Working from home was once rare, but now millions do it. Like most changes, it brings both gains and costs.

The gains are real. There is no long drive to work, which saves time and money. A worker can start soon after waking and use the saved hours for family or rest. The home is quiet, without the noise of a busy office.

But there are costs too. At home, work and rest share the same walls, and the line between them can blur. Some people find it hard to stop working when the desk is ten steps from the bed. Others feel lonely, missing the small talk and shared lunches of an office.

The best home workers set clear limits: a fixed start, a fixed stop, and a space used only for work. Freedom, it turns out, needs a little structure to work well.

passages.title: Why Jet Lag Happens
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Fly across many time zones, and your body arrives before your inner clock does. This tired, foggy feeling is called jet lag. Inside every person is a kind of clock that tells the body when to sleep and when to wake. It is set mostly by light.

For a long time this clock matched the sky where you lived. Then a fast plane drops you in a place where noon feels like midnight to your body. Your inner clock still runs on the old time and takes several days to catch up. That is why, in a new time zone, you may feel wide awake at three in the morning and sleepy at noon.

Light is the best tool to fix it. Spend time outdoors in daylight, and your clock begins to reset to the new place. Going the slow way, by ship or by train, jet lag barely happens at all, because the body has time to adjust.

passages.title: Turning Scraps into Soil
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every kitchen makes waste: apple cores, coffee grounds, old bread, potato peels. Most of it goes into the trash and then to a dump. But there is an older, better path for this waste. It can become rich soil, through a slow, natural process called composting.

Composting is simple. You gather food scraps and yard waste, such as dead leaves, in a pile or a bin. Tiny living things, from worms to bugs to unseen microbes, feed on the waste and break it down. Air and a little water help them work. Over weeks or months, the pile shrinks and darkens, until the scraps are gone and dark, crumbly soil is left.

Gardeners call this soil black gold, because it feeds plants so well. Composting turns a daily waste into something useful, keeps trash out of the dump, and gives back to the earth what came from it.
