skillTips.inference: The text never says Marta sleeps in daylight. You get it from the clock times plus the curtains.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the nearby actions. Loaves go into an oven, so they must be bread.
skillTips.detail: Detail questions here are time questions. Match the time in the question to the time in the text.

passages.title: The Bicycle Shop
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Nadia opened the bicycle shop at eight, though few people came before noon. The shop smelled of rubber and oil. Along one wall hung wheels of every size, like a row of thin moons.

A boy came in with a flat tire and no money. He put the bicycle on the rack and looked at the floor. Nadia found the hole, patched it, and pumped the tire hard. Then she asked him to sweep the back room. He swept it twice.

After that, the boy returned every Saturday. He learned to straighten a bent wheel and to tighten a loose chain. He was clumsy at first, but his hands grew patient.

In the spring, Nadia gave him a key. She did not explain it, and he did not ask. He simply arrived earlier the next morning and turned on the lights himself.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A shop that sells wheels of every size
A boy who cannot pay to fix his bicycle
How a boy slowly earns a place in a repair shop
Why Saturday is the busiest day of the week
questions.explanation: The passage moves from one free repair to weekly visits to a key of his own. The subject is the boy earning his place.

questions.stem: What did Nadia ask the boy to do instead of paying?
choices: Sweep the back room
Come back the next Saturday
Bring her a new tire
Turn on the shop lights
questions.explanation: After patching the tire, she asked him to sweep the back room, and he swept it twice.

questions.stem: What does giving the boy a key most likely mean?
choices: She wants him to lock up and stop visiting.
She trusts him to open the shop on his own.
She is selling the shop to him.
She has lost her own key.
questions.explanation: The next morning he arrives earlier and turns on the lights himself. The key lets him open the shop, which shows trust.

questions.stem: In this passage, clumsy describes someone who
choices: works very quickly
is unfriendly to customers
moves without skill or control
is afraid of machines
questions.explanation: It is contrasted with hands that grew patient after practice, so clumsy means awkward and unskilled at first.

lesson.strategy: This is a story of slow change. Read it as a ladder: one visit, then many visits, then a key. Watch how each paragraph raises the boy's position in the shop.

signals.phrase: though few people came before noon
signals.means: the shop is quiet, so there is time to teach
the single visit becomes a routine
the writer is about to show improvement later
months have passed; the change is complete

vocab.inContext: covered the hole in the tire so the air stayed in
awkward, not yet skilled with his hands
calm and unhurried, working without rushing

skillTips.main-idea: When a story spans months, the main idea is usually the change, not any single scene.
skillTips.inference: The key is never explained. Use the action right after it to decide what it means.
skillTips.vocabulary: Look for contrast words like but. Clumsy is the opposite of the patient hands he gets later.
skillTips.detail: Small actions matter here. The sweeping is the payment, so it is a likely detail question.

passages.title: The Rooftop Garden
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For eleven years Ines lived on the top floor and never went up to the roof. Then the building manager handed her a key and said the roof was hers if she wanted it.

The first summer, everything died. The wind was too strong, and the black tar floor turned the dark pots into ovens. Ines carried water up six flights and watched the tomato leaves curl.

The second summer she built a low wall of bricks and set the pots behind it. She used pale buckets instead of dark ones. Beans climbed a net. Mint spread until she had to pull it out by the handful.

Now the neighbors come up in the evening with folding chairs. Nobody planned this. They talk about the heat and the price of onions while the city turns orange below them. Ines says little. She waters, and she listens.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A woman learns by failing first, and her roof garden becomes a shared place
City roofs are too hot for any plant to survive
Neighbors argue about the rising price of onions
A building manager rents out a roof to make money
questions.explanation: The first summer fails, the second summer works, and by the end the roof draws the neighbors. Both parts together are the point.

questions.stem: Why did the plants die the first summer?
choices: Ines forgot to water them.
The wind was strong and the dark pots became too hot.
The neighbors took the tomatoes.
There was no soil anywhere on the roof.
questions.explanation: The text names two causes: wind that was too strong and black tar that turned the dark pots into ovens.

questions.stem: What does the line about nobody planning it suggest about the evening gatherings?
choices: The building manager invited the neighbors.
Ines built the garden in order to make friends.
The gatherings grew on their own, without being intended.
The neighbors come only to complain about the heat.
questions.explanation: Ines wanted a garden, not a meeting place. The short sentence tells you the company was an unplanned result.

questions.stem: In six flights, a flight is
choices: a set of stairs between two floors
a journey by airplane
a heavy water bucket
a tool used in a garden
questions.explanation: She carries water up from her apartment to the roof, so the flights are stairs between floors.

lesson.strategy: The passage is built in three time blocks: first summer, second summer, now. Compare them. What failed, what she changed, and what appeared that she never planned.

signals.means: opens the failure block
opens the repair block; expect the fixes here
the present result of both summers
the writer marks the ending as an accident, not a goal

vocab.inContext: the black waterproof surface of the roof, which holds heat
sets of stairs between one floor and the next
to bend and dry up from heat

skillTips.main-idea: If a passage has a failure and a success, the main idea usually covers both, not just one.
skillTips.inference: A very short sentence in a long paragraph is a signal. Ask why the writer stopped there.
skillTips.vocabulary: Everyday words can have special uses. Flights here has nothing to do with planes.
skillTips.detail: When a cause has two parts, the right answer usually keeps both.

passages.title: The Last Train
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The last train leaves at 12:40, and the platform is never crowded. There is a cleaner with a wide broom, two students asleep on a bench, and a man with a violin case.

The man does not play. He carries the case in both arms, the way people carry a sleeping child. Some nights he sits under the sign and reads the timetable as though it were news.

Tonight a girl asks him if he is a musician. He says he was, many years ago, and that the case is empty now. He uses it for bread, papers, and a folded jacket.

The girl does not know what to say, so she says nothing. They ride four stops together without speaking. When he stands to leave, he lifts the case with both arms again, exactly as before.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Late trains are dangerous for young people
How to travel cheaply after midnight
A girl learns to play the violin
A quiet meeting that reveals a man's lost life as a musician
questions.explanation: The short exchange on the platform and train is there to show who the man used to be and what he still carries.

questions.stem: What does the man keep in the violin case?
choices: A violin he never plays
Bread, papers, and a folded jacket
Money and train tickets
Nothing at all
questions.explanation: He says the case is empty of the instrument and that he uses it for bread, papers, and a folded jacket.

questions.stem: Why does he still carry the empty case so carefully?
choices: The case is extremely heavy.
He is afraid someone will steal it.
It still holds meaning from the life he had.
Station rules require him to hold it that way.
questions.explanation: He holds it like a sleeping child even though the violin is gone, and he lifts it the same way at the end. The care is about his past, not the contents.

questions.stem: In this passage, a timetable is
choices: a list of train departure and arrival times
a long bench on the platform
a free evening newspaper
a ticket good for one ride
questions.explanation: He reads it on the platform as though it were news, and it belongs to the station, so it lists train times.

lesson.strategy: This is a scene, not a plot. Read the man's hands. The writer repeats one gesture at the start and at the end, and that repetition carries the meaning.

signals.means: sets a fixed, late, quiet scene
this is a repeated habit, not just tonight
the story narrows from habit to one specific evening
closes the circle; nothing about him has changed

vocab.inContext: the raised place beside the track where people wait
a long brush for sweeping floors
the printed list of train times

skillTips.main-idea: In a quiet scene, ask what the writer wants you to notice about one character.
skillTips.inference: Repeated actions carry feeling. Compare the first description of the case with the last.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the place. A word used at a station usually belongs to trains.
skillTips.detail: Listen for lists. Bread, papers, and a jacket is a list, and lists are easy detail questions.

passages.title: The Key With No Lock
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Old Pavel repaired locks for forty years, and he believed that every lock was a small argument about trust. A lock does not stop a determined thief, he liked to say; it only makes an honest hesitation possible.

One October a woman brought him a key with no lock. She had found it in her late father's coat. It was brass, heavy, and stamped with a number that meant nothing to her. Could he tell her what it opened?

Pavel turned it under the lamp for a long minute. The wear on the teeth told him it had been used often, and then not at all for many years. Beyond that, he said, a key by itself says very little.

The woman looked disappointed, and he understood why. She had not come about a door. She had come hoping the key would explain her father, and no key does that.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Old locks are easy for thieves to open
A woman wanted the key to explain her father, not to open a door
Pavel teaches a customer how to repair a lock
Brass keys were common forty years ago
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the turn: her real question was about her father, and an object cannot answer that.

questions.stem: Where did the woman find the key?
choices: In her late father's coat
In Pavel's workshop
Inside an old brass box
Under a lamp at home
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says she had found it in her late father's coat.

questions.stem: What did the wear on the teeth tell Pavel?
choices: The key had never been used.
The key had belonged to a thief.
The key was used a great deal and then stopped being used.
The lock it opened had been repaired recently.
questions.explanation: He reads the marks as heavy use followed by a long period of no use at all.

questions.stem: In this passage, hesitation means
choices: a short pause before acting
a strong metal bar
a written promise
a loud warning alarm
questions.explanation: Pavel says a lock makes an honest hesitation possible: it gives an honest person a moment to stop and think, not a barrier.

lesson.strategy: The passage opens with an idea, gives one case, then turns. Expect the last paragraph to reinterpret everything before it: the question asked was not the question meant.

signals.means: marks a personal belief the story will test
the general belief now meets one specific case
the limit of what evidence can prove
the turn begins; the real reason is coming

vocab.inContext: a pause in which an honest person reconsiders
a heavy yellow metal used for keys
marked by pressing a number into the metal

skillTips.main-idea: When a story ends with a correction, the main idea lives in the correction.
skillTips.inference: Pavel never says the owner stopped using it. He reads the object; you read him reading it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Abstract nouns take meaning from their sentence. Hesitation sits next to honest, so it is about a choice.
skillTips.detail: Details here are small and physical: brass, a number, a coat. Note them as you read.

passages.title: Fog On The Crossing
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The crossing takes twenty-two minutes in clear weather and anything at all in fog. Captain Ruiz had learned not to trust her eyes on mornings like this one, when the harbor lights turned into soft grey stains and the far shore stopped existing.

She trusted the compass, the chart, and the count. Two hundred seconds on this heading, then a slow turn to port. Passengers hated the sound of the horn, but the horn was not for them; it was a question thrown into the white, and the answer, if one came, was another boat.

A new deckhand asked whether she was ever frightened. Ruiz said that fear was the wrong instrument. Fear made people steer toward whatever they could see, and on a morning like this one, what you could see was the least reliable thing on the water.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Fog makes ferry crossings faster
Passengers should not be allowed to hear the horn
A deckhand learns how to steer the boat
In fog the captain trusts instruments and method instead of her eyes
questions.explanation: Every part supports this: she distrusts sight, she names compass, chart and count, and she calls fear the wrong instrument.

questions.stem: How long does the crossing take in clear weather?
choices: Two hundred seconds
Nineteen minutes
Twenty-two minutes
Four minutes
questions.explanation: The first sentence gives twenty-two minutes in clear weather. Two hundred seconds is the length of one heading, not the whole crossing.

questions.stem: Why does Ruiz sound the horn?
choices: To learn whether another boat is nearby
To wake the sleeping passengers
To tell the harbor that she is running late
To warn passengers about the coming turn
questions.explanation: The horn is called a question thrown into the white, and the answer would be another boat. It is a way of finding traffic she cannot see.

questions.stem: In this passage, a turn to port means turning toward
choices: the entrance of the harbor
the left side of the boat
the open sea
the back of the boat
questions.explanation: It appears with a compass heading as a steering direction, so port is the ship term for the left side, not a place.

lesson.strategy: This passage argues by replacing one thing with another: eyes replaced by instruments, fear replaced by method. Each paragraph names what is rejected and what is trusted instead.

signals.means: the time is unpredictable; the normal rule fails

signals.phrase: She trusted the compass, the chart, and the count
signals.means: the list of what replaces eyesight

signals.phrase: but the horn was not for them
signals.means: correcting a wrong assumption about purpose

signals.phrase: on a morning like this one
signals.means: the claim is limited to fog conditions, not always

vocab.inContext: the instrument that shows direction
the left side of a boat, used as a steering direction
a junior crew member who works on deck

skillTips.main-idea: Look for the pattern of rejection. What the captain refuses to trust points at the main idea.
skillTips.inference: The horn is explained with a metaphor. Translate the metaphor into plain purpose.
skillTips.vocabulary: A common word can be technical at sea. Ask what a sailor would mean by it.
skillTips.detail: Numbers are traps here. Two numbers appear, and they measure different things.

passages.title: Room Nine
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Room 9 held eleven paintings, and for nineteen years Teodor stood among them. Visitors moved through in about four minutes. They photographed the large battle scene by the door, glanced at the portraits, and left.

Teodor watched the small canvas in the corner: a kitchen table, a bowl, a window with weak northern light. Nobody stopped for it. In nineteen years he had seen perhaps forty people stop, and he remembered most of them.

He could not have said what the painting meant. He knew instead where the varnish had cracked, how the bowl went cold and silver in February, how the same brown warmed in July when the room's own light changed. He had not studied it. He had simply been present while it was there, which is a different kind of knowing, and possibly not a smaller one.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Museum guards should be trained in art history
Room 9 needs stronger lighting for its paintings
Long, quiet attention creates a knowledge different from study
Visitors always prefer large paintings to small ones
questions.explanation: The final sentences say it directly: he had not studied the painting, yet years of presence gave him a different kind of knowing.

questions.stem: About how many people did Teodor see stop at the small canvas?
choices: Eleven
Four
Nineteen
About forty
questions.explanation: In nineteen years he had seen perhaps forty people stop. Eleven is the number of paintings and nineteen the number of years.

questions.stem: The last sentence suggests that Teodor's kind of knowing is
choices: clearly less valuable than an expert's study
possibly as valuable as expert study, though different in kind
exactly the same as reading a book about the painting
useless, because he cannot explain the painting's meaning
questions.explanation: The careful phrase possibly not a smaller one refuses to rank his knowledge below study, while still calling it different.

questions.stem: In this passage, varnish is
choices: a clear coating on the surface of the painting
the wooden frame around the picture
the signature of the painter
a kind of light from a window
questions.explanation: It is something on the painting that can crack over time, which points to the protective surface layer.

lesson.strategy: Read this as a contrast between two ways of seeing: the visitors' four minutes and the guard's nineteen years. The last paragraph tells you what the guard gained instead of meaning.

signals.means: sets the long time scale against the visitors' four minutes
isolates the small canvas as the true subject
swaps one kind of knowledge for another

signals.phrase: which is a different kind of knowing
signals.means: the writer states the idea plainly at the end

vocab.inContext: the cloth a painting is made on, used here to mean the painting itself
paintings of people
the clear protective layer over the paint

skillTips.main-idea: When two time scales are compared, the main idea is usually about what the longer one gives.
skillTips.inference: Weigh hedging words. Possibly not a smaller one is a careful claim, not a strong one.
skillTips.vocabulary: Ask what can do the action. Only a surface layer can crack on a painting.
skillTips.detail: Three numbers appear close together. Match each number to its own noun.

passages.title: The Mapmaker Of Valea
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The ministry sent Aurel to redraw the map of Valea because the old one had become a polite fiction. Roads on paper ended in open fields. A bridge marked in confident black had gone into the river during a flood eight years earlier, and the village had never replaced it, because the people who needed it had already left.

Aurel worked slowly, and the slowness bothered him. A map is a claim about permanence, he thought, and Valea was a place in the middle of subtraction. Each week another shutter closed for good. If he drew the school, would the school still be there when the ink dried in an office two hundred kilometers away?

In the end he drew everything that stood, and then he added a small date in the corner, smaller than the scale and smaller than his own name. It was the most honest mark on the sheet. It told the reader that the map was not a description of Valea, but a description of one particular Tuesday.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Valea urgently needs a new bridge over the river
A map claims permanence, so Aurel dates his to keep it honest
Government offices are too far from the villages they govern
Aurel works too slowly for the ministry that hired him
questions.explanation: The whole passage builds the tension between a map's claim to permanence and a shrinking village, and it resolves with the date.

questions.stem: Why was the bridge never replaced?
choices: The river had become too wide to cross
The ministry forgot that the bridge existed
A new road had made the bridge useless
The people who needed it had already left
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives the reason directly: the people who needed it had already left.

questions.stem: Why is the small date called the most honest mark on the sheet?
choices: It shows which official drew the map
It proves the ministry approved the work
It admits the map is only true for one moment
It helps the reader measure real distances
questions.explanation: Because Valea keeps shrinking, everything else on the map may already be false. Only the date makes no promise about the future.

questions.stem: In this passage, subtraction describes a place that is
choices: being measured and counted carefully
steadily losing people and buildings
divided into several smaller districts
growing quickly and without a plan
questions.explanation: It sits beside closing shutters, a lost bridge, and departed residents, so it means continuous loss.

lesson.strategy: This passage runs on one tension: a map promises that things stay, but Valea is disappearing. Track that conflict through three moves - the broken old map, Aurel's doubt, and his small solution at the end.

signals.phrase: because the old one had become a polite fiction
signals.means: the old map lies gently; accuracy has already failed once

signals.phrase: A map is a claim about permanence
signals.means: the abstract idea the whole passage turns on

signals.phrase: a place in the middle of subtraction
signals.means: the village is actively shrinking, not stable
his answer to the problem is coming now

vocab.inContext: the quality of staying the same over time
steady removal; the village losing people and buildings
the printed ratio showing how map distance matches real distance

skillTips.main-idea: In an idea-driven story, find the abstract sentence. Here it is the claim about permanence.
skillTips.inference: Ask what the date does that nothing else on the map can do. That gap is the answer.
skillTips.vocabulary: Math words used about places are figurative. Read the surrounding losses to fix the meaning.
skillTips.detail: Causes are stated plainly even in dense text. The bridge sentence contains its own because.

passages.title: Two Rules Of The Workshop
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Herr Bruns had two rules. A clock that runs fast is worse than a clock that has stopped, and the second rule was that the first rule applied to people as well.

His apprentice, Liesl, disliked the second rule until the winter she rushed a repair for an impatient customer. The clock kept good time for three days and then failed in a way that cost four times the original work. A stopped clock announces its failure, Bruns told her afterward; a fast clock hides its failure inside a plausible answer, and the owner arranges a whole day around that answer before discovering the error.

Liesl thought about this far longer than she expected to. The lesson was not really about clocks. It was about the difference between being wrong and being wrong convincingly, and she came to believe that the second was the more expensive condition, in workshops and everywhere else.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: The correct method for repairing a clock that runs fast
Liesl's decision to leave the workshop after a bad repair
Hidden, believable errors cost more than obvious ones
Customers should never rush the people who serve them
questions.explanation: The clock is an example. The closing paragraph states the real subject: being wrong convincingly is the more expensive condition.

questions.stem: What happened after Liesl rushed the repair?
choices: The clock kept good time for three days, then failed expensively
The customer refused to pay anything at all
Bruns repaired the same clock again that afternoon
The clock stopped before it left the workshop
questions.explanation: The text says it kept good time for three days and then failed in a way that cost four times the original work.

questions.stem: According to Bruns, why is a fast clock worse than a stopped one?
choices: A fast clock is much harder to build
A stopped clock is cheaper to repair
A fast clock makes far more noise
People arrange a whole day around a wrong time without knowing it
questions.explanation: A stopped clock shows its failure at once. A fast clock gives a believable time, so the damage spreads before anyone notices.

questions.stem: In this passage, plausible means
choices: extremely loud
easy to believe
completely correct
very old
questions.explanation: The fast clock hides its failure inside an answer that looks reasonable, so plausible means believable, not true.

lesson.strategy: The passage moves from rule to example to principle. Read the two rules first, then watch the broken clock prove them, then let the last paragraph lift the lesson off clocks and onto people.

signals.means: the frame; expect both rules to be tested

signals.phrase: until the winter she rushed a repair
signals.means: the turning point where the rule stops being abstract
the explanation of the rule comes here

signals.phrase: The lesson was not really about clocks
signals.means: the writer tells you to generalize

vocab.inContext: a learner who works under a skilled craftsman
believable on the surface, though false
a state to be in, here the state of being wrong

skillTips.main-idea: When a story says the lesson is not about its objects, follow that instruction to the general claim.
skillTips.inference: Compare the two failures side by side: one announces itself, one hides. The cost follows from that.
skillTips.vocabulary: Plausible and true are different. Watch for words that describe how something seems.
skillTips.detail: Keep the numbers straight: three days of good time, four times the cost.

passages.title: The Letter Writer
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For thirty years Senora Bermudez wrote letters for people who could not, or would not, write their own. Her table stood at the north end of the market, between the notary and a woman selling brooms, and the price was the same for a love letter as for a complaint to the water company, which she considered a matter of principle rather than of pricing.

Her clients arrived with a grievance and left with a sentence. That was the whole craft. A man would talk for twenty minutes about the fence his brother had moved, and she would write four lines that made no accusation at all, because she had learned that an accusation invites a defense, whereas a description invites a reply.

The irony was not lost on her. She was praised throughout the market as an honest woman, and yet her entire trade consisted of making people sound better than they had sounded to her. She never resolved this. She only noticed, each evening, that the letters she was proudest of were the ones from which she had removed the most.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A writer whose craft is removal, and the quiet contradiction it leaves her with
A market where most customers could not read or write
The difficulty of writing complaints to a water company
A woman who charged far too little for skilled work
questions.explanation: The passage defines her craft as cutting a long grievance down to a few lines, then examines the honesty problem that this creates for her.

questions.stem: What did Senora Bermudez charge for a love letter?
choices: More than she charged for a complaint
Less than the notary beside her charged
The same as for a complaint to the water company
Nothing, when the client was poor
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the price was the same for a love letter as for a complaint to the water company.

questions.stem: Why did she avoid writing accusations?
choices: Accusations were forbidden in the market
An accusation makes the reader defend himself instead of answering
She did not believe what her clients told her
Accusations took more words and therefore more time
questions.explanation: The text contrasts them directly: an accusation invites a defense, while a description invites a reply. She wanted a reply.

questions.stem: In this passage, a grievance is
choices: a small payment for a service
a wish to travel somewhere far away
a formal legal document
a complaint about being wronged
questions.explanation: Clients arrive with one and describe things like a brother moving a fence, so a grievance is a sense of having been wronged.

lesson.strategy: Three paragraphs, three layers: what she does, how she does it, and what it costs her conscience. The last paragraph reverses the surface picture, so do not stop reading at the praise.

signals.phrase: a matter of principle rather than of pricing
signals.means: her flat price is a moral choice, not a business one
the writer defines her skill in one blunt line: reduction

signals.phrase: because she had learned that an accusation invites a defense
signals.means: gives the practical reason behind her restraint

signals.phrase: The irony was not lost on her
signals.means: signals the contradiction; expect the praise to be undercut

vocab.inContext: an official who witnesses and certifies documents
a complaint or sense of having been treated unfairly
a statement that someone did something wrong

skillTips.main-idea: In an ironic passage, the main idea usually spans both the praise and the doubt that follows it.
skillTips.inference: Trace her reasoning chain: accusation causes defense, description causes reply, so choose description.
skillTips.vocabulary: Formal nouns are defined by their examples. The fence story tells you what a grievance is.
skillTips.detail: Details hide inside long sentences. Slow down at the clause about price.

passages.title: Why We Use Money
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before money, people traded goods for goods. This is called barter. A farmer with eggs could trade them for shoes. But barter has a problem. The farmer must want shoes, and the shoemaker must want eggs at the same time. If the shoemaker wants bread instead, no trade happens.

Money solves this problem. Money is a thing that everyone agrees to accept. The farmer sells eggs for coins. Later he uses the coins to buy shoes. He does not need to find one person who wants exactly what he has.

Money also stores value. Eggs go bad in a week, so a farmer cannot save them. Coins do not go bad. He can hold them for a year and still buy something with them.

Money is also a way to measure. When every price is written in the same unit, people can compare a shirt and a chair in a second. Barter has no simple unit, so every trade needs a new negotiation.

questions.stem: What is this passage mainly about?
choices: How farmers raise chickens and sell eggs
Why money works better than trading goods for goods
How shoemakers decide the price of shoes
Why most coins are made of metal
questions.explanation: Each paragraph names one job money does better than barter: it removes the matching problem, it stores value, and it gives one unit for prices.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why can a farmer not save eggs?
choices: Eggs go bad in a week.
Eggs are too heavy to carry.
Nobody wants to buy eggs.
Eggs cost more than coins.
questions.explanation: The text says directly: "Eggs go bad in a week, so a farmer cannot save them."

questions.stem: The passage suggests that barter only works when
choices: one person owns more goods than the other
both people live in the same town
each person wants what the other person has
all prices are written in coins
questions.explanation: The failed trade happens because the shoemaker wants bread, not eggs. So both sides must want each other's goods at the same time.

questions.stem: In this passage, "barter" means
choices: keeping money for a long time
writing all prices in one unit
borrowing goods from a neighbor
trading goods directly for other goods
questions.explanation: The word is defined by the sentence before it: "people traded goods for goods. This is called barter."

lesson.strategy: This passage is a problem-then-solution list. The first paragraph gives the problem with barter; each paragraph after that gives one job money does. Read for the first sentence of each paragraph, because each one announces the job.

signals.means: The writer is defining a term. The meaning is in the sentence just before it.
A turn. What follows is the weakness of the old way.
The solution starts here. Everything after is a benefit of money.

signals.phrase: Money is also a way to measure
signals.means: The third job in the same list. The pattern is repeated on purpose.

vocab.inContext: trading goods for other goods, with no money in between
one shared way of counting, so prices can be compared
a talk between two people to agree on the terms of a trade

skillTips.main-idea: When paragraphs repeat one word ("Money..."), that word is the topic. The main idea is what the passage claims about it.
skillTips.inference: Use the small story in the text. Ask why the eggs-for-shoes trade failed, then turn that reason into a general rule.
skillTips.vocabulary: "This is called X" always points backward. Read the sentence before, not after.
skillTips.detail: Detail answers are usually one clean sentence in the text. Find the sentence with the same key word as the question ("save", "eggs").

passages.title: When Prices Rise
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Inflation means that prices, taken together, rise over time. A single price can jump for its own reasons, as when a bad harvest raises the cost of coffee, but inflation is broader. It is the general level of prices moving up, so each unit of money buys a little less than it did before.

Economists track this with a price index. They choose a basket of goods that an ordinary household buys, such as food, rent, fuel, and clothing, and they measure what that same basket costs each month. If the basket cost 100 last year and 104 now, prices have risen about four percent.

Mild inflation is normal, and most central banks aim for a small, steady rate. The trouble begins when inflation is fast or hard to predict. Savers lose, because money kept in a drawer quietly loses purchasing power. Lenders lose too, since they are repaid in money worth less than the money they handed over. Borrowers, oddly, can gain.

That is why inflation is not only an economic event. It moves wealth from one group to another, and nobody ever decided that it should.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Coffee becomes expensive after a bad harvest.
Central banks should stop prices from ever changing.
Inflation is a general rise in prices that quietly shifts wealth between groups.
A price index is the best way to measure a country's total wealth.
questions.explanation: The passage defines inflation, shows how it is measured, then names the winners and losers. The last paragraph states the point: wealth moves without a decision.

questions.stem: In the example, the basket cost 100 last year and 104 now. The passage says prices rose about
choices: one percent
four percent
forty percent
one hundred percent
questions.explanation: The text states it directly: "If the basket cost 100 last year and 104 now, prices have risen about four percent."

questions.stem: Based on the passage, who is most likely to gain from fast inflation?
choices: someone keeping cash in a drawer
a bank that lent money at a fixed rate
a person who lent savings to a friend
a person who borrowed money and repays it later
questions.explanation: The passage says savers and lenders lose, and that "Borrowers, oddly, can gain." The first three choices are all savers or lenders.

questions.stem: As used in this passage, a "basket" is
choices: a fixed set of goods used to compare costs over time
a container people carry food home in
the total money a household earns in a month
a shop that sells many different products
questions.explanation: The text explains it: economists "choose a basket of goods that an ordinary household buys" and measure what that same basket costs each month.

lesson.strategy: This is a definition, then a method, then consequences. Paragraph one says what inflation is, paragraph two says how it is measured, paragraph three says who wins and loses. Track the shift from 'what it is' to 'who it hits'.

signals.means: A contrast. One price rising is not inflation; the writer is narrowing the definition.

signals.phrase: Economists track this with a price index
signals.means: The passage is moving from meaning to measurement. A method follows.
A turn from normal to harmful. The list of losers starts here.

signals.phrase: That is why inflation is not only an economic event
signals.means: The conclusion. The writer is stating the larger meaning of everything above.

vocab.inContext: a number that tracks how a group of prices changes over time
a fixed list of everyday goods used for a fair comparison
buying; "purchasing power" is how much your money can buy

skillTips.main-idea: In a passage that ends with "That is why...", the main idea is usually in that final sentence, not the first.
skillTips.inference: Sort the named groups into winners and losers first. Then check which group each answer choice belongs to.
skillTips.vocabulary: When a common word (basket) is used in a technical way, ignore the everyday meaning and use the sentence around it.
skillTips.detail: Number questions are traps for skimmers. Go back and read the exact sentence with the numbers in it.

passages.title: Sharing The Risk
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine a simple model with one thousand similar houses. An insurer estimates that about one covered house fire will occur during the year, although no one knows which house it will be. This is an illustration, not a universal fire rate. Real risk changes with place, building, weather, coverage, and time.

Insurance exists because many owners would rather face a smaller, predictable cost than a rare, ruinous loss. Each household pays a premium into a common pool. When a covered loss occurs, the pool pays according to the policy. One household’s event is hard to predict; patterns across many similar risks can be estimated more reliably.

Two problems can follow. If coverage removes too much consequence, an owner may take less care because the pool will pay. Economists call this moral hazard. If people with the highest risks are much more likely to buy coverage, claims may exceed what the original price assumed.

Insurers respond with deductibles, inspections, coverage rules, and prices based on relevant risk. These tools are imperfect and can raise questions about access and fairness. The aim is to spread severe losses while keeping the pool able to pay and preserving reasons to reduce preventable harm.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: One house in every thousand burns everywhere each year
Insurance removes every reason to prevent damage
Insurance pools uncertain individual losses and uses rules to keep that sharing workable
A premium guarantees that every possible loss is covered
questions.explanation: The passage explains pooling, prediction, problems, and the tools used to manage them.

questions.stem: What does each household pay into the common pool?
choices: A fire rate
A weather report
A building permit
A premium
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that each household pays a premium.

questions.stem: Why is the one-in-a-thousand figure labeled an illustration?
choices: Actual fire risk varies with place, building, weather, coverage, and time
Insurers never use estimates for groups of houses
Every house has exactly the same chance of damage
The model predicts which named house will burn
questions.explanation: The opening explicitly lists conditions that make a real rate vary.

questions.stem: In this passage, “moral hazard” refers to
choices: charging the same price for every possible risk
taking less care because another party will bear much of the loss
predicting exactly which household will file a claim
refusing to pay a premium into a shared pool
questions.explanation: The passage names moral hazard after describing reduced care when the pool will pay.

lesson.strategy: Separate the hypothetical model from a measured rate. Then follow the economic structure: pool, group estimate, two problems, and responses. The final paragraph adds the tradeoff between solvency, incentives, access, and fairness.

signals.means: Prevents a teaching number from becoming a universal factual rate.
Names the shared fund at the center of insurance.
Signals the move from mechanism to side effects.
Adds limits and fairness concerns to the proposed responses.

vocab.inContext: the payment made for insurance coverage
money collected from many policyholders to pay covered losses
amounts policyholders pay before insurance pays a covered claim

skillTips.main-idea: Include both risk sharing and the rules needed to keep the pool workable.
skillTips.inference: A hypothetical rate illustrates pooling; the listed real-world variables prevent universal use.
skillTips.vocabulary: Technical terms are defined immediately through an example or action.
skillTips.detail: A premium enters the pool; a deductible is paid when a covered claim occurs.

passages.title: The Box That Moved Trade
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For most of history, loading a ship was slow human work. Dockworkers carried sacks, barrels, and crates one at a time and fitted them into the hold like puzzle pieces. A ship could spend more days sitting at the pier than crossing the ocean, and handling the cargo often cost more than the voyage itself.

In 1956, an American trucking businessman named Malcolm McLean tried something different. He loaded fifty-eight truck trailers, stripped down to steel boxes, onto a converted tanker called the Ideal-X and sent it from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas. Cranes lifted the boxes on and off. Nobody touched the goods inside.

The idea only worked once the boxes became uniform. After container sizes were standardized, the same box could pass from crane to truck to train to ship without being opened, and ports rebuilt themselves around it.

The result was a quiet collapse in the cost of moving goods. A factory no longer had to sit near its customers. Long supply chains across many countries became practical. A plain steel box changed world trade more than most trade agreements ever have.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: The life of an American trucking businessman
Why dockworkers lost their jobs at the pier
How ships were built in the middle of the last century
How a standard steel box made shipping cheap enough to reshape trade
questions.explanation: McLean is one step in the story. The passage begins with the old cost of loading and ends with the collapse in shipping cost and its effect on trade.

questions.stem: How many truck trailers did the Ideal-X carry?
choices: eighteen
fifty-eight
one hundred
five hundred
questions.explanation: The text says he "loaded fifty-eight truck trailers, stripped down to steel boxes, onto a converted tanker called the Ideal-X."

questions.stem: Why did the idea need boxes of one standard size?
choices: So equipment everywhere could handle the same box without special work
So the boxes would be light enough for workers to lift by hand
So governments could tax each box at the same rate
So the goods inside would not be damaged by seawater
questions.explanation: The passage says that after sizes were standardized, the same box could pass from crane to truck to train to ship without being opened.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the "hold" is
choices: the rope used to tie a ship to the pier
the crew's living area on a ship
the space inside a ship where cargo is stored
the office where shipping prices are agreed
questions.explanation: Workers "carried sacks, barrels, and crates" and "fitted them into the hold", so the hold is where cargo goes.

lesson.strategy: This is a before-and-after story with a cause in the middle. Paragraph one is the old world, paragraph two is the event, paragraph three is the condition that made it work, paragraph four is the result. Read for the four stages, not the details.

signals.means: Opens the 'before' picture. Expect an old, slow way of doing things.
The turning point. A date this specific marks the event the passage is built around.

signals.phrase: The idea only worked once the boxes became uniform.
signals.means: A condition. The invention alone was not enough; agreement on one size was.

signals.phrase: The result was a quiet collapse in the cost of moving goods.
signals.means: The consequences start here. Everything after is an effect, not a cause.

vocab.inContext: the storage space below the deck of a ship
the structure a ship ties up to while it is loaded
made to one agreed size so all the parts fit together

skillTips.main-idea: In a history passage, the main idea is usually the effect at the end, not the person in the middle.
skillTips.inference: Ask what would break if the condition were removed. Here: different box sizes would force reloading by hand again.
skillTips.vocabulary: Ship and trade words can be guessed from the action around them. Cargo goes in, so it is a space.
skillTips.detail: Numbers and place names are easy to confuse. Reread the one sentence that holds them all.

passages.title: Two Tasks, One Worker
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine two neighbors, a doctor and a gardener. The doctor is better than the gardener at medicine, and, as it happens, she is also faster at weeding a flower bed. Since she is better at both tasks, common sense says she should simply do both. Economics says otherwise.

What matters is not who is better in absolute terms, but what each person gives up. An hour the doctor spends weeding is an hour not spent treating patients, and that hour of medicine is worth far more than the weeding. For the gardener, an hour of weeding costs him almost nothing else, because he has no medical practice to abandon. His disadvantage in every task is real, yet his sacrifice is smaller. That relative cheapness is called comparative advantage.

So both neighbors gain when the doctor treats patients, the gardener weeds, and the two of them trade. The same logic scales up to countries. A wealthy nation can be more productive than a poorer one at building aircraft and at sewing shirts, and still end up richer by building aircraft and buying shirts.

The idea is hard to accept precisely because it does not reward being best. It rewards giving up the least.

questions.stem: What is the central claim of the passage?
choices: Doctors should not waste time on gardening.
Rich countries should produce everything they need themselves.
Trade pays off based on what each side gives up, not on who is better.
A worker who is worse at every task cannot help anyone.
questions.explanation: The last two lines state it: the idea "does not reward being best. It rewards giving up the least."

questions.stem: According to the passage, the doctor is
choices: better than the gardener at both medicine and weeding
better at medicine but slower at weeding
worse at medicine but faster at weeding
equally skilled at both tasks
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says she is better at medicine "and, as it happens, she is also faster at weeding a flower bed."

questions.stem: What does the passage imply about a country that produces everything less efficiently than its trading partner?
choices: It should stop trading until its factories improve.
It can only gain by trading with equally poor countries.
It should export the single good it is worst at making.
It can still gain from trade, because it gives up less by specializing.
questions.explanation: The gardener is worse at everything and still gains, because his sacrifice is smaller. The passage says the same logic scales up to countries.

questions.stem: As used here, "sacrifice" means
choices: the money a worker is paid for an hour of labor
what a person gives up by choosing one task over another
the effort needed to learn a difficult new skill
a gift offered to a neighbor to start a trade
questions.explanation: The paragraph defines it by example: an hour weeding is an hour not treating patients. The sacrifice is the forgone task.

lesson.strategy: This passage sets a trap and then springs it. It first states the answer common sense gives, then overturns it with one reframing: stop asking who is better, start asking who gives up less. Read the second paragraph slowly, since the whole argument lives there.

signals.means: The thesis. The rest of the passage only illustrates this one sentence.

signals.phrase: That relative cheapness is called comparative advantage.
signals.means: The term is being defined by the example that came just before it.

signals.phrase: The same logic scales up to countries.
signals.means: A shift from a small story to the general rule. Expect the parallel case next.

signals.phrase: It rewards giving up the least.
signals.means: The compressed conclusion, written to be remembered.

vocab.inContext: measured on its own, without comparing costs; simply better at the task
the valuable thing you lose by making a choice
able to make more output from the same time and effort

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage says "common sense says X... Economics says otherwise", the main idea is never X.
skillTips.inference: Map the story onto the general case yourself. The gardener is the poorer country; the doctor is the richer one.
skillTips.vocabulary: Abstract words here are defined by the example beside them, not by a dictionary sentence.
skillTips.detail: Read comparisons twice. "Better at both" and "better at one" look similar and change every answer.

passages.title: The Seller Knows More
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In a used car market, the seller has driven the car for years and the buyer has looked at it for twenty minutes. That gap is called asymmetric information, and it can wreck a market without anyone telling a single lie.

Suppose half the cars offered are sound and half are hiding faults. A buyer who cannot tell them apart will not pay the full price of a sound car; he will offer something in the middle, to cover the risk of a bad one. But that middling price insults the owner of a genuinely good car, who takes it off the market instead. The share of faulty cars therefore rises, buyers lower their offers again, and more honest sellers walk away. Quality can spiral downward until only the worst cars remain.

The remedies all attack the information gap rather than the price. A warranty lets an honest seller promise something a dishonest one cannot afford. Independent inspections, service records, and a dealer's reputation do similar work: they make the hidden condition of the car visible and costly to fake.

Trust, seen this way, is not merely a private virtue. It is infrastructure, and markets that lack it shrink.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage's argument?
choices: When sellers know much more than buyers, good products can be driven out of a market.
Most used car sellers deliberately deceive their buyers.
Buyers should always pay the full price for a used car.
Warranties are the only honest way to sell any product.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the downward spiral caused by the information gap, and notes it needs no dishonesty at all.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the owner of a genuinely good car do when offered a middling price?
choices: lowers the price further to close the sale
offers the buyer a warranty instead
takes the car off the market
pays for an independent inspection
questions.explanation: The text says the middling price "insults the owner of a genuinely good car, who takes it off the market instead."

questions.stem: Why does the passage suggest a warranty helps solve the problem?
choices: It lowers the price of every car in the market.
Only a seller with a sound car can afford to make that promise.
It forces buyers to inspect the car themselves.
It transfers ownership of the car more quickly.
questions.explanation: The text says a warranty "lets an honest seller promise something a dishonest one cannot afford", which is a signal buyers can trust.

questions.stem: In this passage, "asymmetric information" means
choices: information that turns out to be false
information that is expensive to collect
information published by a government office
one side of a deal knowing far more than the other
questions.explanation: It names the gap in the first sentence: the seller has years of experience with the car, the buyer has twenty minutes.

lesson.strategy: This is a causal chain with a feedback loop, then a set of fixes. Follow paragraph two step by step: mixed quality leads to a middle price, which drives out good cars, which lowers quality again. Then check that each remedy in paragraph three attacks the information, not the price.

signals.phrase: That gap is called asymmetric information
signals.means: The term is defined by the sentence before it: unequal knowledge between the two sides.

signals.phrase: until only the worst cars remain.
signals.means: The loop closes here. This is the outcome the whole chain was building toward.

signals.phrase: attack the information gap rather than the price.
signals.means: A category statement. Every example that follows is one instance of the same fix.
A metaphor. Trust is being reclassified from a personal virtue to a public system.

vocab.inContext: unequal between two sides; one party holds more than the other
fixes for a problem
the shared foundation a system needs to work at all

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea often sits where the writer says what is NOT required. Here: no dishonesty is needed.
skillTips.inference: For 'why does this fix work' questions, look for the cost difference between the honest and dishonest party.
skillTips.vocabulary: A defined term usually sits one sentence after the situation it names. Read the pair together.
skillTips.detail: Track who does what. Buyer, honest seller, and dishonest seller each take a different action.

passages.title: The Price Of Borrowing
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An interest rate is a price: what borrowed money costs for a year. Most prices are settled by the people trading, but in a modern economy a central bank has strong influence over the short-term rate, and it uses that influence deliberately.

The chain runs roughly like this. When the central bank raises its rate, banks pay more for funds and charge more for loans. Home loans, business credit, and car finance all grow expensive. Households postpone purchases, and firms delay building the new factory. Spending slows across the economy, and with it the upward pressure on prices. Lowering the rate reverses the chain and encourages borrowing.

The difficulty is timing. The effects arrive slowly, often a year or more after the decision, so the bank must act on a forecast of an economy it cannot yet see. Move too late and inflation settles in. Move too hard and the cooling turns into a recession, with real unemployment attached to it.

This is why the language of central bankers is so careful. Expectations move markets by themselves, and a single unguarded sentence can do the work of a rate change before the rate has changed at all.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly explaining?
choices: How banks decide which customers deserve a loan
How a central bank steers spending by changing the price of borrowing, and why that is hard
Why home loans are more expensive than car finance
How households decide when to buy a new factory
questions.explanation: Paragraph two gives the mechanism, paragraph three gives the difficulty, paragraph four gives the consequence for how bankers speak.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do households do when the central bank raises its rate?
choices: They postpone purchases.
They borrow more quickly, before rates rise again.
They move their savings out of banks.
They ask their employers for higher wages.
questions.explanation: The chain states it: "Households postpone purchases, and firms delay building the new factory."

questions.stem: Why must a central bank act on a forecast rather than on what it can see?
choices: Because the data it receives is usually incorrect
Because governments forbid it from reading current figures
Because its decisions affect the economy only after a long delay
Because forecasts are more accurate than measurements
questions.explanation: The passage says effects arrive "often a year or more after the decision", so today's choice must be aimed at a future economy.

questions.stem: As used in this passage, a "recession" is
choices: a sudden rise in the price of borrowing
a promise made by a central banker
a rule that limits how much a bank may lend
a period when the economy shrinks and people lose jobs
questions.explanation: The word appears where cooling goes too far: "the cooling turns into a recession, with real unemployment attached to it."

lesson.strategy: The core of this passage is one cause-and-effect chain, stated in order. Read paragraph two as a sequence of links, then read paragraph three as the two ways the chain can go wrong. If you can retell the chain in your own words, the questions are easy.

signals.phrase: The chain runs roughly like this.
signals.means: A sequence is starting. Expect each sentence to cause the next one.

signals.phrase: Lowering the rate reverses the chain
signals.means: The same mechanism running backwards. You do not need a new explanation.
A shift from how it works to why it fails. The problems follow.

signals.phrase: This is why the language of central bankers is so careful.
signals.means: A conclusion drawn from everything above, not a new topic.

vocab.inContext: on purpose, as a chosen policy rather than by accident
to delay something to a later time
a prediction of what the economy will do next

skillTips.main-idea: When one paragraph gives a mechanism and the next gives its limits, the main idea covers both, not just the mechanism.
skillTips.inference: The reason is usually a fact stated somewhere else in the passage. Here the delay explains the need for a forecast.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read the whole clause the word sits in. "with real unemployment attached to it" defines recession for you.
skillTips.detail: In a chain, each actor does one specific thing. Match the actor in the question to the right link.

passages.title: What A Price Knows
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Consider the tin inside a soldering iron. Suppose a mine floods and the world supply of tin falls. No committee announces this. Yet within days the price rises, and thousands of manufacturers who have never heard of that mine begin, quietly, to economize: substituting other metals where they can, redesigning a joint, salvaging scrap they used to throw away. Each of them acts on a single number. None of them needs the story behind it.

This is the argument that a price is not merely a cost but a message. The knowledge required to run an economy, who has a spare warehouse, which machine sits idle, what a customer will tolerate, exists nowhere in summary form. It is scattered across millions of heads, much of it tacit, some of it barely expressible by the person holding it. A planner cannot gather what is only revealed in the act of trading.

The claim is powerful, and it is also incomplete. Prices are mute about anything nobody is charged for: polluted air, an emptied fishery, a road worn thin by trucks. The signal is real, but it carries only what the market has been made to count.

The honest conclusion is neither worship nor dismissal. Prices are a remarkable instrument with a known blind spot.

questions.stem: Which best states the passage's position?
choices: Prices are set by committees that watch the world's mines.
Central planning works better than markets when knowledge is scattered.
Prices carry scattered knowledge efficiently, but stay silent about costs no one is charged for.
Manufacturers should ignore price changes they do not understand.
questions.explanation: The passage praises the price signal for two paragraphs, then names its limit, and refuses both worship and dismissal at the end.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do manufacturers do when the price of tin rises?
choices: They investigate which mine has flooded.
They substitute metals, redesign joints, and salvage scrap.
They ask a committee for permission to raise their own prices.
They stop producing until the price falls back.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph lists exactly these three responses, and adds that none of them needs the story behind the number.

questions.stem: The passage implies that a central planner's deepest problem is that
choices: the knowledge needed is scattered and often never put into words
planners are less intelligent than traders
there are too many warehouses to count accurately
computers are too slow to process economic data
questions.explanation: The text says the knowledge exists nowhere in summary form, is tacit, and is only revealed in the act of trading.

questions.stem: As used here, "tacit" describes knowledge that is
choices: written down in official records
shared freely with competitors
known to be false but repeated anyway
held by someone without being put into words
questions.explanation: It sits beside "barely expressible by the person holding it", so tacit knowledge is real but unspoken.

lesson.strategy: This passage argues in three moves: a vivid example, the general claim drawn from it, then a limit placed on that claim. Do not stop after the praise. The word 'incomplete' turns the argument, and the final paragraph balances the two halves.

signals.means: The point of the example: coordination happens with no central instruction.

signals.phrase: a price is not merely a cost but a message.
signals.means: The example ends, the general claim begins here.

signals.phrase: The claim is powerful, and it is also incomplete.
signals.means: The turn. Everything after this qualifies what came before.

signals.phrase: The honest conclusion is neither worship nor dismissal.
signals.means: The writer rejects both extremes, so any all-or-nothing answer is wrong.

vocab.inContext: to use less of something because it has become costly
understood but never spoken or written down
a tool used to do a job, here the job of coordinating an economy

skillTips.main-idea: In a balanced argument, the main idea contains both the strength and the limit. Single-sided answers are traps.
skillTips.inference: Gather the scattered clues, then say them in one sentence. Nowhere in summary form + tacit + only revealed in trading = the planner cannot collect it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Hard words here are glossed by the phrase next to them. "barely expressible" explains "tacit".
skillTips.detail: When the text lists three actions, check that the answer choice keeps all three and adds nothing.

passages.title: The Storm That Builds
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Economic growth is usually pictured as accumulation: more machines, more roads, more skill. The uncomfortable half of the picture is subtraction. A genuinely better way of doing something does not sit politely beside the old way; it dismantles it. The refrigerator ended the ice-cutting trade. The spreadsheet emptied rooms of clerks who once added columns by hand. Growth arrives as demolition and construction at the same address.

The arithmetic favors the change, and the arithmetic is also cold. Gains are spread thin, a few dollars a year to millions of consumers who never notice them. Losses are concentrated: a wage, a craft, sometimes a whole town, carried by people who notice nothing else. Those who lose can name exactly what they lost; those who gain usually cannot name what they gained. Political resistance to progress is therefore not irrational. It is a reasonable answer to the question of who pays.

Nor is the adjustment automatic. A displaced worker of fifty-five does not glide into the growing industry. Retraining is slow, and the new jobs often appear in a different city.

Which suggests the useful question is not whether to permit the storm, but who is asked to stand in it, and what is owed to them afterward.

questions.stem: What is the passage's central argument?
choices: Economic growth has slowed because workers resist new machines.
New technology should be delayed until every worker is retrained.
Growth is best measured by counting machines and roads.
Progress destroys as it builds, and its losses fall on a few while its gains spread thin.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one gives the destruction, paragraph two gives the uneven split of gains and losses, and the ending asks who bears the cost.

questions.stem: Which example does the passage give of a trade that a new invention ended?
choices: ice-cutting, ended by the refrigerator
shipbuilding, ended by the spreadsheet
farming, ended by the railway
printing, ended by the telephone
questions.explanation: The text states: "The refrigerator ended the ice-cutting trade." The spreadsheet is the second example, and it replaced clerks.

questions.stem: Why does the passage call resistance to progress reasonable rather than irrational?
choices: Because new technology usually fails to work as promised
Because the losers are few and know exactly what they are losing, while the winners barely notice their gains
Because governments always compensate displaced workers too generously
Because most consumers would prefer the older products
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts thin, unnoticed gains with concentrated, sharply felt losses, then calls resistance a reasonable answer to who pays.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "displaced" worker is one who
choices: has moved to a new city for a better salary
has lost a job because the work itself disappeared
has been promoted into a growing industry
has refused to learn a new skill
questions.explanation: The word follows the examples of trades that were dismantled, and precedes the difficulty of retraining and moving to new jobs.

lesson.strategy: The passage builds a moral argument out of an economic one. It first shows that growth destroys, then shows that the destruction is unevenly shared, then refuses the easy conclusion. Watch the last line: it changes the question rather than answering it.

signals.phrase: The uncomfortable half of the picture is subtraction.
signals.means: The thesis. The passage will argue that growth removes as much as it adds.

signals.phrase: demolition and construction at the same address.
signals.means: A metaphor summarizing the examples above it. Building and destroying are the same event.
One side of a deliberate contrast. Its pair, spread-thin gains, sits in the sentence before.

signals.phrase: not whether to permit the storm
signals.means: The conclusion reframes the debate instead of taking a side in it.

vocab.inContext: a steady piling up of more and more of something
packed into a small group instead of spread out
pushed out of a job because that kind of work no longer exists

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage says the usual picture is only half right, the main idea is the missing half.
skillTips.inference: Compare the two groups the writer sets against each other. The reason for the conclusion is almost always in that contrast.
skillTips.vocabulary: Guess from the surrounding story. Retraining and moving cities tell you what displaced must mean.
skillTips.detail: Examples come in pairs here. Keep each invention with its own trade.

passages.title: Counting What Counts
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Gross domestic product counts the market value of everything a country produces in a year. It is the number governments cite, the number headlines shorten to growth, and the number that decides, in practice, whether a decade is judged a success. It is also, by construction, a strange instrument.

GDP counts transactions, so it is blind to work nobody is paid for. A parent raising a child, a neighbor sitting with an elderly friend, a meal cooked at home: all invisible. Hire someone to do the same tasks and the figure rises, though the work performed has not changed. It is equally indifferent to what the spending is for. Repairing a city after a flood, treating illness caused by dirty air, replanting a burned forest, each registers as activity. Damage, once paid for, looks like progress.

Its defenders make a fair reply. GDP was designed to measure production, not virtue, and it does that narrow job with unusual consistency across countries and decades. The failure is not in the gauge but in the reverence.

Still, a number kept because it is easy to measure will, given enough time, quietly redefine what a society treats as worth having.

questions.stem: Which best expresses the passage's overall claim?
choices: GDP is calculated incorrectly in most countries.
GDP measures paid production well; the danger lies in treating it as a measure of a good life.
GDP should be replaced immediately with a measure of happiness.
Unpaid work is the largest part of any modern economy.
questions.explanation: The passage lists the blind spots, then grants that GDP does its narrow job well, and locates the failure "not in the gauge but in the reverence."

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens to GDP when you pay someone to cook a meal you used to cook yourself?
choices: It falls, because your own labor is no longer counted.
It stays the same, because the meal is identical.
It rises, although the work performed has not changed.
It cannot be measured, because meals are not traded.
questions.explanation: The text says: "Hire someone to do the same tasks and the figure rises, though the work performed has not changed."

questions.stem: What does the passage imply about spending to rebuild after a flood?
choices: It raises GDP even though it only restores what was already there.
It is left out of GDP because the loss came first.
It counts twice, once as damage and once as repair.
It shows that GDP measures human wellbeing accurately.
questions.explanation: Repair after a flood "registers as activity", and the passage concludes that damage, once paid for, looks like progress.

questions.stem: As used in the third paragraph, "reverence" means
choices: a careful method of calculation
a rule written into law
a comparison made between countries
treating something with far too much respect
questions.explanation: The failure is not in the gauge, the tool, but in how people regard it. Reverence is deep, uncritical respect.

lesson.strategy: This is a critique that gives ground before it lands. Paragraph two lists two blind spots, paragraph three concedes the defenders' point, and the last line delivers the real warning. Notice the target moves: the problem is not the number, it is our respect for the number.

signals.phrase: It is also, by construction, a strange instrument.
signals.means: The critique opens. "by construction" means the oddity is built in, not a mistake.

signals.phrase: Damage, once paid for, looks like progress.
signals.means: The second blind spot, stated as a paradox to make it stick.

signals.phrase: Its defenders make a fair reply.
signals.means: A concession. The writer will now argue the other side honestly.

signals.phrase: The failure is not in the gauge but in the reverence.
signals.means: The exact target of the critique. The tool is fine; our treatment of it is not.

vocab.inContext: not caring about a difference; treating unlike things the same
a measuring tool, here the GDP figure itself
deep respect, given here without enough questioning

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage concedes a point to its opponents, the main idea must survive that concession. Choose the balanced answer.
skillTips.inference: Apply the stated rule to the new case. GDP counts transactions, so any paid repair adds to it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast words help. "not in the gauge but in the reverence" tells you one is a tool and one is an attitude.
skillTips.detail: For before-and-after questions, find the sentence that names both states: unpaid, then paid.

passages.title: The Ship That Was Rebuilt
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An old story from Greece describes a wooden ship kept in a harbor as a monument. Every year, workers pulled out the planks that had rotted and put new ones in their place. After many years, not one original piece was left. The ship still had the same shape, the same name, and the same spot at the dock. But was it still the same ship?

Later thinkers made the puzzle harder. Suppose someone collected every discarded plank and built a second ship out of them. Now two ships float in the harbor. One has continuity of place and use. The other has the original material. Each has a fair claim to the name.

The point is not to find the winning answer. The point is that a plain word like sameness hides two different tests. Sometimes we mean the same stuff. Sometimes we mean the same pattern, kept going through steady repair. A person is like the ship. The body's material is replaced over the years, yet memories and habits continue. Philosophy calls this a problem of identity, and the story shows how an ordinary word can carry a hidden question.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: A famous ship in Greece fell apart because its planks rotted.
A plain word like sameness can stand for two different tests.
Wooden ships need repair more often than stone monuments do.
Philosophers have agreed which ship deserves the original name.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states the point directly: the word for sameness hides two tests, same material and same continuing pattern.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what was the second ship built from?
choices: New planks cut for the harbor.
Planks taken from another ship at the dock.
The old planks that had been removed and thrown away.
The stone base of the monument.
questions.explanation: The text says someone collected every discarded plank and built a second ship out of them.

questions.stem: The passage suggests a person is like the repaired ship because
choices: people are born in one place and stay there for life.
a person can be given a new name at any time.
no one can remember what they were like as a child.
the body's material is replaced while memories and habits continue.
questions.explanation: The passage compares the two tests of sameness to a person: material changes, but the pattern of memory and habit keeps going.

questions.stem: In this passage, discarded means
choices: thrown away as no longer wanted.
counted carefully.
painted a new color.
sold for a high price.
questions.explanation: The discarded planks are the rotted ones the workers had already pulled out and replaced, so they were thrown away.

lesson.strategy: This passage is a story followed by a lesson. Read the first two paragraphs as the setup of a puzzle, then slow down at the third paragraph, where the writer stops telling and starts explaining. The final paragraph names the idea the story was built for.

signals.phrase: But was it still the same ship?
signals.means: The question the whole passage exists to raise; everything after it is an answer attempt.

signals.phrase: Later thinkers made the puzzle harder.
signals.means: A second, tougher version of the same problem is coming.

signals.phrase: The point is not to find the winning answer.
signals.means: The writer is telling you not to hunt for a solution; the real lesson is elsewhere.

signals.phrase: Philosophy calls this a problem of identity
signals.means: A name is being given to the idea, which usually marks the main point.

vocab.inContext: an object kept on display to remember something
thrown away because it was no longer wanted
staying unbroken in the same place and use over time

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer says the point is not X, the sentence right after it usually gives the real point.
skillTips.inference: Watch for a comparison at the end of a passage. The story about the ship is there to say something about people.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the action nearby. The planks were rotted and pulled out, so discarded must mean thrown away.
skillTips.detail: Two ships appear in paragraph two. Before answering, check which ship each fact belongs to.

passages.title: The Man Who Asked Questions
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Socrates walked through Athens and asked people simple questions. What is courage? What is justice? The people he asked were often confident. They were generals, poets, and craftsmen who used these words every day. But after a few careful questions, their answers fell apart. They had a skill, not a definition.

In Plato's account, a friend of Socrates went to the oracle at Delphi and was told that no one was wiser than Socrates. Socrates found this strange, because he did not believe he knew much. So he tested the claim by questioning the people who seemed wise. He came to a modest conclusion. He was wiser in one narrow way only: he did not pretend to know what he did not know.

This is why his method is still taught. It treats a question as a tool, not as a sign of weakness. A confident answer can be tested; an untested answer only feels solid. Socrates wrote nothing down.
