What survives is a habit of mind, carried on by his students, that asks a speaker to say clearly what a common word actually means.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Books that Socrates wrote about courage and justice.
Advice the oracle at Delphi gave to generals and poets.
Why a method of questioning matters more than a store of answers.
How Athens punished people who used words without defining them.
questions.explanation: The whole passage builds to the third paragraph: what survives is a habit of questioning, not a set of answers.

questions.stem: In Plato's account, what was the oracle at Delphi told to say?
choices: That Socrates should stop asking questions.
That no one was wiser than Socrates.
That the craftsmen of Athens were the wisest people.
That Socrates knew nothing at all.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two says the friend was told that no one was wiser than Socrates.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about the generals, poets, and craftsmen?
choices: They could use the words well without being able to define them.
They refused to speak with Socrates.
They had studied philosophy for many years.
They agreed with Socrates from the start.
questions.explanation: The text says they used these words every day but their answers fell apart, and that they had a skill, not a definition.

questions.stem: In this passage, modest describes a conclusion that is
choices: expensive to reach.
cheerful in tone.
kept secret from students.
small and not boastful.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is that he was wiser in one narrow way only, which is a small claim rather than a proud one.

lesson.strategy: This is a portrait built from three moves: what Socrates did, a story that explains why, and why it still matters. The last paragraph carries the argument, so read the first two for evidence and the third for the claim.

signals.phrase: But after a few careful questions, their answers fell apart.
signals.means: But marks the turn: confidence meets testing and loses.

signals.phrase: He came to a modest conclusion.
signals.means: A summary of his finding is coming in the next sentence.

signals.phrase: This is why his method is still taught.
signals.means: The writer moves from story to argument; the main claim follows.

signals.phrase: What survives is a habit of mind
signals.means: The lasting result is named here, in contrast to written books.

vocab.inContext: a holy place where an answer from a god was given
small and careful, not proud or overstated
never checked by questions, so only appearing solid

skillTips.main-idea: A passage about a person is usually about an idea. Ask what the writer says survives him.
skillTips.inference: Two short sentences placed side by side often carry the inference: a skill, not a definition.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read the sentence after modest. The narrow claim that follows tells you the word means small.
skillTips.detail: Names and places (Plato, Delphi) are anchors. Return to the exact sentence rather than trusting memory.

passages.title: What Is Up To You
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Epictetus was born into slavery in the Roman Empire and later won his freedom. He taught at a school in Greece, and he wrote no books; his students wrote down his lessons. His central idea is easy to state and hard to live.

He divided the world into two piles. In the first pile are the things that are up to us: our judgments, our aims, our own effort. In the second pile is everything else: our body, our reputation, the weather, other people, the results of our work. Trouble begins, he taught, when we treat the second pile as if it were the first. We demand that a train run on time, that a stranger be fair, that an illness wait. Then we are surprised by grief.

The advice is not to stop caring. It is to move the weight of our caring onto the part we actually hold. An archer can choose the bow, the stance, and the release. A gust of wind is not hers. If she measures herself by the arrow alone, she hands her calm to the air.

questions.stem: What is the central teaching described in the passage?
choices: Put your effort into what you control and accept what you do not.
Stop caring about work, health, and other people.
Write your lessons down so that students remember them.
Freedom from slavery is the source of a calm mind.
questions.explanation: The two piles and the archer both make the same point: care about your own judgment and effort, not the outcome.

questions.stem: Which of these does the passage place in the second pile?
choices: Our judgments.
Our aims.
Our reputation.
Our own effort.
questions.explanation: Reputation is listed in the second pile, along with the body, the weather, other people, and results.

questions.stem: The example of the archer suggests that a person should
choices: avoid any activity that wind can disturb.
judge herself by her preparation and release, not by where the arrow lands.
practice until luck no longer matters.
treat skill as less important than luck.
questions.explanation: The bow, the stance, and the release are hers; the wind is not. So the fair measure is the part she controls.

questions.stem: In this passage, gust means
choices: a long season of storms.
a steady, gentle breeze.
a warm current near the ground.
a short, sudden rush of wind.
questions.explanation: The gust is the uncontrolled air that pushes the arrow, which points to a sudden burst of wind.

lesson.strategy: The passage is one idea shown three ways: a sorting rule, a list of daily examples, and a picture. When you meet the archer, map her back onto the two piles instead of reading her as a new topic.

signals.phrase: He divided the world into two piles.
signals.means: A sorting structure is being set up; expect two lists to follow.

signals.phrase: when we treat the second pile as if it were the first.
signals.means: The cause of the problem is named here.

signals.phrase: The advice is not to stop caring.
signals.means: The writer blocks a likely misreading before giving the real advice.

signals.phrase: A gust of wind is not hers.
signals.means: The image restates the second pile in one line.

vocab.inContext: what other people think and say about you
how the archer places her feet and body before shooting
a sudden short push of wind

skillTips.main-idea: When a text sorts things into groups, the main idea is usually the rule for sorting, not the items.
skillTips.inference: Match each part of the picture to the idea: bow and stance to the first pile, wind to the second.
skillTips.vocabulary: Nearby contrast helps. The archer controls the bow; the gust is what she cannot control.
skillTips.detail: For list questions, go back and read the list itself. The two piles look similar in memory.

passages.title: Shadows On The Wall
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the Republic, Plato asks his readers to imagine prisoners who have spent their whole lives chained in a cave, facing a blank wall. Behind them burns a fire, and between the fire and their backs other people carry carved objects along a low road. The prisoners see only the shadows these objects cast on the wall, and because they have never seen anything else, they take the shadows for the whole of reality. They even give prizes to whoever is quickest at predicting which shadow will come next.

Suppose one prisoner is released and dragged up into daylight. The ascent is painful, and his eyes, trained on dimness, are useless at first. Only slowly can he look at the objects themselves, and later at the sun that makes them visible.

The sharp part of the story is the return. When he goes back down to tell the others, his eyes no longer handle the darkness, so he stumbles and misjudges the shadows. To the prisoners, the journey has plainly made him worse at the one skill they respect. Plato's warning is that education can look like damage to those who lack it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Prisoners in ancient Greece were often kept in caves near fires.
Shadows are easier to study than the objects that make them.
Plato believed that strong daylight harms the eyes.
Learning changes what a person can see, and can look like loss to those who have not learned.
questions.explanation: The last sentence states it: education can look like damage to those who lack it, which the return scene has just shown.

questions.stem: In the story, what makes the shadows on the wall?
choices: Carved objects carried along a road in front of a fire.
The prisoners' own hands.
Sunlight coming through the mouth of the cave.
Paintings left by earlier prisoners.
questions.explanation: The text says other people carry carved objects between the fire and the prisoners' backs, and those objects cast the shadows.

questions.stem: Why do the prisoners believe the freed man has been harmed?
choices: He comes back with injuries from the climb.
He can no longer judge the shadows as well as they can.
He refuses to describe the sun to them.
He has forgotten their names.
questions.explanation: Prizes go to whoever predicts shadows best. Since he now stumbles and misjudges them, he looks worse by their only measure.

questions.stem: In this passage, ascent means
choices: an argument about what is true.
a long period of rest.
the act of climbing upward.
a spoken agreement.
questions.explanation: He is dragged up into daylight, so the ascent that is painful is the climb out of the cave.

lesson.strategy: This is an extended image with a moral at the end. Track one thing at a time: what the prisoners can see, what changes for the one who leaves, and what happens when he comes back. The last sentence tells you what the image was for.

signals.phrase: because they have never seen anything else
signals.means: Gives the cause of their mistake, not a criticism of their intelligence.
Signals that gaining knowledge is described as hard, not pleasant.

signals.phrase: The sharp part of the story is the return.
signals.means: The writer flags the key scene; the main point is close.

signals.phrase: education can look like damage to those who lack it.
signals.means: The moral of the image, stated plainly.

vocab.inContext: threw a shadow onto a surface
the climb up and out of the cave
weak light, almost darkness

skillTips.main-idea: In a story with a moral, read the last sentence first if you are lost. Then check that the scenes support it.
skillTips.inference: Use the prisoners' standard, not yours. They judge by skill at shadows, so his loss is judged by that.
skillTips.vocabulary: Verbs nearby fix the meaning: dragged up tells you ascent is a climb.
skillTips.detail: Physical set-ups are easy to mix up. Redraw the scene in your head: wall, prisoners, fire, road behind them.

passages.title: From Is To Ought
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Reading the moral writers of his time, David Hume noticed a quiet move that almost nobody defended. An author would begin with ordinary claims about how the world is: people live in groups, promises make trade possible, cruelty causes pain. Then, without warning, the sentences would change shape. Instead of saying what is the case, they would say what ought to be done. Hume's complaint was not that the conclusion was wrong. It was that a new kind of word had entered the argument without being introduced.

The gap matters because facts and values answer different questions. A description tells you how things stand; a prescription tells you what to do about it. From the fact that a food is natural, nothing at all follows about whether you should eat it, until someone adds a value: that natural things are good for us. That added step is where the real disagreement usually hides, and it is the step most arguments skip.

This is why careful thinkers ask for the missing premise. Naming it does not settle the dispute. It moves the argument to the place where the dispute actually lives.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly arguing?
choices: The moral writers of Hume's time reached false conclusions.
An argument that moves from facts to duties hides a value that should be named.
Facts always matter more than values in a discussion.
Natural food is better for people than other food.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the silent jump from is to ought and ends by asking for the missing premise to be named.

questions.stem: What was Hume's complaint?
choices: That authors used too many examples taken from trade.
That authors described the world inaccurately.
That a new kind of word entered the argument without being introduced.
That authors refused to state any conclusion.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says this directly, and adds that his complaint was not that the conclusion was wrong.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do arguments about what is natural often go wrong?
choices: People disagree about which foods count as natural.
Nature itself changes over time.
The word natural has no meaning at all.
The value step, that natural things are good for us, is added without defense.
questions.explanation: The example says nothing follows from natural until a value is added, and that this added step is where disagreement hides.

questions.stem: In this passage, a prescription is
choices: a statement about what should be done.
a careful report of the facts.
a medicine bought at a shop.
a summary of an author's life.
questions.explanation: It is set against description: a description says how things stand, a prescription says what to do.

lesson.strategy: This passage names a mistake, then explains why it matters, then says what to do about it. The contrast between is and ought runs through all three paragraphs, so hold that pair in mind and sort each sentence into one side or the other.

signals.phrase: Then, without warning, the sentences would change shape.
signals.means: Marks the exact moment of the jump the passage is about.

signals.phrase: Hume's complaint was not that the conclusion was wrong.
signals.means: Blocks a wrong reading; the objection is about the method, not the result.

signals.phrase: facts and values answer different questions.
signals.means: Because introduces the reason, which is the core of the argument.

signals.phrase: This is why careful thinkers ask for the missing premise.
signals.means: Moves from analysis to practical advice.

vocab.inContext: a statement of what someone should do
a starting claim an argument depends on
the real disagreement between two sides

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage repeats a contrast (is versus ought), the main idea is almost always about that contrast.
skillTips.inference: Apply the general rule to the example. The food case is a test of the rule, not a separate topic.
skillTips.vocabulary: Paired sentences define each other: description tells how things stand, so prescription tells what to do.
skillTips.detail: Watch for was not sentences. They tell you exactly what the writer is not claiming.

passages.title: Choosing Behind A Veil
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1971 the political philosopher John Rawls proposed a test for fair rules. Imagine that you must design the basic institutions of a society, its laws, its schools, its share-out of wealth, before you learn anything about your own place inside it. You do not know whether you will be rich or poor, healthy or ill, a member of the majority or of a small minority. Rawls called this chosen blindness the veil of ignorance.

The device works by removing bias at its source rather than by asking people to resist it. Under normal conditions, a rule that favors the strong is attractive to the strong. Behind the veil, that attraction disappears, because you might turn out to be anyone. Self-interest and fairness stop pulling in opposite directions.

Rawls argued that people reasoning this way would not gamble on landing at the top. They would secure a floor first: basic liberties for everyone, and unequal rewards allowed only when they also lift the position of the worst off. Whether or not you accept his conclusion, the test is portable. Before defending a rule, ask whether you would still defend it without knowing which side of it you would stand on.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Rawls proved that every society must pay everyone the same.
Only people who are poor can write fair rules.
Not knowing your own position is a way to test whether a rule is fair.
Bias disappears once people promise to be honest.
questions.explanation: The veil is presented as a test: it removes the knowledge that would make a rule attractive for selfish reasons.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do people behind the veil not know?
choices: How wealth is shared out in the society.
Whether they will be rich or poor, healthy or ill.
Which laws already exist.
How the schools are organized.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph lists exactly this: rich or poor, healthy or ill, majority or minority.

questions.stem: Why do self-interest and fairness stop pulling in opposite directions behind the veil?
choices: Because people become kinder when they cannot see one another.
Because the rules are decided by a vote.
Because the strong lose their advantages while the veil is in place.
Because anyone who harms a group might turn out to belong to it.
questions.explanation: The passage says the attraction of a rule favoring the strong disappears because you might turn out to be anyone.

questions.stem: In this passage, portable means
choices: easy to carry over and use in other cases.
hard to explain to others.
already written into law.
accepted by everyone.
questions.explanation: The writer says the test is portable and then shows how to use it on any rule, whatever you think of Rawls's conclusion.

lesson.strategy: The passage introduces a device, explains the mechanism behind it, then reports a result and hands you a usable rule. Notice that the last two sentences separate the tool from Rawls's own conclusion, so you can accept one without the other.

signals.phrase: Rawls called this chosen blindness the veil of ignorance.
signals.means: A definition; the term is being fixed for the rest of the passage.
Explains the mechanism, which is the heart of the passage.

signals.phrase: Behind the veil, that attraction disappears
signals.means: Shows the effect of the device on the previous sentence's example.
Separates the conclusion from the method, and signals the takeaway.

vocab.inContext: the large, lasting structures of a society, such as laws and schools
basic freedoms guaranteed to every person
able to be carried to other situations and still work

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage names a device, ask what the device is for. That purpose is usually the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Follow the because clauses. The reason for a claim is often stated one sentence later.
skillTips.vocabulary: An abstract use of a concrete word (portable) keeps the concrete sense: it can be carried elsewhere.
skillTips.detail: Lists inside a long sentence are common test targets. Reread the list before choosing.

passages.title: The Butterfly And The Sleeper
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A short story closes one of the chapters of the Zhuangzi, a Chinese text from roughly the fourth century BCE. The writer dreams that he is a butterfly, drifting and content, with no awareness at all of being a man. Then he wakes, unmistakably himself. The passage ends with a question rather than a lesson: was he a man who dreamed of a butterfly, or is he now a butterfly dreaming that it is a man?

Read quickly, this looks like simple doubt about what is real. Read slowly, it makes a different point. Inside the dream, nothing was missing. The butterfly did not feel like an imitation of something else; it was completely a butterfly. The difficulty is that certainty arrived in both states, so certainty cannot serve as the judge between them.

The chapter is about the limits of a fixed viewpoint. Every position feels like the center when you are standing in it. Zhuangzi does not conclude that nothing is real. He suggests that the boundary between things is drawn by the one who is looking, and that a mind able to move between positions sees more than a mind that has settled into one.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A method for remembering dreams after waking.
The limits of any single, fixed point of view.
Proof that the waking world is only a dream.
The life of butterflies in ancient China.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states it: the chapter is about the limits of a fixed viewpoint, not about proving the world unreal.

questions.stem: How does the passage in the Zhuangzi end?
choices: With a rule for telling dreams from waking life.
With a description of the butterfly's death.
With a question rather than a lesson.
With advice for the writer's students.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the passage ends with a question rather than a lesson, and then gives the question.

questions.stem: Why can certainty not decide between the two states?
choices: Because certainty is always a mistake.
Because the writer could not remember the dream clearly.
Because dreams are shorter than waking life.
Because both states felt completely real from the inside.
questions.explanation: Inside the dream nothing was missing, and waking felt unmistakable, so the feeling of certainty appears in both.

questions.stem: In this passage, imitation means
choices: a copy that stands in for the real thing.
a sudden feeling of fear.
a careful drawing of an animal.
a small kind of insect.
questions.explanation: The butterfly did not feel like a copy of anything; the sentence contrasts imitation with being completely a butterfly.

lesson.strategy: Read this as a story, then a correction, then a claim. The middle paragraph explicitly tells you that the fast reading is wrong, so treat the sentences after it as the real argument.

signals.phrase: The passage ends with a question rather than a lesson
signals.means: Warns you not to look for a stated moral in the story itself.

signals.phrase: this looks like simple doubt about what is real.
signals.means: Sets up a misreading that the next sentence will replace.

signals.phrase: Inside the dream, nothing was missing.
signals.means: The key evidence: the dream state was complete, so it cannot be ranked as lesser.

signals.phrase: feels like the center when you are standing in it.
signals.means: The general lesson, applied beyond dreams.

vocab.inContext: moving lightly with no direction or effort
a copy of a real thing rather than the thing itself
the line that separates one thing from another

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer offers a quick reading and a slow one, the main idea lives in the slow one.
skillTips.inference: Ask what evidence sits behind a claim. Certainty appears in both states, which is why it cannot judge.
skillTips.vocabulary: Negative sentences define by contrast: not an imitation, but completely a butterfly.
skillTips.detail: Questions about how a text ends are answered by the text about the text, not by the story's events.

passages.title: Where The Heap Ends
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Take ten thousand grains of sand piled on a table. That is a heap. Remove one grain and it is still a heap, since a single grain cannot be the difference between a heap and no heap. Apply that reasonable-looking rule again and again, and it carries you, one harmless step at a time, to the claim that one grain is a heap. The ancient Greeks named this the sorites, from their word for heap, and it has resisted easy solutions for well over two thousand years.

Each part of the argument looks safe on its own. The starting case is obvious, the final case is absurd, and every step between them is one that nobody wants to reject. Something must therefore be wrong with an assumption we never stated: that a vague word marks a sharp line somewhere, waiting to be discovered.

The paradox is not a trick about sand. It appears wherever consequences are attached to vague terms, such as bald, poor, dangerous, or adult. A law must draw a line that reality does not contain, and the line will be arbitrary. That is not a reason to draw no line. It is a reason to defend a line by what it does for us, rather than by pretending that nature marked the spot in advance.

questions.stem: What is the main claim of the passage?
choices: Heaps of sand cannot be measured accurately.
Vague words should be kept out of the law.
Vague words have no sharp boundary, so lines must be defended by their usefulness.
The ancient Greeks solved this problem two thousand years ago.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph draws the conclusion: the line is arbitrary, and it must be defended by what it does for us.

questions.stem: Where does the word sorites come from?
choices: The name of the philosopher who invented it.
The Greek word for heap.
A Latin word meaning line.
The name of a Greek city.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the Greeks named it the sorites, from their word for heap.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why is a law that fixes an exact age for adulthood arbitrary?
choices: Lawmakers do not study philosophy.
Everyone grows up at exactly the same rate.
Such laws are changed every few years.
Growing up happens in small degrees with no natural cut-off point.
questions.explanation: Adult is listed as a vague term, and the passage says a law must draw a line that reality does not contain.

questions.stem: In this passage, arbitrary means
choices: fixed at a point that nature does not decide for us.
chosen by a court after a trial.
written in old and difficult language.
impossible for anyone to enforce.
questions.explanation: The line is called arbitrary right after the claim that reality contains no such line, so nothing in nature fixes it.

lesson.strategy: This passage runs an argument to an absurd result, then diagnoses which hidden assumption caused it, then turns the diagnosis into practical advice. Follow the chain rather than judging any single step, because each step is designed to look acceptable alone.

signals.phrase: Apply that reasonable-looking rule again and again
signals.means: Signals repetition of a small step, which is how the paradox is built.

signals.phrase: Each part of the argument looks safe on its own.
signals.means: Tells you the fault is not in one step but in the whole set.

signals.phrase: The paradox is not a trick about sand.
signals.means: Moves the discussion from the example to real-world cases.

signals.phrase: A law must draw a line that reality does not contain
signals.means: The practical consequence, and the basis for the final advice.

vocab.inContext: single tiny pieces of sand
having no exact edge between applying and not applying
set at a point that nothing in nature fixes for us

skillTips.main-idea: In a paradox passage, the main idea is the diagnosis, not the puzzle. Look for the sentence naming the hidden assumption.
skillTips.inference: Carry the general rule to a new case. If adult is vague, any exact age must be a chosen line.
skillTips.vocabulary: Abstract words are often defined by the sentence beside them, not by a dictionary phrase.
skillTips.detail: Small factual notes (where a word comes from) hide inside long sentences. Slow down at names.

passages.title: The Machine That Feels Like Life
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1974 the philosopher Robert Nozick described a machine that could give you any experience you wanted. You would float in a tank with your brain wired to it, and you would feel yourself writing a novel, earning a friend's trust, climbing a mountain, each sensation exactly as vivid as the real thing and none of it detectable from the inside. You could program a lifetime in advance. Nozick then asked a question that sounds simple and is not: would you plug in?

Most people say no. That answer is awkward for any theory that treats pleasant experience as the only thing that finally matters, because the machine supplies more of it, more reliably, than any life outside could. If experience were the whole of the good, refusing would be an error rather than a preference.

Nozick reads the refusal this way: we want to do certain things, not merely to have the experience of doing them, and we want to be a certain kind of person, while a body floating in a tank is not any kind of person. The thought experiment does not prove this. What it does is bring into the open a commitment we rarely notice, that contact with reality is part of what we are after, and not only a means to feeling good.

questions.stem: What does the experience machine test?
choices: Whether people can tell a dream from waking life.
Whether pleasure can be measured by science.
Whether machines will one day replace human work.
Whether pleasant experience is the only thing people finally care about.
questions.explanation: The passage says the common refusal is awkward for any theory that treats pleasant experience as the only thing that matters.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is true of experiences inside the machine?
choices: They feel exactly as vivid as real ones and cannot be noticed from the inside.
They fade after a few hours of use.
They can only repeat memories the person already has.
They feel slightly flat compared with real life.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says each sensation is exactly as vivid as the real thing and none of it is detectable from the inside.

questions.stem: Why is the common refusal awkward for a theory that counts only pleasant experience?
choices: Because the machine would be expensive to build.
Because the machine supplies more pleasure than real life, so refusing would count as an error.
Because most people change their minds after trying it.
Because pleasure cannot be programmed in advance.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states this: if experience were the whole of the good, refusing would be an error rather than a preference.

questions.stem: In this passage, detectable means
choices: worth repeating.
able to be measured in money.
able to be noticed.
harmful over a long time.
questions.explanation: Nothing inside the machine can be told apart from real experience, so nothing about it can be noticed from the inside.

lesson.strategy: This is a thought experiment used as evidence. Read paragraph one for the setup, paragraph two for the pressure it puts on one theory, and paragraph three for what the writer thinks the refusal reveals. Note the careful limit at the end: the experiment exposes a belief, it does not prove one.

signals.phrase: asked a question that sounds simple and is not
signals.means: The hinge of the passage; everything after it interprets the answer.
The datum the argument works from, stated as a plain fact about responses.

signals.phrase: refusing would be an error rather than a preference.
signals.means: A conditional that shows the cost of the theory being tested.

signals.phrase: The thought experiment does not prove this.
signals.means: The writer limits the claim, so do not read the next sentence as proof.

vocab.inContext: strong and clear to the senses
able to be noticed or told apart
a value we already hold, even without saying it

skillTips.main-idea: A thought experiment is always aimed at some claim. Find the claim it makes trouble for.
skillTips.inference: If-then sentences carry the reasoning. Read them slowly and check what follows from what.
skillTips.vocabulary: Break the word apart: detect plus able gives able to be noticed, which the sentence confirms.
skillTips.detail: Descriptions packed with commas hide details. Reread the list of what the machine can supply.

passages.title: A Person Through Other Persons
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Several southern African languages carry a saying usually rendered in English as: a person is a person through other persons. The word often attached to it is ubuntu. Translated carelessly, it sounds like a warm reminder to be kind. Read as philosophy, it is a claim about what a person is, and it disagrees with a habit that much European thought treats as obvious.

That habit begins with the individual as a finished unit, reasoning and choosing, complete before any relationship starts, and then explains community as something such individuals build for their own advantage. The ubuntu claim reverses the order. Personhood is not the raw material of community; it is an achievement produced inside it. You become a self through a language you did not invent, obligations you did not choose, and recognition you cannot give yourself.

The practical difference shows up in how a wrong is handled. If persons are separate units, justice is largely a matter of assigning what each one is owed. If persons are made in relation, a wrong tears a shared fabric, and repair, restoring the relationship rather than only balancing the account, becomes part of what justice means. The two pictures can reach the same verdict in a given case, yet they measure success by different things.

questions.stem: What is the main claim of the passage?
choices: Ubuntu treats personhood as something produced inside relationships, not before them.
Southern African languages are hard to translate into English.
Community exists because individuals build it for their own advantage.
Justice always means giving each person exactly what is owed.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states the reversal: personhood is not the raw material of community but an achievement produced inside it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the European habit of thought assume?
choices: That language shapes the self before anything else.
That obligations come before individual choices.
That the individual is a finished unit before any relationship starts.
That community cannot be explained at all.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two describes the habit exactly that way, and then says ubuntu reverses the order.

questions.stem: Why would the ubuntu view give repair a larger role in justice?
choices: Because paying money is difficult in poorer communities.
Because a wrong is treated as damage to a shared fabric between people.
Because courts move more slowly than private conversations.
Because the person who did wrong is not held responsible.
questions.explanation: If persons are made in relation, the harm is to the relation, so restoring it is part of putting things right.

questions.stem: In this passage, rendered means
choices: repeated many times over.
argued against in public.
kept hidden from outsiders.
expressed in another language.
questions.explanation: The saying is rendered in English, which means it is put into English words.

lesson.strategy: This passage compares two pictures of what a person is, then shows what changes downstream. Keep a two-column map in your head: individual-first on one side, relation-first on the other, and place each sentence on the correct side.

signals.phrase: it sounds like a warm reminder to be kind.
signals.means: Names the shallow reading so it can be replaced by the real claim.

signals.phrase: The ubuntu claim reverses the order.
signals.means: The pivot of the comparison; what came first now comes second.

signals.phrase: The practical difference shows up in how a wrong is handled.
signals.means: Moves from theory to consequence; an example follows.

signals.phrase: The two pictures can reach the same verdict
signals.means: A concession: the views can agree in outcome while differing in reasoning.

vocab.inContext: put into the words of another language
duties you owe to others whether or not you chose them
being seen and accepted as a person by others

skillTips.main-idea: When two views are compared, the main idea is the second view's correction of the first.
skillTips.inference: Trace the consequence. If harm is to a relationship, the fix must involve the relationship.
skillTips.vocabulary: Formal words often have plain equivalents nearby: rendered in English simply means expressed in English.
skillTips.detail: Long sentences with several clauses hold the tested detail. Split them at the commas and reread.

passages.title: The Stone That Talked Back
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1799, French soldiers were digging near a town in Egypt. One of them found a broken slab of dark stone. The stone was covered with writing. It had three kinds of script cut into its surface: Egyptian hieroglyphs at the top, a second Egyptian script in the middle, and Greek at the bottom.

Scholars could read the Greek. The Greek text said that all three sections carried the same message, a decree written by priests for a king. So the stone was a kind of key. If the message was the same, the unknown signs could be matched to known words.

The work was still slow. For more than twenty years, scholars argued about what the signs meant. Many people believed that hieroglyphs were only pictures of ideas. In 1822, a French scholar named Jean-Francois Champollion showed that many of the signs stood for sounds, like the letters in an alphabet. With that idea, the old writing began to make sense.

The stone itself is not beautiful. It is grey, cracked, and incomplete. But it opened three thousand years of Egyptian records to modern readers.

questions.stem: What does the passage mainly explain?
choices: Why French soldiers were sent to Egypt in 1799
How one stone allowed scholars to read ancient Egyptian writing again
How museums decide which objects to display
Why Greek became the main language of Egypt
questions.explanation: The passage follows the stone from its discovery to the moment its three scripts made hieroglyphs readable again.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which text on the stone could scholars already read?
choices: The hieroglyphs at the top
The second Egyptian script in the middle
The Greek at the bottom
A Latin note added later
questions.explanation: The text says plainly, 'Scholars could read the Greek,' which sat at the bottom of the stone.

questions.stem: Why was it important that the three sections carried the same message?
choices: It proved that the stone was very old
It meant a text people could read could be compared with signs they could not
It showed that the priests spoke three languages
It made the stone worth more money
questions.explanation: If the meaning is the same in all three, the known Greek gives a starting point for guessing the unknown signs. That is why the writer calls the stone a key.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'decree' means
choices: an official order or announcement
a religious song
a map of a temple
a private letter
questions.explanation: The decree was 'written by priests for a king' and carved in public on stone, so it is an official announcement, not a private or musical text.

lesson.strategy: This passage tells a story in time order: a discovery, a problem, a solution, and what it meant. Follow the dates, because each one moves the story to the next step. The last paragraph shifts from the object to its value, so read it as the writer's judgement, not as new facts.

signals.means: The story is starting at a fixed moment. Expect dates to organise the passage.

signals.phrase: So the stone was a kind of key
signals.means: A conclusion drawn from the sentence before it. This is the writer explaining why the stone matters.
A turn. The solution was found, but the problem was not over yet.
'But' contrasts the plain look of the stone with its huge importance.

vocab.inContext: a thick, flat piece of stone
an official order announced by rulers or priests
people who study a subject deeply, here ancient languages

skillTips.main-idea: In a story-shaped passage, the main idea is usually the change from beginning to end. Here: unreadable writing becomes readable.
skillTips.inference: When a text calls something 'a kind of key', ask what door it opens. The answer is almost always the inference the question wants.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the words around the target word. 'Written by priests for a king' tells you a decree is official and public.
skillTips.detail: Dates and lists of parts (top, middle, bottom) are common detail-question targets. Slow down and match them exactly.

passages.title: One Penny, Any Distance
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before 1840, sending a letter in Britain was awkward work. The person who received the letter usually paid for it, not the sender. The price depended on the distance and on the number of sheets of paper. A long letter from far away could cost a working man a full day of pay. Many people simply refused their letters at the door.

A reformer named Rowland Hill argued that this system wasted money. Clerks spent hours counting sheets and measuring routes. He proposed one flat price for any light letter, paid in advance by the sender.

In 1840 the Post Office issued a small rectangle of paper with glue on the back and the head of Queen Victoria printed in black ink. It cost one penny. People stuck it on the letter, and the letter travelled anywhere in the country.

The result surprised almost everyone. Letters became cheap enough for ordinary families, and the number sent in Britain rose sharply within a few years. Other countries copied the idea. The little black stamp had turned writing home into a normal habit instead of a luxury.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
choices: why Queen Victoria appeared on British coins
how paper and glue were made in 1840
how a prepaid stamp made letters cheap and common
why British people stopped writing letters
questions.explanation: Every paragraph builds one line: the old system was costly, Hill proposed a flat prepaid price, the stamp appeared, and letter writing spread.

questions.stem: Before 1840, who usually paid for a letter?
choices: the sender
the person who received it
the Post Office itself
the clerk who carried it
questions.explanation: The second sentence states it directly: the receiver paid, not the sender.

questions.stem: Why did many people refuse their letters at the door?
choices: They could not read
They were angry with the sender
The cost of accepting the letter was too high for them
They preferred to collect letters at the post office
questions.explanation: The refusal is placed right after the sentence about a letter costing a day of pay, so money is the reason.

questions.stem: In the last sentence, 'luxury' means
choices: a habit that is hard to stop
something expensive that ordinary people cannot easily afford
a government rule
a long journey
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts a 'normal habit' with a luxury, and the passage has already shown that letters used to be too expensive for ordinary families.

lesson.strategy: This is a problem-and-solution passage. The first paragraph is the problem, the second and third are the fix, and the last is the result. When you meet a passage like this, hold two pictures in your head: life before the change and life after it.

signals.means: Marks the 'old world' section. Everything here describes the problem.

signals.phrase: A reformer named Rowland Hill argued
signals.means: A person enters with an argument. Expect his idea next.
This is the proposed solution, not yet a fact.
The results paragraph begins. What follows is the effect of the change.

vocab.inContext: someone who works to change a system and make it better
officially produced and released for public use
an expensive thing that most people cannot afford often

skillTips.main-idea: In problem-solution texts, the main idea is the solution plus its effect, not the problem alone.
skillTips.inference: Put two neighbouring sentences side by side. Cost, then refusal, means cost caused the refusal.
skillTips.vocabulary: Look for contrast words like 'instead of'. The opposite word ('normal habit') defines the target word.
skillTips.detail: Watch for who does what: sender, receiver, clerk, Post Office. Detail questions often swap these roles.

passages.title: The Machine In The Wreck
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1901, sponge divers sheltering from a storm anchored near the small Greek island of Antikythera. Under the water they found an ancient shipwreck loaded with bronze and marble statues. Among the cargo was a shapeless lump of corroded metal, about the size of a thick book. It sat in a museum for months before anyone noticed the gear teeth inside it.

The lump is now called the Antikythera mechanism, and it is roughly two thousand years old. More than thirty bronze gears survive, cut by hand and fitted together in layers. When the handle was turned, pointers moved across dials on the front and the back. The dials tracked the sun and the moon, showed the phases of the moon, and predicted eclipses years ahead.

Nothing else of that quality has been found from the ancient Mediterranean world. Modern imaging has read faint inscriptions hidden under the corrosion, a kind of instruction manual for the device. Yet the mechanism raises a hard question. If someone could build this, similar machines almost certainly existed. Either they were lost, melted down for their metal, or they are still lying somewhere underwater.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Sponge diving was dangerous work in 1901
Ancient statues are usually found in shipwrecks
A corroded lump from a shipwreck turned out to be a complex ancient machine that still raises questions
Modern imaging can read any ancient writing
questions.explanation: The passage moves from an ignored lump, to what the machine did, to the open question it leaves behind.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did the dials show?
choices: the sun and moon, the moon's phases, and coming eclipses
the depth of the sea near the island
the names of the ship's crew
the price of bronze in Greek markets
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists exactly these three functions.

questions.stem: What does the writer suggest about the mechanism?
choices: It was made by a civilisation no historian has heard of
It was probably not the only machine of its kind
It was built recently and dropped into the sea
It was useless to the people who owned it
questions.explanation: 'If someone could build this, similar machines almost certainly existed' says the skill was not a single accident, so other machines are likely.

questions.stem: 'corroded' describes metal that has been
choices: polished until it shines
broken apart by a hammer
damaged and eaten away over long exposure
painted a dark colour
questions.explanation: The metal is 'shapeless' and later has 'corrosion' hiding its writing, so the word means slowly eaten away, not cleaned or struck.

lesson.strategy: The passage has three moves: discovery, description, and an unanswered question. Notice that the writer waits until the end to raise the question, so the last paragraph carries the argument, not just extra facts. Read the final three options as one thought, not as three separate claims.

signals.phrase: It sat in a museum for months before anyone noticed
signals.means: Signals that the object's value was hidden at first. Expect a reversal.

signals.phrase: Nothing else of that quality has been found
signals.means: A comparison to everything else known. The writer is marking the object as unique so far.

signals.phrase: Yet the mechanism raises a hard question
signals.means: 'Yet' turns the passage from description to argument.
A conditional. The writer is reasoning from one fact to a likely conclusion.

vocab.inContext: slowly eaten away and damaged by seawater over centuries
words cut or scratched into a hard surface
moments when the sun or moon is darkened by a shadow

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage ends on a question, the main idea usually includes that question, not only the object described.
skillTips.inference: 'If X, then probably Y' sentences are inference gifts. The answer is Y, stated in other words.
skillTips.vocabulary: Related forms help. 'Corroded' and 'corrosion' appear in the same passage, and the second one tells you it is a substance that covers and hides.
skillTips.detail: Lists joined by commas ('tracked, showed, predicted') are prime detail targets. Check every item before choosing.

passages.title: Merchants Without A King
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Medieval merchants travelled with one constant problem: nobody protected them. A ship could be seized, a cargo taxed twice, a debt ignored in a foreign court. Beginning in the twelfth century, traders from the towns of northern Germany started to solve this together. They signed agreements, shared armed escorts at sea, and demanded the same privileges in every port they entered. The loose network they built became known as the Hanseatic League.

It was never a country. It had no king, no fixed borders, and no standing army. What it had was leverage. Cities such as Lubeck and Hamburg controlled the route between the herring and timber of the Baltic and the cloth and wine of the west. When a ruler broke an agreement, the League could simply stop trading with his ports until he changed his mind.

At its height the League linked well over a hundred towns and kept permanent trading houses in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod. Its decline came slowly. Atlantic routes opened, strong nation-states grew, and princes who had once needed the merchants began to tax them instead. By the seventeenth century the League met for the last time.

questions.stem: The passage mainly explains
choices: how a group of trading towns gained real power without becoming a state
how herring is caught in the Baltic Sea
why Lubeck became the capital of Germany
how medieval kings built their navies
questions.explanation: The middle paragraph states the core claim: no king, no borders, no army, but leverage. The rest shows how that power grew and faded.

questions.stem: Where did the League keep permanent trading houses?
choices: Venice, Rome, Paris and Cairo
London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod
Lisbon, Seville, Genoa and Athens
only in the towns of northern Germany
questions.explanation: The final paragraph names these four cities exactly.

questions.stem: Why could the League force a ruler to keep his agreements?
choices: It could send a large professional army against him
It could stop the trade that his ports depended on
It could choose a new ruler for his land
It controlled the courts where he was judged
questions.explanation: The passage says the League had no army, and that it could stop trading with a ruler's ports until he changed his mind. That is economic pressure, not force.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'leverage' means
choices: a heavy tool used for lifting
money kept safe in reserve
the power to make others act by controlling something they need
a written peace treaty
questions.explanation: The word is defined by the example that follows it: the League controlled a trade route, so rulers had to listen.

lesson.strategy: This passage defines something by saying what it is not, then what it is. Paragraph two is the heart: three negatives ('no king, no fixed borders, no standing army') followed by one positive ('leverage'). Read the third paragraph as a rise-and-fall summary.

signals.means: The origin story starts here. Expect the reason the League formed.
Definition by negation. The writer is clearing away a wrong assumption first.
The key claim of the whole passage. Everything after it is evidence.
The turn from growth to fall. Causes of the decline follow.

vocab.inContext: taken by force, without permission
special rights given to one group and not to others
power that comes from controlling something other people need

skillTips.main-idea: When a text says 'It was never X. What it had was Y', Y is the main idea. Find that sentence pair first.
skillTips.inference: Use what the text rules out. No army means the pressure had to be economic, so pick the trade answer.
skillTips.vocabulary: Abstract nouns are often explained by the sentence right after them. Read one sentence past the hard word before you guess.
skillTips.detail: Place names in a list are easy to confuse. Match the whole list, not just the first name.

passages.title: The Island Of Glass
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1291 the rulers of Venice ordered every glass furnace in the city moved to Murano, an island in the lagoon. The official reason was fire. Venice stood on wooden piles, its workshops were packed close together, and a furnace burning day and night was a danger to everything around it.

The move had a second effect, whether or not anyone planned it. Once the glassmakers all lived on one small island, their knowledge stayed there. Masters gained real status; they were allowed to wear fine clothes, and their daughters could marry into noble families. They were also forbidden to leave. A master who set up a furnace abroad could lose his family's protection at home, and agents of the Republic were sent to bring him back.

Behind that quiet border the craft advanced quickly. Murano workshops learned to burn away the green tint of ordinary glass and produced a clear, colourless glass they called cristallo, thin enough to bend light like rock crystal. Mirrors, lenses and drinking glasses from the island sold across Europe for centuries. The secrets did leak in the end, as secrets do, but by then Murano's name was itself the product.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
choices: Venice was destroyed by fire many times
Glass can only be made well on islands
Noble families in Venice controlled every trade
Moving the furnaces to one island protected the city and also concentrated a valuable craft
questions.explanation: The passage gives the fire reason, then the 'second effect' of keeping skill and secrecy in one place, and finally the results of that concentration.

questions.stem: What was the official reason for moving the furnaces to Murano?
choices: the risk of fire in a city built of wood
the smell of smoke in the streets
a shortage of sand inside Venice
an order from a foreign king
questions.explanation: 'The official reason was fire', explained by the wooden piles and crowded workshops.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the Republic restricted the masters' travel because
choices: travel in the Middle Ages was too dangerous for skilled men
it wanted to keep their methods from spreading to other countries
the masters had committed crimes in the city
the island needed more men to fight fires
questions.explanation: The paragraph links the island to knowledge staying in one place, then lists rewards for staying and punishments for leaving. The point is control of the technique.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'tint' means
choices: a faint colour in something
a thin crack in a surface
a strong smell
the weight of a material
questions.explanation: The workshops burned away the 'green tint' to make glass 'clear, colourless', so a tint is a light shade of colour.

lesson.strategy: The passage separates a stated reason from a deeper consequence. Paragraph one gives the public explanation; paragraph two gives what the rule actually produced. When a text says 'the official reason', read on and expect an unofficial one.

signals.means: 'Official' hints that this is not the whole story.

signals.phrase: The move had a second effect
signals.means: Here comes the consequence that matters most to the writer.

signals.phrase: They were also forbidden to leave
signals.means: 'Also' pairs the reward with the restriction: privilege and control together.
A dry aside. The writer treats leaking secrets as normal and expected.

vocab.inContext: a very hot enclosed fire used to melt materials such as sand into glass
a shallow area of sea water partly closed off from the open sea
a faint colour, here the green shade of ordinary glass

skillTips.main-idea: If a passage names two effects, the main idea usually joins them, not just one of them.
skillTips.inference: Reward plus punishment aimed at the same behaviour tells you what the rulers wanted. Ask what the rule was protecting.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast is a definition tool: 'green tint' against 'clear, colourless' tells you tint means colour.
skillTips.detail: Distinguish the stated reason from the real result. Detail questions ask what the text says, not what you conclude.

passages.title: The Potato and the Great Irish Famine
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Potatoes reached Europe from the Andes in the sixteenth century. In Ireland, the crop produced many calories on small plots and became especially important to poor tenant families. By the 1840s, poverty and an unequal landholding system left many people heavily dependent on potatoes while they had little money or land for alternatives.

In 1845, potato blight began ruining harvests, and it returned in later years. Yet blight alone does not explain the scale of the Great Irish Famine. Ireland still produced other foods, and food continued to leave Ireland through trade. Many hungry families could not afford that food or control the land that produced it. Relief policy also mattered. British government programs changed over time, but public works and other aid proved inadequate, while policies shaped by laissez-faire ideas limited responsibility. Evictions made the crisis worse for many tenants.

The catastrophe had several causes: a destructive plant disease, deep dependence on one crop, poverty, land and trade structures, and an insufficient state response. About one million people died, and many more emigrated. Remembering all of those causes does not make the blight unimportant. It explains why the same crop failure became a human disaster of such enormous size.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly arguing?
choices: The potato was the main cause, while land and policy played almost no role.
Ireland stopped producing every kind of food, so poverty, money, and land access no longer mattered.
Blight became catastrophic through crop dependence, poverty, land structures, and inadequate policy.
Tenant families had many alternatives, but they chose to depend only on potatoes.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph gathers the interacting causes: disease, dependence, poverty, land and trade structures, and state response.

questions.stem: What does the passage say continued even while people were hungry?
choices: Food continued to leave Ireland through trade.
Potato harvests continued without damage.
Every tenant continued to control a large farm.
Relief programs continued to meet every need.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that Ireland produced other foods and that food continued to leave through trade.

questions.stem: Why did the presence of other food not prevent widespread hunger?
choices: The blight made every other food in Ireland poisonous and unsafe to sell.
People had forgotten how to prepare any food that did not contain potatoes.
Many families lacked the money or control of land needed to obtain it.
The government did not know that farms were still producing other kinds of food.
questions.explanation: The passage connects hunger to poverty, prices, and lack of control over the land, not simply to the amount of food produced.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, “relief” means
choices: a map of higher and lower ground
a feeling of surprise after good news
a law requiring exports to increase
aid given to people during a crisis
questions.explanation: Public works and other aid are examples of relief offered during the crisis.

lesson.strategy: Build a multi-causal explanation instead of looking for one villain or one mechanism. Paragraph one explains vulnerability, paragraph two separates the blight from access and policy, and paragraph three combines the causes. Use each claim at the level of certainty the passage gives it.

signals.means: Moves from the crop’s arrival to the conditions just before the crisis.

signals.phrase: Yet blight alone does not explain
signals.means: Rejects a one-cause account and opens the wider explanation.
Adds government choices to disease and economic conditions.
Introduces the synthesis that states the main idea.

vocab.inContext: a person who farms or lives on land controlled by an owner
a plant disease that destroys or damages a crop
aid provided to people during a crisis

skillTips.main-idea: Prefer the option that preserves all the major causes. A choice naming only blight or only policy is incomplete.
skillTips.detail: For a direct fact, return to the sentence about other foods and trade in paragraph two.
skillTips.inference: Connect production with access: food can exist while people without money or land still cannot obtain it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the nearby examples “public works and other aid” to define relief in this historical context.

passages.title: A Map Against A Theory
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the summer of 1854, cholera killed hundreds of people within a few streets of Soho, in London. Most doctors of the time blamed bad air rising from filth, a theory so widely accepted that it hardly needed defending. A physician named John Snow disagreed. He suspected that cholera was swallowed rather than breathed, and that the carrier was drinking water.

Snow could not see the organism; nobody could yet. So he argued with geography instead. He marked each death on a street map and looked for a pattern. The deaths clustered tightly around one public pump on Broad Street. The exceptions were as useful as the cluster: a nearby workhouse with its own well lost almost nobody, and a brewery whose workers drank beer lost nobody at all. A widow who had moved to a cleaner district still died, because she liked the taste of that water and had it carried to her.

Snow persuaded the parish to remove the pump handle. The outbreak was already fading, so the removal cannot be credited with ending it, and the theory of bad air survived for years afterwards. What survived longer was the method: collect the cases, plot them on a map, and let the pattern point at the cause.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: John Snow discovered the organism that causes cholera
John Snow used a map of deaths to argue that cholera travelled in water
The Broad Street pump held the only clean water in Soho
Removing the pump handle ended the outbreak at once
questions.explanation: The passage is about how Snow reasoned from the distribution of deaths, since he could not see the cause itself.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which group lost nobody at all?
choices: the workers at the brewery
the people in the workhouse
the doctors working in Soho
the families living closest to the pump
questions.explanation: The workhouse lost 'almost nobody'; only the brewery, where workers drank beer, lost 'nobody at all'.

questions.stem: Why does the story of the widow strengthen Snow's argument?
choices: She was old and already weak
She breathed clean air but still drank the pump water, and still died
She had visited Soho on the day she died
She worked at the brewery and drank no beer
questions.explanation: If bad air caused cholera, a woman in a cleaner district should have been safe. The one thing she shared with the victims was the water.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'clustered' means
choices: were spread evenly across the city
happened at exactly the same hour
were grouped closely together in one area
were counted more than once by mistake
questions.explanation: The deaths gathered 'tightly around one public pump', so clustered means grouped in a small space.

lesson.strategy: This passage sets one theory against another and decides between them with evidence. Read the middle paragraph as a list of tests: the cluster is the main evidence, and the exceptions are the control cases. The final paragraph deliberately limits the claim, so notice what the writer refuses to say.

signals.phrase: A physician named John Snow disagreed
signals.means: The conflict begins. One accepted view, one challenger.

signals.phrase: So he argued with geography instead
signals.means: Explains his method. Everything after this is evidence from place, not from biology.

signals.phrase: The exceptions were as useful as the cluster
signals.means: Tells you the following cases are counter-examples that test the theory.

signals.phrase: What survived longer was the method
signals.means: The real conclusion. The lasting result was how he reasoned, not what happened to the pump.

vocab.inContext: gathered close together in one small area
a sudden appearance of a disease in many people at once
a small local district with its own officials

skillTips.main-idea: In argument passages, the main idea is the method or claim that wins, not the most dramatic event.
skillTips.inference: Exceptions carry the logic. Ask what the exception has, or lacks, that the victims did not.
skillTips.vocabulary: Adverbs help: 'clustered tightly around' shows closeness in space rather than in time.
skillTips.detail: Watch the strength of words. 'Almost nobody' and 'nobody at all' are different answers to the same question.

passages.title: The Clocks The Trains Set
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For most of human history, noon was a local fact. A town set its clocks by the sun directly overhead, so a clock in one city ran several minutes ahead of a clock a hundred miles to the west. Nobody minded. A traveller on horseback arrived long after such a difference had stopped mattering.

Railways destroyed that tolerance. Trains ran on published timetables and shared single tracks, and a few minutes of disagreement between two stations was no longer an inconvenience but a collision. From 1840 British railway companies began keeping London time along their whole lines, printing it in their schedules and hanging it in their stations. Local time slowly gave way to what people called railway time.

The same pressure produced the same answer elsewhere. In 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada divided the continent into standard zones and reset their clocks on a single day. Cities followed the railroads rather than the other way round; national law caught up decades later.

It is worth noticing who decided. No parliament designed modern time. A private industry needed its network to agree, imposed a standard because coordination was cheaper than accidents, and the public accepted it because the trains would not wait.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Railways forced towns to give up local time and accept a shared standard
Clocks were badly made before the nineteenth century
Governments invented time zones to help travellers
Trains in Britain were often late
questions.explanation: Each paragraph advances one claim: local time worked until railways made disagreement dangerous, so a shared standard spread.

questions.stem: What happened in 1883, according to the passage?
choices: British railways first began keeping London time
The United States passed a law creating time zones
Railroads in the United States and Canada divided the continent into standard zones
European cities agreed on a single world clock
questions.explanation: 1840 is the British date; 1883 is the North American railroad decision, and the national law came 'decades later'.

questions.stem: Why did differences in local time matter so little before railways?
choices: Very few people owned any kind of clock
Travel was slow, so small differences had no practical effect
Every town used the same clock tower
Clouds usually hid the sun at noon
questions.explanation: The horseback traveller arrives 'long after such a difference had stopped mattering', which points at the speed of travel.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, 'imposed' means
choices: suggested politely and left optional
established by force of authority or power
removed completely
borrowed from another country
questions.explanation: The industry set the standard for its own reasons and the public 'accepted it because the trains would not wait', so the standard was pressed on people, not offered.

lesson.strategy: The passage compares a before-state and an after-state, then repeats the pattern in a second country to show it was not an accident. The last paragraph steps back and comments on who held the power. Read it as analysis, not as more history.

signals.means: Two blunt words that close the 'before' picture: the old system caused no pain.
The turning point of the passage. What follows explains why the change became necessary.

signals.phrase: The same pressure produced the same answer elsewhere
signals.means: Signals a parallel case. Expect a second country with the same outcome.

signals.phrase: It is worth noticing who decided
signals.means: The writer moves from events to interpretation. The point of the passage is in this paragraph.

vocab.inContext: printed lists of the times when trains arrive and leave
set in place by an authority, whether people agreed or not
getting separate parts to act in agreement with each other

skillTips.main-idea: Before-and-after passages state the main idea at the hinge sentence. Find the sentence where the old world breaks.
skillTips.inference: Concrete images do argumentative work. The slow horse explains why nobody needed exact time.
skillTips.vocabulary: Check who acts on whom. 'A private industry imposed a standard' shows power flowing one way.
skillTips.detail: Two dates in one passage invite a swap. Attach each date to its own country before answering.

passages.title: When The Palaces Went Quiet
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Around 1200 BC the eastern Mediterranean held a set of kingdoms that knew one another well. Egyptian, Hittite, Mycenaean and Levantine courts exchanged letters, gifts, brides and complaints in a shared diplomatic language. Within roughly two generations most of that world was gone. Palaces burned, cities emptied, and in Greece the script used for palace accounts stopped being written at all.

The temptation is to look for a single villain, and the surviving texts offer one: raiders from the sea. But raiders had come before without ending anything. What made this period fragile was the system itself. Bronze demands copper and tin, and tin arrived from sources hundreds of miles away, so every blade and plough in the region rested on long supply lines that no single king controlled. Drought, earthquake, revolt and raiding each strained those lines; together they cut them, and palaces that existed to gather and redistribute imported goods had nothing left to hand out.

What followed was not silence. Smaller settlements survived, alphabetic writing spread among traders who had no palace to serve, and iron, whose ore is common almost everywhere, slowly replaced the metal that had required an empire to obtain.

Read closely, the collapse is less a story about invaders than about interdependence without a spare part.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the writer's main argument?
choices: Sea raiders alone destroyed the Bronze Age kingdoms
The collapse came less from invaders than from a connected system with no backup
Iron was superior to bronze in every practical way
Writing was invented only after the Bronze Age ended
questions.explanation: The writer rejects the single-villain reading and restates the claim in the last line: interdependence without a spare part.

questions.stem: What does the passage say stopped in Greece?
choices: the mining of copper ore
the building of seagoing ships
the writing of the script used for palace accounts
the exchange of royal letters with Egypt
questions.explanation: The first paragraph ends with exactly this detail: the script for palace accounts stopped being written.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention that tin came from sources hundreds of miles away?
choices: To show that ancient sailors were skilled navigators
To explain why bronze objects were beautiful
To show that ordinary tools depended on trade routes that could break
To prove that tin was worth more than gold
questions.explanation: The detail supports the claim about fragility: everyday blades and ploughs relied on supply lines nobody controlled.

questions.stem: In the last sentence, 'interdependence' refers to
choices: the ability of each kingdom to live without trade
a condition in which each part relies on the others
a long war between neighbouring kingdoms
the sharing of one written language
questions.explanation: The passage has shown kingdoms and tools relying on distant partners, so interdependence names that mutual reliance, which failed when the links broke.

lesson.strategy: This is an argument that replaces a simple cause with a structural one. Paragraph two states the opposing view, concedes what is true in it, and then explains the deeper mechanism. The final line compresses the whole argument, so use it to check your reading of everything above.

signals.phrase: The temptation is to look for a single villain
signals.means: The writer names a common explanation in order to argue against it.

signals.phrase: But raiders had come before without ending anything
signals.means: The counter-evidence. One 'but' sentence dismisses the simple cause.

signals.phrase: What made this period fragile was the system itself
signals.means: The thesis. Everything after this explains the mechanism.
Corrects an expected image. The collapse changed the world rather than emptying it.

vocab.inContext: easily broken, here because too many parts depended on each other
to collect goods centrally and hand them out again
a situation where every part relies on the others to function

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage argues against a named explanation, the main idea is the replacement, not the rejected cause.
skillTips.inference: Ask why a specific fact is included. Distance of the tin supply is there to prove fragility.
skillTips.vocabulary: Break long words into parts. 'Inter' means between, 'dependence' means relying on, so the whole word means mutual reliance.
skillTips.detail: Pick details from the exact sentence, not from your general sense of the period. Only the palace-account script is said to stop.

passages.title: The Book Of Judgement
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Twenty years after taking England by force, William the Conqueror sent officials into almost every shire with the same list of questions. Who held this land before the conquest, who holds it now, how many ploughs, how many mills, how many people, and what is the whole worth? Answers were given by juries of local men, checked against the answers of other juries, and written down in compressed Latin. The survey began in 1085 and the main volume was finished with unusual speed.

The king's clerks called it a description. The English called it Domesday, the day of judgement, because there was no appeal against what it recorded. That name is the clearest surviving evidence of how the survey felt to the people it counted.

Its purpose is still argued. Some historians read a tax register; others read a legal record fixing who owned what after two decades of confiscation, which was convenient for a ruling class that had arrived recently and by violence. The two readings are not exclusive.

Either way the book did something quietly radical. It made land, labour and livestock legible to a central government, and what a state can see it can assess, and what it can assess it can tax.

questions.stem: Which statement best states the main idea?
choices: William the Conqueror wrote England's first book of law
The survey proves that England was a wealthy country in 1086
A royal survey made the country visible to the state, which is why it mattered
Local juries usually lied to the king's officials
questions.explanation: The last paragraph names the deep result: the survey made land, labour and livestock legible, and therefore taxable.

questions.stem: According to the passage, where did the officials get their answers?
choices: from juries of local men, checked against other juries
from tax records already kept in London
from monks who owned most of the land
from measurements taken by the king's soldiers
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says answers came from local juries and were cross-checked against other juries.

questions.stem: Why does the writer call the name 'Domesday' useful evidence?
choices: It shows that priests carried out the survey
It shows how the people being counted experienced the survey
It proves the whole survey was completed in one day
It tells us that the king chose the title himself
questions.explanation: The clerks called it a description; the people called it judgement day. The popular name records their feeling, since there was no appeal.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, 'legible' means
choices: written in beautiful handwriting
able to be seen and understood clearly
protected by law from change
divided into equal shares
questions.explanation: The sentence continues 'what a state can see it can assess', so legible here means visible and understandable to the government.

lesson.strategy: The passage moves from method, to popular name, to a debate about purpose, to the writer's own conclusion. Notice the two-voice contrast in paragraph two: the clerks' word against the people's word. The chain of clauses at the end ('see, assess, tax') is the argument in miniature.

signals.phrase: The king's clerks called it a description
signals.means: The official view. A second, unofficial view is about to follow.
Signals debate. Expect at least two competing readings and no final verdict.

signals.phrase: The two readings are not exclusive
signals.means: The writer refuses the either-or choice. Both explanations can hold at once.

signals.phrase: Either way the book did something quietly radical
signals.means: The writer sets the debate aside and states the conclusion that matters.

vocab.inContext: an old English administrative district, like a county
the taking of property by an authority, without payment
clear enough to be read and understood, here by a government

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage reports a scholarly debate, the main idea is often what the writer says holds true 'either way'.
skillTips.inference: Names and nicknames carry attitude. Compare who chose each word before deciding what it reveals.
skillTips.vocabulary: Follow the chain. 'Legible' is defined by the next clause: what a state can see it can assess.
skillTips.detail: The method sentences early in the passage are dense. Reread them slowly; detail questions live there.

passages.title: Why Spreading Study Works
