Sunde had spent his second life discovering that faithfulness to a text and faithfulness to its effect are different loyalties, and the tribute he finally received belonged to the man he had stopped being.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the passage's central point?
choices: Translators should never alter a poet's original wording.
Sunde's publisher and his readers wanted incompatible things from the same books.
Sunde came to believe that being true to a poem's effect is not the same as being true to its words, and he was finally honoured for the approach he had abandoned.
The reputation of a translator depends mostly on the poet he chooses.
questions.explanation: The closing sentences name both halves: two different kinds of faithfulness, and a tribute that belonged to the man he had stopped being.

questions.stem: How did the critics respond to Sunde's early volumes?
choices: They called the exactness of the work rigor and praised it.
They said the footnotes ruined the poems.
They ignored them until the later volumes appeared.
They accused him of inventing lines the poet never wrote.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says critics called this rigor, and he accepted the compliment for a decade.

questions.stem: Why is the scholar's praise described as an irony?
choices: The scholar had not read the poet in the original language.
The obituaries had already said the same thing.
Sunde had asked in his will that the early volumes be withdrawn.
It honours the method Sunde judged a failure and abandoned, not the one he spent his second life defending.
questions.explanation: Sunde had concluded that his early literal work lost the poems. Being praised for exactly that work reverses his own verdict on it.

questions.stem: In "The irony arrived posthumously," posthumously means:
choices: very slowly, over many years
after the person's death
without any public notice
in a foreign country
questions.explanation: The passage opens with his obituaries and ends with a scholar assessing his completed career, so the praise reaches him only after he has died.

lesson.strategy: This is a two-period portrait built for a final reversal: early method, late method, then a judgement that lands on the wrong one. Track the pair of opposed values (exactness against effect) and hold both until the last sentence, where the irony depends on remembering which method Sunde himself rejected.

signals.phrase: people who had not compared the two halves of his work.
signals.means: An early warning that the praise is unearned or misplaced. It sets up the ending.
Opens period one. Expect a contrasting period two.

signals.phrase: The later volumes were another matter.
signals.means: The pivot into period two, with the opposite method.
The writer names the reversal outright; the sentences after it explain what was reversed.

vocab.inContext: faithfulness: how closely a translation stays true to the original
someone who translates word for word rather than by sense or effect
after the person has died

skillTips.main-idea: With a two-period structure, refuse any answer that names only one period. The main idea must contain the contrast and its outcome.
skillTips.inference: Irony questions are checked against the character's own judgement. Sunde called his early work a failure; that is the fact the praise collides with.
skillTips.vocabulary: Formal words are often unlocked by frame details: obituaries at the start and a scholar reviewing a finished career at the end fix 'posthumously' as after death.
skillTips.detail: Attribute each opinion to its owner: critics, publisher, readers, scholar. The passage gives each a different verdict.

passages.title: The Lake’s Winter Lid
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Drop a stone into water and it sinks. Place an ice cube in water and it floats. The reason is density: ice has less mass packed into each bit of space than liquid water does.

As water freezes, its molecules join in an open pattern with small gaps. The same amount of water takes up more room as ice. Because it is less dense than the liquid around it, the ice stays on top.

This matters in a lake. On a cold day, ice forms at the surface instead of dropping to the bottom. The floating sheet acts like a lid and slows the loss of heat. Water can remain liquid beneath it, giving fish, frogs, and other organisms a winter habitat.

If ice were denser than liquid water, new ice would sink. More water at the surface could then freeze and sink too. A lake might freeze much more deeply. The floating lid does not protect every lake in every condition, but its position at the top often leaves living space below.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How stones change when they enter cold water
Why ice floats and often leaves liquid habitat beneath a lake’s surface
How frogs make a lake freeze during winter
Why every lake keeps the same temperature
questions.explanation: The passage explains the density of ice, then shows how floating ice can protect liquid water below.

questions.stem: What does a floating sheet of ice do?
choices: It pulls every fish toward the surface
It makes the lake water turn salty
It slows heat loss from the water below
It causes new ice to sink to the bottom
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the sheet acts like a lid and slows the loss of heat.

questions.stem: What would happen first if ice were denser than liquid water?
choices: The lake would become warmer than summer air
Water molecules would lose their mass
All organisms would immediately leave the lake
New ice would sink after it formed
questions.explanation: Something denser than the liquid around it sinks, so newly formed ice would drop.

questions.stem: In this passage, “density” describes
choices: how much mass is packed into an amount of space
how cold something feels to a hand
how quickly something changes shape
how clear a liquid appears
questions.explanation: The first paragraph defines density as how much mass is packed into each bit of space.

lesson.strategy: Read this as cause, position, and consequence. The open pattern makes ice less dense; lower density keeps it on top; the surface lid slows heat loss. Check that each answer follows that chain.

signals.means: Names the idea that explains the opening contrast.
Connects the molecular pattern to floating.
Moves from the explanation to its effect on a habitat.
Introduces a counterfactual that tests the density rule.

vocab.inContext: how much mass is packed into a given amount of space
the tiny units of water that form an open pattern in ice
a place where organisms can live

skillTips.main-idea: The passage needs both halves: why ice floats and what a floating lid changes in a lake.
skillTips.inference: Apply the density rule to the imagined case. If solid ice were denser, it would sink.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the definition after the colon in paragraph one rather than guessing from “heavy.”
skillTips.detail: The third paragraph directly names the lid’s job: it slows the loss of heat.

passages.title: Counting Toward Thunder
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A flash of lightning and the crash of thunder begin at the same moment. You see the flash first because light travels much faster than sound. Light crosses the sky almost at once. Sound needs about three seconds to travel one kilometre.

So you can turn the delay into a measurement. Count the seconds between the flash and the first rumble, then divide by three. The answer is the rough distance to the strike in kilometres. Nine seconds means the lightning was about three kilometres away.

Thunder itself is made of air. Lightning heats the narrow channel it passes through to a temperature far hotter than the surface of the sun. The air in that channel expands in an instant and pushes hard on the air around it. That push spreads outward as a wave, and your ear hears a crash.

Near strikes sound sharp and short. Distant ones sound like a long roll, because the sound reaches you from different parts of the same long channel at slightly different times.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Thunder is more dangerous than lightning.
Counting seconds is the only safe thing to do in a storm.
The gap between the flash and the crash has a simple cause, and it can be used to measure distance.
Sound and light leave a lightning strike at different moments.
questions.explanation: The passage explains why the sound arrives late, turns that delay into a distance, and then explains what makes the sound.

questions.stem: How far does sound travel in about three seconds, according to the passage?
choices: One kilometre
Three kilometres
Nine kilometres
As far as light does
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states that sound needs about three seconds to travel one kilometre.

questions.stem: A person counts fifteen seconds between the flash and the crash. What does the passage suggest?
choices: The lightning was weaker than usual.
The sound and the light started at different times.
The strike was about fifteen kilometres away.
The strike was about five kilometres away.
questions.explanation: The rule given is to divide the seconds by three, so fifteen seconds means roughly five kilometres.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'channel' means:
choices: the narrow path the lightning follows through the air
a wide, open field below the cloud
a deep cut in the ground
a way of sending a radio signal
questions.explanation: The text says lightning heats 'the narrow channel it passes through', so the channel is the thin path of the strike.

lesson.strategy: The passage moves from an observation, to a rule you can use, to the cause behind it. Hold on to the numbers in the first two paragraphs, because one question will ask you to use them. The last paragraph explains a difference in sound, not a difference in danger.

signals.phrase: You see the flash first because
signals.means: A cause is about to be given for something you already noticed.

signals.phrase: So you can turn the delay into a measurement.
signals.means: The writer shifts from fact to practical use. A method follows.

signals.phrase: That push spreads outward as a wave
signals.means: One step in a chain: heat, then push, then wave, then sound.

signals.phrase: different parts of the same long channel
signals.means: The reason for the long rolling sound of far-off thunder.

vocab.inContext: the waiting time between the flash and the sound
a low, rolling sound
the narrow path the lightning cuts through the air

skillTips.main-idea: If a text gives a method, the main idea usually includes both the method and the reason it works.
skillTips.inference: Some inference questions ask you to apply a rule to a new number. Find the rule, then do the small calculation.
skillTips.vocabulary: Adjectives next to a word are clues. 'Narrow channel it passes through' tells you channel is a path.
skillTips.detail: Watch for two similar numbers (three seconds, three kilometres). Reread which one goes with which unit.

passages.title: Two Lives, One Body
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The grey-green crust on an old stone wall looks like a single plant. It is not a plant at all, and it is not a single organism. A lichen is a partnership: a fungus that builds the body, and an alga or a bacterium that makes food inside it.

The division of labour is clear. The fungus cannot make its own food, but it can grip bare rock, hold water, and shield its partner from strong light. The alga has no roots and no shelter, but it can turn sunlight into sugar. Together they live where neither could live alone, on gravestones, on bark, on stone in the high mountains.

The cost of the arrangement is speed. Many lichens grow less than a millimetre a year, and some patches on Arctic rock are centuries old. The cost is also exposure. A lichen has no waxy skin and no way to shut itself off from the air, so it absorbs whatever the air carries, clean or dirty. Where pollution is heavy, lichens thin out and vanish before most other life shows harm. Scientists read that absence as a warning.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: Lichens are unusual plants that grow on stone walls and gravestones.
A lichen is two organisms living as one, and that deal brings both power and cost.
Fungi are more important to a lichen than algae are.
Air pollution is the greatest danger facing mountain plants.
questions.explanation: The passage defines the partnership, shows what each partner gives, then names its two costs: slow growth and exposure to the air.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the fungus contribute to the partnership?
choices: It turns sunlight into sugar.
It grows roots deep into the rock.
It grips the rock, holds water, and shields its partner from strong light.
It filters dirty air before the alga can absorb it.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists exactly these three jobs for the fungus; making sugar from sunlight is the alga's job.

questions.stem: Lichens have disappeared from the trees of a city park. What can you reasonably infer?
choices: The air in that area is probably polluted.
The trees in the park are too young to carry lichens.
The lichens have moved to the stone walls nearby.
The park receives too much sunlight for any lichen.
questions.explanation: The text says lichens absorb whatever the air carries and vanish first where pollution is heavy, and that scientists read their absence as a warning.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'shield' means:
choices: measure carefully
feed steadily
carry from place to place
protect from something harmful
questions.explanation: The fungus shields its partner from strong light, that is, it protects the alga from light that would harm it.

lesson.strategy: This passage corrects a wrong first impression, then explains a trade. Paragraph two is the benefit side, paragraph three is the cost side. Track who does what: mixing up the fungus and the alga is the easiest mistake here.

signals.phrase: It is not a plant at all
signals.means: The writer is correcting what you assumed in the first sentence.

signals.phrase: The division of labour is clear.
signals.means: A list is coming: which partner does which job.

signals.phrase: Together they live where neither could live alone
signals.means: The core claim, that the pair can do what each alone cannot.

signals.phrase: The cost of the arrangement is speed.
signals.means: A turn from benefits to costs. A second cost will follow.

vocab.inContext: two different living things working together as one body
protect from harm, here from light that is too strong
being open to whatever is in the air, with no protection

skillTips.main-idea: When a text names both a benefit and a cost, the main idea has to hold both. A choice that keeps only one half is too narrow.
skillTips.inference: The last line, 'Scientists read that absence as a warning', invites you to apply the idea to a new place. Use the stated cause.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read what the word acts on: 'shield its partner from strong light' shows shield is about protection.
skillTips.detail: For two-partner texts, make a quick mental table: fungus does X, alga does Y. Then match the option to the right column.

passages.title: What Sleep Does With The Day
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Sleep looks like a pause, but the brain does not stop. In the hours after learning, it replays the day.

Researchers who record brain activity in sleeping animals see the same patterns of firing that appeared during the day's tasks, run again in compressed bursts. The idea, supported by many experiments, is that a new memory first sits in a fast, fragile store and is slowly copied into a slower, more durable one. Sleep is when much of that copying happens.

Human studies point the same way. People who learn a list of words and then sleep remember more of it than people who learn the same list and stay awake for the same number of hours. The advantage is not simply time away from the material; a nap of an hour or two can produce it, while the same hours spent awake and busy usually do not.

This is why an all-night session before an exam is a poor trade. Extra hours of reading buy material that the brain is given no time to file. That filing is called consolidation, and it is not a luxury added after learning. It is the second half of learning itself.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly arguing?
choices: Animal brains and human brains work in exactly the same way.
Students should read less and rest more in general.
Word lists are the best way to test memory.
Sleep is an active part of learning, not simply a rest afterwards.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph builds the claim that memory is copied and fixed during sleep, ending with 'It is the second half of learning itself.'

questions.stem: What do researchers see in the brains of sleeping animals?
choices: Firing patterns from the day's tasks running again in compressed bursts.
Almost no activity until the animal wakes.
New patterns that never appeared while the animal was awake.
Activity only in animals that learned nothing that day.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states this directly: the same patterns of firing from the day's tasks, run again in compressed bursts.

questions.stem: Two students study the same material. Alba studies for two hours and sleeps eight. Ben studies for four hours and sleeps four. What does the passage suggest?
choices: Ben will remember more, because he read the material twice as long.
Alba may remember more, because her brain gets more time to file what she read.
Neither will remember anything without a nap during the day.
Both will remember the same amount, since they were awake for equal time.
questions.explanation: The passage says extra reading buys material the brain has no time to file, and that sleepers recall more than those who stay awake.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'fragile' describes a memory store that is:
choices: extremely large
shared between two people
easily lost or damaged
very slow to fill
questions.explanation: The fragile store is contrasted with a 'more durable' one, so fragile means easily lost, not lasting.

lesson.strategy: This is an argument built from two kinds of evidence: animal recordings first, then human experiments. The last paragraph turns the evidence into advice. Read for the contrast pair fast and fragile against slow and durable, because the whole argument sits on it.

signals.phrase: but the brain does not stop
signals.means: A contrast with the everyday view of sleep. The real claim starts here.

signals.phrase: The idea, supported by many experiments, is that
signals.means: The writer is careful: this is a theory with evidence, not a proven fact.

signals.phrase: Human studies point the same way.
signals.means: A second, independent line of evidence agreeing with the first.

signals.phrase: an all-night session before an exam is a poor trade.
signals.means: The turn from evidence to practical conclusion.

vocab.inContext: easily lost, not yet firmly held
lasting, able to survive over time
the brain's work of filing a new memory into lasting storage

skillTips.main-idea: When each paragraph adds evidence for one claim, the last sentence is often the cleanest statement of the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Apply the argument to the case in the question. Ask which person the text's rule would favour, and why.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast pairs teach meaning. 'Fragile' sits opposite 'more durable', so it must mean the reverse.
skillTips.detail: Careful phrases like 'supported by many experiments' matter. A choice that states the theory as certain is a different claim.

passages.title: The Diary Inside A Tree
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Cut across the trunk of an old oak and you meet a set of rings. In climates with a real winter, the tree adds one ring a year: pale, quick wood in spring, dark, tight wood late in the season. Count the rings and you have the age of the tree. Measure their width and you have something better, a record of the years themselves.

A wet, mild year leaves a wide ring. A drought leaves a narrow one. Because every tree in a region meets the same weather, the trees of that region share one pattern of wide and narrow bands, like a barcode.

That shared pattern lets researchers reach back further than any living tree. A beam cut from an old farmhouse carries rings too, and if the outer rings of the beam match the inner rings of a living trunk, the two records can be joined. Chain enough overlaps together and the sequence runs back thousands of years, with every ring tied to an exact calendar year.

Archaeologists use those sequences to date buildings and ships. Climate scientists use them to test what the weather did long before anyone wrote it down.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How to tell an oak tree from other kinds of tree.
Why old farmhouses were built from oak beams.
How tree rings record past years and can be joined into a long dated record.
Why trees grow faster in warm regions than in cold ones.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from one tree's rings, to the shared regional pattern, to chained overlaps that reach back thousands of years.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does a narrow ring show?
choices: That the tree was cut down that year.
That the year was dry.
That the tree was very young.
That two rings grew in one season.
questions.explanation: The text pairs a wet, mild year with a wide ring and a drought with a narrow one.

questions.stem: What must be true before a wooden beam can be given an exact calendar date?
choices: The tree it came from must still be alive somewhere.
The beam must come from the same farmhouse as another dated beam.
The beam must be older than any living tree in the region.
Its ring pattern must overlap with a pattern that is already dated.
questions.explanation: Dating works by matching the beam's rings to an existing sequence; without an overlap, the beam cannot be tied to calendar years.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'beam' means:
choices: a long piece of timber used to build with
a line of bright light
a wide smile
a ring of new spring wood
questions.explanation: The beam is 'cut from an old farmhouse' and 'carries rings', so it is a piece of building timber.

lesson.strategy: The passage widens step by step: one tree, then one region, then thousands of years. Each paragraph depends on the one before it, so if a step is unclear, go back rather than forward. The final paragraph only names who uses the method.

signals.phrase: In climates with a real winter
signals.means: A limit on the claim. The one-ring-a-year rule does not hold everywhere.

signals.phrase: Because every tree in a region meets the same weather
signals.means: The cause that makes the shared pattern possible.
A comparison. The pattern is unique and can be matched, like a code.

signals.phrase: reach back further than any living tree.
signals.means: The key move of the passage: from living wood to old wood.

vocab.inContext: a long stretch of time with too little rain
a long piece of cut timber inside a building
a run of years placed in order, one after another

skillTips.main-idea: In a step-by-step explainer, the main idea is the whole chain, not the first step. Prefer the choice that covers the last step too.
skillTips.inference: Ask what a method needs in order to work. Here, matching requires an overlap, even though the text never says 'must'.
skillTips.vocabulary: A word with several everyday meanings, like 'beam', is fixed by its verbs: it is cut, and it carries rings.
skillTips.detail: Pairs (wide and wet, narrow and dry) are common detail traps. Reread the pairing before you answer.

passages.title: Why Antibiotics Lose Power
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An antibiotic does not teach bacteria to resist it. The resistance is already present in a handful of cells, produced by ordinary copying errors long before the drug arrives. What the drug does is edit the population: it kills the cells that cannot survive it and leaves the rare ones that can. Those survivors then divide in an emptied field, with their competition gone, and within days the resistant type is no longer rare.

Two features of bacteria make this loop unusually fast. The first is speed of reproduction; a population can double in twenty minutes, so a number of generations that a mammal would need centuries to produce can pass in a single weekend. The second is that bacteria trade genes sideways. A small loop of DNA carrying a resistance gene can move from one cell to another, and even between species, so a trait that arose in one lineage need not stay there.

Every use of an antibiotic applies this pressure, which is why quantity matters more than intent. Prescriptions written for viral infections, which antibiotics cannot touch, and routine doses given to healthy farm animals both add selection without adding benefit. The drug is not wearing out; the target is changing.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage's central claim?
choices: Antibiotics grow weaker each time they are manufactured.
Bacteria learn to defend themselves after meeting a drug.
Antibiotics select bacteria that were already resistant, and heavy use speeds that selection.
Farm animals are the only serious source of resistant bacteria.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says resistance exists before the drug arrives and that the drug edits the population; the last says every use adds pressure.

questions.stem: How can a resistance gene reach bacteria of a different species?
choices: A small loop of DNA can move from one cell into another.
The bacteria must first be exposed to a viral infection.
Copying errors happen at the same moment in both species.
The gene passes only from parent cell to daughter cell.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes bacteria trading genes sideways: a small loop of DNA can move between cells and even between species.

questions.stem: Why does the passage treat an antibiotic prescribed for a cold as harmful?
choices: Because colds become more severe when they are treated with drugs.
Because the drug cannot act on a virus, yet it still selects resistant bacteria in the body.
Because patients with colds usually take too small a dose.
Because viruses can carry resistance genes to bacteria.
questions.explanation: The text says antibiotics cannot touch viral infections but such prescriptions still 'add selection without adding benefit'.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'applies this pressure', 'pressure' refers to:
choices: the physical force of the drug on a cell wall
the urgency doctors feel when a patient is ill
the cost of buying antibiotics in large amounts
the killing of vulnerable cells, which favours resistant ones
questions.explanation: Pressure here is selection pressure: the drug removes cells that cannot survive, so survivors are favoured.

lesson.strategy: The passage opens by rejecting a common belief, then replaces it with a mechanism, then gives two reasons the mechanism runs fast, then draws a practical conclusion. Notice that the whole argument turns on one distinction: creating resistance versus selecting it. Hold that distinction and the rest follows.

signals.phrase: What the drug does is edit the population
signals.means: The replacement idea. This is the writer's real thesis.

signals.phrase: Two features of bacteria make this loop unusually fast.
signals.means: A preview of a two-part list. Expect 'the first' and 'the second'.

signals.phrase: The second is that bacteria trade genes sideways.
signals.means: The second item, and a new route for resistance that is not inheritance.

signals.phrase: which is why quantity matters more than intent
signals.means: The conclusion drawn from the mechanism: amount of use, not the reason for it, drives the problem.

vocab.inContext: one line of descent, a family of cells from a common ancestor
the process by which some cells survive and others do not, changing the mix
a force pushing a population to change, not a physical push

skillTips.main-idea: When a text says what something is not, the main idea is the correction that follows, stated in full.
skillTips.inference: Combine two separate lines: antibiotics do nothing to viruses, and every use adds selection. The harm sits where those meet.
skillTips.vocabulary: Technical uses of ordinary words ('pressure', 'selection') are defined by the process around them, not by their everyday sense.
skillTips.detail: Two-part lists reward care. Check whether a choice belongs to 'the first' feature or 'the second' before you pick it.

passages.title: The Colour Of Air
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Air has no colour of its own, yet the sky overhead is blue and the same sky turns orange at the end of the day. Both facts come from one process, and that process depends on size.

Sunlight is a mixture of wavelengths, and the molecules of nitrogen and oxygen in the air are far smaller than any of them. When a wave meets a particle much smaller than itself, the particle does not block the wave; it takes in a little energy and sends it out again in every direction. This redirection is called scattering, and it is biased: the shorter the wavelength, the more it is scattered. Blue light, being short, is thrown sideways across the whole sky, while red light mostly continues straight ahead. Looking anywhere except at the sun, you see the light that was scattered, so you see blue.

At sunset the geometry changes. The sun sits low, so its light crosses far more air before it reaches you, and the blue is scattered away long before it arrives. What survives the journey is the long end of the spectrum. The orange of a sunset is not something added to the light; it is what is left after the blue has been taken out.

questions.stem: What does the passage set out to explain?
choices: How a blue sky and an orange sunset arise from the same scattering of light.
Why nitrogen and oxygen are the most common gases in the air.
How the human eye separates one colour from another.
Why sunlight grows weaker as the day goes on.
questions.explanation: The opening promises that both facts come from one process, and the passage then traces that single process through both cases.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does sunset light lose its blue?
choices: The sun emits less blue light in the evening.
Cooler evening air absorbs blue light completely.
Its light crosses far more air, so the blue is scattered away before it arrives.
Clouds near the horizon block the shorter wavelengths.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the low sun's light crosses far more air, and the blue is scattered away long before it reaches you.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, how would the daytime sky look from a place with far thinner air?
choices: Brighter blue, because thin air scatters more light.
Darker, because less air means less scattered light to see.
Orange all day, because red light travels straight.
Unchanged, because scattering does not depend on how much air there is.
questions.explanation: The sky's blue is scattered light. The sunset paragraph shows that more air means more scattering, so less air means less scattered light and a darker sky.

questions.stem: The passage calls scattering 'biased'. Here that means the process:
choices: is unfair to observers on the ground
happens only at certain times of day
cannot be measured accurately
affects some wavelengths far more than others
questions.explanation: The sentence explains itself: the shorter the wavelength, the more it is scattered. The effect is uneven across colours.

lesson.strategy: One mechanism, two results. Paragraph two builds the mechanism, paragraph three applies it to a new geometry. When you meet the word 'biased', slow down: the clause right after it is the rule that the whole passage rests on.

signals.phrase: Both facts come from one process
signals.means: A promise of unity. Expect one explanation to cover both the blue sky and the orange sunset.

signals.phrase: the shorter the wavelength, the more it is scattered
signals.means: The central rule. Everything after this is an application of it.
A pivot. The rule stays the same; only the path of the light is different.

signals.phrase: it is what is left after the blue has been taken out
signals.means: The conclusion, stated as subtraction rather than addition.

vocab.inContext: the different lengths of light wave that together make sunlight
light being taken in by a tiny particle and sent out again in all directions
the full range of colours in sunlight, from short to long waves

skillTips.main-idea: A first paragraph that names two puzzles and one cause is telling you the main idea outright. Choose the option that keeps both puzzles.
skillTips.inference: Extend the stated rule to a new case. More air means more scattering, so ask what less air must do.
skillTips.vocabulary: When a writer uses an odd word and then a colon or comma, the definition usually follows immediately.
skillTips.detail: Causal detail questions test direction. Check whether the text says the light changed or the path through the air changed.

passages.title: A Clock In Dead Wood
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
High in the atmosphere, cosmic rays strike nitrogen atoms and turn a few of them into carbon-14, a rare and unstable form of carbon. It mixes into the air as carbon dioxide, plants take it in, animals eat the plants, and every living body ends up holding about the same proportion of it as the air does.

Death closes that account. Nothing new comes in, and the carbon-14 already present breaks down at a fixed rate: half of it is gone in about 5,730 years, half of the remainder in the next 5,730, and so on. Measure how much is left in a piece of charcoal, bone, or cloth, and you can work out how long ago the exchange with the atmosphere stopped. After roughly fifty thousand years so little remains that the method runs out.

There is a complication. The proportion of carbon-14 in the air has not been constant; it has drifted with changes in the sun and, more recently, with the burning of fossil fuels. So raw measurements are corrected against samples of known age, tree rings above all, before a date is announced. The clock is real, but it has to be set.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why cosmic rays are dangerous to living things.
How carbon-14 dating works, and why its results must be corrected.
Why charcoal and bone survive longer than cloth.
How plants take carbon dioxide out of the air.
questions.explanation: The first two paragraphs explain the method; the third explains the complication and the correction that follows from it.

questions.stem: Why does the method stop working after roughly fifty thousand years?
choices: Bones and cloth have usually rotted away by then.
Cosmic rays stop reaching the atmosphere at that depth of time.
So little carbon-14 remains that there is nothing to measure.
The rate of breakdown changes once a sample is very old.
questions.explanation: The text states that after roughly fifty thousand years so little remains that the method runs out.

questions.stem: A sample holds about one quarter of the carbon-14 it began with. Roughly how old is it?
choices: About 2,900 years
About 5,730 years
About 23,000 years
About 11,500 years
questions.explanation: Half is lost in about 5,730 years and half of the rest in the next 5,730, so a quarter left means about two such steps, near 11,460 years.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'constant' means:
choices: staying the same over time
happening again and again
easy to measure
very small in amount
questions.explanation: The text says the proportion has not been constant, then adds that it has drifted, so constant means unchanging.

lesson.strategy: Read this as method, then limit, then correction. The second paragraph carries the numbers you will need, so read it slowly and note that the halving repeats. The final short sentence is the writer's summary of the whole argument.

signals.means: A pivot from the living exchange to the decay clock. The metaphor marks the start of the method.

signals.phrase: half of it is gone in about 5,730 years
signals.means: The key quantity. The word 'half' repeating tells you the loss is by steps, not steady.
A qualification is coming. The method as described is not quite enough.

signals.phrase: The clock is real, but it has to be set.
signals.means: The closing judgement: the method works, but only after correction.

vocab.inContext: breaking down over time into something else
the share of one thing within a whole
unchanging from one age to the next

skillTips.main-idea: If a passage adds a problem at the end, the main idea includes it. A choice describing only the clean method is incomplete.
skillTips.inference: Repeated halving questions need two steps, not one. Count how many halvings the amount implies.
skillTips.vocabulary: A negative ('has not been constant') plus its restatement ('has drifted') gives you the meaning for free.
skillTips.detail: When several limits are mentioned, match the exact one the question asks about, not the first limit you remember.

passages.title: The Sugar Pill Problem
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Give a patient an inert tablet, tell them it is a strong painkiller, and a fair number will report less pain. The result is real and repeatable, and it is why medicine cannot judge a treatment by asking whether patients improved. Almost everyone improves after treatment. The question is whether they improved because of it.

Several forces push the same way at once. Illness is not steady; people seek help when symptoms peak, and symptoms that peak tend to fall again on their own. Expectation shapes what is felt, and the ritual around a treatment, the examination, the confident voice, the price, has effects of its own. Reporting is not neutral either: a patient who has been given something, and a doctor who gave it, both have quiet reasons to notice improvement.

The controlled trial exists to strip these out. Two groups, assigned at random, receive the real treatment or a convincing imitation, and neither the patients nor the staff judging them know which is which. Whatever the two groups share is subtracted; only the difference is credited to the drug.

The design is powerful, and it is not perfect. Placebo effects act mainly on what a patient reports, such as pain, sickness, and mood, and much less on what an instrument measures.

questions.stem: What is the passage's central argument?
choices: Placebo tablets should be prescribed more often, since they clearly work.
Doctors deliberately mislead patients about which treatment they receive.
Because many forces make patients seem better, only a controlled comparison can credit a treatment.
Pain is the only symptom that medicine can measure reliably.
questions.explanation: The passage names the forces that mimic a cure, then presents the controlled trial as the way to separate the drug's effect from everything else.

questions.stem: In the controlled trial described, who does not know which treatment a patient received?
choices: Only the patients.
Neither the patients nor the staff judging them.
Only the staff who prepare the tablets.
Nobody: the assignment is announced at the start.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says neither the patients nor the staff judging them know which is which.

questions.stem: A clinic reports that seventy percent of its patients improved after starting a new therapy. How would this passage read that figure?
choices: As strong evidence that the therapy works, since most patients got better.
As proof that the therapy is no better than a placebo.
As a sign that the clinic treated unusually mild cases.
As nearly uninformative, because most patients improve anyway and no comparison group is given.
questions.explanation: The passage says almost everyone improves after treatment, so a figure without a comparison group cannot show that the therapy caused the change.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'inert' means:
choices: having no active effect of its own
unpleasant to swallow
very strong in small amounts
sold without a prescription
questions.explanation: The inert tablet is the fake treatment; it is contrasted with a real painkiller, so inert means it does nothing on its own.

lesson.strategy: Track the problem-and-solution structure. Paragraph two lists confounding causes; paragraph three explains the design that separates them; paragraph four adds a limitation. Keep improving after treatment distinct from improving because of treatment.

signals.phrase: The question is whether they improved because of it.
signals.means: The thesis, stated as a distinction between sequence and cause.

signals.phrase: Several forces push the same way at once.
signals.means: A list is coming, and the items all point in the same misleading direction.

signals.phrase: The controlled trial exists to strip these out.
signals.means: The turn from problem to solution.

signals.phrase: The design is powerful, and it is not perfect.
signals.means: A concession. What follows limits the claim just made.

vocab.inContext: having no active effect, doing nothing by itself
the set of familiar actions around a treatment, which carries meaning for the patient
free of any leaning, here free of reasons to see improvement

skillTips.main-idea: In problem-and-solution writing, the main idea joins both halves. A choice naming only the problem or only the solution is too small.
skillTips.inference: Test a new number against the writer's rule. If the passage says a figure alone proves nothing, apply that to the case in the question.
skillTips.vocabulary: Unfamiliar adjectives are often fixed by their opposite in the same sentence: inert tablet against strong painkiller.
skillTips.detail: Blinding questions turn on who knows what. Reread the exact list of people the text names.

passages.title: Air From Another Age
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Snow that falls on central Antarctica may remain instead of melting. Later snow buries it, pressure turns it into ice, and closing pores trap samples of the surrounding air. A bubble is not labeled with a year, but it preserves gases from an atmosphere far older than any instrument record.

Drilling brings the layers up in order, with younger ice above older ice. Earlier Antarctic cores produced a continuous climate record reaching about eight hundred thousand years. A newer core from Little Dome C reaches at least 1.2 million years, although researchers must still analyze and date its deepest sections carefully. “Oldest” therefore describes both an achievement and an active measurement problem.

Two kinds of evidence come from a core. Air bubbles let researchers measure gases such as carbon dioxide and methane. The ice itself holds indirect temperature clues. Ratios of heavier and lighter forms of oxygen and hydrogen vary with the conditions in which snow formed.

The gas record and the temperature clues do not share exactly the same age at a given depth: air is sealed only after snow has already begun becoming ice. Scientists model that age difference and compare several dating clues. An ice core is a powerful archive not because every layer speaks plainly, but because many physical records can be tested in one ordered column.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Deep ice preserves ancient gases and climate clues that require careful dating and comparison
Antarctic ice gives one perfectly labeled measurement for each year
Only air bubbles can reveal anything about past climate
The newest core has already answered every question about ancient air
questions.explanation: The passage describes the two records, the new reach, and the dating work required to compare them.

questions.stem: How far back does the newer Little Dome C core reach?
choices: At least 12,000 years
At least 1.2 million years
About 120,000 years
About 800,000 years only
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the newer core reaches at least 1.2 million years.

questions.stem: Why might trapped air and nearby ice have slightly different ages?
choices: Methane makes every bubble younger than the ice
Drilling changes old ice into new snow
Air is sealed after the snow has already begun turning into ice
Oxygen cannot remain inside an ice sheet
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says air closes into bubbles only after snow has begun becoming ice.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, “archive” means
choices: a machine that predicts future weather
a shelter used by a drilling team
a single bubble with a printed date
an ordered store of records for later study
questions.explanation: The core stores several records in an ordered column, like an archive kept for study.

lesson.strategy: Track what is directly measured, what is inferred, and what must be dated. The new 1.2-million-year reach updates the scale, while the final paragraph prevents “archive” from sounding automatic or perfectly labeled.

signals.phrase: far older than any instrument record
signals.means: Explains why trapped air is valuable evidence.
Updates the former eight-hundred-thousand-year record.
Signals the parallel gas and temperature explanations.

signals.phrase: do not share exactly the same age
signals.means: Introduces the dating complication readers must retain.

vocab.inContext: small spaces in compacting snow where air can be trapped
comparisons between amounts of heavier and lighter forms
an ordered store of records preserved for later study

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the preserved evidence and the interpretation work; neither alone captures the passage.
skillTips.inference: Follow the sequence from fallen snow to sealed pore to explain the age difference.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “many physical records” explains why the core is called an archive.
skillTips.detail: Keep the old and new records separate: about 800,000 years versus at least 1.2 million.

passages.title: Why Leaves Change Color
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In summer, most leaves are green. The green comes from a substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll helps the tree make food from sunlight. The tree makes so much of it that green covers every other color. Leaves also hold yellow and orange colors all summer long. We cannot see them. The strong green hides them.

In autumn, the days get shorter and the air gets cold. The tree gets less sunlight, so making food becomes hard. The tree stops making chlorophyll. The old green fades away. Now the yellow and orange show. They were always there.

Some trees, like maples, also make a new red color in autumn. Bright days and cool nights help this red grow strong. Then the tree seals the small tube that joins each leaf to the branch. Water and food stop moving. The leaf dries, and the wind takes it down. The tree rests through the winter. In spring, new leaves open, and the green returns.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Trees make brand new yellow and orange colors when the weather turns cold.
Autumn colors appear mostly because the green that hid them fades away.
Leaves fall because the wind gets much stronger in autumn.
Maple trees are the only trees that change color in autumn.
questions.explanation: The text says the yellow and orange are in the leaf all summer but are hidden by the strong green. When the tree stops making chlorophyll, the green fades and those colors show. Red is the one new color, and only in some trees.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does chlorophyll do for the tree?
choices: It keeps the leaf warm in cold air.
It seals the tube between the leaf and the branch.
It carries water up from the roots.
It helps the tree make food from sunlight.
questions.explanation: The third sentence states it directly: chlorophyll helps the tree make food from sunlight. Sealing the tube is a separate step the tree takes later.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a leaf falls mainly because
choices: the tree itself cuts off the leaf's water and food
autumn wind is much stronger than summer wind
the yellow and orange colors make the leaf heavier
insects damage the leaf during the summer
questions.explanation: The tree seals the tube, so water and food stop moving and the leaf dries. The wind only takes down a leaf the tree has already closed off. Weight and insects are never mentioned.

questions.stem: In this passage, "fades" means
choices: grows brighter
spreads wider
slowly becomes weaker until it is gone
turns into red
questions.explanation: "The old green fades away" comes right after the tree stops making chlorophyll, and right before the hidden colors show. So the green is slowly weakening and disappearing.

lesson.strategy: This passage follows the seasons in order: summer, then autumn, then winter and spring. Read it as a simple time line and ask at each step what the tree stops doing. The key sentence is short and easy to miss: the yellow and orange were in the leaf the whole time.

signals.phrase: In summer, most leaves are green.
signals.means: The starting point of the time line. Everything later is a change from this.

signals.phrase: In autumn, the days get shorter
signals.means: A time marker. The season has turned, so expect the tree's behavior to change.
"so" links a cause to its result: less sunlight causes the food problem.
The main point in one short sentence. Nothing new appeared; something was uncovered.

vocab.inContext: the green material in a leaf that turns sunlight into food
slowly loses strength and disappears
closes something tightly so nothing can pass through

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage explains a change, the main idea is usually the reason for the change, not the list of steps.
skillTips.inference: An inference is a small step past the words. The text says the tree seals the tube and the leaf dries; you conclude that the tree, not the wind, starts the fall.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the sentences around a word. "Fades" sits between "stops making chlorophyll" and "now the yellow shows," so it must mean the green is going away.
skillTips.detail: Detail answers are stated in one sentence. Find that sentence and match it word for word before choosing.

passages.title: The Tern's Long Year
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The Arctic tern is a small white seabird with a sharp red bill. It weighs about as much as an apple. Yet no animal on Earth travels farther in a year.

Each northern summer, the tern nests near the Arctic. When the cold returns, it leaves. It flies south across the Atlantic to the sea ice around Antarctica, where the southern summer is just beginning. Months later, it turns around and comes back.

Scientists once could only guess at the route. Then they fitted terns with tiny trackers, light enough for a small bird to carry. The data showed a journey of about seventy thousand kilometres a year, and a path that was not straight. The birds curved across the ocean to catch helpful winds, because fighting the wind costs energy they cannot spare.

A tern may live more than thirty years. Over such a life, its flights add up to more than two trips to the moon and back. Because it follows summer from one end of the planet to the other, it also sees more daylight than any other creature alive.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: how scientists build trackers that are small enough for birds
why the Atlantic Ocean has such strong winds
how a very small seabird makes the longest journey of any animal
why terns choose to nest in cold places instead of warm ones
questions.explanation: Every paragraph supports one claim made in the first paragraph: no animal travels farther in a year. The trackers and the winds are details that explain how the journey was measured and flown.

questions.stem: About how far does a tern travel in one year, according to the tracking data?
choices: about seven thousand kilometres
about seventy thousand kilometres
about thirty thousand kilometres
about two million kilometres
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives the figure directly: about seventy thousand kilometres a year. Thirty is the bird's possible age in years, not a distance.

questions.stem: Why do the terns curve across the ocean instead of flying straight?
choices: A straight route would carry them over land, where they cannot rest.
The trackers only record data along certain paths.
They are following older birds who know the way.
A longer path with helpful winds costs them less energy than a short, hard one.
questions.explanation: The text says they curve to catch helpful winds because fighting the wind costs energy they cannot spare. So the longer route is the cheaper one.

questions.stem: In "energy they cannot spare", the word "spare" means
choices: have extra of, and so can afford to give up
store safely for the winter
share with other birds
measure with care
questions.explanation: The sentence explains why the birds avoid fighting the wind. They have no energy to waste, so "cannot spare" means they have none extra to lose.

lesson.strategy: The first paragraph makes a surprising claim, and the rest of the passage backs it up with numbers and reasons. Read paragraph one as the thesis, then check what each later paragraph adds: the route, the measurement, the total over a lifetime. Watch for the word "because"; it marks the two explanations.

signals.phrase: Yet no animal on Earth travels farther in a year.
signals.means: "Yet" flips the small size into a surprise. This sentence is the claim the passage will prove.
A repeating time marker. The story is about a yearly cycle, not one trip.

signals.phrase: because fighting the wind costs energy they cannot spare
signals.means: A reason. It explains why a longer curved route is smarter than a straight one.

signals.phrase: it follows summer from one end of the planet to the other
signals.means: Another reason, this time for the daylight claim that closes the passage.

vocab.inContext: the path taken from one place to another
small devices that record where an animal goes
to have enough extra that you can afford to lose some

skillTips.main-idea: When paragraph one states something surprising, the main idea is usually that claim, not the evidence that follows.
skillTips.inference: Join two facts: the path is curved, and fighting wind is costly. The conclusion is that the birds trade distance for easier flying.
skillTips.vocabulary: A word inside a "because" clause is explained by the clause's job. "Spare" appears in a reason for saving effort, so it must be about having extra.
skillTips.detail: Numbers are easy to mix up. Match the number to its unit: seventy thousand kilometres, thirty years.

passages.title: The Cactus and the Rain
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The saguaro is the tall cactus of the Sonoran Desert, in Arizona and northern Mexico. Rain there is rare, and it arrives in short, heavy storms. A plant that cannot use that water within a few hours will not get another chance for months.

The saguaro is built for those hours. Its roots are shallow, but they spread out wide, reaching about as far from the plant as the plant is tall. They sit just under the surface, where the first rain lands. When a storm passes, the roots drink fast.

The body of the cactus is folded like an accordion. As water comes in, the folds open and the trunk grows thicker. A large saguaro full of water can weigh more than a ton. In the dry months the folds close again, and the plant stands thin.

Everything else about the saguaro is slow. It may need ten years to grow as tall as your thumb, and fifty years or more before its first arm appears. A patient plant can live more than a hundred and fifty years in a place where nothing is easy.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: The saguaro grows fast so that it can reach water deep underground.
The Sonoran Desert receives more rain than most people believe.
The saguaro is built to catch rare rain quickly and then live slowly on it.
The arms of the saguaro are its most important part.
questions.explanation: The passage pairs two ideas: fast collection during the short storms, and a slow life between them. The other choices contradict the text, which says the roots are shallow and growth is slow.

questions.stem: How far do the roots of a saguaro spread?
choices: about as far from the plant as the plant is tall
only a few centimetres in each direction
deep down, below the reach of rain
as far as the nearest other cactus
questions.explanation: Paragraph two states the comparison directly. The text also says the roots are shallow, which rules out the deep answer.

questions.stem: Why are shallow roots an advantage for this cactus?
choices: They keep the tall plant from falling over in strong wind.
They allow it to reach underground rivers.
They stay cooler than deep roots during the day.
The rain comes in short storms, so the water is near the surface and must be taken quickly.
questions.explanation: The passage says storms are short and the roots sit where the first rain lands. Shallow roots reach that water before it is lost. Wind, rivers and temperature are never mentioned.

questions.stem: In this passage, "rare" means
choices: worth a great deal of money
not happening often
hard to see with the eye
spread over a wide area
questions.explanation: The next sentences explain the word: rain arrives in short storms, and then there is no more for months. So "rare" here is about how seldom it happens.

lesson.strategy: This passage sets a problem in paragraph one and then answers it part by part: roots, body, and finally speed of growth. Read it as problem then solutions. Notice that the last paragraph turns the passage around, from fast to slow.

signals.phrase: Rain there is rare, and it arrives in short, heavy storms.
signals.means: The problem. Everything after this is the plant's answer to it.

signals.phrase: The saguaro is built for those hours.
signals.means: A topic sentence. The paragraph that follows will show how it is built.

signals.phrase: As water comes in, the folds open
signals.means: "As" links two things happening together, showing cause and effect inside the plant.

signals.phrase: Everything else about the saguaro is slow.
signals.means: A turn. The passage switches from speed to patience.

vocab.inContext: happening only a few times, not often
close to the surface, not deep
a musical instrument with folds that open and close, used here to picture the cactus body

skillTips.main-idea: If a passage has two halves that seem opposite, the main idea usually holds both together, not just one.
skillTips.inference: Link the shape of the plant to the shape of the weather. Short storms explain shallow roots.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read one sentence past the hard word. Here the storms and the months of waiting define "rare" for you.
skillTips.detail: When a passage gives a comparison instead of a number, keep the comparison whole: as far out as the plant is tall.

passages.title: What Beavers Build
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A beaver does not build a dam because it wants a pond. It builds because it cannot stand the sound of running water. Play a recording of a stream beside a dry bank, and a beaver will pile branches and mud against the loudspeaker.

That simple rule changes whole valleys. Branch by branch, the dam slows the stream, the water spreads out behind it, and a pond forms. In the middle of the pond the beaver builds a lodge, and the door of the lodge sits under the water, where a wolf cannot follow.

The pond is useful to more than the beaver. Slow water drops the mud and sand it was carrying, so the valley floor rises and turns soft. Water sinks into the ground instead of rushing away, and the ground stays wet through dry weeks. Frogs, fish, insects and birds arrive.

The beaver has no plan for any of this. It answers one sound, and a wetland appears behind it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Beavers plan wetlands so that frogs and fish will have a home.
Beavers harm valleys by stopping the streams that run through them.
One simple instinct in the beaver builds a whole wetland it never intended.
Wolves are the main reason that beavers live in ponds.
questions.explanation: The passage begins with the simple trigger, shows the large results, and ends by saying the beaver has no plan for any of it. That contrast is the point.

questions.stem: Where is the door of the beaver's lodge?
choices: on the dry bank behind the dam
under the water
at the top of the lodge
inside the dam itself
questions.explanation: Paragraph two says the door sits under the water, where a wolf cannot follow.

questions.stem: What does the loudspeaker example show?
choices: Beavers are drawn to any loud noise.
Beavers must have running water in order to drink.
People can teach beavers to build in new places.
The building behaviour is set off by a sound, not by a plan for a pond.
questions.explanation: There is no stream at the loudspeaker, only the sound, and the beaver still builds. That separates the trigger from any goal. Nothing in the text says beavers respond to noise in general.

questions.stem: In "beside a dry bank", the word "bank" means
choices: a business that keeps people's money
a long row of machines
the sloping ground at the edge of water
a thick pile of snow
questions.explanation: The word appears where a stream would normally be, and the writer marks it "dry" to show there is no water there now. So it is the land at a water's edge.

lesson.strategy: The passage moves from a very small cause to a very large effect, then names the gap between them. Read paragraph one for the trigger, paragraphs two and three for the chain of results, and the last two sentences for the point. Follow the words "because" and "so" to keep the chain in order.

signals.phrase: because it cannot stand the sound of running water.
signals.means: The real cause, given in place of the obvious one. "Because" marks it.

signals.phrase: That simple rule changes whole valleys.
signals.means: A jump in scale. The passage now moves from one animal to a landscape.

signals.phrase: so the valley floor rises and turns soft
signals.means: "so" marks a result inside the chain of effects.

signals.phrase: The beaver has no plan for any of this.
signals.means: The final turn. Big results here come from instinct, not intention.

vocab.inContext: the sloping ground along the edge of a stream
the dome of sticks and mud a beaver lives in
low ground that stays wet, where water plants and animals live

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer ends by denying something ("has no plan"), that denial is often the main idea.
skillTips.inference: An experiment in a passage is there to prove one thing. Ask what changed and what stayed the same: sound stayed, water was gone.
skillTips.vocabulary: Common words have uncommon meanings. If "bank" sits next to a stream, choose the meaning that fits water, not money.
skillTips.detail: Small location words matter. "Under the water" is the whole answer, and it also explains the wolf.

passages.title: The Trade Under the Forest
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Walk through a forest and you see trunks and leaves. Most of the living exchange, though, happens under your boots.

Nearly all forest trees share their roots with fungi. The fungus grows fine threads through the soil, far thinner than any root and far more numerous. Those threads reach into spaces a root could never enter, and they pull out water and minerals such as phosphorus. In return, the tree hands over sugar it has made from sunlight. Neither partner could do the other's work well, so each pays for a service it cannot perform.

Because the threads of one fungus can touch several trees, a forest can be joined underground. Careful experiments have followed marked carbon from one tree into a neighbour through such a link, and that finding is solid.

What the link means is less settled. It is tempting to call the network a system for sharing, as if the trees were feeding the weak ones. But a fungus is not a charity. It is a partner with its own interests, and some of that movement may serve the fungus more than any tree. The connection is proven. The kindness is not.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage as a whole?
choices: Fungi live on trees as pests and slowly drain their sugar.
Trees and fungi trade what each cannot make, and while the underground link is proven, the idea that trees share out of kindness is not.
Scientists have shown that strong trees deliberately feed weaker ones.
Forest soil holds far more minerals than most people expect.
questions.explanation: The first half explains the trade and the proven link. The last paragraph pulls back from the warm interpretation. Both halves belong in the main idea.

questions.stem: What does the tree give the fungus?
choices: water pulled from small spaces in the soil
phosphorus and other minerals
sugar it has made from sunlight
fine threads that spread through the soil
questions.explanation: The other three items all belong to the fungus's side of the trade. The tree's payment is sugar made from sunlight.

questions.stem: The writer would most likely agree that
choices: a headline saying "trees feed their weak neighbours out of care" claims more than the evidence supports
the carbon experiments were poorly designed
tree roots and fungal threads never actually touch
forests would grow better if the fungi were removed
questions.explanation: The writer calls the connection proven but the kindness unproven, and warns that a fungus has its own interests. That is a caution about the interpretation, not about the experiments.

questions.stem: In "What the link means is less settled", the word "settled" means
choices: calm and quiet
paid in full
moved into a new home
agreed on and decided
questions.explanation: It contrasts with the previous sentence, where a finding is called solid. If the finding is agreed, the meaning is not yet agreed.

lesson.strategy: This passage builds a claim and then limits it. Paragraphs two and three explain a real exchange and a real measurement; the last paragraph separates what was measured from what people like to believe about it. Read for the hinge sentence where the writer stops describing and starts judging.

signals.phrase: the tree hands over sugar it has made from sunlight.
signals.means: "In return" marks the second half of an exchange. Both sides are now on the table.

signals.phrase: What the link means is less settled.
signals.means: The hinge. Facts stop here and interpretation begins.

signals.phrase: But a fungus is not a charity.
signals.means: "But" rejects the appealing reading offered in the sentence before.

signals.phrase: The connection is proven. The kindness is not.
signals.means: The conclusion, split into two short lines to keep proof and story apart.

vocab.inContext: attractive and easy to believe, even if it may be wrong
an organisation or person that gives help without asking anything back
finally agreed and no longer argued about

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage ends by qualifying its own story, the main idea must include the limit, not only the discovery.
skillTips.inference: To infer an author's view, find where the author disagrees with someone. Here it is "a fungus is not a charity."
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast is a definition tool. "Less settled" opposes "solid", so settled must mean agreed.
skillTips.detail: In a trade, keep the two sides separate. List who gives what before answering.

passages.title: Salmon Find the Way Home
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A young salmon leaves a small stream, swims to the sea, and spends years there. Then, as an adult, it comes back. Not to the coast in general, but to the same stream where it hatched.

It solves the problem in two steps. Far out at sea, the fish appears to read the Earth's magnetic field, which differs slightly from place to place and works like a rough map. That map is good enough to bring the salmon near the right stretch of coast, but not good enough to pick one creek out of a hundred.

Close to shore, the salmon switches to smell. As a young fish it learned the particular odour of its home water: the soil, the plants, the rock the stream ran over. Now it tests the water at each junction and turns toward the smell it remembers.

The journey ends in exhaustion. Pacific salmon spawn once and then die, and their bodies stay in the stream. Bears drag some of them into the trees. Chemical tests can find, in the wood of forests beside such streams, nitrogen that came from the open ocean and was carried inland inside fish.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Salmon use two different methods, one at sea and one near the coast, to return to the exact stream where they hatched.
Bears depend on salmon for most of their yearly food.
Salmon prefer salt water and stay in the ocean as long as they can.
The Earth's magnetic field is the same in every part of the ocean.
questions.explanation: The middle paragraphs are organised as step one and step two of a single navigation problem. The bears and the nitrogen come after the journey and are not the subject.

questions.stem: What does the salmon use to choose the right creek once it is close to shore?
choices: the temperature of the water
the smell of its home water
the direction of the current
the position of the sun
questions.explanation: Paragraph three says the salmon switches to smell and turns toward the odour it learned as a young fish.

questions.stem: Why is the magnetic map not enough on its own?
choices: It only works during the night.
It stops working once the fish becomes an adult.
It brings the fish to the right region but cannot separate one creek from its neighbours.
It points the fish in the wrong direction near land.
questions.explanation: The text says the map is good enough for the right stretch of coast but not for picking one creek out of a hundred. That gap is exactly what smell fills.

questions.stem: In this passage, "junction" means
choices: a place where waters meet and the fish must choose a way
a deep pool where fish rest
the mouth of a river at the sea
a narrow gap between two rocks
questions.explanation: The salmon tests the water at each junction and then turns. A choice of direction is only needed where two waters meet.

lesson.strategy: The passage announces its own structure: two steps, then an ending. Use the announcement as a map, and read each middle paragraph as one step with its own limit. The final paragraph is not navigation at all; it follows the fish's body after death.

signals.phrase: It solves the problem in two steps.
signals.means: A structure sentence. Expect exactly two methods, in order.
Marks step one and the place it applies.

signals.phrase: but not good enough to pick one creek out of a hundred
signals.means: The limit of step one. It creates the need for step two.

signals.phrase: Close to shore, the salmon switches to smell.
signals.means: Marks step two, with both the place and the method.

vocab.inContext: a smell, especially one that can be recognised
a point where two streams or paths join
to lay eggs, of fish

skillTips.main-idea: A sentence like "in two steps" usually names the shape of the whole passage. Build the main idea around it.
skillTips.inference: Look for a stated limit. Whatever a method cannot do explains why the next method exists.
skillTips.vocabulary: Watch the verb next to the word. "Tests the water at each junction and turns" tells you a choice of route is happening.
skillTips.detail: Keep the two steps in their places: magnetic field at sea, smell near shore. Mixing them is the usual mistake.

passages.title: Two Lives in One
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The grey-green crust on an old stone wall is not one organism. A lichen is a fungus living together with a partner that can feed it: an alga, a bacterium that works like one, or both. The fungus builds the body and holds the water. The partner turns sunlight into sugar. Apart, neither would last long on bare rock; together they cover mountains.

For a century, textbooks called this a partnership of two. Then researchers looked at the cells more closely and found a third member in many lichens, a yeast that had been present all along and missed by everyone. The old picture was not wrong so much as too small.

Lichens grow at a pace that is hard to imagine. Some spread less than a millimetre a year, so a patch the size of a coin may be older than the wall it sits on. They also work on the stone, releasing weak acids that loosen its grains and begin the slow business of making soil.

They have one weakness. A lichen takes in whatever the air carries and cannot spit any of it out again. Where the air is dirty, the crust disappears, which is why a wall covered in lichen is also a report on the air around it.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the passage?
choices: Lichens grow much faster than most people believe.
A lichen is a partnership of more than one kind of life; it grows very slowly, it makes soil, and it fails where the air is dirty.
Lichens are small plants that prefer to live on stone walls.
The yeast is the most important member of every lichen.
questions.explanation: The four paragraphs cover the partnership, the correction to it, the slow growth and rock work, and the weakness. Only one choice holds those together, and the others contradict the text.

questions.stem: What did researchers find when they examined lichen cells more closely?
choices: that the alga was doing all of the work
that lichens grow faster in clean air
that a yeast was also present in many lichens
that the fungus was in fact a bacterium
questions.explanation: Paragraph two states it: a third member, a yeast, had been there all along and was missed.

questions.stem: A wall in a city centre is bare, while a wall of the same age in the countryside is covered in lichen. What does the passage most support?
choices: The city wall is built from a different kind of stone.
The countryside wall gets more rain.
The city wall is cleaned by people more often.
The city air carries more pollution.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says a lichen absorbs whatever the air carries and disappears where the air is dirty, so its absence is evidence about the air. Stone type, rain and cleaning are never discussed.

questions.stem: In "Lichens grow at a pace that is hard to imagine", the word "pace" means
choices: a single step taken while walking
the speed at which something happens
a distance measured on foot
the open space around a plant
questions.explanation: The next sentence gives millimetres per year, which is a rate. So "pace" means how fast or slow the growth is.

lesson.strategy: Each paragraph here does one job: define, correct, describe, then warn. Read the second paragraph carefully, because it revises the definition you were just given. The last paragraph turns a weakness into a use for people.

signals.means: A negative opening. The writer removes a wrong idea before giving the right one.

signals.phrase: neither would last long on bare rock; together they cover
signals.means: A contrast pair that shows why the partnership exists.
A shift from strengths to a limit. Expect the drawback next.

signals.phrase: a wall covered in lichen is also a report on the air
signals.means: "which is why" draws a conclusion from the weakness just described.

vocab.inContext: a thin hard layer on the surface of something
a simple living thing, like a very small water plant, that makes food from sunlight
the speed at which something develops

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage corrects itself midway, the main idea should reflect the corrected version, not the first one.
skillTips.inference: Absence can be evidence. If lichen dies in dirty air, a bare wall points to dirty air.
skillTips.vocabulary: Look for a measurement after the word. Millimetres a year defines "pace" as a rate.
skillTips.detail: Note who found what and when. The yeast is a recent finding, not part of the century-old picture.

passages.title: Forests That Need Fire
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Some trees do not merely survive fire; they wait for it. The lodgepole pine seals many of its cones shut with resin, and those cones can hang closed on the branch for years. Only heat melts the seal. When a fire passes, the cones open and drop their seed onto ground that has just been cleared of competitors and dusted with ash. A disaster, from the seed's point of view, is a delivery.

The giant sequoia depends on the same arrangement and on a second favour. Its seedlings cannot start in deep litter or in shade; they need bare soil and open sky. Fire supplies both, burning off the layer of dead needles and thinning the smaller trees that would otherwise close the roof of the forest.

This explains an uncomfortable result of good intentions. For much of the twentieth century, fire in North American forests was fought wherever it appeared. The forests did not become safer. Dead wood built up year after year, young trees crowded in, and the fires that finally came were hotter and harder to stop than the ones that had been prevented. Removing a frequent small disturbance did not remove disturbance. It saved it up.

questions.stem: What is the central argument of the passage?
choices: Fire is purely destructive and should be stopped as early as possible.
Lodgepole pines and sequoias are the tallest trees in North America.
Some trees depend on fire, and decades of preventing fire made the later fires worse.
Ash from burnt wood is the best fertiliser available to a young tree.
questions.explanation: The first two paragraphs show trees that need fire; the third shows what happened when fire was removed. The argument joins the two.

questions.stem: What makes the lodgepole pine's sealed cones open?
choices: heat, which melts the resin holding them shut
heavy rain after a long dry season
the weight of winter snow on the branch
birds that break them apart for the seed
questions.explanation: The passage says the cones are sealed with resin and that only heat melts the seal.

questions.stem: Why did fighting every fire fail to make the forests safer?
choices: The firefighters were poorly trained and equipped.
The fuel that small fires would have removed built up until the fires that came were far hotter.
Trees stopped producing seed once fires were prevented.
