The regional climate grew drier in every single year of the century.
questions.explanation: The passage lists dead wood building up and young trees crowding in, then says the eventual fires were hotter and harder to stop. The closing line calls this saving disturbance up.

questions.stem: In "seedlings cannot start in deep litter", the word "litter" means
choices: rubbish dropped by visitors to the forest
a group of young animals born at one time
the layer of dead needles and leaves lying on the ground
loose stones washed downhill by rain
questions.explanation: The next sentence says fire burns off the layer of dead needles, which is the same thing named again. So litter here is fallen plant material.

lesson.strategy: The passage argues by cases: two trees that need fire, then one policy that ignored the need. Read the first sentence as the thesis and watch for the paragraph that turns from biology to human decisions. The last two sentences state the cost of that decision in the plainest words in the passage.

signals.phrase: Some trees do not merely survive fire; they wait for it.
signals.means: The thesis. "Not merely" tells you the usual idea is about to be pushed further.
The key mechanism, isolated in a short sentence so it cannot be missed.

signals.phrase: This explains an uncomfortable result of good intentions.
signals.means: The pivot from nature to policy, and a warning that the result will be unwelcome.

signals.phrase: The forests did not become safer.
signals.means: Contradicts what the reader expects from the action just described.

vocab.inContext: a sticky substance made by a tree, here hardened to hold cones shut
the layer of dead leaves and needles on the forest floor
an event that breaks up a system, such as a fire in a forest

skillTips.main-idea: In an argument passage, the main idea usually spans the examples and the conclusion drawn from them.
skillTips.inference: Trace the chain: no small fires, so fuel accumulates, so the eventual fire burns hotter. Inference is often just following the chain one link past the text.
skillTips.vocabulary: A writer often renames a hard word in the next sentence. "Litter" reappears as "the layer of dead needles".
skillTips.detail: Attach each mechanism to the right tree: resin cones to the lodgepole, bare soil and open sky to the sequoia.

passages.title: What the Ice Leaves Behind
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A glacier is snow that never had a summer. Where more falls in winter than melts in the warm months, the layers press down on one another until the air is squeezed out and the pile turns to ice. Once the ice is thick enough, its own weight makes it move, and a mass that looks perfectly still is in fact travelling downhill.

Its power comes from what it carries. Stones frozen into the base act like the teeth of a file, scratching parallel lines into the bedrock beneath. Meltwater seeps into cracks, freezes, expands, and prises whole blocks free, which the ice then carries away. Working together, these two actions widen a valley as well as deepen it, which is why an old glacial valley has a broad, U-shaped floor while a river valley narrows to a V.

The evidence outlasts the ice by a very long time. Ridges of mixed rubble mark where the edge of a glacier once stood. Boulders sit in open fields hundreds of kilometres from the mountain they were broken from, and the minerals in them tell geologists which mountain that was. Long after the last of the ice is gone, the land keeps a record of where it went and how far.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
choices: Glaciers move so slowly that they change almost nothing around them.
Glaciers form from packed snow, cut the land with the rock they carry, and leave marks that outlast the ice itself.
Rivers and glaciers shape their valleys in exactly the same way.
Most large boulders in open fields were moved there by farmers.
questions.explanation: The three paragraphs are formation, erosion, and evidence. Only one choice covers all three, and the passage directly contradicts the others.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what shape is the floor of an old glacial valley?
choices: a narrow V
a broad U
a flat circle
a deep round hole
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the two: the glacial valley is broad and U-shaped, while a river valley narrows to a V.

questions.stem: A geologist finds a large boulder in a flat field, hundreds of kilometres from the only mountain made of that rock. What does the passage best support?
choices: The boulder formed in place out of the local bedrock.
A river carried the boulder there during a great flood.
Ice once crossed this land and brought the boulder from that mountain.
The boulder arrived from space as a meteorite.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph describes exactly this case: far-travelled boulders whose minerals identify the mountain, left behind by ice that has since melted.

questions.stem: In this passage, "bedrock" means
choices: the solid rock lying underneath the loose surface material
a bed of soft sand at the bottom of a lake
a heap of stones left behind by a glacier
ice that has been pressed until it is hard
questions.explanation: Stones in the base of the glacier scratch lines into the bedrock beneath, so it is the firm rock under the ice and the loose material.

lesson.strategy: This passage runs a causal chain from snow to ice to movement to erosion to evidence. Read each paragraph as one link and keep asking what causes what. The comparison of U and V shapes is the passage's test of whether you followed the mechanism.

signals.phrase: A glacier is snow that never had a summer.
signals.means: A definition disguised as an image. It tells you the whole formation story in one line.

signals.phrase: Its power comes from what it carries.
signals.means: A topic sentence. The paragraph will describe the tools, not the ice itself.

signals.phrase: these two actions widen a valley as well as deepen it
signals.means: Two causes are combined into one result, which then explains the valley's shape.

signals.phrase: The evidence outlasts the ice by a very long time.
signals.means: A turn from process to the record it leaves. Expect clues, not action.

vocab.inContext: a slow-moving mass of ice formed from packed snow
the solid rock that lies under soil and loose stone
broken stone of mixed sizes

skillTips.main-idea: For a process passage, name the beginning and the end of the chain. Here: snow at one end, lasting evidence at the other.
skillTips.inference: Use the passage's own example as a rule. It explains far-travelled boulders, so apply that explanation to a new boulder.
skillTips.vocabulary: Break the word apart and check the sentence. "Bed" plus "rock", scratched from below, gives solid rock underneath.
skillTips.detail: When two shapes are compared, hold both: U for ice, V for river. Half the pair is not an answer.

passages.title: Honest Liars
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A yellow and black band on an insect is a sentence addressed to birds. Its meaning is roughly: swallow me and regret it. Because a young bird has to learn that lesson the hard way, on a real mouthful, the warning works only if it is usually true.

Which is what makes the hoverfly interesting. It has no sting and nothing unpleasant to offer, yet it wears the wasp's colours and is left alone. It profits from a reputation it never earned and pays nothing for the lesson that protects it. The arrangement is parasitic on honesty.

It is also self-limiting. The mimic's safety rests on the odds a predator faces, and as harmless copies grow common relative to genuine wasps, more encounters end pleasantly and the band loses its force. Deceit of this kind cannot spread far without destroying the credit it draws on, which makes it rare in nature: a cheat that must stay rare to keep cheating.

The other strategy is stranger. Several species that are all genuinely unpleasant sometimes converge on one shared pattern, so a bird's single bad experience teaches it to avoid them all. Nobody is lying, and each species is spared its share of the tuition. Here the resemblance is not theft but a bill split between honest neighbours.

questions.stem: What does the passage as a whole set out to show?
choices: Birds are unable to tell any two insects apart.
Warning colours have become useless because so many insects copy them.
Wasps and hoverflies are close relatives that share an ancestor.
There are two kinds of look-alike: one that free-rides on a true warning and is limited by its own success, and one in which genuinely dangerous species share the cost of teaching predators.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs two and three describe the cheat and its built-in limit; the last paragraph presents the honest alternative. The passage is a comparison of the two.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens as harmless copies become common relative to genuine wasps?
choices: Wasps begin to change their own colours.
More encounters end pleasantly for the predator, and the warning loses its force.
Predators stop hunting insects altogether.
The copies slowly develop a real sting of their own.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states it directly. The mimic's protection depends on the odds, and common mimics improve those odds for the bird.

questions.stem: Why can the honest look-alikes stay common without losing their protection, while the hoverfly cannot?
choices: Because every one of them really is unpleasant, so more of them makes the lesson stronger rather than weaker.
Because they are larger and therefore easier for a bird to see.
Because birds never manage to learn their pattern at all.
Because they live in places where predators happen to be rare.
questions.explanation: The mimic weakens the signal because it makes the warning false more often. When all the sharers are genuinely unpleasant, every extra encounter confirms the warning instead of undermining it.

questions.stem: In "each species is spared its share of the tuition", the word "tuition" means
choices: the food that a predator eats
the pattern carried on the wings
the cost of teaching the predator its lesson
a formal school attended by young birds
questions.explanation: The lesson costs the insects that get eaten while a bird learns. Sharing one pattern splits that price, which the writer then calls a bill split between neighbours.

lesson.strategy: Hold onto the condition stated at the end of paragraph one. The next two paragraphs test a mimic that weakens the warning, while the last presents a strategy that preserves it. Use the short paragraph openings to mark the change between cases.

signals.phrase: the warning works only if it is usually true
signals.means: The condition the whole argument depends on. Judge every later case against it.
A second turn. The cheat is not only unfair, it contains its own brake.
A structural pivot to the second case, and a hint that it will overturn expectations.
Marks the key difference from the earlier case, in the plainest possible words.

vocab.inContext: living off something else without giving anything back
to come to resemble one another, arriving at the same form
the price paid for teaching, here the cost of educating the predator

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage sets out two contrasting cases, the main idea is the contrast itself, not either case alone.
skillTips.inference: Reason from the stated condition. If the warning must usually be true, then any copy that makes it false more often weakens itself.
skillTips.vocabulary: Money words used about animals are metaphors. "Credit", "bill" and "tuition" all treat a reputation as something bought and paid for.
skillTips.detail: Track direction carefully. It is the ratio of copies to real wasps that matters, not the number of copies on its own.

passages.title: Wangari Maathai and the Trees
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Wangari Maathai grew up in a village in Kenya. As a girl she carried water from a clean stream near her home. Trees stood along the banks and held the soil in place.

She was a strong student. She won a place at a college in the United States and studied biology there. When she came home, she saw that many trees were gone. The streams ran brown with mud, and women walked far to find firewood.

In 1977 she started a simple plan. She asked rural women to plant seedlings and to care for them. For each tree that lived, the women earned a small payment. The plan grew into the Green Belt Movement, and over the years the women planted tens of millions of trees.

Some officials did not like her. She was arrested more than once, and the police beat her. She kept working. In 2004 she won the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it. The prize honored a plain idea: caring for the land is also caring for peace.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Maathai studied biology in the United States and then taught school.
Maathai turned tree planting by rural women into a movement that also stood for peace.
Kenya lost its streams because the rain stopped falling.
Maathai wanted women to walk shorter distances for firewood.
questions.explanation: The passage follows one line: she saw the land damaged, organized women to plant trees, and the Nobel Prize connected that work to peace. The other choices are small details or things the text never says.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did the women receive for their work?
choices: A place at a college in the United States
Free firewood from the government
A small payment for each tree that lived
A tree to keep inside their homes
questions.explanation: The text says, 'For each tree that lived, the women earned a small payment.' Payment depended on the tree surviving, not on planting alone.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about how Maathai answered danger?
choices: She kept working even though it was dangerous.
She stopped planting trees for several years.
She moved to the United States to be safe.
She asked the officials to join her movement.
questions.explanation: The text places 'She kept working' right after the arrests and the beating. That order tells you the danger did not stop her. Nothing says she left or paused.

questions.stem: In the passage, what are 'seedlings'?
choices: Tools for digging holes
Bags of clean water
Yearly payments to workers
Very young plants
questions.explanation: The women 'plant seedlings and care for them,' and later 'the women planted tens of millions of trees.' So a seedling is a young tree before it grows.

lesson.strategy: This is a simple life story told in time order: childhood, study, the problem she found, the plan, the prize. Read it as four steps and put a mental mark at each date. When a date appears, ask what changed at that moment.

signals.phrase: In 1977 she started a simple plan.
signals.means: A turning point. Everything after this sentence is the plan and its results.
A condition. The money came only when a tree survived, so care mattered more than planting.

signals.phrase: Some officials did not like her.
signals.means: A problem is coming. Expect trouble in the next sentences.

signals.phrase: In 2004 she won the Nobel Peace Prize
signals.means: The result of the whole story. The writer is closing the arc that began in 1977.

vocab.inContext: very young trees, small enough to carry and plant by hand
living in the countryside, away from cities
people with power in the government

skillTips.main-idea: In a life story, the main idea is usually the work the person is remembered for, not the first thing they did. Ask: what does the last paragraph say the whole life added up to?
skillTips.inference: When two sentences sit side by side with no 'because', the writer still wants you to connect them. Arrests, then 'She kept working' means she chose to continue.
skillTips.vocabulary: For an unknown noun, look for the verb next to it. 'Plant seedlings' tells you a seedling is something you put in the ground.
skillTips.detail: Details with numbers and dates are easy to check. Go back to the exact sentence instead of trusting memory.

passages.title: Hokusai and Mount Fuji
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Katsushika Hokusai was born in Japan in 1760. He began drawing as a boy and never really stopped. He worked in woodblock printing, a craft in which a drawing is carved into blocks of wood and then printed on paper many times. Because prints were cheap, ordinary people could own his pictures.

Hokusai changed his artist name more than thirty times. Each new name marked a new stage in his work. He drew fishermen, farmers, bridges, ghosts, and quiet streets. He also filled sketchbooks with quick studies of hands, faces, and animals.

In his seventies he made his most famous series, Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. In every print the mountain appears somewhere, sometimes wide and calm, sometimes small behind a wave or a roof. The best known image shows a huge wave curling over small boats while Fuji sits quietly in the distance.

Hokusai died in 1849, at about eighty-eight. Late in life he wrote that he was still learning, and that his real work would begin only if he lived many more years.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Hokusai grew rich because his prints were expensive.
Woodblock printing began in Japan in 1760.
Hokusai drew all his life, and his cheap prints reached ordinary people.
Hokusai painted only Mount Fuji during his whole career.
questions.explanation: The passage stays on two points: he never stopped working, and prints put his pictures in ordinary hands. He drew many subjects, not only Fuji, and the text never mentions wealth.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why could ordinary people own Hokusai's pictures?
choices: Because prints were cheap
Because he gave them away at temples
Because the government bought them for the public
Because he painted each one by hand
questions.explanation: The text gives the reason directly: prints were cheap, so ordinary people could own them. Printing from wood blocks is the opposite of painting each picture by hand.

questions.stem: What does his habit of changing his artist name more than thirty times suggest about him?
choices: He wanted to hide from the people who bought his prints.
He kept changing the way he worked, again and again.
He was not allowed to keep one name.
He shared his workshop with thirty other artists.
questions.explanation: The text says each new name 'marked a new stage in his work,' so the names track changes in his art. Hiding, rules, and other artists are never mentioned.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'studies' means:
choices: rooms where an artist works
lessons taken at a school
books written about art
quick practice drawings
questions.explanation: The word sits inside 'filled sketchbooks with quick studies of hands, faces, and animals.' In a sketchbook, a study is a practice drawing, not a lesson or a room.

lesson.strategy: This life story is told in time order, but each paragraph also answers one question: how he worked, how he changed, what he made, how he ended. Read one paragraph, name its question, then move on. That keeps the many names and dates from blurring together.

signals.means: A cause. The next part of the sentence is the effect it produced.

signals.phrase: Each new name marked a new stage in his work.
signals.means: The writer explains the meaning of a strange fact, so you do not have to guess.

signals.phrase: In his seventies he made his most famous series
signals.means: The high point of the story. Slow down here.

signals.phrase: Late in life he wrote that he was still learning
signals.means: A closing idea about his character, not a new event.

vocab.inContext: a skilled kind of making, learned by practice
a set of prints that belong together and share one subject
quick practice drawings made to learn a shape

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage repeats an idea in different words ('never really stopped', 'still learning'), that repetition is pointing at the main idea.
skillTips.inference: A strange fact plus the writer's short explanation is an invitation to infer. Thirty names plus 'a new stage' means his art kept changing.
skillTips.vocabulary: The same word can mean different things. Let the sentence around it decide: 'studies' inside a sketchbook must be drawings.
skillTips.detail: Cause questions ask for the reason the text gives, not the reason you think is true. Look for 'because'.

passages.title: Sequoyah Creates a Cherokee Syllabary
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the early 1800s, Cherokee people already spoke a rich language, but it did not yet have a widely used writing system. Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, saw how English writing carried messages. He began searching for a way to represent Cherokee speech on a page.

At first, Sequoyah tried to make one symbol for each word. There were far too many words for that plan. He changed his method and made symbols for the syllables, or sound units, used in Cherokee. He completed a set of eighty-five characters. A syllabary is not an alphabet: its characters represent syllables rather than single letters.

Sequoyah tested the system with his daughter. They could exchange written messages even when they had not heard each other speak. The test showed that the marks carried Cherokee words.

The Cherokee Nation adopted the syllabary in 1825, and many Cherokee people learned it rapidly. In 1828, the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper began printing in both Cherokee and English. Sequoyah did not create the Cherokee language. He created a writing system that Cherokee speakers used to record and share their existing language.

questions.stem: Which statement best gives the passage’s main idea?
choices: Sequoyah invented the Cherokee language and then taught its existing speakers how to write and speak it.
Sequoyah created a syllabary that enabled Cherokee speakers to write their existing language.
Sequoyah replaced Cherokee speech with English letters borrowed for a new alphabet.
Sequoyah built a printing press that could publish only English-language newspapers.
questions.explanation: The passage is specifically about Sequoyah creating a syllabary for the existing Cherokee language.

questions.stem: Why did Sequoyah abandon one symbol for every word?
choices: His daughter could not hear any spoken Cherokee during their later test.
The Cherokee Nation required him to use letters from an English alphabet.
The Cherokee language had too many words for a separate symbol for every word.
Newspapers of the period could print numbers but could not print written words.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says there were far too many words for a one-symbol-per-word system.

questions.stem: What did the test with Sequoyah’s daughter show?
choices: The characters worked only when both people spoke each written message aloud.
The writing system still needed thousands of symbols before it could carry a message.
The symbols represented English words instead of the sounds used in spoken Cherokee.
The writing could carry Cherokee words between people on its own.
questions.explanation: Because they exchanged messages without hearing each other, the marks themselves had to carry the Cherokee words.

questions.stem: A “syllabary” is a writing system whose characters represent
choices: whole books or stories rather than units of sound
syllables in spoken words
single numbers used to count printed characters
only the names of people, places, and newspapers
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines a syllabary by contrasting syllables with the single letters of an alphabet.

lesson.strategy: Keep language and writing system separate. Paragraph one names the existing spoken language, paragraph two defines the syllabary, paragraph three tests it, and paragraph four shows adoption. The final contrast prevents the misleading claim that Sequoyah created Cherokee itself.

signals.means: Establishes that Cherokee existed before this writing system.
Marks the shift from a failed word-symbol plan to syllables.

signals.phrase: A syllabary is not an alphabet
signals.means: Defines the precise type of writing system by contrast.

signals.phrase: did not create the Cherokee language
signals.means: Corrects the title-level misconception directly.

vocab.inContext: a craftsperson who makes or repairs objects made of silver
sound units that form spoken words
a writing system with characters representing syllables

skillTips.main-idea: Use the precise title: Sequoyah created a Cherokee syllabary, not the Cherokee language.
skillTips.detail: The failed plan and its problem are both stated at the start of paragraph two.
skillTips.inference: Messages exchanged without spoken clues show that the marks themselves carried language.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the explicit contrast: a syllabary represents syllables, while an alphabet represents letters.

passages.title: Rachel Carson's Careful Case
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Rachel Carson trained as a marine biologist at a time when very few women held science jobs in the United States government. She joined the federal fisheries agency in the 1930s and spent her first years writing radio scripts and pamphlets about fish and the sea. The work paid poorly, but it taught her something valuable: how to explain science to people who had never studied it.

Her books about the ocean sold well, and by the 1950s she could write full time. Then letters began to reach her about birds dying after fields and neighborhoods were sprayed with chemical pesticides. Carson spent four years reading studies, checking claims, and writing slowly, because she expected the chemical industry to attack her.

Silent Spring appeared in 1962. It did not demand that all pesticides be banned. It argued something narrower and harder to dismiss: that powerful chemicals were being spread across the country without anyone measuring what they did to the rest of the living world. Companies called her emotional and unqualified. The evidence held. Carson died of cancer in 1964, before she could see the laws her book helped set in motion.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: Carson proved that every pesticide should be banned at once.
Carson used her gift for explaining science to build a careful, limited case about untested spraying.
Carson spent her career writing radio scripts for a government agency.
The chemical companies won the public argument over Silent Spring.
questions.explanation: The passage joins her early training in plain explanation to the book she later wrote, and stresses that her claim was narrow. The text says directly that she did not demand a total ban, and that her evidence held.

questions.stem: How long did Carson work on Silent Spring before it appeared?
choices: One year
Ten years
Since the 1930s
Four years
questions.explanation: The text says she 'spent four years reading studies, checking claims, and writing slowly.' The 1930s date belongs to her government job.

questions.stem: Why did Carson check her claims so slowly and carefully?
choices: She expected the chemical industry to attack her work.
Her publisher refused to print anything unchecked.
She had no training in science.
The government required proof before she could publish.
questions.explanation: The passage gives the reason in the same sentence: 'because she expected the chemical industry to attack her.' Careful work was a defense against that attack.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'dismiss' means:
choices: to send a worker away from a job
to explain something in simple words
to reject an idea as not worth taking seriously
to test a claim a second time
questions.explanation: Her argument was 'harder to dismiss,' that is, harder for opponents to wave away. The job meaning of the word does not fit an argument.

lesson.strategy: Trace the causal chain: an early writing job develops a skill, that skill meets new evidence, and careful limits strengthen the resulting book. In paragraph three, note what the book did not claim before reading what it did claim.

signals.phrase: The work paid poorly, but it taught her something valuable
signals.means: A 'but' reversal: a bad-sounding fact is about to be reframed as an advantage.

signals.phrase: It did not demand that all pesticides be banned.
signals.means: The writer clears away a common misreading before giving the real claim.

signals.phrase: It argued something narrower and harder to dismiss
signals.means: Here comes the true argument, and a reason why its narrowness is a strength.
A short verdict sentence. The attacks failed; the facts did not.

vocab.inContext: chemicals sprayed to kill insects and other pests
to brush an argument aside as unworthy of a serious answer
lacking the training to speak on the subject: an insult here, not a fact

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer says what a work did NOT claim, the sentence right after it holds the main idea. Do not stop at the negative.
skillTips.inference: A 'because' clause often answers an inference question before you ask it. Read to the end of the sentence.
skillTips.vocabulary: Pick the meaning that matches what the word is being applied to. You dismiss an argument the way you dismiss a worker, but only one fits here.
skillTips.detail: Passages carry several time spans. Match the number to the right event: four years of research, not thirty years of career.

passages.title: Hedy Lamarr's Hidden Workbench
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Hedy Lamarr was one of the best known film actresses of the 1930s and 1940s. Studios sold her as a beautiful face, and interviewers rarely asked her about anything else. In private she kept a small workbench in her home and spent evenings sketching inventions.

Before she left Europe she had been married to an arms manufacturer, and she had sat through years of business dinners about weapons. She had listened. One problem stayed with her: a radio-guided torpedo could be pushed off course if an enemy jammed the single frequency that carried its orders.

With the composer George Antheil she worked out an answer. Instead of one steady frequency, the transmitter and the torpedo would hop together through a changing sequence of frequencies, in step, like two players reading the same roll of music. An enemy listening on one channel would catch only a fragment.

They received a patent in 1942. The Navy did not use it. Decades later, related ideas, spreading a signal across many frequencies, became ordinary in wireless communication, and Lamarr was finally known as an inventor and not only as a face.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
choices: Lamarr left Europe in order to become a film star.
The Navy improved its torpedoes with Lamarr's help.
A famous actress used what she had overheard about weapons to invent a signal that was hard to jam.
Music and radio depend on exactly the same machines.
questions.explanation: The passage links three things: her public image, the weapons talk she absorbed, and the invention that came out of it. The text states plainly that the Navy did not use the patent.

questions.stem: What problem were Lamarr and Antheil trying to solve?
choices: An enemy could jam the single frequency that controlled a torpedo.
Torpedoes moved too slowly in cold water.
Radios cost the Navy too much money.
Composers were not allowed to file patents.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two names the problem: one control frequency could be jammed, pushing the torpedo off course. The hopping design answers exactly that.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about how Lamarr was treated during her film career?
choices: The studios encouraged her inventing.
She earned less money than other actresses.
Interviewers asked her mostly about science.
People saw her looks and ignored her mind.
questions.explanation: Studios 'sold her as a beautiful face', interviewers asked nothing else, and her workbench stayed private. The closing line (known at last as an inventor, not only a face) confirms the reading.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'transmitter' means:
choices: a person who repairs radios
the device that sends out the radio signal
the wire running inside a torpedo
the written record of a patent
questions.explanation: The transmitter and the torpedo 'hop together' through frequencies, so the transmitter is the sending side of the pair. The torpedo receives; the transmitter sends.

lesson.strategy: This passage sets a public image against a private one, then explains a technical idea with a comparison. Read paragraph one as the mask and paragraph two as what was behind it. When you reach the music image, use it; it is there to make the invention easy to picture.

signals.phrase: In private she kept a small workbench in her home
signals.means: 'In private' flips the picture built in the first two sentences.
A short sentence used for emphasis: this detail matters more than it looks.
A contrast is coming: the old way, then the new way.

signals.phrase: The Navy did not use it.
signals.means: A flat, unexpected turn. The invention worked but went nowhere at the time.

vocab.inContext: blocked a radio signal on purpose with interference
the machine that sends the radio orders out
a small broken piece of the signal, too little to be useful

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage contrasts how someone was seen with what they actually did, the main idea usually lives in the gap between the two.
skillTips.inference: Read the last sentence again. Writers often place the inference they want you to draw at the very end.
skillTips.vocabulary: Split a long word into parts you know: 'transmit' plus '-er' gives you the thing that transmits.
skillTips.detail: For a problem-solution passage, name the problem in your own words before checking the choices. The right answer will match it.

passages.title: Twenty-Nine Years From Home
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1325 a young scholar named Ibn Battuta left Tangier, in Morocco, to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He was twenty-one and traveled alone. He expected to be gone for a year or two. He came home about twenty-nine years later.

The pilgrimage became a habit of moving. He crossed North Africa and Arabia, sailed down the East African coast, rode north into the grasslands of Central Asia, and served for years as a judge in Delhi. He was robbed, shipwrecked, promoted, and dismissed. What carried him was less courage than a network: across a huge region, Muslim merchants, judges, and rulers shared a language of law and hospitality, and a traveling scholar could expect a bed and a meal from strangers.

Back in Morocco, the sultan asked him to dictate his travels to a young writer at the court. The book that resulted mixes what Ibn Battuta saw with stories he collected along the way, so historians read it with care. Even so, it remains one of the fullest pictures we have of the fourteenth-century world, drawn by someone who actually crossed it.

questions.stem: Which statement best states the main idea?
choices: Ibn Battuta was the first person to sail down the East African coast.
Ibn Battuta's book is completely accurate and needs no checking.
Ibn Battuta became a judge in Delhi and stayed there for life.
A short pilgrimage grew into nearly thirty years of travel, helped by a shared world of law and hospitality.
questions.explanation: The passage opens with the gap between one or two years and twenty-nine, then explains what made such travel possible. It says the book must be read with care, and that he returned to Morocco.

questions.stem: About how long was Ibn Battuta away from home?
choices: About one year
About ten years
About twenty-nine years
About fifty years
questions.explanation: The text says he came home 'about twenty-nine years later.' The year or two was only what he expected.

questions.stem: Why do historians read his book with care?
choices: It was written in a language no one can read today.
It mixes what he saw himself with stories he heard from others.
He never actually left Morocco.
The sultan rewrote the ending.
questions.explanation: The text gives the mixture as the reason: seen events and collected stories sit side by side, so a reader cannot always tell which is which.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'hospitality' means:
choices: welcoming guests and caring for them
medical treatment for the sick
the law of a foreign country
payment made for a night's stay
questions.explanation: It appears beside the idea that a traveler 'could expect a bed and a meal from strangers.' That is guest-welcome, and it is free, so payment is wrong.

lesson.strategy: The passage opens with a gap (one or two years expected, twenty-nine years spent) and then explains it. Read paragraph two for the explanation, not for the list of places. The last paragraph shifts from the man to his book and how much we should trust it.

signals.phrase: He expected to be gone for a year or two.
signals.means: Sets up a contrast. The next sentence will break the expectation.

signals.phrase: The pilgrimage became a habit of moving.
signals.means: A summary line for the whole middle of the story: one trip turned into a way of life.

signals.phrase: What carried him was less courage than a network
signals.means: The writer corrects an easy assumption and gives the real cause.

signals.phrase: so historians read it with care
signals.means: A judgment about the source. The book is useful but not fully reliable.

vocab.inContext: a journey made to a holy place for religious reasons
the custom of feeding and housing travelers who arrive as strangers
to speak the words aloud so another person can write them down

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage sets up a gap between what was expected and what happened, the main idea is usually the explanation of the gap.
skillTips.inference: 'Less X than Y' tells you the writer is rejecting the obvious explanation. The real cause always follows.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the nearby example, not the word's shape. 'Hospitality' looks like 'hospital', but the bed and meal for strangers give the true sense.
skillTips.detail: When two numbers appear close together, check which one is expectation and which is fact.

passages.title: Zora Neale Hurston Listens
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Zora Neale Hurston arrived in New York in the 1920s with a gift for talk and very little money. She studied anthropology under a professor who insisted that no culture was primitive, only unfamiliar. That training changed how she heard her own hometown. The stories traded on porches in Eatonville, Florida (the town where she grew up, one of the first self-governing Black towns in the country) were not quaint local color. They were a literature, already complete, waiting only to be written down.

So she went back with a notebook and, later, a recording machine. She gathered folktales, work songs, sermons, and jokes across the South and the Caribbean, and she published them alongside her novels. Her method was unusual for its time: she refused to translate Black speech into standard English for the comfort of white readers, and she wrote about ordinary desire and pleasure rather than only about suffering.

That refusal cost her. Prominent critics of her own generation judged her work politically useless. Her books went out of print, and she died in 1960 with almost no money and no headstone. A later generation of writers found her again, and the novel she published in 1937 is now read in classrooms everywhere.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Hurston invented the folktales that she published as research.
Trained to see her own community as culture, Hurston recorded it on its own terms and paid for that choice in her lifetime.
Hurston left Florida because there was nothing there worth writing about.
Critics of the 1930s agreed that Hurston's work mattered.
questions.explanation: The three paragraphs give training, method, and cost. She collected rather than invented, went back to Eatonville rather than away from it, and the critics of her time dismissed her.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Hurston refuse to do?
choices: Translate Black speech into standard English for white readers.
Publish the folklore she had collected.
Study anthropology in New York.
Return to Eatonville after leaving it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two states the refusal directly. She did publish the folklore, did study anthropology, and did go back to Eatonville with a notebook.

questions.stem: What does 'she died in 1960 with almost no money and no headstone' most strongly suggest?
choices: Her family had moved far away from her.
She had never managed to publish a book.
She had asked to be buried without a marker.
By the end of her life her work had been largely forgotten.
questions.explanation: The sentence sits between 'her books went out of print' and 'a later generation found her again.' That frame makes neglect, not choice or family, the point.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'quaint' means:
choices: hard to translate accurately
recently invented
charming in an old-fashioned way, and so not taken seriously
recorded by an outsider
questions.explanation: The writer denies the word: the porch stories were 'not quaint local color' but 'a literature'. So quaint names the small, decorative view she rejected.

lesson.strategy: This passage argues, it does not just report. Paragraph one gives the idea that reframes everything (culture is not primitive, only unfamiliar), paragraph two shows the method that follows from it, and paragraph three counts the cost. Watch for sentences built as 'not X but Y'; they carry the argument.

signals.phrase: That training changed how she heard her own hometown.
signals.means: A hinge sentence. An idea learned in school is about to be applied to her own life.
A rejection. The writer denies one description in order to insist on a stronger one.

signals.phrase: Her method was unusual for its time
signals.means: A signal that the next details define her difference from other writers.
Consequence marker. The rest of the paragraph lists the price she paid.

vocab.inContext: the study of human cultures and how people live together
pretty and old-fashioned in a way that keeps something from being taken seriously
her decision not to change Black speech for white readers

skillTips.main-idea: In an argued biography, the main idea combines the person's choice and its consequence. A choice with no cost is only half the passage.
skillTips.inference: Read a hard sentence together with the sentences on both sides. Neighbors supply the meaning that the sentence alone leaves open.
skillTips.vocabulary: When a word appears inside a denial ('not quaint'), its meaning is the view the writer is arguing against.
skillTips.detail: Distractors are often true statements about other parts of the text. Match the exact action the question asks about.

passages.title: Humboldt’s Network of Knowledge
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
From 1799 to 1804, Alexander von Humboldt traveled through Spanish America with Aimé Bonpland, a French botanist and physician. They measured temperature and altitude, collected specimens, and compared plants across climates. A rare passport from the Spanish Crown gave them unusual access to colonial territories. Their journey was never the work of one observer moving through empty landscapes.

Indigenous guides and knowledge holders, boat crews, interpreters, local residents, and scholars helped the travelers choose routes and understand plants and places. In the Orinoco region, Indigenous geographic knowledge was essential to navigation. Humboldt and Bonpland learned through these encounters, although later European publications often placed Humboldt’s name in the foreground and made other contributors harder to see.

Humboldt’s distinctive achievement was to synthesize many observations. On the Andes, patterns of vegetation changing with altitude helped him picture nature as an interconnected system. Near Lake Valencia, he connected plantation agriculture and forest clearing with changes in water and climate. These comparisons challenged the idea that natural facts should be studied only as isolated items.

His work remains influential, but a fuller biography changes the lone-genius story. It credits Bonpland and local and Indigenous expertise, and it recognizes that colonial permission shaped where the expedition could travel and whose knowledge entered print.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly arguing?
choices: Humboldt worked alone and discovered all places and natural knowledge entirely unknown to the people living there.
The expedition collected plants but avoided comparing environments or connecting observations.
Colonial officials denied all travel permission, so the expedition remained in one port city.
Humboldt’s synthesis mattered, but it depended on Bonpland, local and Indigenous knowledge, and colonial access.
questions.explanation: The passage retains Humboldt’s systems insight while placing it inside a network of collaborators, knowledge, and political access.

questions.stem: Who traveled with Humboldt through Spanish America?
choices: Edward Jenner, an English physician who studied smallpox vaccination
Aimé Bonpland, a botanist and physician
Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who developed a writing system
James Phipps, the child who participated in Jenner’s experiment
questions.explanation: The opening sentence identifies Aimé Bonpland and his fields of work.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the Spanish Crown’s passport?
choices: To show that scientific travel was shaped by colonial political power
To prove that the travelers personally owned every place and specimen they encountered
To show that royal permission made local guides and knowledge holders unnecessary
To explain the instrument the travelers used to measure altitude on the Andes
questions.explanation: The passport gave unusual entry into colonized territories, so political permission affected where the expedition could work.

questions.stem: In the passage, “synthesize” means
choices: hide the sources of each piece of information in a later publication
collect many specimens while avoiding comparisons among them
combine many observations into a connected understanding
translate each observation word for word into another language
questions.explanation: The following sentences show Humboldt combining observations of altitude, vegetation, land use, water, and climate.

lesson.strategy: Read a biography for both contribution and conditions. Paragraph one names the expedition pair and colonial access; paragraph two restores contributors; paragraph three identifies Humboldt’s synthesis; paragraph four recombines them into a networked account.

signals.phrase: never the work of one observer
signals.means: Rejects the empty-landscape and lone-traveler frame.
States a concrete dependence on Indigenous geographic knowledge.
Identifies Humboldt’s contribution without assigning all discovery to him.
Introduces the revised account of credit and access.

vocab.inContext: connected with rule imposed by an outside imperial power
combine many observations into a connected understanding
deep knowledge or skill developed through experience

skillTips.main-idea: Preserve both parts: Humboldt’s synthesis and the people and political conditions that enabled it.
skillTips.detail: The opening sentence names Bonpland and describes his fields.
skillTips.inference: A royal passport is evidence that access to places and knowledge was structured by colonial authority.
skillTips.vocabulary: The Andes and Lake Valencia examples show separate observations being combined into systems.

passages.title: The Composer Nobody Printed
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Fanny Mendelssohn was trained beside her younger brother Felix and, by the account of their teachers, matched him. She read scores fluently, played long piano works from memory, and began composing as a child. But their father wrote to her that music would be a profession for Felix and, for her, only an ornament of family life. In that sentence a career closed.

She composed anyway (more than four hundred pieces), and her music circulated in a narrow world. Sunday concerts at the family house in Berlin drew serious musicians, and she led and performed there for years. What she lacked was print. A few of her songs did reach the public in the 1820s and 1830s, but under her brother's name, inside collections he published; one story has him explaining that awkward arrangement to a queen who praised a song he had not written.

At forty she decided to publish under her own name, against her family's advice. The first works appeared in 1846. She died the next year, at forty-one, with most of her manuscripts still unheard. They sat in archives for over a century. That is why her rising reputation today is not a rediscovery of a forgotten composer but the first real hearing of one.

questions.stem: Which statement best states the main idea?
choices: Felix stole his sister's songs and was punished for it.
Fanny stopped composing after reading her father's letter.
Fanny composed all her life, but the door to publication stayed shut until she opened it herself, too late.
The Sunday concerts in Berlin were the most important musical events in Europe.
questions.explanation: The passage tracks one thing across three paragraphs: she had the talent and the output, but not print, until 1846, a year before her death. The text says she composed anyway, and the songs under Felix's name are described as an arrangement, not a theft.

questions.stem: Under what name did some of Fanny's songs first reach the public?
choices: Under no name at all
Under her brother's name
Under an invented Italian name
Under her married name
questions.explanation: The text says a few songs reached the public 'under her brother's name, inside collections he published.' The queen story depends on that fact.

questions.stem: Why does the writer call her new fame 'the first real hearing' rather than a rediscovery?
choices: Because her music was written only for private homes.
Because her brother's fame was always greater than hers.
Because nobody performs her works even today.
Because most of her music was never published, so it was never widely known and then forgotten.
questions.explanation: To rediscover something, the public must have known it first. Her manuscripts sat unheard in archives, so today's audience is hearing the music for the first time, not again.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'ornament' means:
choices: a pleasant decoration rather than serious work
a musical instrument played at home
a written contract with a publisher
a public performance for money
questions.explanation: Her father contrasts a profession for Felix with an ornament for her. The contrast makes ornament mean something decorative and secondary.

lesson.strategy: Read for the hidden subject: access to print, not talent. The first paragraph closes the door, the second shows work continuing behind it, and the third opens it too late. Preserve the ending’s distinction between rediscovery and a first real hearing.

signals.phrase: In that sentence a career closed.
signals.means: A short summary line. One letter, not a lack of ability, decided her future.
Names the exact missing thing. Everything else (skill, audience, output) she had.
Signals that her decision to publish was an act of resistance, not a normal step.

signals.phrase: forgotten composer but the first real hearing of one
signals.means: A 'not X but Y' correction. The writer refuses the easy word and insists on a sharper one.

vocab.inContext: a decoration; something pleasant but not serious work
handwritten scores that were never printed
collections where old documents are stored and preserved

skillTips.main-idea: Ask what single thing the passage keeps returning to. Here it is publication, not talent, and that is the main idea.
skillTips.inference: A 'not X but Y' ending tells you the writer expects the reader to reach for X. The reason Y is truer is usually stated just before.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrasted pairs define each other. 'Profession' for him and 'ornament' for her fixes the meaning of both.
skillTips.detail: Dates that sit one year apart matter. Publishing in 1846 and dying in 1847 is the whole point of the paragraph.

passages.title: Vivian Maier's Hidden Negatives
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 2007 a young man in Chicago bought a box of negatives at a storage auction for a few hundred dollars. He was researching a neighborhood and hoped for old street scenes. What he had bought, it turned out, was the life's work of a woman who had shown it to almost no one.

Vivian Maier spent forty years as a nanny for families in Chicago and New York. On her days off, often with a child in tow, she walked the city with a twin-lens camera held at her waist, a design that let her look down into the viewfinder and photograph people who never noticed. She made well over a hundred thousand exposures. Thousands of rolls were never developed. She had no exhibition, no gallery, no reviews.

The story is usually told as a happy accident: genius saved from a dumpster. It is worth pausing on the other reading. A person who photographs relentlessly for four decades and never shows the work may not be waiting to be discovered. She kept her rooms locked and gave strangers a false name. Her fame is entirely posthumous, arranged by people she never met, out of images she chose not to publish, which is a kind of luck, and also a question no one can now ask her.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea of the passage?
choices: A nanny in Chicago sold her photographs at a storage auction.
Twin-lens cameras take better street photographs than other cameras.
A man researching a neighborhood became a famous photographer.
Maier's huge hidden body of work made her famous after death, and the writer questions the cheerful way that story is usually told.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs one and two supply the discovery and the scale of the work; paragraph three turns and challenges the standard telling. She did not sell the work, and the buyer is not the photographer.

questions.stem: What was the buyer hoping to find when he bought the box?
choices: Portraits of famous people
Rolls of film that had never been developed
Old street scenes for his neighborhood research
Letters written by a nanny
questions.explanation: The text says he 'was researching a neighborhood and hoped for old street scenes.' The undeveloped rolls were part of what he actually got, not what he wanted.

questions.stem: What does the writer suggest by mentioning the locked rooms and the false name?
choices: That Maier may have wanted both her life and her work kept private.
That Maier had stolen the camera she used.
That Maier was secretly planning an exhibition.
That Maier could not afford to rent a gallery.
questions.explanation: Those two facts arrive right after the claim that she may not have been waiting to be discovered. They are offered as evidence of a wish for privacy, which is what makes her posthumous fame uneasy.

questions.stem: In the passage, 'posthumous' means:
choices: shared only with close friends
happening after a person's death
earned through long, hard work
printed in a daily newspaper
questions.explanation: Her fame was 'arranged by people she never met' and rests on a question 'no one can now ask her.' Both phrases place the fame after she died.

lesson.strategy: Treat the first two paragraphs as report and the third as argument. The invitation to pause is the hinge. After it, locked rooms and a false name support a counter-reading, while the final judgment deliberately leaves luck beside an unanswered question.

signals.phrase: work of a woman who had shown it to almost no one.
signals.means: 'It turned out' marks a reversal of expectation, and previews the passage's real subject: work kept hidden.

signals.phrase: The story is usually told as a happy accident
signals.means: 'Usually told' distances the writer from that version. A challenge is coming.

signals.phrase: It is worth pausing on the other reading.
signals.means: The explicit turn of the argument. Everything after this is the counter-case.
Sets up the irony: she has everything an artist wants, and none of it in her lifetime or by her choice.

vocab.inContext: developed film images from which photographic prints are made
single shots taken on film; one press of the shutter
arriving only after her death

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage tells a familiar story and then says 'the other reading', the main idea includes the doubt, not just the story.
skillTips.inference: Small biographical facts placed after a claim are evidence for it. Ask why the writer chose those two details and no others.
skillTips.vocabulary: Latin-based words often carry a hidden time marker. Let the surrounding phrases ('never met', 'no one can now ask her') fix the timing.
skillTips.detail: Separate what a person wanted from what they got. The question here is about hope, not about the actual contents of the box.

passages.title: Ten Minutes of Walking
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When I cannot solve a problem, I stop and go for a walk.

At my desk, I stare at the same screen and the same words. My mind goes in a small circle. Outside, the street gives me new things to look at. A bus, a dog, a red door. My body moves, and my thoughts begin to move too.

I do not try to think hard while I walk. That is the point. I let the problem sit in the back of my mind. Often, by the time I come home, one small part of it has become clear. The answer was not on the street. It was already in my head, but it needed room.

Ten minutes is enough. A walk is a cheap tool, and I keep forgetting to use it.

questions.stem: What is the main point of this essay?
choices: Walking is the best kind of daily exercise.
A short walk can help a stuck mind find an answer.
Working at a desk is bad for the body.
Streets are more interesting than offices.
questions.explanation: The writer walks when a problem will not move, and comes home with one part of it clear. The essay is about thinking, not about exercise.

questions.stem: According to the essay, what happens when the writer stays at the desk?
choices: New ideas arrive slowly but surely.
The writer falls asleep.
The writer's mind goes in a small circle.
The writer writes the answer down.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says directly: 'My mind goes in a small circle.'

questions.stem: What does the essay suggest about where the answer came from?
choices: It was already in the writer's head and only needed space.
The writer saw the answer written on a red door.
A person on the street explained it.
It came from working harder at the desk.
questions.explanation: The writer corrects the reader: 'The answer was not on the street. It was already in my head, but it needed room.'

questions.stem: The writer calls a walk a "cheap tool". Here, cheap means
choices: of poor quality
not polite
difficult to arrange
costing almost nothing and easy to use
questions.explanation: Nothing in the essay says the walk works badly. The point is that it takes ten minutes and no money, so 'cheap' means it costs almost nothing.

lesson.strategy: This is a short personal essay built on one contrast: the desk and the street. Read the first line as the writer's claim, then watch the middle paragraph set the two places side by side. The last short paragraph gives the practical rule.

signals.phrase: When I cannot solve a problem
signals.means: The opening states the situation the whole essay answers.
Marks the key idea: not thinking hard is deliberate, not lazy.

signals.phrase: Often, by the time I come home
signals.means: Signals the result of the walk; the outcome comes right after.
A short closing sentence that turns the essay into advice.

vocab.inContext: to look at one thing without moving your eyes
here, the same thoughts repeating with no progress
costing almost nothing to do

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea is the writer's claim, not the examples. The bus, the dog and the red door only support it.
skillTips.inference: Use the writer's own correction ('not on the street') to throw out any choice about the street.
skillTips.vocabulary: Everyday words often carry a second meaning. Ask what the word is doing in this sentence.
skillTips.detail: Detail answers repeat the essay's own words. Find the sentence that holds the key word, then read it exactly.

passages.title: The Small Notebook
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
I carry a small notebook in my pocket. It is not for deep thoughts. It is for the things I would lose.

A name I must not forget. The number of the bus that goes to the airport. A word I heard and liked. I write them down in one line, and then I stop thinking about them. That is the gift. My head does not have to hold them anymore.

Some people say a notebook makes the memory lazy. I think the opposite is true. When small facts are safe on paper, my mind is free for larger work. I do not spend the morning trying to remember a phone number.

Once a week, I read the pages again. Most lines are useless. Two or three are not. Those I copy into a better place. The rest I let go without regret.

questions.stem: What is the writer's main point about the notebook?
choices: Writing small things down leaves the mind free for larger work.
A notebook is the best gift for a friend.
People should write long thoughts every day.
Paper is safer than a phone.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states it: when small facts are safe on paper, the mind is free for larger work.

questions.stem: How often does the writer read the old pages?
choices: Every morning
Once a week
Once a month
Never
questions.explanation: The last paragraph begins, 'Once a week, I read the pages again.'

questions.stem: What does the writer think about most of the lines in the notebook?
choices: Every line will be useful later.
The lines should be shown to other people.
Each line must be copied twice.
Most lines can be thrown away, and that is fine.
questions.explanation: 'Most lines are useless' and the rest are let go 'without regret'. The writer expects to keep only two or three.

questions.stem: The writer says, "I think the opposite is true." This means
choices: the same thing is true
nobody knows what is true
the reverse of what those people say is true
the point is unimportant
questions.explanation: Some people say the notebook makes memory lazy. The writer claims the reverse: it frees the mind.

lesson.strategy: This essay lists small examples first and gives the reason later. Read the second paragraph as evidence and the third as the argument. When the writer names an objection, expect his answer in the very next sentence.

signals.phrase: It is not for deep thoughts.
signals.means: Tells you what the notebook is NOT for; the real use follows.
Names the benefit; the idea itself sits in the sentence before.

signals.phrase: Some people say a notebook makes the memory lazy.
signals.means: Introduces the opposing view, which the writer then rejects.

signals.phrase: Once a week, I read the pages again.
signals.means: Signals a routine; facts about time and amount usually follow.

vocab.inContext: here, weak from not being used
the reverse; the other way around
a sad feeling about something you lost or did

skillTips.main-idea: When an essay names an objection and answers it, the answer is usually the main idea.
skillTips.inference: 'Most lines are useless' plus 'without regret' tells you how the writer feels about throwing them away.
skillTips.vocabulary: 'Opposite' points backwards. Reread the sentence before it to know what is being reversed.
skillTips.detail: Numbers and time words ('once a week', 'two or three') are the easiest details to check.

passages.title: In Praise of Repair
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
My kettle stopped working last winter. The shop told me a new one would cost less than a repair, so I almost threw it away. Instead I opened it with a screwdriver and found a loose wire. Ten minutes later it boiled water again.

The lesson was not that I am clever. I am not. The lesson was that the kettle was never a mystery. It was a small machine with five or six parts, and it had failed in a way I could see. Because I had never opened one, I assumed the inside was beyond me.

We are trained to be users of objects, not owners of them. A sealed case tells you politely that the inside is none of your business. But a thing you cannot open is a thing you cannot keep, and a thing you cannot keep is a thing you must buy twice.

Repair is not only cheaper. It is a way of refusing to be a stranger in your own house.

questions.stem: What is the essay mainly arguing?
choices: Kettles are easy to build at home.
Repair is worth doing because it keeps you the owner of your things.
New machines are always worse than old ones.
Shops give bad advice on purpose.
questions.explanation: The last two paragraphs move past money: a thing you cannot open is a thing you must buy twice, and repair keeps you from being a stranger in your own house.

questions.stem: What was wrong with the kettle?
choices: It had no water inside.
The shop had sold a broken model.
A wire inside was loose.
The screwdriver was the wrong size.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the writer opened it and 'found a loose wire'.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention that he had never opened a kettle before?
choices: To explain why he wrongly believed the inside was too hard for him.
To show that he is a trained engineer.
To prove that kettles are dangerous.
To suggest he should have bought a better brand.
questions.explanation: He says the machine 'was never a mystery' and that he assumed the inside was beyond him only because he had never looked.

questions.stem: A "sealed case" is one that is
choices: painted in a bright color
sold at a high price
very heavy to lift
closed so that it cannot easily be opened
questions.explanation: The sentence says the case tells you the inside is none of your business, so 'sealed' means shut against opening.

lesson.strategy: This essay starts with one small story and then widens into an argument. Read paragraph one as the event, paragraph two as what it taught, and paragraphs three and four as the general claim. Watch for sentences that block a wrong reading before giving the right one.

signals.phrase: The lesson was not that I am clever.
signals.means: Blocks a wrong conclusion; the real lesson comes next.

signals.phrase: I assumed the inside was beyond me.
signals.means: Gives the cause of the writer's mistaken belief.

signals.phrase: But a thing you cannot open
signals.means: 'But' turns the paragraph from description into argument.
'Not only' warns that the bigger reason is about to arrive.

vocab.inContext: not tight or firmly fixed in place
closed so that it cannot be opened
believed something without checking it

skillTips.main-idea: In a story-plus-argument essay, the main idea is in the argument, not the story. Read the final paragraph first if you are unsure.
skillTips.inference: When a writer says why he was wrong, the inference question usually asks about that reason.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the sentence that follows the hard word. Here it explains what a sealed case does to you.
skillTips.detail: Concrete nouns are easy anchors. Search for 'wire', 'screwdriver', 'shop' and read those lines closely.

passages.title: The Long Rise
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Bread teaches a kind of patience that is hard to fake. Flour, water and a little yeast will become bread whether you hurry or not, but the two loaves are not the same.

Warm dough rises fast. The yeast makes carbon dioxide quickly, the bread puffs up, and in two hours you can eat. Cold dough rises slowly, sometimes overnight in a refrigerator. During that long wait, other things happen. Enzymes break starch into simpler sugars, and the dough gathers a deeper, slightly sour flavor that speed cannot produce.

So the slow loaf is not better because waiting is noble. It is better because waiting is when the chemistry gets done. The time is not empty. It only looks empty to us, because nothing on the surface moves.

I think about this when a piece of work feels stalled. Some processes have a minimum time, and no amount of attention will shorten it. The honest question is not how to hurry them. It is what to do while they finish.

questions.stem: What is the essay's main claim about the slow loaf?
choices: Waiting is a virtue that makes people better cooks.
Cold dough is safer to eat than warm dough.
It is better because the chemistry needs time, not because waiting is good in itself.
Bread made in two hours cannot rise at all.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says it plainly: the slow loaf is not better because waiting is noble, but because waiting is when the chemistry gets done.

questions.stem: According to the essay, what do enzymes do during the long, cold rise?
choices: They kill the yeast.
They break starch into simpler sugars.
They make the carbon dioxide.
They cool the refrigerator.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says enzymes break starch into simpler sugars. Carbon dioxide is made by the yeast, not the enzymes.

questions.stem: What does the writer suggest about work that feels stalled?
choices: It should be handed to someone else.
More attention will always speed it up.
It is usually a sign of a bad plan.
Part of it needs a minimum time, so the useful question is what to do meanwhile.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says no amount of attention will shorten a minimum time, and asks what to do while the process finishes.

questions.stem: When a piece of work feels "stalled", it is
choices: stopped and not moving forward
finished too early
shared with a team
done carelessly
questions.explanation: The sentences after it talk about time that cannot be shortened, so 'stalled' means stuck, making no visible progress.

lesson.strategy: The essay compares two things (warm dough and cold dough) and then applies the comparison to something else entirely. Track the two sides in paragraph two, find the conclusion in paragraph three, and read the last paragraph as the transfer to daily work.

signals.means: Opens the comparison; the cold-dough sentence answers it.

signals.phrase: During that long wait, other things happen.
signals.means: Promises an explanation; the science follows immediately.
The turn of the essay: waiting is work you cannot see.

signals.phrase: I think about this when a piece of work feels stalled.
signals.means: Moves from bread to the wider lesson about any slow process.

vocab.inContext: the soft mix of flour and water before baking
natural substances that cause chemical changes
stopped, making no progress

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer says 'not because X, but because Y', Y is the main idea.
skillTips.inference: The bread is an example. The inference question usually asks about the thing the example stands for.
skillTips.vocabulary: Guess a hard word from the sentences around it before you look at the choices.
skillTips.detail: Watch out for choices that swap two facts from the same paragraph, like yeast and enzymes.

passages.title: Quiet Rooms
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A public library is one of the few rooms left where nobody wants anything from you. You do not have to buy a coffee to sit down. No one asks for your name at the door. You can stay four hours and leave with nothing.

That sounds like a small thing. It is not. Almost every other indoor space in a city is rented in some way: you pay for the chair, or you pay with your attention, or you pay by agreeing to be a customer. The library breaks the pattern. Its only condition is quiet.

I notice who uses these rooms. Students, of course. But also people between jobs, people waiting for a shift to start, people whose homes are too crowded to think in. For them the shelves are not the point. The point is a chair, warmth, and the right to be somewhere without spending.

A city that keeps such rooms is saying something about itself. It is saying that presence does not have to be bought.

questions.stem: What is the essay mainly saying about libraries?
choices: They should buy more books.
Cities have become too noisy for study.
A library matters as free public space, not only for its books.
Students need more chairs than they are given.
questions.explanation: The essay's subject is a room where nobody wants anything from you, and it ends on the right to be somewhere without spending.

questions.stem: What does the essay say is the library's only condition?
choices: A membership card
Quiet
Buying a coffee
Giving your name
questions.explanation: 'The library breaks the pattern. Its only condition is quiet.' The card, the coffee and the name are all things the essay says are NOT required.

questions.stem: What does the essay suggest about some of the people it describes?
choices: They come for the chair and the warmth more than for the books.
They are all university students.
They dislike reading.
They pay a small fee to enter.
questions.explanation: 'For them the shelves are not the point. The point is a chair, warmth, and the right to be somewhere without spending.'

questions.stem: In "Its only condition is quiet", condition means
choices: the state of the building
an illness
a change in the weather
a rule you must meet to be allowed in
questions.explanation: The paragraph lists things other places demand of you. The library demands only one thing, so 'condition' is a requirement.

lesson.strategy: The essay defines the library by what it does not ask of you, so read the negatives carefully. Paragraph two supplies the contrast with the rest of the city; paragraph three shows who the space is really for. The last two lines carry the value judgement.

signals.means: States the essay's central claim in the first sentence.

signals.phrase: That sounds like a small thing. It is not.
signals.means: A correction; the writer is about to explain why it is large.
Contrast marker; the pattern was described just above it.

signals.phrase: For them the shelves are not the point.
signals.means: Tells you the books matter less than the space for these visitors.

vocab.inContext: a rule that must be met
too full of people
simply being in a place

skillTips.main-idea: Ask what the writer values, not what the place contains. The books are barely mentioned.
skillTips.inference: 'The shelves are not the point' invites you to name what the point actually is.
skillTips.vocabulary: An abstract noun like 'condition' takes its meaning from the sentences around it.
skillTips.detail: When a text lists what is NOT required, wrong choices are often built from that list.

passages.title: The Use of Boredom
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Boredom has a bad name, and it earned some of it. Nobody enjoys the flat, gray hour when nothing seems worth doing. But I have come to think that hour has a function, and that we have quietly deleted it from our lives.

Consider what boredom actually is. It is the state of having attention available and nothing obvious to spend it on. That is an uncomfortable position, and the mind treats it as a problem to solve. Left alone, it starts producing: a half-idea, an old memory, a plan for Saturday. The discomfort is the engine.

Now consider the phone. The moment attention comes free, there is something to spend it on, endlessly and at almost no cost. The unpleasant gap closes before it can do any work. We have not defeated boredom; we have removed the pressure that boredom used to create.

I am not arguing for suffering. I am arguing that a mind with nothing to do is not idle. It is searching, and searching is expensive to interrupt.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the essay's argument?
choices: Boredom becomes pleasant once you accept it.
Phones should be banned from public places.
Boredom does useful work, and constant distraction removes it.
People today are lazier than people used to be.
questions.explanation: The essay claims boredom has a function, that the mind starts producing when left alone, and that the phone removes the pressure that made this happen.

questions.stem: How does the essay define boredom?
choices: A lack of sleep.
Having attention available with nothing obvious to spend it on.
A wish to be with other people.
Sadness with no clear cause.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two gives the definition word for word.

questions.stem: What does the essay imply the phone does to the mind?
choices: It teaches the mind to search faster.
It makes old memories sharper.
It causes physical tiredness.
It closes the uncomfortable gap before the mind can produce anything.
questions.explanation: The discomfort is called 'the engine'. The phone closes the gap at once, so the engine never runs.

questions.stem: The writer says a mind with nothing to do is not "idle". Idle here means
choices: doing no work at all
moving quickly
feeling angry
fast asleep
questions.explanation: The next sentence corrects the idea: the mind is searching, so it is not doing nothing.

lesson.strategy: This is a two-case argument: first what boredom is, then what the phone does to it. Read paragraph two as the definition and paragraph three as the contrast. The final paragraph narrows the claim so you do not overstate it.

signals.means: Opens with the common view the essay will argue against.
Compresses the argument into one image: the bad feeling drives the thinking.
Turns to the second case; expect a contrast with the paragraph above.

signals.phrase: I am not arguing for suffering.
signals.means: Limits the claim, so the reader does not take it too far.

vocab.inContext: a useful job that something does
an unpleasant feeling
doing nothing at all

skillTips.main-idea: An essay that opens with a common view usually states its own view right after 'But'.
skillTips.inference: Link the image ('the engine') to the later case (the phone) to see what the writer left unsaid.
skillTips.vocabulary: When a word appears in a negative sentence ('is not idle'), the meaning is what the writer denies.
skillTips.detail: A definition question wants the writer's definition, not the dictionary one.

passages.title: Every Map Is Wrong
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
