questions.explanation: The sentence says the sound was chosen before she was born and links to nothing else about her. A label names without describing.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that you would remember a name better if
choices: you met the person in a quieter room
the person had an unusual job
it connected to something you already knew
you heard it spoken more loudly
questions.explanation: The rule is that memory holds what connects. Names fail because they connect to nothing, so a name with a connection would hold better.

lesson.strategy: Two reasons for one everyday problem. The first takes three paragraphs and rests on a comparison between a job and a name. The second gets four lines. Watch for the sentence that announces the second reason, or you will read straight past it.

signals.phrase: it is not a sign of a poor memory
signals.means: Clears away the obvious explanation before the real one arrives.

signals.phrase: Memory holds on to things that connect to other things.
signals.means: The rule the passage rests on. Everything after it tests names against this rule.
The comparison snaps shut. The job had connections; the name has none.
A plain marker that a new cause is being added, not the old one repeated.

vocab.inContext: join on to something else you already know
hold on to something, so it has a place to stay
a name put on something that does not describe it

skillTips.main-idea: Two reasons are given, but only one is developed at length. The main idea is the connection rule, with the second reason as an addition.
skillTips.inference: The passage explains why names fail to stick. Reverse that explanation to see what would make one stick instead.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Label" is explained by the words around it: chosen before she was born, linked to nothing about her.
skillTips.detail: The list after "nurse" has four items. Match all of them, not just the first one you recognize.

passages.title: The First Street Lights
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For most of history, a city went dark at sunset. Anyone who had to go out carried a lantern, or paid a boy with a torch to walk in front of them. Some towns ordered every household to hang a lamp by its door on winter nights. The light was thin, and it ended where the house ended.

In January 1807, a street in London called Pall Mall was lit with gas. Pipes ran under the pavement, and a small flame burned at the top of each post. The light was steady, and it did not blow out. Within twenty years, gas lamps stood in cities across Europe and America.

Someone still had to walk those streets each evening with a ladder and a flame. Lamplighters had a route and a time, and people set their evenings by them. Electricity ended that work. A whole street could be lit from one switch, by a person who never left the room.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How city streets went from carried lanterns to gas lamps and then to electric light.
Why gas lamps were dangerous in cold weather.
How London grew larger after 1807.
Why people stopped going out after dark.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph is one stage of the same change, and the last one closes it with electricity.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did some towns order every household to do?
choices: Hang a lamp by its door on winter nights.
Pay a boy to carry a torch through the street.
Keep a candle burning until sunrise.
Stay indoors after the sun went down.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states the rule directly. Paying a boy with a torch was a private choice, not an order.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "lantern" is
choices: a lamp fixed to the top of a post
a light you carry, with the flame held inside a case
a pipe that brings gas under a street
a ladder used to reach a high lamp
questions.explanation: It is what a person carried when going out at night, before any street had lamps of its own.

questions.stem: Why did electricity end the lamplighter's work?
choices: Cities had grown too large for anyone to walk across.
Gas pipes were dug up and taken away.
Electric lamps were cheaper to buy than gas lamps.
One switch could light a whole street, so nobody had to walk it.
questions.explanation: The last sentence describes a person who never left the room lighting a whole street. If nobody walks the route, the job is gone.

lesson.strategy: A short history in three stages: carried light, gas light, electric light. Each paragraph is one stage, and each stage removes something the stage before it needed. Read for what disappears, not only for what arrives.

signals.phrase: For most of history, a city went dark at sunset.
signals.means: Sets the starting condition. Everything after this is a change away from it.
A date marks the turn. The first stage has ended and the second begins.

signals.phrase: Someone still had to walk those streets
signals.means: "Still" signals that the change was not complete. A limit is coming.
The final stage, stated as a loss as much as a gain.

vocab.inContext: a light you carry, with the flame inside a case
the hard walking path at the side of a street
a fixed path that someone follows each time

skillTips.main-idea: Three stages, one subject. Choose the answer that names the change across all three, not the one that stops at gas.
skillTips.inference: The last two sentences give a cause without using the word "because." Put the one switch and the person who never left the room together.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Lantern" sits next to people who had to go out at night. What they carried tells you what it is.
skillTips.detail: The household rule is in the first paragraph and the lamplighters are in the third. Go back to the right paragraph before choosing.

passages.title: The Farmer Who Photographed Snow
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Wilson Bentley was a farmer in Vermont. He was also the first person to photograph a single snow crystal.

He was fifteen when his mother gave him an old microscope. He caught snowflakes on a black board, carried them into a cold shed, and looked. What he saw would melt in a minute, and he could not draw fast enough. So he asked for a camera, and his family bought one that cost more than the farm could easily spare.

It took him two winters to get one picture. He was nineteen. He kept going for forty-six more years, in a shed with no heat, working in the cold so that his subject would not vanish. He made more than five thousand photographs of snow crystals.

He never sold many. He gave prints away and charged little, and in his village he was known mostly as a strange, patient neighbor. The pictures outlasted the opinion. Almost every image of a snowflake we know began in that shed.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Snow crystals melt too quickly to be studied properly.
A Vermont farmer spent his life photographing snow crystals.
Cameras were rare and costly on farms in the 1800s.
A microscope is the best tool for studying snow.
questions.explanation: The passage is about one man and one long task. The camera and the microscope are tools in that story.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how long did it take Bentley to get his first picture?
choices: Two winters.
Forty-six years.
Fifteen years.
A single night.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens with it. Forty-six years is how long he worked afterward, and fifteen is his age when he got the microscope.

questions.stem: In this passage, "patient" describes someone who
choices: is waiting to be seen by a doctor
is gentle and quiet with other people
works quickly but very carefully
keeps working at something slow without giving up
questions.explanation: Two winters for one picture, then forty-six years in an unheated shed. The numbers around the word show what it means here.

questions.stem: "The pictures outlasted the opinion" suggests that
choices: photographs last longer than snow does
he became famous while he was still alive
what his village thought of him mattered less in the end than his work
he changed his neighbors' minds about him
questions.explanation: The opinion is the village calling him strange. The pictures are still with us, so the work outlived the judgement.

lesson.strategy: A life told through one stubborn task. Watch the numbers: fifteen, two winters, nineteen, forty-six years, five thousand. They carry a point the sentences never state outright. The last line puts the value of the work outside his lifetime.

signals.phrase: the first person to photograph a single snow crystal
signals.means: The claim the passage supports. Read everything after it as how he did it.

signals.phrase: It took him two winters to get one picture.
signals.means: The cost of the work, given as a plain fact. Expect more numbers like it.
A turn from what he achieved to how little it was valued at the time.
The closing judgement, weighing his work against what his village thought.

vocab.inContext: a solid with a regular shape, here one piece of snow
a tool that makes very small things look large
willing to keep going slowly, without hurrying or quitting

skillTips.main-idea: This is about a person and one task. A main idea has to join them: who he was and what he spent his life doing.
skillTips.inference: The last paragraph never says he was ignored. It says he charged little and was thought strange. Read the tone as well as the facts.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Patient" is proved by the numbers near it: two winters, forty-six years, a shed with no heat.
skillTips.detail: The numbers are easy to mix up. Two winters is the first picture; forty-six years is everything that came after.

passages.title: Why Password Advice Changed
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Password advice has changed. Many sites once demanded a short string with a capital letter, a number, and a symbol. Current guidance puts more weight on length, uniqueness, and tools that reduce what a person must remember.

Length matters because every unpredictable character can multiply the possible strings. Symbols can enlarge that set too, but forced rules often lead people to predictable swaps, such as replacing a letter with a similar-looking number. No chart can promise one cracking time for every password. The rate depends on the password, the way a site protects it, the attacker’s equipment, and whether guesses happen online or against stolen data.

Reuse creates a different danger. If one service is breached, attackers may try the same email and password elsewhere. A unique password for each account limits that chain.

A password manager can create and store long, random passwords. Multi-factor authentication adds another check, and passkeys can avoid a shared password altogether. When a person must remember a password, a long and unusual passphrase may be easier than a short jumble. The goal is not one magic recipe. It is to make guessing difficult and one stolen secret less useful.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why every password can be cracked in the same number of hours
Why symbols make a password weaker in every situation
How websites prevent all attacks on stored data
How current password advice combines length, uniqueness, and safer tools
questions.explanation: The passage explains length, attack conditions, unique passwords, managers, MFA, and passkeys.

questions.stem: Why can no chart promise one cracking time for every password?
choices: The rate depends on the password, protection, equipment, and kind of attack
Every attacker must type guesses by hand
All websites use exactly the same protection
Long passwords contain no characters that a machine can test
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly lists the conditions that change a guessing rate.

questions.stem: In this passage, “unique” means
choices: made entirely from symbols
used for only one account
changed at the end of every day
shared with a trusted friend
questions.explanation: A unique password is different for each account, so one breach does not open the others.

questions.stem: Why does password reuse make one breach more damaging?
choices: A reused password becomes shorter each time
A password manager publishes every stored password
Attackers can try the same credentials on other accounts
Multi-factor authentication stops working on all sites
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explains that attackers may test the stolen email and password elsewhere.

lesson.strategy: Organize the passage into three risks and responses: guessability, reuse, and memory burden. Notice the limits in paragraph two; attack conditions prevent a universal cracking-time claim.

signals.means: Introduces the shift from composition rules to broader guidance.
Signals an important limit on fixed cracking-time claims.
Moves from guessing strength to damage across accounts.
Summarizes why several protections work together.

vocab.inContext: broken into so that protected account data may be exposed
different for each account rather than reused
a longer password made from an unusual sequence of words

skillTips.main-idea: The answer should include both stronger secrets and tools that limit memory and reuse.
skillTips.inference: Trace the stolen credential from one breached service to attempts at other services.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “for each account” gives the local meaning of unique.
skillTips.detail: For cracking time, return to the four conditions listed in paragraph two.

passages.title: Your Name in a Loud Room
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At a crowded party you can follow one voice and let the rest of the room become noise. It feels like closing a door. Then someone across the room says your name, and you hear it.

Both of those are true, and together they say something odd about attention. If the door were really shut, your name could not get through. If it were open, you would be flooded.

A researcher named Colin Cherry tested this in the 1950s. He played two different recordings, one into each ear, and asked people to repeat one of them aloud as it went. They managed it. Afterwards they could report almost nothing about the ignored ear: not the topic, not the words. But in a later study built on his method, about a third of listeners noticed their own name when it was slipped into the ear they were ignoring.

So the ignored channel is not switched off. Something keeps reading all of it, cheaply and without your knowledge, and interrupts you when it finds something that matters.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: People are unable to follow two conversations at the same time.
The sound you are ignoring is still being checked for things that matter.
Crowded parties are difficult places to hold a conversation.
Hearing works better than sight in a noisy room.
questions.explanation: The passage sets up a puzzle, uses the study as evidence, and answers it in the last paragraph: something keeps reading the ignored side.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what could Cherry's listeners report about the ignored ear?
choices: The topic, but not the exact words.
Their own name, and nothing else.
Almost nothing: not the topic and not the words.
Everything they had heard on that side.
questions.explanation: The passage says they could report almost nothing, and then names both things they missed. The name result came from a later study.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "channel" is
choices: a station on a television set
a narrow path cut to carry water
the part of the ear that carries sound inward
one stream of sound among several you could listen to
questions.explanation: The word arrives right after an experiment with two recordings and two ears, and it is the one being ignored. It names a stream of sound.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that attention works less like a door and more like
choices: a switch that is either on or off
a room that slowly fills with noise
a filter that keeps checking whatever it lets past
a memory that stores everything it hears
questions.explanation: A shut door would block the name and an open one would flood you. What is left is something that lets most through unread but still watches it.

lesson.strategy: The passage sets up a contradiction and then resolves it with an experiment. Read the second paragraph slowly, since it names both halves of the puzzle. The last paragraph is the answer, and it quietly corrects the door image from the opening.

signals.phrase: It feels like closing a door.
signals.means: An image the passage will later argue against. Hold on to it loosely.
Marks the contradiction. Two things that seem to conflict are about to be reconciled.

signals.phrase: about a third of listeners noticed their own name
signals.means: The crucial exception. Not everything in the ignored ear was lost.

signals.phrase: Something keeps reading all of it
signals.means: The resolution. Attention filters, but the filter is never idle.

vocab.inContext: the mind's choice of what to follow and what to let go
left unattended on purpose while you follow something else
one stream of sound among several arriving at the same time

skillTips.main-idea: The experiment is evidence, not the point. The point is what it shows about the side you are not listening to.
skillTips.inference: The door image is offered and then undercut. When a passage sets up an image early, check whether its ending still supports it.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Channel" arrives late, after two recordings and two ears. Use that setup to fix what it means.
skillTips.detail: The study has two separate results: nothing remembered, and a third hearing their name. Keep them apart when you answer.

passages.title: The Woman Who Drew the Sea Floor
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1948, Marie Tharp took a job at a laboratory in New York that studied the ocean floor. She was a trained geologist and a skilled mapmaker. She was not allowed on the research ships, because women were thought to bring bad luck at sea.

So she worked ashore with whatever the ships sent back. Bruce Heezen and others crossed the Atlantic, bouncing sound off the bottom and writing down how long each echo took to return. Tharp turned those columns of numbers into a picture of the sea floor, drawing by hand, profile by profile.

A shape kept appearing. Down the middle of the Atlantic ran a long range of mountains, and along the top of that range ran a narrow valley, like a crack. She said it looked like a rift, a place where the floor was being pulled apart. Heezen called the idea girl talk.

Then someone plotted the earthquakes of the Atlantic on the same map. They fell in a line, inside her valley. Heezen stopped calling it girl talk.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Bruce Heezen discovered a mountain range under the Atlantic.
Echo sounding is the most accurate way to measure an ocean.
Earthquakes happen more often in the Atlantic than elsewhere.
Kept off the ships, Marie Tharp drew the sea floor from numbers and found a rift nobody had seen.
questions.explanation: The passage joins the obstacle, the work she did instead, and what that work revealed. The other choices take one piece out of context.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why was Tharp not allowed on the research ships?
choices: Women were thought to bring bad luck at sea.
She had no training in geology.
She was needed on shore to draw the maps.
The ships had no room for extra staff.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives the reason directly, and it has nothing to do with her skill: she was a trained geologist and mapmaker.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "rift" is
choices: a disagreement between two scientists
a place where something is being pulled apart
a tall ridge of underwater mountains
the echo of a sound returning from the sea floor
questions.explanation: The passage defines it in the same sentence, right after the comma: a place where the floor was being pulled apart.

questions.stem: Why did the earthquake map change Heezen's mind?
choices: It proved that the mountain range was really there.
It was drawn by someone other than Tharp.
It showed that the ships had measured the depths wrongly.
It put earthquakes exactly where she said the floor was splitting.
questions.explanation: Two maps made from unrelated data agreed. Earthquakes falling inside her valley is what a splitting floor would produce.

lesson.strategy: A story about evidence. Track three things: what she was refused, what she built out of second-hand data, and what finally settled the argument. The turn comes when an independent map lands on top of hers and agrees with it.

signals.phrase: She was not allowed on the research ships
signals.means: The obstacle. Everything she does afterward is shaped by working from shore.
How the raw data was made. She never saw the ocean floor, only numbers.
The discovery begins. A pattern found across many drawings, not in one.

signals.phrase: Heezen stopped calling it girl talk.
signals.means: The reversal, shown as a change in behavior rather than an admission.

vocab.inContext: a scientist who studies rock and the structure of the earth
a side view of the ground, drawn as a single line
a split, or a place where something is being pulled apart

skillTips.main-idea: A life story's main idea joins the person to what changed because of them. Keep both the obstacle and the discovery in your answer.
skillTips.inference: The passage never explains why the earthquake line mattered. Set the two maps side by side and ask what their agreement proves.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Rift" is defined in the same sentence, just after the comma. When a hard word is followed by a comma, read on before guessing.
skillTips.detail: The reason she stayed ashore is given once, in the first paragraph, and it says nothing about her ability.

passages.title: The Shade That Moved
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On the hottest day of summer, one tree stood in the field. Its shade was cool and dark. A young ram got there first. "This shade is mine," he said. He butted away the old ewe and the lambs. They went to the stone wall and lay in its thin shadow.

The ram slept. But the sun does not stand still. All afternoon it slid across the sky, and the shadow slid with it. The ram woke on hot, bare grass. The tree's shade now lay by the wall, where the others rested. The old ewe looked up. "There is room," she said. He came, and the shade held them all.

What you grab can move. What is shared makes room.

questions.stem: What lesson does this fable teach?
choices: Sheep should always rest near stone walls on hot days.
The strongest animal deserves the best place in the field.
Grabbing a good thing for yourself can leave you with nothing, while sharing makes room for all.
Summer afternoons are too hot for sleeping outside.
questions.explanation: The ram grabs the shade and loses it when the sun moves, while the ewe shares her spot even after being pushed away. The last two lines state the moral directly: what you grab can move, and what is shared makes room.

questions.stem: Why does the old ewe say "There is room"?
choices: She chooses to be kind to the ram even though he pushed her away.
She is afraid the ram will butt her again.
She wants the ram to guard the wall from other sheep.
She needs the ram to keep the lambs warm.
questions.explanation: The story never says the ewe forgives the ram, but her actions show it. He butted her away in the morning, yet when the shade comes to her side, she invites him in. Her three words are kindness he did not earn.

questions.stem: In this fable, "butted" means the ram:
choices: called loudly to the other sheep
pushed the others away with his head
walked slowly around the tree
shared the shade with the flock
questions.explanation: Rams push with their heads. The sentence says he "butted away the old ewe and the lambs," and the next sentence shows the result: they had to leave and go to the wall. So the word means a forceful push, not a call or a walk.

questions.stem: Where did the ewe and the lambs go after the ram took the shade?
choices: To the far side of the field
Under a second tree
Into a cool stream
To the stone wall and its thin shadow
questions.explanation: The text states it directly: "They went to the stone wall and lay in its thin shadow." There is no second tree or stream in this story.

lesson.strategy: A fable: one hot day, one selfish grab, one turn. The ram takes the shade; the sun quietly takes it back. Watch "But the sun does not stand still": that sentence starts the turn. The last two short lines say the moral, so read the story as proof of those lines.

signals.means: The selfish grab. A fable sets up a choice like this so it can test it; expect a turn.

signals.phrase: But the sun does not stand still.
signals.means: The turn begins. "But" warns you the ram's plan is about to fail, and no animal will cause it.
The kindness at the end. The ewe offers what the ram refused to offer her.
The moral, said plainly. The whole story exists to prove this one line.

vocab.inContext: pushed with the head, the way rams fight
the cool, dark area where a tree blocks the sun
empty and uncovered: grass with no shade left on it

skillTips.main-idea: In a fable the main idea is the moral. Test the closing lines against the story: does the ram's afternoon prove them? The answer must fit the ram's loss and the ewe's offer at once.
skillTips.inference: The ewe's feelings are never named. Compare how the ram treats her in the morning with what she says at the wall; her actions carry what the fable does not say.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the result to test a word. Right after the ram "butted away" the others, they leave for the wall, so the word must mean something forceful, not friendly.
skillTips.detail: Track the shade like an object: under the tree at noon, "by the wall" in the afternoon. Where each sheep lies depends on where the shade is at that moment.

passages.title: Two Piles of Acorns
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
All autumn, Pip the squirrel worked to have the biggest store in the wood. She buried acorns everywhere: under roots, near the stream. She did not mark the spots. "More," she said. "More is what matters."

Her neighbor Hazel buried only forty acorns and pressed a small white stone over each one. Pip laughed at the little pile.

Then snow covered the wood. Pip dug here and there and found almost nothing. Her acorns were everywhere, and so they were nowhere. Hazel followed her stones and found every one. She shared with Pip until spring.

A small store you can find beats a big store you lose.

questions.stem: What lesson does this fable teach?
choices: A supply you can find when you need it is worth more than a bigger one you cannot.
Squirrels should bury their acorns near streams.
Working hard in autumn is a waste of time.
Laughing at a neighbor always brings bad luck.
questions.explanation: The fable sets Pip's huge unmarked pile against Hazel's forty marked acorns, then lets winter test both. The last line states the moral: a small store you can find beats a big store you lose. Hard work is not the problem; losing track of it is.

questions.stem: Why does Pip find almost nothing when the snow comes?
choices: Other squirrels stole her acorns during autumn.
The stream washed her acorns away.
She buried her acorns too deep to dig up.
She did not mark her spots, so she cannot remember where her acorns are.
questions.explanation: Put two clues together: early on, "She did not mark the spots," and later, her acorns "were everywhere, and so they were nowhere." The acorns still exist; she just cannot find them. No thief, flood, or deep hole appears in the story.

questions.stem: In "the biggest store in the wood," the word "store" means:
choices: a shop that sells food
a supply saved up for later
a hole under a tree root
a pile of white stones
questions.explanation: No one buys or sells anything in this fable. Pip is burying acorns to eat in winter, so her "store" is the food she has saved up. The other common meaning of the word, a shop, does not fit a forest.

questions.stem: How many acorns did Hazel bury?
choices: Fourteen
Four hundred
Forty
The story does not say
questions.explanation: The text states it in one sentence: "Her neighbor Hazel buried only forty acorns." The word "only" is there to contrast her count with Pip's everywhere-pile.

lesson.strategy: A fable built on a contrast: Pip's huge unmarked pile against Hazel's forty acorns under white stones. Hold the two squirrels side by side as you read. "Then snow covered the wood" is the test, and the last line turns the contrast into the moral.

signals.means: Pip's belief, said out loud. The fable is built to put this idea through a winter test.

signals.phrase: a small white stone over each one
signals.means: Hazel's method. It looks like a tiny detail, but it decides the ending.
The turn. Winter arrives, and both squirrels' autumn choices get graded.
The twist in one phrase: food you cannot find might as well not exist.

vocab.inContext: a supply of food saved for later, not a shop
to leave a sign on a spot so you can find it again
the nuts of an oak tree, buried by squirrels for winter

skillTips.main-idea: Check the last line against both squirrels: does Pip's winter prove it? Does Hazel's? A fable's moral must fit the whole contrast, not just one character's luck.
skillTips.inference: The fable never says in one place why Pip fails. Link her early choice about the spots to the phrase "they were nowhere": the cause sits two paragraphs before the result.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Store" has two everyday meanings. Test each against the scene: no one is buying or selling in this wood, so pick the meaning that fits burying food for winter.
skillTips.detail: Numbers stick to the wrong squirrel easily. Reread who buried forty and who buried "everywhere" before answering any counting question.

passages.title: The Fox and the Spring Ice
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the last week of winter, a young fox came to the wide pond. Home was on the far side. Walking around would take all morning. Walking across the ice would take ten minutes.

An old goose stood by the bank. "Spring is close," she said. "The ice is thin now. Go around."

"The ice held me all winter," said the fox, and he trotted out. Halfway across, the ice groaned. Then it cracked, and the fox dropped into the freezing water. He kicked his way back and climbed out. Then he walked around the pond after all, shivering, slower than ever.

A shortcut you do not test can be the longest way home.

questions.stem: What is the lesson of this fable?
choices: Foxes should never trust what geese tell them.
A shortcut can cost more than the long way if you do not check that it is still safe.
Ponds are dangerous in every season of the year.
Walking all morning makes a young animal stronger.
questions.explanation: The fox skips the safe route to save time, ignores a warning, and ends up making the coldest, slowest trip of all. The last line names the mistake: a shortcut you do not test can be the longest way home.

questions.stem: What is wrong with the fox's reason, "The ice held me all winter"?
choices: The season is changing, so what was true in winter is no longer true.
The fox never actually crossed the ice in winter.
The ice was always too thin, even in the coldest weeks.
The goose had broken the ice earlier that day.
questions.explanation: The goose gives the clue: "Spring is close... The ice is thin now." The fox trusts the past, but the pond has changed with the season. His fact was true once; it just is not true anymore.

questions.stem: In this fable, "groaned" means the ice:
choices: melted into water at once
turned soft and white
slid under the fox's feet
made a low, deep sound as it strained
questions.explanation: Read the order of events: the ice groaned, then it cracked. The groan is the sound of ice straining under weight, a warning that comes just before the break.

questions.stem: How long would walking around the pond take?
choices: Ten minutes
One hour
All morning
Two days
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives both times: around takes all morning, across takes ten minutes. Ten minutes belongs to the ice route, not the safe one.

lesson.strategy: A fable with a warning in the middle. The fox weighs ten minutes against all morning, hears the goose, and trusts the past instead. Watch the word "now" in "The ice is thin now": the whole story turns on the season changing. The last line hands you the moral to check.

signals.means: The goose's warning rests on the season changing. What the fox knows about the ice is out of date.

signals.phrase: The ice held me all winter
signals.means: The fox's reason. It sounds solid; the fable will test whether the past still counts.
A warning sound before the crack. The story gives the fox one last chance to turn back.

signals.phrase: A shortcut you do not test
signals.means: The start of the moral. The fable blames the not-testing, not the shortcut itself.

vocab.inContext: made a low, deep sound under weight, a sign of strain
ran at an easy, confident pace
shaking from cold

skillTips.main-idea: The moral line names the fox's mistake exactly. Reread his choice at the bank and ask which part of the last line he skipped; that part is the heart of the lesson.
skillTips.inference: Set the goose's "The ice is thin now" beside the fox's "The ice held me all winter." Both can be true. Work out why one of them no longer helps him.
skillTips.vocabulary: Sound words like "groaned" take their meaning from what follows. The next sentence starts with "Then it cracked"; let the order of events define the word.
skillTips.detail: Two times sit in one paragraph: ten minutes and all morning. Match each time to its route before you answer.

passages.title: The Frog That Freezes
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The wood frog lives in cold northern forests. It cannot dig deep or fly south. So in late autumn it lets winter win. The frog hides under leaves. When hard frost comes, ice forms under its skin. Its heart slows, then stops. It does not breathe. All winter it lies still, like a frog made of glass.

But the frog is not dead. Before it freezes, its body fills with sugar. The sugar works like antifreeze in a car. It keeps the ice from cutting the soft parts inside. In spring the ground warms, and the ice inside melts. Its heart gives one beat, then another. Soon the frog hops off to find a pond.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why ponds in northern forests freeze over in winter.
How frogs dig deep holes to escape the frost.
Why sugar is an important food for forest animals.
How the wood frog survives winter by freezing and then thawing out alive.
questions.explanation: The passage covers the whole cycle: the frog freezes in autumn, lies still all winter, and wakes when the ice inside it melts. The sugar and the frost are parts of that story, not the main point on their own.

questions.stem: Why does the wood frog "let winter win"?
choices: It enjoys the cold more than other frogs do.
It has no way to escape the cold, so freezing is its only choice.
The ice keeps it safe from hungry animals.
It is too old to travel to a pond.
questions.explanation: The second sentence is the clue: the frog "cannot dig deep or fly south." Other animals escape winter by going under it or leaving. This frog can do neither, so its body found a third way: go through the freeze instead of around it.

questions.stem: In "All winter it lies still," the word "still" means:
choices: even now
calm, like quiet water
without moving
in the same place every year
questions.explanation: "Still" has several meanings. This one follows "Its heart slows, then stops" and "It does not breathe": the sentence is describing a body with no movement at all.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the sugar in the frog's body do?
choices: It keeps the ice from cutting the soft parts inside.
It makes the frog's heart beat faster.
It melts the ice in early spring.
It feeds the frog while it sleeps.
questions.explanation: The passage states the sugar's job right after the antifreeze comparison. Melting is a different step; the warm spring ground does that, not the sugar.

lesson.strategy: A nature passage in two halves. The first half sounds like a death: the heart stops, the breathing stops, "a frog made of glass." The second half opens with "But the frog is not dead" and explains the trick. Read the first half slowly, then let the second half solve it.

signals.means: A surprising move. The frog does not fight or flee the cold; it goes through it.

signals.phrase: like a frog made of glass
signals.means: A picture of the frozen frog: hard, still, and breakable-looking.

signals.phrase: But the frog is not dead.
signals.means: The turn. Everything before this looked like an ending; the explanation starts here.
A comparison to something familiar: the sugar blocks ice damage the way antifreeze does.

vocab.inContext: freezing cold that turns water to ice; a "hard frost" is a deep freeze
without moving
turns from ice back into water

skillTips.main-idea: This passage explains one animal's winter trick from start to finish. A good main-idea answer must include both halves (the freezing and the waking), not just the strange first paragraph.
skillTips.inference: The reason for the frog's choice sits in the second sentence, before anything strange happens. Ask what this frog cannot do, and the freezing starts to look like a plan.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Still" changes meaning by sentence. Test each meaning against the neighbors here: a stopped heart and no breathing point to only one of them.
skillTips.detail: The sugar has one job and the spring ground has another. When a question asks what one thing does, check which sentence names that thing as the doer.

passages.title: How a Duck Stays Dry
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Rain rolls off a duck's back and never soaks in. This is not luck. The duck builds it.

Near its tail, the duck has a small gland that makes oil. The duck takes oil with its beak and rubs it over each feather. This careful work is called preening. The oil wears off, so the duck preens every day.

The feathers do their part too. They lie over each other like tiles on a roof, and tiny hooks zip each feather to the next. Rain hits this oily roof and rolls away in drops. Under it, the duck's soft down stays dry and warm. That is why a duck can sit on a cold pond all day.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Ducks spend most of their day swimming on cold ponds.
A duck keeps itself dry through its own work: oil from a gland, spread over feathers that overlap like a roof.
Rain is dangerous for most water birds.
A duck's down feathers are warmer than any coat.
questions.explanation: The passage opens with the claim ("This is not luck. The duck builds it") and then gives the two parts of the build: the oil and the overlapping feathers. The other choices each grab a single detail.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if a duck could not preen for many days?
choices: Its gland would make more oil on its own.
Its feathers would grow closer together.
The oil would wear off and rain would start to soak in.
The duck would stop needing to swim.
questions.explanation: The passage says "The oil wears off, so the duck preens every day." Daily preening is what replaces the lost oil. Take the preening away and the oil keeps wearing off with nothing to replace it, so the water gets through.

questions.stem: In this passage, "preening" means:
choices: spreading oil over the feathers with the beak
sleeping with the head under a wing
diving for food under the water
calling loudly across a pond
questions.explanation: The passage defines the word right where it appears: the duck "takes oil with its beak and rubs it over each feather," and the next sentence names that work preening.

questions.stem: Where does the duck's oil come from?
choices: From the pond water
From the food the duck eats
From the tips of its wing feathers
From a small gland near its tail
questions.explanation: One sentence states it: "Near its tail, the duck has a small gland that makes oil." The pond, the food, and the wings are never given as sources.

lesson.strategy: A how-it-works passage with two parts that work together. Part one is the oil and the daily preening; part two is the feather roof with its tiny hooks. Keep asking what each part does alone, then what they do together when the rain hits.

signals.means: The opening claim. The passage promises to show the work behind the dry back.
A problem inside the system. It explains why the preening must happen every day.
A comparison: the feathers overlap the way roof tiles do, so water runs off instead of in.

vocab.inContext: a small body part that makes something: here, oil
a bird's careful cleaning and oiling of its feathers
the soft, fluffy feathers closest to a bird's body

skillTips.main-idea: The first paragraph makes a claim in three short sentences, and the rest of the passage is the proof. A main-idea answer should cover the claim and both parts of the proof.
skillTips.inference: The passage tells you what the duck does every day and why. To predict what happens without that habit, run the system forward with one part missing.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Preening" is defined by the sentence just before it is named. When a passage teaches a term, the meaning usually sits right beside it.
skillTips.detail: The gland, the hooks, and the down each live in one sentence. Match the question's thing to its own sentence instead of answering from the picture in your head.

passages.title: The Umbrella Box
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The rain started at three. Ren stood at the school door with no umbrella and ten blocks to walk.

Mr. Otis, the janitor, was mopping the hall. He looked at the rain, then at Ren. He took his own umbrella from a hook. "Take it," he said. "Bring it back tomorrow."

Ren brought it back dry the next morning. "Thank you," he said. "Pass the favor on," said Mr. Otis. "That is all the rent I charge."

On Saturday, Ren found two old umbrellas at home. On Monday he set a box by the school door with a sign: TAKE ONE. BRING IT BACK. By spring, the box held nine umbrellas, and no one walked home wet.

questions.stem: What is this story mainly about?
choices: A small kindness from a janitor grows into a box of umbrellas that helps the whole school.
Ren learns to check the weather before leaving home.
Mr. Otis wants students to pay to borrow umbrellas.
A school makes a new rule about lost umbrellas.
questions.explanation: The story moves from one lent umbrella to a box of nine. The turn is Mr. Otis's condition ("Pass the favor on") which Ren turns into something that keeps working without him. The rent line is a joke, not a price.

questions.stem: What does Mr. Otis mean by "That is all the rent I charge"?
choices: Ren must pay him a small amount of money.
He wants Ren to return two umbrellas instead of one.
He wants no payment; passing the favor on is enough.
He plans to start renting umbrellas to students.
questions.explanation: Rent is normally money paid for borrowing something. But Mr. Otis names his "rent" in the line just before: "Pass the favor on." He is saying the only cost of the loan is a kindness to someone else.

questions.stem: In "Pass the favor on," a "favor" is:
choices: a payment made on time
a kind act done to help someone
a school rule about the rain
a borrowed thing that must be returned
questions.explanation: The favor in the story is Mr. Otis lending his own umbrella to a stuck student, help given freely. The last choice is close but wrong: the umbrella is the thing; the favor is the act of lending it.

questions.stem: What did the sign on the box say?
choices: PASS THE FAVOR ON
UMBRELLAS FOR SALE
RETURN TO MR. OTIS
TAKE ONE. BRING IT BACK.
questions.explanation: The text gives the sign in capital letters: "TAKE ONE. BRING IT BACK." The first choice mixes in Mr. Otis's spoken words, which never appear on the box.

lesson.strategy: A story that moves in three steps: one loan, one condition, one invention. Track the umbrella count as you read: one lent, two found at home, nine by spring. The numbers quietly show a kindness spreading. Mr. Otis's two short lines carry the meaning.

signals.means: A loan, not a gift. Half of these words come back in capitals on Ren's sign.
The condition of the loan. Ren answers it with a box, not with more words.

signals.phrase: By spring, the box held nine umbrellas
signals.means: The result, given as a number. One favor became nine because it kept moving.

vocab.inContext: a person who cleans and takes care of a building
a kind act done to help someone
money paid to borrow or use something that is not yours

skillTips.main-idea: Ask what changed between the first rainy day and spring. The story's point lives in that change, not in any single scene at the door.
skillTips.inference: Mr. Otis speaks twice and explains nothing. Read his lines as instructions, then watch what Ren builds with them; the story answers for him.
skillTips.vocabulary: The story shows the favor before naming it: an umbrella handed over in the rain. Tie the word to that scene, not to a dictionary.
skillTips.detail: The sign is printed in capital letters in the text. For any question about exact words, go back and copy them with your eyes; near-matches are the trap.

passages.title: The Nest in the Flower Pot
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
All winter, Maya planned her balcony garden. She drew maps: beans here, tomatoes there, one big blue pot for sunflowers in the sunny corner.

In March she took her soil out. But in the blue pot sat a brown bird on a nest of twigs and string. Two pale eggs lay under her.

Maya wanted that corner. It got the best sun. She stood a long time with her trowel. Then she watered around the pot.

The chicks hatched in April and flew in May. Maya planted her sunflowers late, and they bloomed small. But all summer the bird sang from her rail, and Maya thought her garden had grown more than flowers.

questions.stem: What is this story mainly about?
choices: How to plant sunflowers in a balcony pot.
A bird that takes over a garden every spring.
Maya gives up her best spot for a nesting bird and finds the trade worth it.
Why sunflowers need the sunniest corner to grow tall.
questions.explanation: The story is built around Maya's choice. Her plan wanted the sunny corner, the bird got it, and the last line weighs the result: small sunflowers, but a garden that "had grown more than flowers."

questions.stem: Why does Maya stand "a long time with her trowel"?
choices: She is tired from carrying the soil.
She is afraid the bird will peck her.
She cannot remember her garden map.
She is deciding between her plan and leaving the nest alone.
questions.explanation: The two sentences before set up a pull in each direction: "Maya wanted that corner. It got the best sun." The long pause is the choice being made, and what she does next (watering around the pot) shows which side won.

questions.stem: In "they bloomed small," the word "bloomed" means:
choices: opened their flowers
fell over in the wind
dried up in the heat
grew taller than the rail
questions.explanation: Blooming is what flowers do when they open. The sunflowers were planted late, so they still bloomed (they opened) but small. The sentence is about size, not falling or drying.

questions.stem: What was the nest in the blue pot made of?
choices: Grass and mud
Twigs and string
Leaves and feathers
Paper and cloth
questions.explanation: The text states it directly: "a nest of twigs and string." The string is a city detail: balcony birds build with what they find.

lesson.strategy: A quiet story where the turn is a choice, not an event. Winter holds the plan; March puts a problem in the blue pot; the pause with the trowel is the decision. The last sentence tells you how Maya weighs what she lost against what she got; read it twice.

signals.phrase: one big blue pot for sunflowers
signals.means: The plan. The story will put its problem in exactly this pot.
The want, stated flat. Watch what she does with it two sentences later.
The decision, shown as an action. She keeps gardening but spares the nest.
The last line's hint at meaning: the summer gave her something the map could not.

vocab.inContext: a small hand tool for digging in a garden
broke out of the egg
opened flowers

skillTips.main-idea: Nothing loud happens here. Find the main idea by comparing the winter map with what the balcony actually holds by summer, and asking how Maya feels about the difference.
skillTips.inference: The story never says what Maya is thinking at the pot. Put "Maya wanted that corner" next to what she does with the water, and the pause explains itself.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Bloomed" arrives with a size word after it. Late flowers can still open; let "late" and "small" shape the meaning together.
skillTips.detail: The nest is described once, in the March paragraph. The materials, the bird, and the eggs sit in two sentences; reread them before answering about any of the three.

passages.title: Why Shadows Change Size
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Light moves in straight lines. It cannot bend around you. When you stand in the sun, your body blocks some light, and a dark shape falls on the ground. That shape is your shadow.

Watch it change through one day. In the early morning, the sun sits low in the sky. Its light comes from the side, so your shadow stretches out long and thin. At noon, the sun is high overhead. Light comes down from above, and your shadow shrinks to a small pool at your feet. By evening, the sun is low again, and the shadow grows long on the other side.

Your body never changed. Only the angle of the light did.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Your shadow grows during the day because the sun gets stronger.
A shadow changes size because the angle of the sunlight changes, not because your body does.
Light can bend around objects when the sun is low in the sky.
Shadows appear only in the early morning and the evening.
questions.explanation: The last two sentences state it directly: your body never changed, only the angle of the light did. The morning, noon, and evening scenes all exist to show that one cause.

questions.stem: A flagpole's shadow would be shortest
choices: just after sunrise
in the late evening
whenever the pole is tallest
at noon, when the sun is highest
questions.explanation: The passage links a low sun to long shadows and a high sun to a small pool at your feet. Apply that rule to any object: the shadow is shortest when the sun is highest.

questions.stem: In this passage, "overhead" means
choices: directly above you
far away in the distance
hidden behind a cloud
close to the ground
questions.explanation: The word sits in the noon scene, and the next sentence says light comes down from above. The sentence right after a hard word often carries its meaning.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does your shadow look like at noon?
choices: Long and thin, stretching to the side.
The same as it looked in the morning.
A small pool at your feet.
Twice as tall as your body.
questions.explanation: The noon sentence says the shadow shrinks to a small pool at your feet. Long and thin belongs to morning and evening, when the sun is low.

lesson.strategy: The passage states a rule in its first two sentences, then walks one day from morning to evening as a test of it. Follow the sun's height in each scene and check what the shadow does. The last two sentences separate what changed from what did not.

signals.means: The rule everything depends on. Shadows exist because light cannot bend around you.

signals.phrase: Watch it change through one day.
signals.means: Announces the structure: one example traced through morning, noon, and evening.
The closing contrast. If you did not change, the cause must be the light.

vocab.inContext: directly above you, where the sun sits at noon
gets longer and thinner
the direction the light comes from, from the side or from above

skillTips.main-idea: The morning, noon, and evening scenes are three tests of one rule. The main idea covers all three, not just one time of day.
skillTips.inference: The passage ties shadow length to how low the sun sits. Apply that link to a time or an object the text never mentions.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Overhead" appears in the noon scene, right before light comes down from above. Read the next sentence before choosing.
skillTips.detail: Each time of day gets its own sentence. Find the one scene the question names and match it word for word.

passages.title: Why Popcorn Pops
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A popcorn kernel is a seed with a secret. Under its hard shell sits soft white starch, and inside the starch hides a small drop of water.

Heat the kernel in a pan. The water gets hot and wants to become steam. Steam needs far more room than water, but the hard shell will not let it out. So the steam pushes. It pushes harder and harder, like air filling a balloon.

At last the shell cannot hold. It breaks open with a bang, the steam bursts free, and the starch puffs out and cools into a white cloud. A kernel with a cracked shell never pops. Its steam leaks out slowly, and there is no push.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Popcorn should be cooked slowly so the shell does not crack.
The starch inside a kernel is the part that makes the bang.
Popcorn pops because trapped steam pushes until the sealed shell breaks.
Water and starch never mix inside a seed.
questions.explanation: Every step builds one chain: water becomes steam, the shell traps it, the push breaks the shell. The bang and the white cloud are results of that push.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen to a kernel that has fully dried out, with no water left inside?
choices: It would never pop, because there is nothing to become steam.
It would pop faster, because dry things heat quickly.
It would pop twice, once for the shell and once for the starch.
It would turn into a white cloud without a bang.
questions.explanation: The push comes from water turning to steam. Remove the water and the chain has no first step, just as the cracked shell removes the last one.

questions.stem: In this passage, "bursts" means
choices: leaks a little at a time
breaks out suddenly and with force
cools down into a cloud
grows larger and softer
questions.explanation: The steam bursts free in the same sentence as the shell breaking open with a bang. The moment is sudden and forceful, the opposite of the slow leak in the cracked kernel.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a kernel with a cracked shell never pop?
choices: The starch inside it has already turned white.
Cracked kernels contain no starch at all.
The water inside it is too cold to boil.
Its steam leaks out slowly, so there is no push.
questions.explanation: The last two sentences say it plainly: the steam leaks out slowly, and there is no push. The crack removes the trap that lets pressure build.

lesson.strategy: This is a cause chain: water to steam, steam to push, push to bang. Read it as steps, and at each step ask what the hard shell is doing. The final sentences give a failed case, the cracked shell, which shows you which step the pop cannot live without.

signals.means: Points inward. The passage will open the kernel layer by layer.
The middle of the cause chain. Pressure is building against the shell.

signals.phrase: A kernel with a cracked shell never pops.
signals.means: The test case. Remove the sealed shell and the pop disappears.

vocab.inContext: one seed of popcorn, shell and starch and all
water turned into hot gas, needing far more room
breaks out suddenly and with force

skillTips.main-idea: The bang is the ending, not the point. Look for the step the whole chain depends on, the one the cracked shell takes away.
skillTips.inference: Use the cracked-shell case as your model: take away one part of the chain, water or shell, and ask what fails next.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Bursts" sits beside "breaks open with a bang." The words around it carry its force.
skillTips.detail: The passage names three layers in order: hard shell, soft starch, drop of water. Keep them straight before answering.

passages.title: Why You Can See Your Breath
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On a cold morning, your breath is a small white cloud. On a warm day, the same breath is invisible. Your breath did not change. The air did.

The air you breathe out is warm and full of water. That water is a gas, spread too thin to see. Warm air holds this hidden water easily.

Cold air cannot. When your warm breath meets freezing air, it cools fast, and the hidden water has nowhere to stay. It gathers into tiny drops, thousands of them, each too small to feel. Light bounces off the drops, and you see a white puff.

Real clouds in the sky are made the same way: warm, wet air meeting cold.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: You see your breath when cold air turns its hidden water into tiny drops.
Breathing out water is a sign that cold weather is coming.
Warm air is easier to see than cold air.
Clouds in the sky are made of people's breath.
questions.explanation: The passage opens with a puzzle, same breath on two days, and solves it: cold air cannot hold the hidden water, so it gathers into drops you can see.

questions.stem: Using the passage, why is your breath invisible on a warm day?
choices: You breathe out less water when you are warm.
Tiny drops form, but the sun melts them.
The warm air keeps holding the water as a gas your eyes cannot see.
Light cannot bounce in warm weather.
questions.explanation: The passage says warm air holds the hidden water easily. If the water stays a spread-out gas, no drops form, and there is nothing for light to bounce off.

questions.stem: In this passage, "gathers" means
choices: disappears completely
freezes into ice
spreads out thinner
comes together in one place
questions.explanation: The hidden water gathers into tiny drops. Gas that was spread thin becomes drops, so the water is coming together, the opposite of spreading out.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does the puff of breath look white?
choices: The water inside it is frozen.
Light bounces off the tiny drops.
Cold air is naturally white.
The breath carries dust out of your body.
questions.explanation: The passage states it in one sentence: light bounces off the drops, and you see a white puff. Freezing and dust are never mentioned.

lesson.strategy: The first paragraph is a puzzle: same breath, different days. The next two paragraphs solve it by comparing what warm air and cold air can hold. Track the hidden water through the passage, first as a gas you cannot see, then as drops you can.

signals.phrase: Your breath did not change. The air did.
signals.means: The puzzle and its answer in two short sentences. The rest explains the second one.
Three words that turn the passage. Everything after shows what happens instead.
The last line widens one puff of breath into every cloud in the sky.

vocab.inContext: not able to be seen
comes together in one place
one small cloud of breath

skillTips.main-idea: The answer to the opening puzzle is the main idea. It is about what cold air does to the hidden water, not about the breath itself.
skillTips.inference: The passage says warm air holds hidden water easily. Turn that sentence around to explain the warm-day half of the puzzle.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Gathers" is followed by what it produces: tiny drops, thousands of them. Read past the word before choosing.
skillTips.detail: The white color has its own one-sentence cause near the end. Find the sentence about light.

passages.title: Margaret Knight's Bag Machine
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1868, a paper bag was shaped like an envelope: flat, weak at the bottom, useless for anything heavy.

Margaret Knight worked at a bag factory in Springfield, Massachusetts. Machines were her language. At twelve, she saw a steel shuttle fly off a loom and hurt a worker, and designed a guard to stop it. She studied the bag machines and saw the missing step: none of them could fold a flat bottom.

So she designed one that could. It cut, folded, and glued a bag that stood open on its own, the shape grocery bags still have today. She built a wooden model, then had a machine shop build it in iron.

At that shop, a man named Charles Annan studied her iron model and quietly filed for the patent himself. In court he argued that a woman could not understand such a machine. Knight answered with two years of diaries, drawings, and models. She won, and the patent was issued to her in 1871.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Knight invented a machine that folded flat-bottomed bags, then proved in court that the design was hers.
Charles Annan built the first machine that could glue paper bags.
Paper bags in 1868 were too weak to carry anything heavy.
Factories in Massachusetts refused to hire women as designers.
questions.explanation: The passage joins the invention and the fight over it. The weak envelope-shaped bag is only the setup, and Annan filed for a design the passage shows was hers.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Knight won the case because
choices: the judge had watched her work at the factory
Annan admitted he had copied the iron model
her long record of the design work showed it was hers
the factory owner spoke in her defense
questions.explanation: Annan's argument was about what a woman could understand, not about the machine. Against two years of diaries, drawings, and models, a claim with no record behind it lost.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "patent" is
choices: a written apology ordered by a court
the legal right to own an invention
a wooden model of a machine
a factory's book of safety rules
questions.explanation: Annan filed for the patent on a machine he did not design, and the court issued it to Knight once she proved the design was hers. Both uses point to legal ownership of an invention.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Knight design at age twelve?
choices: A stronger flat-bottomed paper bag.
A machine that wove cloth faster.
An iron model of a loom.
A guard to stop shuttles flying off looms.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says she saw a shuttle fly off a loom and hurt a worker, and designed a guard to stop it. The bag machine came later, at the factory.

lesson.strategy: A maker's story with a fight at the end. Track three things: what the existing machines could not do, what her machine did, and how she proved it was hers. The court case turns on paper, so notice what Knight brings as evidence and what Annan brings instead.

signals.means: Character in four words. The shuttle-guard story right after it is the proof.

signals.phrase: none of them could fold a flat bottom
signals.means: The gap she saw. Her invention is the answer to this exact line.

signals.phrase: quietly filed for the patent himself
signals.means: The theft. The word quietly tells you he knew whose design it was.

signals.phrase: two years of diaries, drawings, and models
signals.means: Her evidence. A record of the work beat a claim with nothing behind it.

vocab.inContext: the legal right to own and sell an invention
a machine that weaves thread into cloth
officially given out

skillTips.main-idea: Join the two halves: the bag machine she built and the court fight that made it legally hers. An answer holding only one half is too small.
skillTips.inference: Ask why Annan argued about her being a woman instead of about the machine itself. What he does not argue tells you what he could not.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Patent" appears twice, filed for and then issued. Both times it is something about an invention that a court can award.
skillTips.detail: The shuttle story happens at age twelve, before the bag factory. Keep the two workplaces separate when you answer.

passages.title: The Man Who Copied a Burr
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1941, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral came home from hunting with his trousers covered in burrs, the prickly seed cases of the burdock plant. So was his dog's fur. Most people pull burrs off and forget them. De Mestral put one under his microscope.

He saw no glue and no thorns. The burr was covered with hundreds of tiny hooks, and every hook had caught a loop: a loop of thread in his trousers, a loop of hair on his dog. Hooks and loops. That was the whole trick, and he thought he could copy it.

The copying took more than ten years. Hooks cut from cotton wore out. Then he tried nylon and found that nylon sewn under heat keeps its hook shape through thousands of openings and closings. He patented his fastener in 1955 and named the company Velcro, from the French words for velvet and hook.

The burdock plant had spent millions of years on the design. He only had to notice it.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Burdock plants are harmful to dogs and hunters.
Cotton is a weaker material than nylon in every product.
De Mestral invented the microscope to study plants.
By studying why burrs stick, de Mestral turned nature's hook-and-loop trick into a fastener.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the burr on his trousers to the hooks under the microscope to the nylon fastener. The main idea joins the noticing to the invention.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a good material for this fastener must
choices: be grown from a plant
keep its shape after many uses
melt as soon as it is heated
be softer than ordinary cloth
questions.explanation: Cotton failed by wearing out, and nylon won by keeping its hook shape through thousands of openings and closings. The requirement follows from that pair of results.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "fastener" is
choices: a device that holds two things together and can open again
a tool for cutting tiny hooks
a kind of prickly seed case
a French word meaning velvet
questions.explanation: He patented it after making hooks that survive thousands of openings and closings, so a fastener must join things and release them. The burr is the seed case, and velvet is only half of the name.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did de Mestral see under the microscope?
choices: A sticky glue coating the burr.
Tiny thorns that pierced the cloth.
Hundreds of tiny hooks, each caught on a loop.
Loops of nylon wrapped around the seeds.
questions.explanation: The passage rules out glue and thorns in the same paragraph, then names the hooks and the loops they caught. Nylon enters the story only years later.

lesson.strategy: An invention story in three moves: notice, understand, copy. The turn is the microscope, where everyone else pulls burrs off and he looks closer. Then track the ten years of copying: what failed, what worked, and why nylon made the difference.

signals.phrase: De Mestral put one under his microscope.
signals.means: The move that makes the story. Curiosity exactly where other people stop.
The whole mechanism in three words. Everything after is engineering.

signals.phrase: Hooks cut from cotton wore out.
signals.means: The failure that explains the nylon choice in the next sentence.

signals.phrase: He only had to notice it.
signals.means: The closing point. The design already existed in nature.

vocab.inContext: prickly seed cases that stick to cloth and fur
a device that holds two things together and can open again
registered as legally his own invention

skillTips.main-idea: The burr, the microscope, and the nylon tape are one arc. The main idea links what he saw in nature to what he built from it.
skillTips.inference: Compare cotton and nylon using only what the passage says each one did. The gap between wearing out and keeping shape is the engine of the answer.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Fastener" arrives after thousands of openings and closings. Those two words are its definition in action.
skillTips.detail: The story runs in order: the 1941 hunt, the microscope, ten years of failed hooks, the 1955 patent. Pin each detail to its stage before you answer.

passages.title: How a Screen Feels a Finger
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A phone screen has no moving parts. Nothing presses in when you tap. So how does the glass know where your finger is?

Under the glass lies a grid of wires, each thinner than a hair, and the phone keeps a faint electric charge spread across it. Your body is mostly salt water, and salt water conducts electricity. The moment your fingertip lands, it draws a little of that charge out of the wires directly beneath it.

The phone notices the loss. It scans the grid many times a second, asking where charge went missing, and that crossing of row and column becomes the spot you touched.

This one fact explains two small mysteries. A wool glove blocks your touch because wool does not conduct, so no charge can leave the screen. And rain makes a phone type nonsense because every drop of water draws off charge exactly the way a finger does.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Phone screens break easily because the glass is so thin.
The screen finds your finger by sensing where its electric charge is drawn away.
Gloves and rain are the two main enemies of a phone.
Salt water is dangerous to electronics of every kind.
questions.explanation: The middle paragraphs answer the opening question: the fingertip draws charge from the grid, and the phone locates the loss. The glove and the rain are consequences used as proof.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, why would the tip of a plastic pen fail to work on the screen?
choices: Plastic does not conduct, so it cannot draw charge from the wires.
Plastic is too smooth for the glass to feel.
A pen tip is too small for the grid to notice.
The pen would scratch the wires under the glass.
questions.explanation: The glove sentence gives the rule: no conduction, no charge leaves, no touch. A plastic tip fails the same test a wool glove fails.

questions.stem: In this passage, "conducts" means
choices: heats up very quickly
stores information safely
lets electricity pass through
repairs itself over time
questions.explanation: Salt water conducts and a fingertip works; wool does not conduct and the touch is blocked. What passes in one case and fails in the other is electric charge.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does rain make a phone type nonsense?
choices: Water reaches the battery and shorts it.
Cold raindrops make the glass shrink.
The grid of wires rusts when it gets wet.
Every drop draws off charge the way a finger does.
questions.explanation: The last sentence states it: each drop of water draws off charge exactly the way a finger does, so the phone reads touches that nobody made.

lesson.strategy: A question-and-answer passage. The first paragraph asks how glass can feel, the middle explains the charge trick, and the last paragraph tests it against two everyday mysteries. If the glove and the rain both make sense to you, you have the mechanism.

signals.phrase: So how does the glass know where your finger is?
signals.means: The question the whole passage exists to answer.
The key fact is about you, not the phone. Your body completes the trick.
The detection step. Missing charge is the signal, not pressure.

signals.phrase: This one fact explains two small mysteries.
signals.means: A test section begins. The glove and the rain are both checks on the mechanism.

vocab.inContext: a pattern of lines crossing in rows and columns
lets electricity pass through
very small, barely there

skillTips.main-idea: The mechanism is the answer to the opening question. The glove and the rain are proof of it, not the point.
skillTips.inference: Both mysteries follow one rule about what conducts. Apply that same rule to any new object touching the screen.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Conducts" is defined by contrast: wool does not conduct, and the touch is blocked. Read what failing to conduct costs.
skillTips.detail: The glove and the rain each get one sentence with its own because. Match the question to the right sentence.

passages.title: How a Microwave Heats Food
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A microwave oven does not heat every material in the same way. Its magnetron produces electromagnetic waves. Inside food, the changing electric field makes polar molecules, especially water molecules, turn back and forth. Moving ions also respond. Their motion transfers energy through the food and produces heat.

Water is important, but it is not the only part of food that absorbs microwave energy. Fats and sugars can absorb some too. That is why a fairly dry food may still become hot. The amount of heating depends on the food, its shape, and how long it is exposed.

Many microwave-safe glass or ceramic plates absorb less energy than the food. Such a plate may stay cooler at first, then warm as heat moves into it from the meal. Some dishes absorb more energy and become hot on their own, so the material and safety label matter.

Waves overlap inside the oven, creating stronger and weaker spots. A turntable moves food through those spots. It cannot guarantee perfectly even cooking, which is why stirring and checking temperature can still be important.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why every dry object remains cold in a microwave
Why a magnetron makes food safe without a temperature check
How microwave energy heats food unevenly and why dishes may heat differently
Why ceramic is the only material allowed in an oven
questions.explanation: The passage explains energy absorption by food, differences among dishes, and the turntable’s role.

questions.stem: Why can a fairly dry food still become hot?
choices: Its shape blocks all waves from leaving the oven
Only its plate can absorb microwave energy
Dry food always contains more water than soup
Fats and sugars can absorb some microwave energy too
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says fats and sugars, not only water, can absorb some microwave energy.

questions.stem: In this passage, “polar” describes a molecule that has
choices: an uneven electrical charge across it
a perfectly round and balanced shape
no response to an electric field
a layer of frozen water around it
questions.explanation: A changing electric field can turn a polar molecule because its electrical charge is unevenly arranged.

questions.stem: What does the turntable do?
choices: It changes fats and sugars into water
It moves food through stronger and weaker wave spots
It prevents every dish from becoming hot
It measures the food’s internal temperature
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says the turntable carries food through stronger and weaker spots.

lesson.strategy: Separate absorption from heat transfer. Food can absorb microwave energy through water and other components; a dish can absorb energy or warm later from the food. The last paragraph adds why motion helps without promising perfect heating.

signals.phrase: not the only part of food
signals.means: Corrects the idea that microwave heating acts on water alone.
Warns that one prediction does not fit every material.

signals.phrase: then warm as heat moves into it
signals.means: Distinguishes direct absorption from heat transferred by food.
Limits what the turntable can accomplish.

vocab.inContext: the device that produces electromagnetic waves in the oven
having an uneven electrical charge that responds to the field
to take in energy from the microwave field

skillTips.main-idea: Choose an answer broad enough to include food, dishes, and uneven heating.
skillTips.inference: Use paragraph two to reject the simple dry-means-cold rule.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read “polar” through the next action: the changing electric field turns the molecule.
skillTips.detail: The turntable changes where the food sits; it does not measure temperature or change ingredients.

passages.title: The Heavy Thumb
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In a market town there lived a miller who sold flour by weight. His scale was honest, but his thumb was not. When he poured flour into the pan, he let his thumb rest on its edge, and the scale read more than the bag held. Each trick earned him a coin, and each coin looked the same as an honest one.

One morning a girl watched the pan instead of the flour. "Your thumb is buying flour too," she said, loud enough for the whole line to hear. The miller laughed and gave her an extra scoop. Nobody laughed with him.

Nothing happened that day. But the baker began weighing his sacks at home. The innkeeper started walking to the mill in the next village, which was farther away but felt nearer. Within a year the miller's scale was honest all day long, because nobody came to test it.

A coin taken by trickery spends your name along with it.

questions.stem: What lesson does this fable teach?
choices: A scale should be tested by the customer before every sale.
Children see more clearly than adults do.
A small cheat earns coins now and costs your good name later.
A merchant should give extra to customers who complain.
questions.explanation: The girl's line exposes the trick, but the real punishment is the quiet drift of customers over the next year. The moral says it plainly: the coin "spends your name along with it."

questions.stem: Why did the mill in the next village feel "nearer" to the innkeeper?
choices: Trust made the longer walk cost less than being cheated.
A new road had shortened the walk between the villages.
The next village sold flour at a lower price.
The innkeeper had quarreled with the girl at the market.
questions.explanation: The text gives no road and no price. "Farther away but felt nearer" measures comfort, not distance: an honest scale is worth a longer walk, so the honest mill feels close.

questions.stem: In this passage, "trickery" most nearly means
choices: skill with a scale
hard bargaining
quick thinking
cheating
questions.explanation: The miller's hidden thumb makes the scale lie, so a coin "taken by trickery" is a coin taken by cheating, not by skill, bargaining, or wit.

questions.stem: What did the baker begin to do after the girl spoke?
choices: He complained to the miller directly.
He weighed his sacks at home.
He walked to the mill in the next village.
