He stopped buying flour at all.
questions.explanation: The passage says "the baker began weighing his sacks at home." It was the innkeeper, not the baker, who started walking to the next village.

lesson.strategy: A fable set in a trade: one small cheat, one witness, one slow punishment. The key is what does not happen. Nobody shouts, and "Nothing happened that day." Watch how each customer quietly protects himself afterward, then read the last line as the bill arriving.

signals.phrase: His scale was honest, but his thumb was not.
signals.means: The setup in one sentence. The tool is fair; the man is not. The fault belongs to the miller alone.
The turn. The punishment is not a scene at the stall; it is what customers quietly do afterward.
Distance measured in trust, not steps. The honest mill costs a walk but no worry.

signals.phrase: spends your name along with it
signals.means: The moral. Every cheated coin pays out reputation too, and that part cannot be earned back at the scale.

vocab.inContext: cheating; winning by a hidden unfair move, like the thumb resting on the pan
a person who runs an inn, a house where travelers pay to eat and sleep
one measure taken with a rounded tool; here, an extra helping of flour

skillTips.main-idea: The moral is the last line, but check it against the middle: the baker and the innkeeper act it out before the fable says it. A right answer must cover both the coin gained and the name lost.
skillTips.inference: The miller "laughed and gave her an extra scoop," and nobody laughed with him. Ask what the silence of the line already knows that the miller has not yet understood.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Trickery" is defined by the thumb: a hidden move that makes an honest scale lie. Tie the word to that picture rather than to a memorized definition.
skillTips.detail: Two customers react in two different ways. Keep the baker's move and the innkeeper's move separate before you answer who did what.

passages.title: The Borrowed Ladder
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Two farmers, Brek and Tomas, kept orchards on the same slope. Neither owned every tool an orchard needs, so they borrowed from each other, as country people do.

Brek treated a borrowed tool better than his own. He returned a ladder the evening he finished with it, and once, finding a rung cracked, he mended it before carrying it back. Tomas returned things when he was asked, and sometimes only when he was asked twice. The saw came back dull. The cart came back with a loose wheel and no word about it.

One autumn, frost was coming, and both men still had apples on the trees. The tallest ladder on the slope belonged to the widow Maren, and both men knocked at her door that morning.

She did not think long. "Brek brings things back," she said. "He may take it now. Tomas may have it after, if the frost waits."

Every borrowed tool is a test, and you do not choose when the grade is given.

questions.stem: What lesson does this fable teach?
choices: Never lend a tool you cannot afford to lose.
How you return what you borrow decides what you are trusted with later.
A tall ladder is worth more than a saw or a cart.
Neighbors should buy their own tools instead of borrowing.
questions.explanation: Maren's choice at the door only announces a grade earned over years of returns. The moral states it directly: every borrowed tool is a test.

questions.stem: Why does Maren decide so quickly at the door?
choices: She had promised the ladder to Brek the week before.
She wants both men gone before the frost arrives.
Tomas has never borrowed anything from her.
Years of watching returned tools have already told her whom to trust.
questions.explanation: The passage shows no promise and no record book. Her four-word reason, "Brek brings things back," points to the habits described earlier, which the whole slope could see.

questions.stem: In this passage, "mended" most nearly means
choices: repaired
replaced
painted
measured
questions.explanation: Brek finds a cracked rung and mends it before carrying the ladder back: he fixes the damage. Replacing or painting the ladder would not answer the crack.

questions.stem: What was wrong with the cart when Tomas returned it?
choices: It had a cracked rung.
It came back a week late.
It had a loose wheel, and he said nothing about it.
It came back dull.
questions.explanation: The text says "The cart came back with a loose wheel and no word about it." The dull edge belongs to the saw, and the cracked rung to the ladder Brek fixed.

lesson.strategy: A fable built on a contrast: two borrowers, one lender, one scarce ladder. Track the pattern of returns, the mended rung against the loose wheel, before the frost arrives. The knock at Maren's door is not the test; it is the day the grades come out.

signals.means: Borrowing is normal here. The fable is not about whether to borrow but about how to return.

signals.phrase: sometimes only when he was asked twice
signals.means: Tomas's habit in one line: things come back late, and only under pressure.
The decision is quick because it was made long ago, by years of watching how each man returns things.

signals.phrase: you do not choose when the grade is given
signals.means: The moral: the test runs silently for years, and the scarce ladder is simply the day results arrive.

vocab.inContext: one crossbar of a ladder, the step your foot lands on
fixed; Brek repairs the cracked rung before returning the ladder
freezing cold that can ruin fruit still hanging on the trees

skillTips.main-idea: Do not stop at "Brek is careful." The fable's point is what his returns buy him at Maren's door. Match your answer to the moral about tests and grades.
skillTips.inference: Maren gives one reason: "Brek brings things back." Ask how she knows. The fable expects you to connect her choice to the borrowing habits in the second paragraph.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Mended" sits next to a cracked rung. Let the broken thing tell you what the verb has to mean.
skillTips.detail: Three tools go home in three states: the ladder's rung, the saw's edge, the cart's wheel. Pin each condition to its tool; the wrong answers swap them.

passages.title: The Knife and the Stone
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A young cook named Pia worked in a harbor kitchen beside an old cook named Ruth. Every morning, before the first order, Ruth drew her knife across a flat stone, ten slow strokes on each side. Pia thought this was wasted time. While Ruth sharpened, Pia was already chopping, and for the first hour she was the faster of the two.

But a knife dulls a little with every cut, and a dull edge does not slice; it tears. By noon Pia was pressing hard and slowing down. Her onions came out crushed, and her wrist ached before the dinner rush. Ruth's knife moved in the evening as it had in the morning, and Ruth went home with an easy hand.

One night Pia asked for her secret. Ruth handed her the stone. "The ten strokes are not a delay before the work," she said. "They are the first part of it."

Care for the tool is part of the trade, not a pause from it.

questions.stem: What lesson does this fable teach?
choices: Keeping a tool sharp is part of the work, not time taken away from it.
Old cooks are always faster than young cooks.
A kitchen should buy new knives before every dinner rush.
Chopping onions is the hardest job in a kitchen.
questions.explanation: Ruth's ten strokes look like a delay and turn out to be why her evening matches her morning. The moral repeats her words: care for the tool is part of the trade.

questions.stem: Why is Pia the faster cook only in the first hour?
choices: Ruth works slowly on purpose to teach her a lesson.
Pia's knife is newer and better made than Ruth's.
Her head start comes from skipping the sharpening, and the cost arrives as her edge dulls.
The kitchen gives Pia the easier orders in the morning.
questions.explanation: The passage gives the rule: a knife dulls a little with every cut. Pia gains an hour by not sharpening, then pays it back in pressing, crushed onions, and an aching wrist.

questions.stem: In this passage, "dulls" most nearly means
choices: becomes dirty
loses its sharp edge
grows heavier
becomes boring
questions.explanation: The same sentence explains it: a dull edge "does not slice; it tears." The word is about the edge failing, not about dirt, weight, or boredom.

questions.stem: What did Ruth do every morning before the first order?
choices: She crushed onions for the lunch pots.
She checked Pia's knife for cracks.
She washed the flat stone in the harbor.
She drew her knife across a stone, ten strokes on each side.
questions.explanation: The second sentence states it exactly: ten slow strokes on each side of a flat stone, every morning before the first order.

lesson.strategy: A fable of two working styles side by side. Follow the clock: first hour, noon, dinner rush, evening. Pia wins early and loses late, and the reason is one plain fact about knives. Ruth's last two lines turn the whole story into the moral.

signals.phrase: ten slow strokes on each side
signals.means: Ruth's ritual, small and exact. The rest of the fable proves this minute earns its time.

signals.phrase: a dull edge does not slice; it tears
signals.means: The mechanism. This one fact explains the crushed onions and the aching wrist.
The turn. The morning's advantage starts to reverse at midday.

signals.phrase: They are the first part of it.
signals.means: Ruth's answer reframes sharpening: not a delay before the work, but the work's first step.

vocab.inContext: loses sharpness; each cut wears the knife's edge down a little
single passes of the blade across the stone
the busiest stretch, when orders come in fastest

skillTips.main-idea: Weigh the whole day, not the first hour. The fable is built so the early winner and the final winner are different cooks, and the moral explains why.
skillTips.inference: The story never says Pia's knife went dull. It gives the rule, "a knife dulls a little with every cut," then shows her pressing and slowing. You connect the rule to her symptoms.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Dulls" is explained by a pair of verbs: a sharp edge slices, a dull one tears. Use that contrast to fix the meaning.
skillTips.detail: The numbers are exact: ten strokes, each side, every morning, before the first order. A close-but-wrong choice will bend one of them.

passages.title: The Shopping Cart
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1937, a grocer in Oklahoma named Sylvan Goldman noticed where his sales stopped. Customers quit shopping when the basket got heavy. The limit on a sale was not money, and it was not appetite. It was arms.

So Goldman put wheels on a folding chair frame and set baskets where the seat had been. Now the store carried the weight. A customer could buy as much as a cart held, which was far more than two hands could.

At first, almost nobody would push one. Men thought the cart made them look weak. Women said it looked like a baby carriage. Goldman hired people to wheel carts around the store and pretend to shop, until pushing one looked normal. It worked.

The cart then quietly redrew the store around itself. The aisles grew wider so carts could pass. Packages grew larger to fill the extra room. A basket asks what you can carry. A cart asks how much you want.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why grocery stores stopped selling baskets in 1937.
How Sylvan Goldman became the richest grocer in Oklahoma.
Why customers in the 1930s distrusted new inventions.
How the shopping cart removed a limit on buying and reshaped the store.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the problem, arms as the limit, to the invention, the resistance, and the store changing around it. Only the last choice covers that whole arc.

questions.stem: Why did Goldman hire people to push carts and pretend to shop?
choices: He needed workers to test whether the wheels would break.
Shoppers copy what looks normal, and the cart's problem was its image, not its use.
The store was too empty, and he wanted it to look busy.
He could not afford to advertise in the newspapers.
questions.explanation: The complaints in the passage are about appearance: looking weak, looking like a baby carriage. Hired shoppers attacked exactly that problem, "until pushing one looked normal."

questions.stem: In this passage, "redrew" most nearly means
choices: sketched a picture of
advertised
changed the shape and layout of
cleaned and repainted
questions.explanation: The sentences after "redrew" list physical changes: wider aisles, larger packages. The store's design was changed, not put on paper.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Goldman build the first cart from?
choices: A folding chair frame with wheels and baskets.
A baby carriage with the seat removed.
A wooden crate from the storeroom.
A delivery wagon cut down to size.
questions.explanation: The passage says he "put wheels on a folding chair frame and set baskets where the seat had been." The baby carriage is what critics said it resembled, not what it was.

lesson.strategy: A cause-and-effect piece told as a story. First find the stated limit, "It was arms." Then track how one tool removes it, gets rejected, gets made normal, and finally reshapes the store. The last two short sentences state the whole idea as a contrast.

signals.means: The problem in three words. Sales were capped by what a body could carry, not by money or appetite.
The obstacle is social, not mechanical. The cart worked; its image did not.
Goldman's fix aims at habit and image. Normal, the passage shows, can be manufactured.

signals.phrase: A cart asks how much you want.
signals.means: The closing contrast: the tool changed the question a shopper answers while walking the aisles.

vocab.inContext: a shopkeeper who sells food; Goldman ran grocery stores in Oklahoma
the walking lanes between store shelves
changed the shape of; the store's layout was rebuilt around the cart

skillTips.main-idea: The cart is the subject, but the point is the limit it removed. An answer that stays at "a man invented a cart" misses why the aisles and the packages changed.
skillTips.inference: Line up the two complaints, looking weak and looking like a baby carriage, with Goldman's fix. Ask what kind of problem hired pretend-shoppers can solve.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Redrew" is figurative. Read the two sentences that follow it; wider aisles and larger packages tell you what kind of drawing this is.
skillTips.detail: The passage names both what the cart was made from and what people said it looked like. A wrong answer will hand you the look-alike instead of the parts.

passages.title: The Match
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For most of history, fire was hard to start and easy to lose. A household kept its fire alive all night, banking the coals in ash so a spark would live until morning. If the fire died, someone struck flint against steel over dry tinder; it could take many tries. Some families sent a child next door to carry home a live coal in a pan. Fire was borrowed like sugar.

In 1826, an English chemist named John Walker stirred a pot of paste, then scraped his mixing stick against the hearth to clean it. The stick burst into flame. One quick pull had made fire. Walker sold his "friction lights" in boxes but never patented them, so the idea spread fast.

The match made fire instant and personal. A lamp could be lit the moment it grew dark, a stove the moment you grew hungry, with no coals to guard and no neighbor to ask. Fire stopped being a thing a family kept and became a thing anyone could make.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why John Walker never became rich from his invention.
How the match turned fire from something kept alive into something made at will.
Why keeping coals alive overnight was dangerous for families.
How chemists in the 1800s tested new kinds of paste.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph shows fire being guarded and borrowed; the last shows it made in one pull. The closing sentence states the change directly: kept became made.

questions.stem: Why did households go to such trouble to keep a fire alive all night?
choices: Starting a fire from nothing was harder than keeping one burning.
Coals were expensive to buy in the morning.
The law required every home to keep a fire lit.
Neighbors refused to share fire with each other.
questions.explanation: The opening gives the rule: fire was "hard to start and easy to lose." Banking coals makes sense only if restarting was the harder job. And neighbors did share; that is what the coal in the pan shows.

questions.stem: In this passage, "banking" most nearly means
choices: saving money for the household
putting a fire out completely
stacking wood beside the hearth
covering coals in ash so they burn low and slow
questions.explanation: The sentence explains itself: coals are banked in ash "so a spark would live until morning." The goal is to keep the fire barely alive, not to end it, and money is not involved.

questions.stem: How did John Walker discover the friction match?
choices: He was trying to invent a safer kind of lamp.
A child brought him a live coal in a pan.
He scraped a paste-covered mixing stick against the hearth, and it caught fire.
He struck flint against steel over a pot of paste.
questions.explanation: The passage says he stirred a pot of paste, scraped the stick against the hearth to clean it, and "The stick burst into flame." The discovery was an accident of cleaning, not a plan.

lesson.strategy: A before-and-after passage. The first paragraph is the before: three ways people managed without matches. The middle is one accident in 1826. The last paragraph is the after. Weigh the closing sentence against the opening one; the whole change sits between "kept" and "made."

signals.phrase: hard to start and easy to lose
signals.means: The old problem in six words. Every habit in the first paragraph exists because of it.
A comparison that shows how ordinary sharing fire was: a common favor between neighbors.
The accident itself. Cleaning a stick, not chasing an invention, produced the match.
Why the idea spread fast: Walker left it free for anyone to copy and sell.

vocab.inContext: covering coals with ash so they burn low and last the night
dry material that catches a spark easily, used to start a fire
legally registered an invention so only the owner may sell it

skillTips.main-idea: Set the first sentence against the last. "Hard to start and easy to lose" becomes "a thing anyone could make." The main idea is that reversal, not Walker's life story.
skillTips.inference: The passage never says why families banked coals. It gives the nightly effort and the cost of losing fire; you supply the reason the effort was worth it.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Banking" here has nothing to do with money. The phrase "so a spark would live until morning" is the definition, sitting right after the word.
skillTips.detail: Three before-the-match habits are listed: banking coals, flint and steel, borrowing a coal. The question asks for one; do not let the others blur into it.

passages.title: The Elevator and the Top Floor
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Elevators existed long before Elisha Otis. What they lacked was a reason to trust one: ropes broke, and a falling platform forgave nobody. So hoists lifted freight, and people took the stairs.

In 1854, at a New York exhibition, Otis stood on a raised platform and ordered the rope cut. The platform dropped an inch and stopped. His invention was not the elevator but the brake, a spring that snapped out and gripped the rails the instant the rope went slack. The show mattered as much as the device. Safety you cannot see has to be performed.

Then the brake quietly repriced the city. Buildings stopped at five or six floors because legs did, and the top floor was the cheapest in the house, given to clerks and storage. Rent fell as stairs rose. Once an elevator made every floor a short ride, the slope flipped. Height stopped costing effort and began buying light, quiet, and a view. The best address moved from the second floor to the roof, and "penthouse," once a word for an attic, became a word for a prize.

Steel frames let cities build tall. It was a brake that made tall worth wanting.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How steel frames allowed the first skyscrapers to rise.
Why nineteenth-century elevator ropes broke so often.
How a brake made elevators trusted and reversed the value of height in buildings.
How Elisha Otis staged the most famous demonstration of his century.
questions.explanation: The passage has two halves that need each other: the brake earning trust, and rents flipping floor by floor. The steel sentence exists only to sharpen that point, and the demonstration serves the trust story.

questions.stem: Why did Otis order the rope cut in public instead of simply selling his brake?
choices: Cutting the rope was the only way to test whether the spring worked.
He wanted to prove his platform was stronger than his rivals' platforms.
Exhibition rules required every machine to be demonstrated.
People would not ride on a promise; the missing piece was belief, and belief needed a show.
questions.explanation: The passage says the show mattered as much as the device, and that safety you cannot see "has to be performed." The obstacle was trust, and a public drop attacked exactly that.

questions.stem: In this passage, "repriced" most nearly means
choices: changed what people would pay for each floor
made every building more expensive
lowered the cost of installing elevators
printed new rent contracts for tenants
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow trace prices moving in both directions: the once-cheap top floor becomes the prize. The brake shifted the pattern of value; it did not raise or lower everything at once.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happened when the rope was cut in 1854?
choices: The spring failed and the platform fell to the floor.
The platform dropped an inch and stopped.
The platform stayed exactly where it was.
Otis stepped off just before the platform slid down the rails.
questions.explanation: The text states it plainly: "The platform dropped an inch and stopped." The small drop matters, because the slack rope is what lets the spring grip the rails.

lesson.strategy: Two arguments joined by one device. First, the elevator's missing part was trust, and trust had to be staged. Second, once trust arrived, the price of height flipped. Read "Rent fell as stairs rose" as the before-picture, then watch the later sentences undo it clause by clause.

signals.means: Why freight rode and people walked: one rope failure was fatal, so trust was everything.
The demonstration. Otis attacks the fear directly, with his own body on the platform.
The old pricing rule in five words. Every flight of climbing made the space above it cheaper.
The reversal: height switches from a cost paid in effort to a luxury worth paying for.

vocab.inContext: simple lifting machines; before the brake, they raised freight, not people
changed the pattern of what people would pay, floor by floor
once a word for an attic, now the most expensive space in a building

skillTips.main-idea: Neither half alone is the answer. The brake explains the trust; the rents explain the stakes. The main idea has to hold "ordered the rope cut" and "the slope flipped" together.
skillTips.inference: The passage calls the show as important as the device. Ask what a public rope-cutting solves that a working brake, sitting in a workshop, cannot.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Repriced" is unpacked by the paragraph around it: cheap top floors becoming the prize. Let the examples define the word before you pick a choice.
skillTips.detail: The demonstration has exact physics: the rope cut, a one-inch drop, the stop. Wrong answers will remove the drop or extend it; the inch is the point.

passages.title: What a Barcode Holds
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On a June morning in 1974, in a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a cashier dragged a pack of chewing gum across a laser scanner, and the register rang up the price by itself. The stripes on the pack were a barcode, and the moment is remembered for what those stripes did not contain.

A barcode holds no price. It holds a number that says what the item is; the price lives in the store's computer. That split sounds small, and it is the whole invention. When the price is printed on every can, changing it means a clerk with a sticker gun and an afternoon of shelves. When the price lives in one machine, changing it is a keystroke. The shelf label can say one thing on Monday and another on Friday, and no can needs touching.

The scanner also made the store observant. Every beep was a record: this item, this hour, this lane. For the first time a grocer knew what was selling while it was selling, and could reorder before a shelf went bare. Faster checkout was the visible gain. The invisible one was that the shop began to watch its shelves, and in time its customers, with the same patient eye.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: The barcode separated an item's identity from its price, and that split changed how stores work.
The first product ever scanned was a pack of chewing gum.
Laser scanners made checkout lines shorter in the 1970s.
Sticker guns were slower than modern shelf labels.
questions.explanation: The passage marks its own center: the split "sounds small, and it is the whole invention." The gum, the lasers, and the stickers are all in service of that one idea.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that before the barcode, stores probably
choices: let cashiers set prices as they liked
sold fewer kinds of chewing gum
changed prices less often, because each change cost hours of relabeling
kept their computers in the checkout lanes
questions.explanation: If changing a price meant "a clerk with a sticker gun and an afternoon of shelves," each change carried a real cost in labor. The passage lets you conclude that stores would do it sparingly.

questions.stem: In this passage, "observant" most nearly means
choices: obedient to rules
noticing and recording what happens
careful with money
visible to customers
questions.explanation: The next sentence supplies the definition: every beep became a record of item, hour, and lane. The store began to notice its own activity, not to follow rules or save money.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what was the first item scanned in 1974?
choices: A can with a price sticker.
A shelf label.
A carton of milk.
A pack of chewing gum.
questions.explanation: The opening sentence states it: a cashier in Troy, Ohio "dragged a pack of chewing gum across a laser scanner." The cans and shelf labels appear later, as examples of pricing.

lesson.strategy: A technology passage with one load-bearing sentence: "A barcode holds no price." Everything before it is scene; everything after is consequence. Track the two gains separately, the visible one at the checkout and the invisible one in the store's records, and notice which the ending treats as larger.

signals.phrase: what those stripes did not contain
signals.means: A flag that the invention's power is an absence. The missing price is the point.
The author marks the core claim outright: the split between identity and price is the idea to hold.
The contrast with the sticker gun. One machine edit replaces an afternoon of shelf work.
The second consequence begins here: scanning turns selling into data while it happens.

vocab.inContext: the checkout machine that totals what a customer pays
one press of a key; here, the entire cost of changing a price
watching closely and keeping track; the store records each sale as it happens

skillTips.main-idea: The gum scan is the scene, not the subject. The passage tells you where its center is: the split that "sounds small, and it is the whole invention." Test each choice against that sentence.
skillTips.inference: The sticker-gun sentence is about cost. Ask what a store does less of when every price change costs an afternoon of shelves, and the answer follows.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Observant" is followed by its evidence: "Every beep was a record." Read one sentence past the word before choosing a meaning.
skillTips.detail: The first scan is precise: June 1974, Troy, Ohio, gum, laser. A distractor will offer you the can or the shelf label from the later pricing example.

passages.title: One Line, Many Windows
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At some banks and airports, customers no longer pick a line. A single roped path snakes toward all the counters, and whoever stands at its head goes to the next window that opens. The snake looks long. It is usually the faster and fairer design.

Consider the alternative: one line per counter. You must guess which line will move, and your wait depends on that guess. Service times are uneven (one customer needs thirty seconds, another ten minutes), and separate lines let one slow case trap everyone behind it while the next line drains.

The single line pools that unevenness. Nobody commits to one counter, so a slow customer delays the whole snake by a little instead of delaying a few people by a lot. And the rule people care most about (first come, first served) actually holds, because no one who arrived later can beat you by picking a luckier lane.

So why do supermarkets keep separate lines? Because a snake of forty people looks alarming at the door, even when it moves quickly. Stores sometimes choose the design that feels shorter over the one that is.

questions.stem: The passage mainly argues
choices: that supermarkets should remove all checkout lines
that waiting in line is unpleasant no matter how the line is designed
that a single line feeding many counters is usually faster and fairer than separate lines
that customers always choose the shortest line available
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states the claim (the snake 'is usually the faster and fairer design') and the middle paragraphs prove it: the single line pools uneven service times and preserves first come, first served.

questions.stem: Why does a slow customer do less damage in a single snaking line?
choices: Because no one is committed to standing behind that customer, so the delay spreads thinly across everyone
Because slow customers are sent to a special counter
Because staff serve slow customers faster when the line is long
Because slow customers usually give up and leave the snake
questions.explanation: The text says nobody 'commits to one counter', so the next free window takes the next person. Combine that with pooling: one slow case delays 'the whole snake by a little' rather than trapping a few people completely.

questions.stem: In this passage, the word 'drains' means the next line
choices: becomes wet and unpleasant
empties as its customers are served
closes before yours does
grows longer and slower
questions.explanation: 'Drains' pictures the neighboring line emptying like water flowing out; its customers keep moving while you stay trapped behind one slow case.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do supermarkets keep separate lines?
choices: Separate lines are cheaper to staff
Supermarket customers refuse to stand in one line
Shopping carts do not fit through a roped path
A long single snake looks alarming at the door, even when it moves quickly
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states it directly: 'a snake of forty people looks alarming at the door, even when it moves quickly', so stores pick the design that feels shorter.

lesson.strategy: This explainer states its claim early (the snake 'is usually the faster and fairer design'), then proves it by contrast. Read the 'one line per counter' paragraph as the problem and the pooling paragraph as its point-by-point answer; the supermarket ending is the exception that tests the rule.

signals.phrase: Consider the alternative: one line per counter.
signals.means: A contrast signal: the weaker design is shown first so the better one is easier to see.

signals.phrase: The single line pools that unevenness.
signals.means: The mechanism in one line: pooling. Everything after explains what pooling fixes.
The fairness rule at stake: the snake keeps it, separate lines break it by luck of the lane.

signals.phrase: the design that feels shorter over the one that is
signals.means: The closing twist: how a line feels can beat how fast it actually moves.

vocab.inContext: gathers many people's uneven waits into one shared line, so no one is stuck alone
not equal from case to case; one customer needs thirty seconds, another ten minutes
frightening to see; a forty-person snake scares shoppers at the door

skillTips.main-idea: Both halves of the claim matter: speed and fairness. Check that your summary covers why the snake wins on each, not only the speed half.
skillTips.inference: Link 'Nobody commits to one counter' to the thirty-seconds-versus-ten-minutes contrast. The inference is about where a delay goes when no one is locked behind it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Words here borrow from water: the path 'snakes', a line 'drains', the single line 'pools'. Read each image by asking what the water picture says about moving customers.
skillTips.detail: The last paragraph asks and answers its own question about supermarkets. For stated-fact questions, reread that sentence rather than reasoning from your own shopping memories.

passages.title: A Sheet That Nearly Keeps Its Shape
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Fold an A4 sheet in half across its long side and the smaller rectangle is nearly the same shape as the whole. The A-series is based on an ideal ratio: the long side divided by the short side equals the square root of two, about 1.414. This is the one rectangular proportion that returns after exact halving.

The ideal rule creates a family of related sizes. A design can shrink from a poster to a flyer without changing proportions, and a copier can use one scale factor between neighboring sizes. The theoretical starting sheet, A0, has an area of one square meter. Each later size has half the preceding area.

Physical paper uses whole-millimeter dimensions and manufacturing tolerances. An A4 sheet is listed as 210 by 297 millimeters, so its measured ratio is close to, not exactly, the mathematical value. A physical A0 sheet is likewise nominally one square meter rather than a perfect geometric object.

The distinction does not weaken the standard. It explains how standards connect an exact idea with objects that must be cut and measured in the real world. North American letter paper uses a different proportion, so halving it does not preserve even the ideal shape. A small mathematical choice can simplify a large system of paper, printing, and machines.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: All paper sheets have exactly the same measured proportions
A-series paper applies an exact geometric ratio through rounded real-world dimensions
A0 paper is always cut without any manufacturing tolerance
North American letter paper uses the square-root-of-two ratio
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes the exact ideal from the close, practical dimensions used for real sheets.

questions.stem: Why can a copier use one scale factor between neighboring A sizes?
choices: Every A-series sheet has the same area
Physical sheets have no measurement tolerances
The ideal proportions repeat when the sheet is halved
A copier changes the shape of every image
questions.explanation: Because the ideal shape repeats, scaling changes size without changing proportions.

questions.stem: In this passage, “nominally” means
choices: secretly larger than every listed dimension
made without using any mathematical idea
available only in North America
by its stated standard or name, though a physical measurement may vary slightly
questions.explanation: The text contrasts the nominal one-square-meter standard with a physical object and tolerances.

questions.stem: What is the theoretical area of an A0 sheet?
choices: One square meter
Two square meters
One square millimeter
Exactly 210 by 297 meters
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives one square meter as the theoretical A0 starting area.

lesson.strategy: Keep ideal geometry and manufactured paper in separate columns. The square-root-of-two rule is exact in the model; millimeter dimensions and tolerances make real sheets close approximations.

signals.means: Marks the exact mathematical model behind the size family.
Keeps the one-square-meter claim in the ideal definition.
States the effect of rounded millimeter dimensions.
Explains why approximation is compatible with useful standardization.

vocab.inContext: a comparison between the long and short side lengths
allowed small differences in manufactured dimensions
by the stated standard, while actual measurement may vary slightly

skillTips.main-idea: Preserve the contrast between an exact model and approximate physical implementation.
skillTips.inference: Repeated ideal proportions explain why one scale factor works between sizes.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast with “perfect geometric object” to understand nominally.
skillTips.detail: Theoretical A0 area and physical millimeter dimensions are different kinds of facts.

passages.title: Why the Wait Feels Long
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
One airport faced constant complaints about slow baggage delivery. Passengers stood eight minutes at the carousel, and the bags could not come faster. So managers moved the arrival gate farther from baggage claim. Passengers now spent six minutes walking and two standing. The total wait was unchanged. The complaints nearly stopped.

A wait has two lengths: the one on the clock and the one in the mind. Psychologists find that occupied time feels shorter than empty time. Walking is doing something; standing at a silent carousel is not, and empty time stretches. Uncertainty stretches it further: an open-ended wait feels longer than a known one, which is why a countdown clock at a bus stop calms riders though the bus comes no sooner.

Designers now build for the waiting mind. Mirrors beside elevators give idle eyes work; a numbered ticket turns a vague wait into a visible line. None of it moves the clock.

There is a limit. A trick that only soothes can excuse a system that should be fixed. But when a delay cannot shrink, the mind's side is all that is left: fill the time, or measure it.

questions.stem: The passage mainly explains
choices: that how long a wait feels depends on the mind as much as the clock, and design can work on the felt side
that airports should deliver baggage faster
that countdown clocks make buses arrive sooner
that walking is healthier than standing
questions.explanation: The airport story sets up the split between clock time and felt time; the rest shows designers working on the felt side (filling time, making it measurable) without changing the clock.

questions.stem: Why did moving the arrival gate reduce complaints even though the total wait stayed the same?
choices: Passengers no longer noticed the carousel existed
The bags arrived earlier once the gate moved
Walking filled the wait with activity, and occupied time feels shorter than standing idle
Tired passengers had no energy left to complain
questions.explanation: Connect the story to the principle stated after it: 'occupied time feels shorter than empty time'. Six minutes of walking is filled time; eight minutes of standing was empty time.

questions.stem: In this passage, the word 'soothes' means
choices: repairs a broken system
makes a wait longer
counts the minutes exactly
calms the feeling without changing the fact
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts a trick 'that only soothes' with 'a system that should be fixed': soothing eases how the wait feels while leaving the delay itself untouched.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how did the airport respond to the complaints?
choices: It hired more baggage handlers
It moved the arrival gate farther from baggage claim
It installed mirrors beside the carousel
It added a countdown clock to the carousel
questions.explanation: The fix is stated plainly: managers 'moved the arrival gate farther from baggage claim', trading standing time for walking time. Mirrors and countdown clocks appear later as other designers' tools.

lesson.strategy: The passage opens with a puzzle (same wait, fewer complaints) and pays it off with one distinction: clock time versus felt time. Hold the airport story in mind as you read; every later example (mirrors, a numbered ticket, the countdown clock) is the same move applied somewhere new.

signals.means: The puzzle in one line: whatever improved, it was not the clock.
The key distinction of the passage; everything after sorts into one length or the other.

signals.phrase: occupied time feels shorter than empty time
signals.means: The central finding: filled minutes shrink in the mind.
A turn: the author marks where perception fixes stop being enough.

vocab.inContext: the rotating belt where passengers wait to collect their bags
filled with activity; occupied minutes feel shorter than idle ones
calms the feeling of waiting without shortening the wait itself

skillTips.main-idea: The airport is a case, not the topic. State the main idea using the distinction it illustrates (the wait on the clock versus the wait in the mind), not just the baggage story.
skillTips.inference: The story ends before the principle is named. Carry 'six minutes walking and two standing' into the second paragraph and match it against what psychologists find about filled time.
skillTips.vocabulary: Test words against their built-in contrasts: 'soothes' sits opposite 'fixed', 'empty' sits opposite 'occupied'. The opposite in the sentence is the definition's other half.
skillTips.detail: Several fixes appear: the moved gate, mirrors, a numbered ticket, a countdown clock. A detail question will ask who used which; keep the airport's own fix separate from the rest.

passages.title: The Screws That Did Not Fit
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the Second World War, American mechanics repairing British equipment kept hitting one failure: the screws did not fit. Both measured in inches, but the angle and spacing of their grooves differed slightly. An American nut would not seat on a British bolt; damaged machines sat idle while fasteners crossed an ocean.

A century earlier, Joseph Whitworth had shown the fix. In 1841 he collected sample screws from workshops across England and proposed one thread for the whole country. It worked: a bolt from one factory fit a nut from another, and machines could be repaired with stock parts instead of hand-fitted ones.

Notice what the standard never claimed: that Whitworth's 55-degree thread was the best angle. A 60-degree thread works too; the Americans used one. The value was not in the number but in the agreement, because interchangeable parts exist only among people who cut the same groove.

The war exposed the limit: an agreement stops at the border of those who joined it. In 1948 Britain, America, and Canada unified their threads. The rule outlives screws: the cost of standardizing is argument today; the cost of not standardizing is discovered later, at the worst time.

questions.stem: The passage mainly argues that
choices: British screws were poorly made until 1948
Joseph Whitworth invented the screw thread
wartime repairs require larger stocks of spare parts
a standard's value lies in shared agreement, not in the particular choice it fixes
questions.explanation: The thread story carries the general claim, stated near the end: 'The value was not in the number but in the agreement'. Both 55 and 60 degrees work; only agreement makes parts interchangeable.

questions.stem: Why did the thread problem surface during the war rather than earlier?
choices: Screw factories closed during the war
The two national standards only collided when one country's mechanics had to repair the other's equipment
Wartime screws were cut less carefully than peacetime ones
Whitworth's standard expired in the 1940s
questions.explanation: Each standard worked within its own borders: 'an agreement stops at the border of those who joined it'. Only when American hands met British bolts did the mismatch start stalling repairs.

questions.stem: As used here, 'interchangeable' parts are parts that
choices: are cheaper than hand-made parts
can be exchanged for money
fit in place of one another, whichever factory made them
must be modified before use
questions.explanation: The word is anchored by the sentence before it: after Whitworth, 'a bolt from one factory fit a nut from another'. Interchangeable parts swap freely because they follow one shared groove.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did Whitworth do in 1841?
choices: He collected sample screws from workshops across England and proposed one thread for the whole country
He unified British and American threads
He invented a 60-degree thread for American factories
He shipped fasteners across the ocean to stalled machines
questions.explanation: The 1841 sentence states it directly: Whitworth gathered sample screws from English workshops and proposed a single national thread. The three-country unification came in 1948, a century later.

lesson.strategy: A story-driven argument: a wartime failure, a century-old fix, then the general rule. Track the two dates (1841 and 1948) as the passage's spine, and at each step ask what the standard covered and, just as important, who had not joined it.

signals.means: The concrete failure the whole argument grows from.

signals.phrase: Notice what the standard never claimed
signals.means: The author redirects you: the point is not which thread angle is best.

signals.phrase: an agreement stops at the border of those who joined it
signals.means: The limit of any standard, and the reason the war exposed the gap.

signals.phrase: the cost of not standardizing is discovered later
signals.means: The closing rule: skipping agreement defers the price to the worst moment.

vocab.inContext: hardware that joins parts: screws, nuts, and bolts
to settle into place; a nut that will not seat cannot tighten on its bolt
merged into one; three countries adopted a single thread in 1948

skillTips.main-idea: The screws are the vehicle, not the destination. A strong main-idea answer generalizes the way the passage does: from thread angles to what any standard is for.
skillTips.inference: Ask why 1841's fix did not prevent the wartime problem. The answer lies in the scope of the agreement, not the quality of the engineering.
skillTips.vocabulary: Terms like 'seat' and 'stock parts' are workshop language. Read the surrounding sentence for what physically happens: a nut settling onto a bolt, a shelf of ready parts.
skillTips.detail: Two standardizations happen a century apart. Pin who joined each (England alone in 1841; Britain, America, and Canada in 1948) before answering any who-did-what question.

passages.title: When Buffers Backfire
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Internet traffic moves in bursts, so every router keeps a buffer: a queue where packets wait when they arrive faster than the link ahead can carry. A modest buffer is useful; it absorbs a burst that would otherwise be thrown away. Engineers reasoned that if some buffer was good, more was safer, and when memory became cheap, buffers grew enormous.

Then fast connections began to feel slow. A video call stutters while a file uploads. Engineers named the sickness bufferbloat. Once a giant buffer fills, each packet waits behind everything ahead; the waiting, not the moving, is the delay.

The deeper fault is a silenced signal. A sender slows down when the network drops its packets: a drop is bad news, but it is also the message that the road is full. A deep buffer delays that message: it stores excess traffic instead of dropping it, so the sender keeps pushing into an ever-longer line. A queue smooths traffic, but it also carries feedback; too deep, and feedback arrives too late to matter.

Modern routers keep their queues deliberately short. The lesson travels beyond networks: in a system steered by feedback, quietly absorbing a problem does not solve it. It postpones the news.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage's central point?
choices: Routers should have no buffers at all
Oversized buffers slow networks by creating long queues and by delaying the congestion signal senders rely on
Video calls use more data than file uploads
Cheap memory made the internet faster for everyone
questions.explanation: The passage gives two linked causes: a full giant buffer makes every packet wait, and storing excess traffic delays the dropped-packet message that tells senders to slow down. A modest buffer stays useful.

questions.stem: Why does a sender keep pushing at full rate even as the queue grows?
choices: Senders are designed to ignore all network conditions
The router asks the sender for more traffic
The signal to slow down is a dropped packet, and the deep buffer keeps storing packets instead of dropping them
Full buffers transmit data faster than empty ones
questions.explanation: The passage says a sender 'slows down when the network drops its packets'. A deep buffer 'stores excess traffic instead of dropping it', so the bad-news message never arrives and the sender pushes on.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'absorbs' a burst means the buffer
choices: takes the sudden extra packets in and holds them instead of losing them
deletes the burst immediately
splits the burst between two routers
slows the burst down permanently
questions.explanation: 'Absorbs' is set against 'thrown away': the buffer soaks up a spike of arriving packets and holds them briefly so none are lost.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what let buffers grow enormous?
choices: Faster video calls
A new internet standard
Complaints from senders
Memory becoming cheap
questions.explanation: The enabling condition is stated directly: engineers assumed more buffer was safer, 'and when memory became cheap, buffers grew enormous'.

lesson.strategy: An explainer with two layers of cause. First take the surface story (big buffer, long queue, long wait), then reread the third paragraph for the deeper one: the queue silences the drop signal. The closing rule about feedback only lands if you hold both layers together.

signals.phrase: if some buffer was good, more was safer
signals.means: The mistaken assumption the passage is built to overturn.
A label attached to the symptoms just described; the example is the definition.

signals.phrase: The deeper fault is a silenced signal.
signals.means: A depth marker: the paragraph before was the symptom, this one is the cause.
The rule in miniature: absorbing a problem delays its message, not its arrival.

vocab.inContext: a queue where packets wait when they arrive faster than the link ahead can carry
briefly freezes and jumps; how a video call behaves when its packets sit in a long queue
more than the link can handle right now; the traffic a router should drop, not store

skillTips.main-idea: Do not stop at 'big buffers are bad'. The passage's point includes why: what a deep queue does to the drop signal. A complete main idea joins the waiting and the silenced message.
skillTips.inference: The third paragraph calls a drop 'bad news' and 'the message that the road is full'. Reason from what happens to a sender who never receives that message.
skillTips.vocabulary: Network terms here are defined by contrast: 'absorbs' against 'thrown away', a queue that 'smooths' against one that silences. Use the paired opposite to fix each meaning.
skillTips.detail: The history is one sentence long: the assumption, then cheap memory, then enormous buffers. Detail questions live in that chain; keep its order straight.

passages.title: When Everyone Claims at Once
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Insurance rests on a quiet assumption: misfortunes arrive one at a time. Fires are scattered, so an insurer with a hundred thousand customers can predict losses like a timetable. The pool works because each loss is independent; one member's bad year says nothing about the others.

Some risks refuse to scatter. A flood does not pick one house in a valley; it takes the valley. An earthquake takes a city's homes in one minute. When losses are correlated, when they arrive together or not at all, the arithmetic of pooling collapses. Most years such a fund pays nothing; then every member claims at once, and the fund fails exactly when needed.

This is why fire cover is cheap and easy while flood and earthquake cover is often costly, capped, or run by governments. Insurers also export the problem: reinsurance (insurance bought by insurers) spreads a valley's flood across pools on other continents, on the bet that distant disasters will not share a year.

Some risks are correlated across the whole planet. A pandemic or a worldwide crash reaches every pool at once, and a pool of pools is still only a pool. The reach of insurance ends where the whole world can have the same bad year.

questions.stem: The passage mainly explains
choices: why fire insurance premiums have risen over time
how governments profit from selling flood insurance
why pooling handles scattered losses well but breaks down when losses strike together
why reinsurance has replaced ordinary insurance
questions.explanation: The structure is a contrast: independent losses make pools predictable; correlated losses (floods, earthquakes, pandemics) make every member claim at once, which is the failure the rest of the passage traces.

questions.stem: Why does reinsurance spread a valley's flood risk across other continents specifically?
choices: Foreign insurers charge lower premiums
Laws forbid holding flood risk in one country
Continents have more money than valleys
Distance makes disasters less likely to strike the same year, restoring the independence pooling needs
questions.explanation: The passage says the spread rests 'on the bet that distant disasters will not share a year'. Reinsurance works by rebuilding independence, the same property that made fire pools predictable.

questions.stem: As used here, losses that are 'correlated' are losses that
choices: have been counted incorrectly
tend to arrive together or not at all
are too small to insure
grow larger every year
questions.explanation: The passage defines the word right where it appears: 'correlated, when they arrive together or not at all'. The flood taking the whole valley is the picture to keep.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does flood and earthquake cover tend to differ from fire cover?
choices: It is often costly, capped, or run by governments
It is illegal in most countries
It is cheaper because floods are rare
It pays claims only to insurers, never to households
questions.explanation: The contrast is stated in one sentence: fire cover is 'cheap and easy' while flood and earthquake cover 'is often costly, capped, or run by governments'.

lesson.strategy: Read this as one assumption stress-tested at growing scale. Paragraph one states it: misfortunes arrive one at a time. Each later paragraph raises the correlation: a valley, then continents, then the whole planet. Watch what happens to the pool at each step.

signals.phrase: misfortunes arrive one at a time
signals.means: The assumption the whole institution rests on; the passage will break it.
The turn: the assumption fails, and the failure cases begin.

signals.phrase: a pool of pools is still only a pool
signals.means: The limit of the reinsurance fix: scaling up cannot create independence.

vocab.inContext: unconnected; one member's loss tells you nothing about another's
insurance that insurers buy, passing part of their risk to other pools
limited to a maximum payout, no matter how large the loss

skillTips.main-idea: The flood is an example, not the subject. Frame the main idea around what correlation does to pooling, so that fires, floods, and pandemics all fit under your statement.
skillTips.inference: Reinsurance is explained as a bet. Ask what the bet assumes about distant disasters, and connect it back to the word 'independent' in paragraph one.
skillTips.vocabulary: 'Correlated' is defined between commas right where it appears. When a technical word arrives with a comma or a parenthesis after it, the definition is usually sitting inside.
skillTips.detail: The pricing consequences sit in one sentence contrasting fire cover with flood and earthquake cover. Match each adjective (cheap, costly, capped) to the right risk before answering.

passages.title: Why the Jeweler Is Downtown
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
No committee assigns jewelers downtown and furniture showrooms to the edge, yet city after city sorts itself the same way. The mechanism is a silent auction. Each plot goes, in effect, to the use that can earn the most from standing on it, and what the center sells is nearness.

A jeweler earns huge value per square foot and needs almost no space, so it outbids nearly everyone for a small central shop. A furniture showroom is the reverse: it needs acres of floor and its customers visit rarely, so it takes cheap land at the edge. Offices crowd the middle to be near workers; farms, needing much land and little nearness, lie furthest out.

Economists call the pattern a bid-rent gradient: rent falls with distance from the center, and each activity settles where its bid still wins. Skyscrapers are the auction made visible: where land grows dear enough, it pays to stack floor upon floor and sell one address many times.

The auction is not the whole story. Zoning can overrule it, forbidding the factory that would outbid the houses. But wherever the rules are silent, the gradient does the sorting, which is why you can arrive in a strange city and guess, correctly, where the jewelers are.

questions.stem: The passage mainly argues that
choices: a city's layout emerges from competing bids for nearness, with each land use settling where its bid wins
zoning laws decide where every business in a city must go
furniture showrooms earn more money than jewelers
skyscrapers exist because architects prefer tall buildings
questions.explanation: The 'silent auction' is the thesis: uses that profit most from nearness outbid others for central land, producing the bid-rent gradient. Zoning appears only as the exception at the end.

questions.stem: Which business would the passage predict bids highest for a small shop at the very center?
choices: A farm supply depot needing storage yards
A business earning high value per square foot from being near many customers
A warehouse whose customers visit once a decade
A factory needing cheap land and wide floors
questions.explanation: The jeweler's logic generalizes: the center rewards uses that turn nearness into 'huge value per square foot' while needing little space. Space-hungry, rarely visited uses lose the central auction.

questions.stem: In this passage, land that 'grows dear' is land that
choices: becomes loved by the people of the city
is set aside for family homes
loses value as the city spreads
becomes expensive
questions.explanation: 'Dear' here is the older sense of costly: where land grows dear enough, 'it pays to stack floor upon floor'; stacking only makes sense when the ground itself is expensive.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what can overrule the auction?
choices: The furniture showrooms at the edge
The bid-rent gradient
Zoning
The price of skyscrapers
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states it directly: 'Zoning can overrule it, forbidding the factory that would outbid the houses'. The gradient sorts only where the rules are silent.

lesson.strategy: An argument from a mechanism: the 'silent auction' explains the map. For each land use (jeweler, showroom, office, farm), note two things: how much it earns from nearness and how much space it needs. The whole gradient follows from that pair.

signals.phrase: The mechanism is a silent auction.
signals.means: The thesis named in one line; every example after is a bid in that auction.

signals.phrase: A furniture showroom is the reverse
signals.means: A mirror-image signal: expect the jeweler's two traits, flipped.
Skyscrapers as evidence: the invisible price gradient printed on the skyline.

signals.phrase: The auction is not the whole story.
signals.means: A scope limit: the author marks where the mechanism yields to written rules.

vocab.inContext: to offer more than a rival; central shops go to whoever can outbid the rest
a steady slope of change; here, rent sliding downward with distance from the center
costly, in the older money sense; land grows dear where nearness is most wanted

skillTips.main-idea: Keep the mechanism, not the shops, at the center of your summary. Jewelers and showrooms are bids; the main idea is what the auction does to the whole map.
skillTips.inference: To predict where a new business lands, weigh its two traits the way the passage does: value per square foot against space needed. The examples give you the scale's two ends.
skillTips.vocabulary: Older money-words appear here: land 'grows dear', a bid 'still wins'. Read them inside the auction picture: everything in this passage is priced, even nearness.
skillTips.detail: The paragraphs of examples never mention limits. The exception to the mechanism arrives only in the final paragraph; look there when asked what constrains the auction.

passages.title: The Discipline You Don't See
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Ask people to picture self-control and they describe a battle: the dieter staring down a slice of cake, the student who silences the phone and grinds through the evening. Discipline, in this picture, is the strength to win such fights, and some people are simply born with more of it.

Researchers who study self-control keep finding something odd. When people who score high on discipline describe their days, they report fewer battles, not more victories. They are not resisting temptation better than the rest of us; they are meeting less of it. The cake is not stared down, because it was never bought. The phone is not silenced heroically, because it charges in another room.

What looks like strength of character is mostly quiet arrangement. The disciplined design their surroundings so that the easy path and the intended path are the same one, and then they walk it without drama. The finding is encouraging, because arrangement can be learned by anyone, and a little humbling, because it means the willpower we admire in others was, most of the time, never used.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the essay's argument?
choices: Discipline is an inborn strength that some people simply have more of.
Dieting fails because cake is too tempting for most people to resist.
People who seem disciplined mostly arrange their lives to meet fewer temptations.
Willpower grows stronger every time a temptation is successfully resisted.
questions.explanation: The battle picture in paragraph one is set up to be knocked down: high scorers report fewer battles, and the essay concludes that apparent strength of character is 'mostly quiet arrangement'.

questions.stem: Which new habit best fits the essay's picture of how disciplined people behave?
choices: Deleting a distracting game instead of promising to open it less.
Keeping cake on the counter to practice resisting it.
Relying on willpower to win each battle as it comes.
Admiring friends who can study with the phone beside them.
questions.explanation: Extend the pattern: the cake 'was never bought' and the phone 'charges in another room'. Both remove the temptation in advance. Deleting the game is the same quiet arrangement; the other choices keep fighting battles.

questions.stem: "The phone is not silenced heroically, because it charges in another room." Heroically here means
choices: quietly and secretly
at the last possible moment
without any clear reason
as if it took great strength or courage
questions.explanation: The word is lightly ironic: the 'because' clause explains that no strength was needed at all, since the phone was never within reach.

questions.stem: According to the essay, what do people who score high on discipline report about their days?
choices: More victories over strong temptations
Fewer battles with temptation
Longer working hours than other people
More careful planning of meals
questions.explanation: The finding is stated as a contrast: 'they report fewer battles, not more victories'. The surprise is the absence of fights, not extra wins.

lesson.strategy: An essay built as picture, evidence, replacement. Paragraph one paints discipline as 'a battle'; paragraph two reports what researchers 'keep finding'; paragraph three states the new claim, 'quiet arrangement'. Read the cake and phone examples as the same mechanism shown twice.

signals.phrase: Discipline, in this picture, is the strength to win
signals.means: Names the common view the essay is about to overturn; 'in this picture' hints it is only a picture.
The turn. Evidence now replaces the opening image.

signals.phrase: they report fewer battles, not more victories
signals.means: The finding that reverses the battle picture: less fighting, not better fighting.
The essay's replacement claim for what discipline is.

vocab.inContext: the way things are set up around you in advance
as if it took great strength or courage
pushes on with steady, tiring effort

skillTips.main-idea: The first paragraph is bait. The claim the essay keeps is the one introduced by 'Researchers... keep finding something odd', not the battle picture before it.
skillTips.inference: The essay never says discipline is fake. Ask what 'never bought' and 'charges in another room' share, then carry that pattern to any new example you are offered.
skillTips.vocabulary: 'Heroically' is ironic here: the sentence explains why no heroism was needed. Let the 'because' clause set the word's tone.
skillTips.detail: The finding is stated as a double contrast: 'fewer battles, not more victories'. Match a choice to both halves, not just one.

passages.title: The Silence Between Strangers
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On trains and in waiting rooms, strangers sit a hand's width apart and say nothing. We treat the silence as a treaty: everyone prefers it, so everyone keeps it. Breaking it feels like a small trespass, which is why the person who chats to seatmates on a morning commute is met with polite alarm.

Psychologists who tested the treaty found that it rests on a misreading. Commuters asked to predict a conversation with a stranger expected awkwardness and rated the quiet ride as the more pleasant option. Commuters assigned to actually talk reported the opposite: the conversations started easily, the strangers seemed pleased to be spoken to, and the talkers stepped off in a better mood than the silent riders. Each side had been waiting for a signal that the other side was also waiting for.

So the silence is not a shared preference. It is a shared guess about other people's preferences, and the guess is wrong on both ends. That reframes a small duty. What we owe strangers may begin lower than charity or rescue: the first word, offered so that the other person is not the one who has to risk it.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the essay's argument?
choices: Talking to strangers on trains is rude and is best avoided.
Strangers stay silent because each side wrongly assumes the other prefers silence.
Commuters enjoy quiet rides far more than conversations.
Charity is the main duty we owe to strangers.
questions.explanation: The essay names the assumption (a 'treaty'), tests it, and replaces it: the silence 'is not a shared preference' but 'a shared guess' that is wrong on both ends.

questions.stem: The essay's mechanism would best explain which of these situations?
choices: A commuter puts on headphones because she truly prefers music to conversation.
Two old friends talk easily for the whole ride.
A tourist asks a stranger for directions and gets a friendly answer.
No student asks a question in a confusing lecture, though most are lost and would welcome one.
questions.explanation: The train's silence is 'a shared guess about other people's preferences'. The lecture hall repeats it: each student reads the others' silence as understanding and keeps quiet, everyone 'waiting for a signal'. The other cases involve a real preference or no misreading at all.

questions.stem: "We treat the silence as a treaty: everyone prefers it, so everyone keeps it." A treaty is
choices: a formal agreement between sides
a punishment for breaking a rule
a long journey taken together
a sudden change of plans
questions.explanation: The essay borrows the language of diplomacy: 'everyone prefers it, so everyone keeps it' describes an agreement both parties honor, which is what a treaty is.

questions.stem: What did the commuters who were assigned to talk report?
choices: The conversations were as awkward as they had feared.
The strangers asked them to stop talking.
The conversations started easily and left them in a better mood.
They missed their stops while talking.
questions.explanation: The results sentence is explicit: conversations 'started easily', strangers 'seemed pleased', and talkers 'stepped off in a better mood than the silent riders'.

lesson.strategy: The essay tests a social rule like an experiment. First the rule ('a treaty'), then the test (predictions versus actual conversations), then the reframe ('a shared guess'). Keep the predictions and the results in separate columns; the argument lives in their mismatch.

signals.phrase: We treat the silence as a treaty
signals.means: States the assumption the essay will put on trial.

signals.phrase: found that it rests on a misreading
signals.means: The turn: the treaty is not what it seemed, and evidence follows.

signals.phrase: waiting for a signal that the other side was also waiting
signals.means: The mechanism: two people each deferring to the other's imagined preference.
The replacement claim for 'a shared preference'; the essay's verdict.

vocab.inContext: a formal agreement between sides
a step onto ground where you have no right to be
a wrong understanding of what others think

skillTips.main-idea: The essay's claim is the correction, not the custom: silence is 'a shared guess', not 'a shared preference'. A good summary must contain the misreading.
skillTips.inference: The mechanism is both sides 'waiting for a signal that the other side was also waiting for'. Test any situation against it: is a real preference at work, or only a guess about one?
skillTips.vocabulary: 'Treaty' and 'trespass' borrow from law and diplomacy. The essay uses them to make an unwritten habit sound like a formal rule; read them through that image.
skillTips.detail: Predictions and results sit in separate sentences. Check which group a choice describes: those asked to predict, or those assigned to talk.

passages.title: Sarajevo and the July Crisis
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, made an official visit to Sarajevo with his wife, Sophie. Bosnia was under Austro-Hungarian rule, and nationalist movements opposed that rule. An earlier attack on the visitors failed. Afterward, Franz Ferdinand chose to visit people affected by the attack at a hospital, but confusion about the changed route caused his car to stop near Gavrilo Princip. Princip, a member of the nationalist conspiracy, assassinated Franz Ferdinand and Sophie.

The route confusion shaped the immediate event, but it does not by itself explain a world war. Europe was already marked by imperial rivalry, military planning, nationalism, and alliances. The assassination became a trigger inside that tense system.

During the July Crisis, leaders made further choices. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, sent Serbia an ultimatum. Serbia accepted many demands but not all of them. Mobilizations and declarations followed as governments responded to both their plans and one another. By early August, several major powers were at war. The Sarajevo assassination mattered greatly, yet war grew from the political conditions and decisions that followed it, not from one driver’s mistake alone.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage’s main idea?
choices: A driver’s mistake made the assassination and every government’s later political and military decision unavoidable.
Europe’s alliances had no role in the crisis because the route confusion alone caused the war.
The official visit to Sarajevo occurred after a world war had already begun across Europe.
Route confusion shaped the assassination; wider tensions and later political choices turned crisis into war.
questions.explanation: The passage separates the chance event in Sarajevo from the political conditions and decisions of the July Crisis.

questions.stem: Why does the passage include the route confusion?
choices: To prove that Princip had no political goal or connection with a nationalist conspiracy
To show that chance shaped the immediate event without fully explaining the later war
To show that all European leaders wanted a world war before the assassination occurred
To claim that the hospital was outside Sarajevo and therefore impossible to visit
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly limits what the route can explain: it affected the encounter, not the whole chain to war.

questions.stem: In the passage, an “ultimatum” is
choices: a set of final demands backed by a threatened consequence
a private travel plan for an official visit through a city
a public celebration held after a visiting official leaves a city
an agreement in which governments end every military plan immediately
questions.explanation: Austria-Hungary sent demands that Serbia had to answer during an escalating crisis, which fits an ultimatum.

questions.stem: What change followed the earlier failed attack?
choices: Franz Ferdinand decided to leave Sarajevo immediately and cancel the rest of the visit.
Princip became the official driver and selected a new route through the city.
Franz Ferdinand chose to visit people affected at a hospital.
European governments ended their military plans and alliances before the July Crisis.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says the hospital visit changed the planned route after the earlier attack.

lesson.strategy: Separate trigger, background conditions, and later decisions. Paragraph one gives the immediate Sarajevo event without graphic detail; paragraph two limits the wrong-turn explanation; paragraph three traces the July Crisis. A cause can matter without being sufficient by itself.

signals.phrase: but confusion about the changed route
signals.means: Identifies the chance element in the immediate encounter.
Limits how much one event can account for.
Connects the assassination with already existing tensions.
Moves responsibility from chance to decisions during the crisis.

vocab.inContext: connected with a movement seeking power or self-rule for a nation
an event that starts a process under conditions already in place
final demands backed by a threatened consequence

skillTips.main-idea: Include both scales: the Sarajevo encounter and the political chain that expanded the crisis.
skillTips.detail: The changed hospital visit appears in paragraph one before the route confusion.
skillTips.inference: The author includes chance, then explicitly limits it; use that boundary when explaining causation.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read ultimatum with the demands, response, and escalation that surround it.

passages.title: The Sentence That Opened the Wall
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
By the autumn of 1989, East Germany was leaking. Hungary had opened its border and thousands of East Germans were escaping through it, while protest marches in Leipzig grew by the week. Hoping to release the pressure, the government drafted a new travel rule: citizens could apply for exit visas through an orderly process beginning the next day.

The official sent to announce it, Günter Schabowski, had missed the meeting and was handed the text minutes before a live press conference on November 9. Asked when the rule took effect, he leafed through his papers and guessed: immediately, without delay. Television carried the sentence into every living room. By late evening tens of thousands of East Berliners stood at the crossings, and the guards had no orders and no way to hold back a crowd that size. Near midnight an overwhelmed officer at one checkpoint gave up and opened the gate.

The state could have corrected the announcement the next morning, and it would have changed nothing. A closed border works only as long as people believe it is closed, and one wrong sentence had ended the belief. The wall stood in concrete for another year, but as a fact of power it fell that night.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: The Berlin Wall was demolished by crowds on November 9, 1989.
Schabowski secretly planned to open the border ahead of schedule.
Hungary forced East Germany to rewrite its travel laws.
A misread announcement released pressure that no correction could take back, because the border ran on belief.
questions.explanation: The story is the press conference and the crowds, but the passage's point is the last paragraph: a border 'works only as long as people believe it is closed', and the belief could not be restored.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say a correction the next morning 'would have changed nothing'?
choices: Because the official papers had been destroyed overnight.
Because once people stopped believing the border was closed, the state could not restore that belief.
Because Schabowski refused to appear on television again.
Because the concrete wall had already been torn down.
questions.explanation: Apply the passage's own rule. The border's power was the public belief that it was closed; after a night of open gates, no announcement could rebuild that belief.

questions.stem: "East Germany was leaking." Leaking here means
choices: running out of money
sharing state secrets with the West
steadily losing citizens through gaps in its borders
flooding after weeks of heavy rain
questions.explanation: The image is explained by the next clause: Hungary's open border let 'thousands of East Germans' escape. The country was losing people the way a pipe loses water.
