skillTips.main-idea: Summarize the full collection path and avoid extending one behavior to every beetle species.
skillTips.inference: The raised body creates a slope, letting gravity move droplets mouthward.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “inland from the Atlantic” shows that fog “drifts” by moving through air.
skillTips.detail: The timing appears immediately before the description of the beetle's raised position.

passages.title: How a Museum Moves a Painting
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Moving a valuable painting begins before anyone lifts its frame. A conservator prepares a condition report, recording cracks, loose paint, and old repairs. Photographs create a baseline. After travel, staff compare the work with this record.

Teams plan the route from one wall to another. They measure doors, lifts, corners, and loading areas, while considering vibration, weather, security, and time outside controlled rooms. A large work may move while a building is closed.

A custom crate protects the painting without pressing on its painted surface. Supports hold safe parts of the frame, cushioning reduces shocks, and materials slow changes in temperature and humidity. Sensors may record conditions inside.

At the destination, handlers do not always unpack immediately. A cold crate in a warm room may need time to adjust, reducing condensation. Staff then inspect the painting against its report. The safest move is a chain of ordinary decisions rather than one heroic lift. Documentation, measurements, packing, timing, and inspection let everyone know what happened at each stage.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A strong handler can safely move a painting without preparation or records.
Paintings are unpacked immediately so a cold crate warms as fast as possible.
A custom crate protects art by pressing firmly against the painted surface.
Museums move paintings safely through coordinated documentation, route planning, protective packing, environmental control, and inspection.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph contributes a stage in the careful chain summarized at the end.

questions.stem: Why might staff wait before opening a cold crate in a warm room?
choices: Gradual adjustment can reduce condensation that might harm the painting.
The painting needs darkness before staff can photograph it.
Waiting makes the crate's route measurements more accurate.
The frame must become cold enough to shrink away from the canvas.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph directly connects delayed unpacking with gradual temperature change and reduced condensation risk.

questions.stem: What does “baseline” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: the lowest edge of a painting's frame
an initial record used for later comparison
a route marked across the gallery floor
a strap placed inside a shipping crate
questions.explanation: Photographs and the condition report document the starting state against which later observations are checked.

questions.stem: What may travel inside the crate to record conditions?
choices: gallery visitors
wall labels
sensors
replacement paintings
questions.explanation: The crate paragraph says sensors may accompany the work and log its environment.

lesson.strategy: Read the passage as a handoff across stages. At each one, identify the risk and its control: records address uncertainty, measurements address fit, crates address shock, and gradual adjustment addresses condensation.

signals.means: Safe transport starts with documentation rather than the moment of lifting.

signals.phrase: without pressing on its painted surface
signals.means: Support must hold safe structural areas, not vulnerable paint.
Arrival does not end environmental risk or the planned procedure.

vocab.inContext: a specialist who cares for and preserves cultural objects
a starting record used to detect later change
liquid formed when water vapor meets a cooler surface

skillTips.main-idea: Collect the stages into one coordinated process instead of choosing a summary focused only on the crate.
skillTips.inference: Link temperature difference to the named danger of condensation and the value of gradual adjustment.
skillTips.vocabulary: The later comparison with the report defines the baseline as the recorded starting condition.
skillTips.detail: The device that logs travel conditions is named at the end of the crate paragraph.

passages.title: Curtains of Light in the North
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An aurora can appear as a pale arc, a moving curtain, or rays across a dark sky. The light forms high in Earth's atmosphere when charged particles from the Sun transfer energy to atmospheric atoms and molecules. Those particles do not fall in a straight line from the Sun to one city.

Earth's magnetic field shapes their route. Many particles are guided toward high latitudes, so auroras are frequent around broad zones near the magnetic poles. Solar activity can disturb the space around Earth and expand the visible area.

Color depends on which atmospheric gas emits light, the energy involved, and altitude. Oxygen commonly contributes green and red light, while nitrogen can contribute blue or purplish shades. One color chart cannot capture every mixture or viewing condition.

The curtain shape also has a physical story. Perspective can turn a thin sheet of emission into folds and rays. Apparent movement reflects changing particle flows rather than fabric waving in air. An aurora therefore links events across enormous scales: activity near the Sun, magnetic guidance around Earth, and collisions among particles in the upper atmosphere. Its beauty is immediate, but its mechanism is a layered interaction.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Auroras arise through interactions among solar particles, Earth's magnetic field, and atmospheric gases, producing varied forms and colors.
Auroras are ordinary sunlight reflected from fabric-like clouds near the ground.
Every aurora displays one color determined only by the outside air temperature.
Charged particles travel in straight lines to cities selected by solar activity.
questions.explanation: The passage develops the particle source, magnetic routing, atmospheric emission, and visible structure.

questions.stem: Why are auroras especially common near high latitudes?
choices: Those regions receive direct sunlight throughout every night.
Earth's magnetic field guides many incoming charged particles toward regions near the magnetic poles.
Only polar air contains oxygen and nitrogen.
High-latitude cities produce more electrical light.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly links magnetic guidance to the broad auroral zones near the poles.

questions.stem: What does “emits” mean in the color paragraph?
choices: stores permanently
bends into a circle
gives off
measures from a distance
questions.explanation: Atmospheric gases receive energy and then give off visible light of various colors.

questions.stem: Which gas commonly contributes green and red auroral light?
choices: helium
hydrogen
water vapor
oxygen
questions.explanation: The third paragraph assigns common green and red contributions to oxygen.

lesson.strategy: Build the mechanism from source to sight: solar particles reach Earth's magnetic environment, are guided toward high latitudes, transfer energy to gases, and produce emissions viewed in perspective.

signals.phrase: do not fall in a straight line
signals.means: The author rejects a direct route before introducing magnetic guidance.
Several variables, not one fixed rule, shape an aurora's color.
The curtain description is visual; its motion comes from changing physical conditions.

vocab.inContext: a natural upper-atmosphere display of colored light
position north or south of Earth's equator
releases or gives off energy as light

skillTips.main-idea: Follow all three interacting systems: solar source, magnetic route, and atmospheric light production.
skillTips.inference: The geographic pattern follows the magnetic field's guidance, not the presence of unique polar gases.
skillTips.vocabulary: Because the paragraph discusses visible colors, “emits light” means gives light off.
skillTips.detail: Keep the gas-color pairings distinct: oxygen is linked to green and red.

passages.title: Kalpana Chawla's Long Route to Space
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
As a student in Karnal, India, Kalpana Chawla watched aircraft and became interested in how machines move through air. Spaceflight was not a nearby or guaranteed path. She first built a foundation through study, earning an engineering degree in aeronautics in India, then continuing her education in the United States in aerospace engineering.

Chawla's work combined theory with exacting computation. She studied how air flows around aircraft and worked with methods for modeling complex moving surfaces. After joining the United States space program, she trained across many systems rather than preparing for one dramatic moment. Astronaut work included simulations, technical assignments, physical practice, teamwork, and repeated responses to possible failures.

She first flew in space aboard the shuttle Columbia in 1997. Her responsibilities included operating a robotic arm and supporting scientific work. The mission also required the crew to respond to a satellite deployment problem, showing that preparation mattered precisely when a plan changed.

Chawla returned to Columbia for a research mission in 2003. The shuttle was lost during reentry, and all seven crew members died. That ending is an essential part of her biography, but it should not flatten the years before it into a prediction. Her career was built through accumulated choices: crossing fields of study, learning unfamiliar systems, and contributing within teams. Remembering Chawla only as someone who “dreamed of space” makes persistence sound magical. Her route shows something more concrete. A distant ambition became work through education, technical depth, patient training, and collaboration, none sufficient alone, but each opening the next stage.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Kalpana Chawla entered spaceflight directly after watching aircraft as a child.
Kalpana Chawla reached space through sustained education, technical work, training, and teamwork rather than ambition alone.
Her astronaut preparation focused on one dramatic task and avoided routine technical systems.
The outcome of her final mission made every earlier achievement unimportant.
questions.explanation: The biography repeatedly turns a distant interest into a sequence of concrete preparation and collaborative responsibilities.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the satellite deployment problem?
choices: It shows that Chawla's robotic-arm training had no practical purpose.
It explains why she decided to leave aerospace engineering.
It demonstrates how broad preparation helps a crew respond when events depart from the plan.
It proves that one astronaut controlled every decision on the mission.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph connects the changed plan directly to the value of preparation.

questions.stem: What does “flatten” mean in the fourth paragraph?
choices: change an aircraft surface into a straight plane
make a biography easier to print
remove gravity during a space mission
reduce a complex life to one dominating event
questions.explanation: The warning asks readers not to let the fatal ending erase the varied years of education and work before it.

questions.stem: What device did Chawla operate on her first spaceflight?
choices: a robotic arm
a printing press
a radio telescope on Earth
a paper-making screen
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names operation of a robotic arm among her responsibilities.

lesson.strategy: Read the biography as a route made of stages, not as destiny followed by tragedy. Track how each stage (education, modeling, systems training, and crew work) creates the capacity for the next.

signals.phrase: not a nearby or guaranteed path
signals.means: The opening rejects the idea that interest alone made spaceflight inevitable.

signals.phrase: rather than preparing for one dramatic moment
signals.means: Astronaut readiness grows through many routine systems and contingencies.
The final loss belongs in the story without replacing the full career.

vocab.inContext: the study and design of flight within an atmosphere

skillTips.main-idea: Summarize the connected forms of preparation that turned an ambition into skilled team contribution.
skillTips.inference: The unexpected satellite problem illustrates why astronauts train for systems and failures beyond a single planned task.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast one fatal event with the many prior years to understand the figurative meaning of “flatten.”
skillTips.detail: The first-flight paragraph names the robotic arm before describing the deployment problem.

passages.title: The Lighthouse Everyone Can Use
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A lighthouse sends a warning beam across dark water. When one ship uses that light to avoid rocks, the beam remains available to another ship. One captain's benefit does not use up the signal.

It can also be difficult to show the beam only to ships that paid for it. Once the light shines, many vessels nearby can see it. Economists use features like these to describe a public good. One person's use does not greatly reduce use by others. Excluding non-payers may also be difficult.

The term does not mean the lighthouse is free to build or maintain. Workers, equipment, and energy still have costs. The example instead explains why collecting payment from each user can be hard and why communities may support a shared service together.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A lighthouse is a public good because it has no building or maintenance costs.
Each ship uses up part of a lighthouse beam and must replace it.
A lighthouse illustrates a public good because many ships can share its beam and excluding users is difficult.
Lighthouse beams can be directed only toward vessels that have paid.
questions.explanation: The passage develops the two relevant features and then separates them from the mistaken idea of zero cost.

questions.stem: Why can charging each ship be difficult?
choices: Every ship owns a separate lighthouse.
The beam disappears after one captain sees it.
Workers cannot determine whether rocks exist.
Nearby ships may see the beam whether or not they paid for it.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says excluding non-payers from an already shining beam may be difficult.

questions.stem: What does “excluding” mean here?
choices: preventing someone from using or receiving something
adding another ship
making a light brighter
counting maintenance costs
questions.explanation: The context concerns keeping non-payers from receiving the visible signal.

questions.stem: What cost does the passage name?
choices: fish caught near shore
equipment

replacement seawater
questions.explanation: The final paragraph lists workers, equipment, and energy as real lighthouse costs.

lesson.strategy: Test the lighthouse against two separate features: shared use does not consume the beam, and non-payers are hard to exclude. Then note that “public good” describes use, not an absence of cost.

signals.means: One ship's benefit leaves the same warning available to others.

signals.means: The signal is hard to restrict after it is provided.
The final paragraph corrects a common misunderstanding about the word “public.”

skillTips.inference: A visible beam reaches nearby ships without checking which captains contributed payment.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase about non-payers shows that “excluding” means preventing access.
skillTips.detail: The final paragraph contains a three-part list of costs; equipment is the middle item.

passages.title: The Case for Taking Notes by Hand
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Writing notes by hand is slower than typing for many people. That limit can become useful. Because a writer cannot capture every sentence, handwriting may force a choice: Which idea matters, and how can it be restated briefly? Selecting and rephrasing can deepen attention.

Slowness is not automatically better, however. A person recording unfamiliar names, exact quotations, or rapid instructions may need the speed and searchability of a keyboard. Digital notes can also be enlarged, reorganized, shared, and made accessible through assistive tools. Handwriting may be painful or impossible for some learners.

The strongest case for handwriting is therefore conditional. Use it when the task benefits from selection, sketches, or a deliberate pace. Use another tool when accuracy, access, or collaboration matters more. The learning comes from what the note-taker does with information, not from a moral quality hidden inside paper or a screen.

questions.stem: What is the essay's main idea?
choices: Handwritten notes always produce deeper learning than any digital method.
Typing is useful only when a person needs to record exact quotations.
The physical material of paper gives notes a special moral value.
Handwriting can encourage selection and rephrasing, but the best note-taking tool depends on the task and learner.
questions.explanation: The essay argues for a conditional advantage, then balances it against speed, access, and collaboration needs.

questions.stem: How can the slowness of handwriting support learning?
choices: It can push a note-taker to identify and restate the most important ideas.
It prevents unfamiliar names from appearing in notes.
It makes every written sentence an exact quotation.
It removes the need to think about organization.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph connects limited capture speed with choosing and rephrasing information.

questions.stem: What does “conditional” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: written in especially neat letters

based on a promise to share notes
certain to work for every learner
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow specify when handwriting fits and when another tool is better.

questions.stem: Which digital advantage is named?

questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists enlargement, reorganization, sharing, and assistive access.

lesson.strategy: Track the essay's qualification words. It explains how a limitation “can” help, then uses “however” and “conditional” to match tools with purposes instead of declaring one universal winner.

The author blocks a universal conclusion from the first benefit.
Purpose and access decide which tool fits a particular learner.

skillTips.inference: Connect slower recording with the need to decide, condense, and express ideas in fresh language.
skillTips.vocabulary: The alternating “use it when” sentences demonstrate that “conditional” means circumstance-dependent.
skillTips.detail: Reorganization appears in the list of operations digital notes can support.

passages.title: The Heron's Second Path
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A heron returned each season to a narrow stream where minnows flashed beneath reeds. One year, the water shrank into warm pools. The heron walked the familiar banks from dawn to noon, finding less food each day.

Overhead, a flock of small birds flew toward hills the heron had never crossed. “My stream is behind me,” he called. “Why should I follow strangers away from it?” The birds answered, “We are flying toward water, not away from home.”

The heron stayed until the deepest pool barely covered his feet. At last, he followed their fading calls. Beyond the first hill lay a wide wetland fed by spring rain. It offered fish, shelter, and reeds unlike those he knew.

When the old stream filled again, the heron returned. He had not abandoned it forever. He had abandoned only the route that could no longer serve his deeper purpose. From then on, he remembered both paths. Loyalty to a place, he learned, need not require refusing every change.

questions.stem: What lesson does the fable teach?
choices: Changing a familiar route can protect a deeper commitment when conditions no longer support the old way.
Loyalty requires staying in one place even after its resources disappear.
Strangers always know a better path than someone who lives nearby.
A difficult journey should never lead back to a familiar home.
questions.explanation: The heron leaves to preserve its life and later returns, showing that adaptation need not betray attachment.

questions.stem: What do the small birds mean by flying toward water?
choices: They want the heron to forget that streams contain fish.
Their change of direction serves the same basic need that once drew the heron to its stream.
They believe every home must be located beyond a hill.
They are carrying water back to the dry pools.
questions.explanation: The birds reframe movement as pursuit of a continuing goal, not rejection of home.

questions.stem: What does “fading” mean in “fading calls”?
choices: changing into a new language
growing angry with the heron
becoming weaker as the birds move farther away
echoing more loudly between hills
questions.explanation: The flock is already traveling away, so its calls diminish with distance.

questions.stem: What is beyond the first hill?
choices: the heron's old stream
a village of lantern makers
a completely dry valley
a wide wetland
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reveals the wetland immediately after the heron crosses the hill.

lesson.strategy: Distinguish destination from purpose. The stream is one place where the heron meets its needs; water, food, and survival are the deeper aims. The return proves that adapting was not permanent rejection.

signals.means: Repeated evidence shows that the familiar route no longer works.

signals.phrase: toward water, not away from home
signals.means: The birds redefine change by the goal it serves.
Experience expands the heron's options instead of erasing the old one.

vocab.inContext: well known through earlier experience
land whose soil is covered or soaked with water
steady attachment or faithfulness to someone or something

skillTips.main-idea: Express the difference between changing a method and abandoning the underlying value or goal.
skillTips.inference: The birds' direction makes sense when water, rather than one stream, is treated as the enduring purpose.
skillTips.vocabulary: Distance and the flock's movement explain why its calls are “fading.”
skillTips.detail: The new landscape is revealed in the first sentence after the heron follows the flock.

passages.title: The Room That Knows Every Fact About Color
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine Mara, a scientist who studies color vision in a room where everything is black, white, or gray. Her screens display no colors. Still, she has learned every physical fact available about human color perception: wavelengths, retinal cells, neural signals, language, and behavior. She can predict what people will say when they see a ripe tomato.

One day, Mara leaves the room and sees red for the first time. Does she learn something? If the experience teaches her what red looks like, then complete physical information may seem to leave out a fact about conscious experience. Philosopher Frank Jackson made a version of this case famous as the knowledge argument.

The conclusion is disputed. Some philosophers say Mara gains new knowledge: she now knows a quality that descriptions could not provide. Others say she gains an ability, such as recognizing or imagining red, without discovering a new fact. Still others argue that she encounters an old physical fact through a new form of representation.

The thought experiment does not depend on whether such a total education is practically possible. Its extreme setup sharpens a distinction between describing a brain process and undergoing an experience. Yet the story alone does not announce which interpretation wins. Like a prism separating one beam, it divides meanings of “knowing” so they can be examined.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The thought experiment proves that wavelengths and retinal cells have no role in seeing color.
The color-room thought experiment tests whether complete physical knowledge includes what a conscious experience feels like.
Mara forgets all physical information as soon as she sees a ripe tomato.
Every philosopher agrees that recognizing red is a newly discovered physical fact.
questions.explanation: The setup and competing interpretations all concern whether experiential knowledge adds something to physical description.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the case to a prism?
choices: Mara uses a prism to create the first red object she sees.
A prism prevents neural signals from reaching the brain.
The case separates several meanings of knowledge so each can be considered distinctly.
All arguments about color can be reduced to measuring one wavelength.
questions.explanation: The final phrase directly explains the metaphor: one term, “knowing,” is divided into examinable meanings.

questions.stem: What does “undergoing” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: describing an event with complete accuracy
predicting another person's words
measuring the length of a light wave
personally experiencing a process or event
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a scientific description with actually having the color experience.

questions.stem: What color does Mara first see after leaving the room?
choices: red
blue
green
gold
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly says that Mara sees red for the first time.

lesson.strategy: Keep three layers apart: Mara's total physical description, her first-person experience, and the rival accounts of what changes. The passage presents the distinction as a question, not a settled proof.

signals.means: The setup makes descriptive knowledge as complete as the scenario permits.
This question is the hinge between the story and the philosophical dispute.
Several interpretations follow, so no single answer should be attributed to the passage.

vocab.inContext: the process of becoming aware through the senses
a way in which information is presented or encoded
personally experiencing something as it happens

skillTips.main-idea: State the test between physical description and felt experience without declaring one disputed answer correct.
skillTips.inference: A prism divides a beam; here the comparison concerns dividing the broad word “knowing” into senses.
skillTips.vocabulary: The direct contrast with “describing” makes “undergoing” an act of personally experiencing.
skillTips.detail: The first experience and the tomato example both identify the focal color as red.

passages.title: Why Plans Take Longer Than Expected
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A team schedules two weeks to redesign a website. Members list the pages, divide the work, and imagine each step proceeding normally. They remember that the last redesign took a month, but dismiss it because that project had different problems. Three weeks later, an overlooked approval and a difficult data transfer have broken the new schedule too.

This pattern is called the planning fallacy: people predict a task by focusing on the current plan while giving too little weight to outcomes from similar past tasks. The inside view asks, “How will we complete these steps?” The outside view asks, “How long did comparable efforts actually take?” Both offer information, but confident schedules often lean heavily on the first.

A detailed plan makes smooth progress easy to picture, while unknown interruptions are hard to represent. Each past delay can also look unique. Treating every obstacle as exceptional prevents the repeated pattern from informing the next estimate.

An outside view begins with a relevant group of earlier projects and their actual durations. Planners can then adjust for important differences in the present case. This is not blind surrender to an average: a smaller team or a tested tool may justify a change. The starting point carries evidence that imagination tends to omit. Longer estimates are not always better, and extra time can create its own waste. The goal is calibration, not pessimism. A useful forecast combines the plan's specific knowledge with the record's inconvenient base rate, then states uncertainty instead of hiding it behind one exact date.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The planning fallacy occurs because people intentionally lie about every project's schedule.
An outside view requires using an average without adjusting for present differences.
Better time forecasts combine detailed current plans with evidence from comparable past tasks and explicit uncertainty.
Accurate planners should always choose the longest estimate anyone proposes.
questions.explanation: The passage diagnoses overreliance on the inside view and recommends a calibrated combination rather than pessimism or blind averaging.

questions.stem: Why can treating every past obstacle as unique worsen future estimates?
choices: It makes current task steps impossible to list.
It forces planners to use exactly the same tools again.
It proves that comparable projects do not exist.
It prevents a repeated history of delays from influencing the next prediction.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says exceptional explanations can hide the overall pattern that the outside view needs.

questions.stem: What does “calibration” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: bringing confidence and estimates into line with actual outcomes
adding the maximum possible delay to every schedule
removing all specific information from a plan
dividing website pages equally among workers
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts calibration with pessimism and calls for forecasts that reflect plans, records, and uncertainty.

questions.stem: What two problems break the example team's schedule?
choices: a missing office and a broken printer
an overlooked approval and a difficult data transfer
a color dispute and a staff holiday
an expired website name and a power cut
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph names the approval and data-transfer problems together.

lesson.strategy: Contrast the inside and outside views as complementary evidence sources. The first maps this task's steps; the second supplies actual durations from related work. The conclusion recommends calibration through both.

signals.means: The team explains away relevant history instead of incorporating it.
A vivid smooth plan can outweigh interruptions that are unknown and hard to imagine.
Past averages are starting evidence that can still be adjusted for real differences.

vocab.inContext: a recurring error in reasoning
similar enough to provide a useful comparison
alignment between predictions and observed results

skillTips.main-idea: Choose the synthesis of current detail, historical outcomes, and uncertainty rather than one view alone.
skillTips.inference: If every delay is dismissed as exceptional, their shared effect never enters the next forecast.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with both optimism and pessimism shows that “calibration” means matching estimates to evidence.
skillTips.detail: The schedule breaks for two named reasons at the end of the website example.

passages.title: Why E-Ink Holds Still
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An electronic-paper display can keep showing a page even when it is not using power. Its screen contains tiny capsules filled with light and dark charged particles. An electric field moves selected particles toward the visible surface.

To make a dark mark, the device brings dark particles to the top in certain places. To make a light area, it moves light particles upward instead. After the field stops, the particles remain largely in position. The image therefore holds still without being redrawn many times each second.

Power is needed when the page changes, and the device still uses energy for other tasks. E-ink is not a glowing screen; it usually reflects surrounding light. Its stable particles explain both the paperlike appearance and the low energy needed to display an unmoving page.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: E-ink redraws every page many times each second to keep it visible.
An electronic-paper screen glows by burning dark particles inside capsules.
E-ink uses no energy when changing pages or performing other device tasks.
E-ink holds an image by positioning charged particles that remain stable after the electric field stops.
questions.explanation: The passage connects electric movement with particle stability and carefully limits the low-power claim.

questions.stem: Why can an unchanged page remain visible with little power?
choices: The selected particles stay near the visible surface after being moved.
The screen stores sunlight inside every capsule.
A hidden printer replaces the page continuously.
The dark particles lose their electric charge forever.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that the particles largely remain in place after the field stops.

questions.stem: What does “reflects” mean in the last paragraph?
choices: creates its own strong light
sends surrounding light back toward the viewer
erases a dark particle
measures electric power
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a reflective e-ink screen with a glowing screen that produces light.

questions.stem: When is display power needed?
choices: only when the page stays still
whenever surrounding light is present
when the page changes
only while the device is turned off
questions.explanation: The final paragraph directly says power is needed when the page changes.

lesson.strategy: Follow one particle through the cause-and-effect chain: an electric field moves it, its surface position sets a light or dark area, and its stability preserves the image after power stops.

signals.means: Electrical forces can move the light and dark material within each capsule.
Particle stability lets a static image persist without constant refreshing.
E-ink typically depends on reflected environmental light.

vocab.inContext: tiny enclosed containers holding the display particles
likely to remain in the same position
sends incoming light back from a surface

skillTips.main-idea: Connect particle movement and later stability; both are necessary to explain e-ink.
skillTips.inference: The image persists because its physical light-dark pattern remains after the moving field ends.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with “glowing” indicates that “reflects” means returning outside light.
skillTips.detail: The last paragraph separates page-change energy from the low cost of displaying a fixed page.

passages.title: Three Stops Early
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When repairs closed her usual station, Priya left the tram three stops early. Rain had blurred the temporary map, so she followed signs through a street she had never noticed. Beside a bakery stood a shop window filled with single gloves, bent keys, and umbrellas tagged with dates.

The owner, Mr. Anwar, explained that he collected objects found on nearby trams. The transit office accepted valuable items, but ordinary things were often discarded before owners knew where to ask. He cleaned them, posted photographs, and waited.

Priya recognized a red lunch tin in the window. Her coworker Elise had searched for it all week because a child's drawing was tucked inside. Priya sent a photograph, and Elise arrived before closing. She offered Mr. Anwar money; he asked her to post the shop's address instead.

When Priya's station reopened, she resumed her usual route. Now she sometimes left three stops early on purpose, carrying a list of objects people had lost.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: An unexpected detour leads Priya to a shop that quietly reunites ordinary lost objects with their owners.
Priya opens a bakery after her tram station closes permanently.
A transit office pays Mr. Anwar to sell valuable lost property.
Elise loses a lunch tin because Priya takes the wrong tram.
questions.explanation: The detour reveals Mr. Anwar's service, enables one reunion, and changes Priya's later route.

questions.stem: Why does Mr. Anwar ask Elise to post the address instead of paying him?
choices: He wants to hide the lunch tin from the transit office.
Making the shop easier to find will help other owners recover their things.
He plans to move the shop before the station reopens.
He believes the drawing belongs in the bakery.
questions.explanation: His work depends on owners knowing where to ask, so publicity supports the service more than one payment.

questions.stem: What does “discarded” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: carefully repaired
officially photographed
thrown away
returned by tram
questions.explanation: The ordinary objects are lost because they may be disposed of before owners locate them.

questions.stem: What is tucked inside the red lunch tin?
choices: a tram ticket
a bakery receipt
a list of lost umbrellas
a child's drawing
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives the drawing as the reason Elise especially wants the tin back.

lesson.strategy: Trace how the detour changes from inconvenience to connection. The lost station leads to a lost-property shop, one recovery demonstrates its value, and Priya's voluntary later trips show a new commitment.

signals.means: The disruption places Priya on an unfamiliar street where discovery becomes possible.

signals.phrase: before owners knew where to ask
signals.means: The main obstacle is not ownership but the missing connection to a recovery place.
Priya later repeats the route by choice to help extend the shop's work.

vocab.inContext: intended to last only for a limited time
thrown away as unwanted
began doing something again after an interruption

skillTips.main-idea: Link the accidental discovery, the lunch-tin reunion, and Priya's later decision to help.
skillTips.inference: Mr. Anwar's stated problem is that owners do not know where to ask, which an address post can solve.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with owners recovering items shows that “discarded” means thrown away.
skillTips.detail: The keepsake inside the tin is named immediately after Priya recognizes it.

passages.title: The Drains Beneath Mohenjo-daro
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the ancient city now called Mohenjo-daro, streets followed an organized layout and many buildings were made from standardized baked bricks. Archaeologists have also found numerous wells, bathing areas, and covered drains. Wastewater could move from some houses into channels along the streets.

These features reveal careful planning and repeated maintenance. Brick covers allowed sections of drain to be opened, while settling spaces could catch solid material before it blocked a channel. Water management was not confined to a single palace. Its structures appeared through residential parts of the city.

The remains, however, do not answer every social question. Similar brick sizes suggest shared standards, but they do not identify the officials or craftspeople who set them. A large bathing structure shows organized construction, yet its exact ceremonies or rules remain uncertain. Drains demonstrate capacity; they do not by themselves prove that every resident received equal service.

Mohenjo-daro belonged to the Indus civilization, whose script has not been securely deciphered. Without readable administrative records, buildings carry much of the evidence. The city's waterworks show technical coordination and daily concern with water, while their silences remind us to separate what ruins support from what we merely expect them to say.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The city's drains prove that every resident received exactly equal public services.
Mohenjo-daro's waterworks show extensive urban coordination, while archaeological remains leave important social questions unanswered.
Readable government records explain who designed every well and bathing area.
Mohenjo-daro had one palace drain but little water management in residential streets.
questions.explanation: The passage presents substantial structural evidence, then repeatedly marks what that evidence cannot establish.

questions.stem: Why are the drain covers important evidence of maintenance?
choices: They converted wastewater back into drinking water.
They displayed the names of all city officials.
Workers could remove them to reach and clear sections of the channel.
They prevented houses from connecting to street drains.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph connects openable brick covers with access to drain sections.

questions.stem: What does “confined” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: written in an undeciphered script
filled completely with solid material
built from standardized bricks
limited to one place or group
questions.explanation: The next sentence contrasts a single palace with structures spread through residential areas.

questions.stem: What material was used for many buildings?
choices: standardized baked bricks
uncut ice blocks
steel panels
woven reed mats only
questions.explanation: The opening sentence describes numerous buildings made from standardized baked bricks.

lesson.strategy: Sort claims into evidence and interpretation. Wells, drains, covers, and standard bricks directly support coordination; statements about leadership, ceremony, or equality require records the remains do not provide.

signals.means: Accessible covers and settling areas imply ongoing work, not construction alone.

signals.phrase: do not answer every social question
signals.means: Physical sophistication does not reveal the whole political or social system.
Unreadable script limits the administrative evidence available to researchers.

vocab.inContext: made to follow a consistent size or design
restricted to a particular place or limit
successfully interpreted or read

skillTips.main-idea: Balance the positive evidence for coordination with the explicit boundaries on social conclusions.
skillTips.inference: A removable cover makes hidden infrastructure accessible, which is necessary for clearing a drain.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast between one palace and residential areas defines “confined” as limited.
skillTips.detail: The building material and its consistent form appear together in the opening sentence.

passages.title: Slime Mold Finds a Short Route
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A slime mold spreading across damp wood has no brain or central planner. In one stage of its life, however, the organism forms a pulsing network that moves nutrients through branching tubes. The network changes: useful tubes strengthen, while poorly used ones may shrink.

In laboratory demonstrations, researchers place food at several points on a surface and let a slime mold grow among them. At first, its branches explore many directions. Over time, routes that connect food efficiently can remain while redundant paths fade. The final network may resemble a compact transport map.

This result does not mean the slime mold draws a map, understands distance, or solves a problem consciously. Local chemical and physical responses can produce organized behavior at a larger scale. Flow through a tube affects that tube's future size, creating feedback across the living network.

Efficiency also has more than one meaning. The shortest set of connections might break if one link is damaged. A network with an extra loop can be longer but more resilient. Researchers therefore compare length, travel efficiency, and tolerance of disruption rather than awarding the organism one score. The slime mold is interesting because coordination emerges without a command center. Countless local adjustments preserve routes that work under particular conditions. What looks like a decision from above can grow from feedback distributed through the whole body.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A slime mold consciously draws transport maps before growing toward food.
The shortest possible network is always the most resilient and useful one.
A slime mold's local feedback can shape efficient, adaptable networks without conscious planning or a central brain.
Every branch in a slime mold network remains the same size throughout its life.
questions.explanation: The passage explains exploration, reinforcement, caution about consciousness, and multiple forms of network quality.

questions.stem: Why might a slightly longer network be useful?
choices: Longer tubes always carry nutrients faster than shorter ones.
Redundant paths prove that the organism has a central planner.
A larger network prevents all local chemical feedback.
An extra route can preserve connections if another part is damaged.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph contrasts absolute shortness with loops that improve resilience under disruption.

questions.stem: What does “redundant” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: unnecessary because another route already serves the connection
especially strong after heavy use
directed by a conscious plan
unable to carry any nutrients
questions.explanation: The redundant paths fade as the network retains routes that connect the food efficiently.

questions.stem: What happens to well-used tubes?
choices: They immediately dry out.
They strengthen.
They turn into food points.
They detach from the network.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says useful tubes strengthen while poorly used tubes may shrink.

lesson.strategy: Track scale carefully. Tube flow changes local growth, repeated local changes reshape the network, and the large pattern looks purposeful. The passage warns against inserting conscious planning into that chain.

signals.means: The organized result must arise through distributed processes.
Early exploration is broad before feedback preserves more useful routes.
The author blocks a metaphorical map from becoming a claim about consciousness.

vocab.inContext: unneeded because another route serves the same function
able to continue working after damage or disruption
a process in which results influence what happens next

skillTips.main-idea: Connect local feedback to the emergent network while preserving the warning against conscious intent.
skillTips.inference: An extra loop provides an alternate path, explaining how more length can increase resilience.
skillTips.vocabulary: Paths disappear as more efficient ones remain, so “redundant” means duplicative and unnecessary.
skillTips.detail: The useful-versus-poorly-used tube contrast appears in the opening description of network change.

passages.title: What a Passport Proves
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A passport is a document issued by a government to identify a person for international travel. It records a name, photograph, birth date, nationality, and anti-forgery features. By issuing it, a government asserts that the holder is the person described and recognizes that person's nationality under its rules.

The document does not by itself promise entry into every country. A destination applies its laws and may require a visa, which is permission or authorization to seek entry for a purpose and period. Some visas are placed in passports; others are recorded electronically. Even a visa is not always a final guarantee, because border authorities may check whether entry conditions are met.

A passport also has an expiration date. Some destinations require it to remain valid beyond the planned trip, and rules vary. Damage, missing pages, or a major mismatch between the holder's current appearance and the document can create additional questions. Travelers must check official requirements for their circumstances rather than relying on a general example.

Because a passport contains personal data, finding someone else's document creates a responsibility to protect it. Posting a full image online may expose the passport number and identity details. Returning it through the issuing authority, police, or an appropriate lost-property service is usually safer than public display. The passport's power is specific. It supports identity and nationality claims and allows a person to request passage across a border. It is not a universal invitation, a record of personal character, or a substitute for every destination's permission.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A valid passport guarantees its holder entry into every country without further checks.
A visa replaces the need for a passport by proving a traveler's personal character.
Publishing a found passport online is the safest way to locate its owner.
A passport supports identity and nationality for travel, but entry rights, validity rules, and privacy duties remain separate.
questions.explanation: The passage defines the passport's claims and then carefully distinguishes visas, border decisions, validity, and data protection.

questions.stem: Why does a visa not always guarantee entry?
choices: Border authorities may still determine whether the traveler meets the destination's conditions.
A visa never records any purpose or permitted period.
Passports automatically expire whenever a visa is issued.
Only the passport's photograph can authorize a border crossing.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that authorities can make a further conditions check even after a visa exists.

questions.stem: What does “asserts” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: hides through encryption
states or affirms as true
questions without evidence
changes after every trip
questions.explanation: By issuing the document, the government formally affirms the holder's identity and nationality claims.

questions.stem: Which information does the passage say a passport generally records?
choices: a complete work history
every city previously visited
a photograph
a list of personal opinions
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph includes a photograph among the usual identity fields.

lesson.strategy: Build a boundary chart around the passport's function. It supports identity and nationality, while a visa, border decision, expiration rule, and privacy practice answer different questions the passport alone cannot settle.

signals.means: Possessing the document is distinct from receiving permission to enter.
Validity requirements depend on the destination and circumstances.
The conclusion narrows the passport's real authority after listing common overclaims.

vocab.inContext: legal membership or recognized connection to a country
formally states that something is true
a false document made to appear genuine

skillTips.main-idea: Define what the document supports and contrast it with the permissions and duties outside that role.
skillTips.inference: A visa is advance authorization, but the later border check still applies the actual entry conditions.
skillTips.vocabulary: The government's act of issuing and recognizing claims shows that “asserts” means formally affirms.
skillTips.detail: The identity-field list in the first paragraph includes the holder's photograph.

passages.title: The Skin on a Drop of Water
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Fill a cup carefully, and the water may rise slightly above the rim before spilling. The curved top looks as if it wears a thin skin. No separate film covers it. The effect comes from attraction among water molecules.

Inside the water, a molecule is pulled by neighbors in many directions. At the surface, there are fewer water molecules above. The unequal pull draws surface molecules inward, making the surface resist being stretched. This behavior is called surface tension.

Surface tension can support a light water strider when its legs spread the force without breaking the surface. It also helps small drops become rounded. The “skin” can still break when enough force is applied. The image is useful, but the surface remains liquid water held together by molecular attraction.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Attraction among water molecules creates surface tension, making a liquid surface behave somewhat like a stretched skin.
A solid film forms over every cup of water before it spills.
Gravity disappears from water molecules located at the surface.
Water striders float because their legs turn liquid into ice.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the unequal surface forces, names surface tension, and applies it without treating the skin as literal.

questions.stem: Why are surface molecules pulled inward?
choices: They are covered by a separate solid layer.
They have fewer water neighbors above them than beside and below them.
Their weight becomes zero at the rim.
Water striders push every molecule downward.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph connects the missing neighbors above with an unequal inward pull.

questions.stem: What does “resist” mean here?
choices: begin immediately
measure accurately
oppose or push against
flow through a hole
questions.explanation: Surface tension makes the top oppose stretching rather than give way without force.

questions.stem: Which animal is supported by surface tension?
choices: a flying fish
a desert beetle
a heron
a water strider
questions.explanation: The final paragraph names a light water strider as an example.

lesson.strategy: Move from the skin comparison to the molecular cause. Unequal attraction at the boundary creates resistance, while the final warning reminds you that no solid covering has formed.

signals.means: The skinlike appearance is a comparison, not a new material on top.
An uneven set of neighboring pulls distinguishes the surface from the interior.
Surface tension resists force only up to a limit.

vocab.inContext: tiny units that make up a substance such as water
the outer boundary of the water
oppose a force or change

skillTips.main-idea: Connect the visible skinlike behavior to attraction among molecules, not to a literal covering.
skillTips.inference: Compare a molecule's neighbors inside the water with the missing neighbors above the surface.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “being stretched” identifies the force that the surface tends to oppose or resist.
skillTips.detail: The animal example appears in the first sentence of the final paragraph.

passages.title: Katherine Johnson Checks the Flight
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Katherine Johnson joined the organization that became NASA as a mathematician. Early computers were people who performed and checked calculations. Johnson analyzed flight paths, bringing strong geometry skills and a habit of asking what each number meant.

For astronaut John Glenn's orbital mission, electronic computers calculated the planned route. Glenn asked for Johnson to check the machine's numbers by hand before launch. Her calculation did not replace every computer. It provided an independent comparison at a time when crewed orbital flight was new and confidence in automated results was still developing.

Johnson also calculated trajectories for other missions and worked with engineers across specialized teams. A safe route involved launch location, speed, Earth's rotation, orbit, and a return corridor. No single person controlled all those systems.

Her famous check matters because trust was earned through demonstrated accuracy. It also shows how new technology and human expertise can support each other. Verification is not distrust for its own sake; it is a method for finding whether two routes to an answer agree.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Katherine Johnson replaced every electronic computer used in the space program.
Katherine Johnson's precise calculations and independent checks helped teams build confidence in early crewed spaceflight.
John Glenn asked Johnson to design the spacecraft's mechanical engines.
Orbital routes depended on one mathematician working without engineers.
questions.explanation: The passage centers on her mathematical expertise, the Glenn check, teamwork, and verification.

questions.stem: Why was Johnson's hand calculation valuable before Glenn's launch?
choices: It allowed the mission to avoid using geometry.
It proved that automated calculation would never be useful.
It offered an independent result that could be compared with the electronic computer's route.
It changed Earth's rotation during the planned orbit.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes two calculation routes whose agreement could strengthen confidence.

questions.stem: What does “verification” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: replacing a team with one expert
guessing a result without calculation
hiding uncertainty from a crew
checking evidence to confirm whether a result is accurate
questions.explanation: Johnson's independent calculation is compared with the machine's answer to verify the route.

questions.stem: Which astronaut requested Johnson's check?
choices: John Glenn
Kalpana Chawla
Neil Armstrong
Mae Jemison
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly names John Glenn.

lesson.strategy: Follow the two calculation paths in the Glenn example: an electronic result and Johnson's independent hand check. Their comparison explains why the story is about verification, expertise, and team trust.

signals.means: The historical job combined producing results with testing their accuracy.
A separate method can reveal disagreement rather than repeating the same error.
The conclusion rejects a simple contest between human mathematics and machines.

vocab.inContext: mathematics concerning shape, position, and space
paths followed by moving objects
a check that confirms accuracy or truth

skillTips.main-idea: Emphasize accurate checking within a broader spaceflight team, not a lone-person or anti-computer story.
skillTips.inference: Two independent routes to the same number make unnoticed error less likely and confidence more justified.
skillTips.vocabulary: The final sentence defines verification through comparing two routes to an answer.
skillTips.detail: The astronaut's name appears in the paragraph about the orbital mission and launch check.

passages.title: The Cost Outside the Receipt
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A delivery company chooses noisy trucks because they are cheap to operate. Customers pay the delivery price, and the company pays for fuel, drivers, and repairs. Residents along the route, however, lose sleep. That disruption is a cost though it appears on neither the company's bill nor the customer's receipt.

Economists call such an effect an external cost, or externality. Part of the consequence of an exchange falls on people who did not choose it. Smoke affecting nearby lungs, bright signs disturbing neighboring homes, or waste damaging shared water can follow the pattern. The term identifies where a cost lands; it does not calculate the harm or select a policy.

When decision makers see only their private costs, an activity may look cheaper than it is for the community as a whole. That difference can lead to more noise or pollution than people would choose if all effects were considered. Responses might include rules, fees, bargaining, changed routes, or cleaner technology, depending on rights, evidence, and practical conditions.

The hidden cost is not imaginary simply because no receipt prints it. Recognizing an externality expands the boundary of the decision: whose time, health, property, or surroundings change when the transaction occurs?

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every cost of a delivery is fully paid by the company and its customers.
The term externality automatically identifies one correct government policy.
An external cost occurs when an activity imposes real burdens on people outside the transaction and its receipt.
A cost becomes imaginary whenever no one can print it on a receipt.
questions.explanation: The delivery example and later cases all show consequences landing on third parties outside the exchange.

questions.stem: Why might a company operate more noisy trucks than a community would prefer?
choices: Residents receive all delivery revenue without paying fuel costs.
Noise makes every truck mechanically cheaper to repair.
A receipt requires companies to increase pollution.
Its private calculation may omit the sleep disruption borne by residents.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links omitted community effects with an activity appearing cheaper and therefore occurring more.

questions.stem: What does “lands” mean in “where a cost lands”?
choices: is experienced or borne by someone
arrives at a delivery address
falls physically from a truck
becomes printed on paper
questions.explanation: The phrase asks which people experience the consequence, even if they are outside the transaction.

questions.stem: What effect do nearby residents experience in the truck example?
choices: lower fuel prices
lost sleep
free deliveries
shorter travel routes
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph states that truck noise causes residents along the route to lose sleep.

lesson.strategy: Draw a boundary around the buyer and seller, then look beyond it. The truck example shows that accounting records can omit consequences borne by neighbors, which is the defining structure of the passage.

signals.means: The contrast shifts attention from transaction participants to affected outsiders.
A third party bears part of the consequence without joining the exchange.
Community cost includes effects missing from the company's private calculation.

vocab.inContext: a disturbance that interrupts normal life
an effect of an activity borne by people outside the exchange
discussion aimed at reaching an agreement

skillTips.main-idea: Define the location of the burden (outside the transaction) rather than focusing only on pollution.
skillTips.inference: Compare the company's listed costs with the residents' omitted sleep loss to explain overuse.
skillTips.vocabulary: The nearby phrase “on people” shows that a cost “lands” where it is experienced.
skillTips.detail: The opening truck example names sleep disruption before introducing the economics term.

passages.title: A Door Left Open
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A community workshop hung a banner saying EVERYONE WELCOME. Its front door was propped open, and members understood that visitors could enter. Yet newcomers paused on the pavement. Through the doorway they saw shelves of tools, people wearing safety glasses, and a desk with no sign.

The organizers blamed shyness. Then they watched one Saturday from a newcomer's point of view. Was the workshop free? Did a visitor need experience? Which tools required training? Could someone enter only to look? The open door answered none of these questions.

The group added a board: “First visit? Start here. Looking is free. Ask us before using a marked tool.” They placed spare safety glasses beside it and marked an accessible route to the desk. A volunteer began greeting people without demanding that they explain a project.

Attendance grew, but the lesson was not that every space needs more signs. Welcome must become legible through the choices a visitor actually faces. A door can be physically open while rules, costs, and risks remain hidden. Conversely, a closed door with a clear bell and instructions may communicate entry better. Stating a value matters because it gives people a promise to evaluate. Design carries the promise into action. The most generous invitation is one that does not require a newcomer to display confusion before receiving the information regulars already possess.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Physically propping open a door gives every visitor all the information needed to participate.
Community spaces should replace personal greetings with as many signs as possible.
Newcomers must explain a complete project before receiving safety information.
A welcoming value becomes effective when a space makes entry, rules, costs, and assistance understandable to newcomers.
questions.explanation: The workshop succeeds when it translates a general banner into practical cues and low-pressure human support.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention a closed door with a bell?
choices: It shows that clear entry instructions can communicate welcome better than physical openness alone.
It proves that all community workshops should remain locked.
It suggests that newcomers prefer ringing loud bells.
It shows that safety glasses are unnecessary behind closed doors.
questions.explanation: The counterexample separates the physical state of a door from the clarity of the invitation.

questions.stem: What does “legible” mean in the fourth paragraph?
choices: written in one particular typeface
easy for a visitor to understand from visible cues
free from every safety rule
known only to regular members
questions.explanation: The board, marked route, and greeting make the workshop's welcome understandable in practice.

questions.stem: What item is placed beside the new board?
choices: a box of finished projects
a locked payment drawer
spare safety glasses
a shelf of blank banners
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says spare safety glasses are placed beside the instructions.

lesson.strategy: Contrast declared welcome with usable welcome. The banner and open door state an intention; the observed questions reveal missing information; the board, route, equipment, and greeting make the intention operational.

signals.means: Physical access does not clarify costs, skill expectations, or safety rules.
A specific first action reduces the newcomer's uncertainty.
The counterexample proves that communication matters more than door position alone.

vocab.inContext: held in an open position with support
designed so people with varied needs can reach or use it
clear enough to be understood in practice

skillTips.main-idea: Move from the banner's abstract promise to the concrete cues that let newcomers act on it.
skillTips.inference: The closed-door example tests whether clarity, rather than physical openness, carries the meaning of welcome.
skillTips.vocabulary: The practical signs and marked route show that “legible” means understandable through visible design.
skillTips.detail: In the improvement paragraph, the equipment placed by the board is spare safety glasses.

passages.title: The Mango Tree and the Vine
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A young vine curled around a mango tree and climbed rapidly toward the sun. From the upper branches, it could see beyond the garden wall. “I rose because I refused to remain low,” the vine told the plants below. “Ambition alone brought me here.” The mango tree said nothing. Its roots drew water through a dry season, and its trunk held steady during wind. Each week, the vine wrapped itself around another branch while praising its own height.

One day, gardeners came to prune dead wood. They cut a cracked branch, not noticing how much of the vine depended on it. The vine fell halfway to the ground. “They have stolen my success,” it cried. An old bean plant growing on a frame replied, “Your reaching was real. So was the branch beneath it.” The vine looked at the spiral marks its stem had left around the tree. For the first time, it saw its path not as empty air conquered, but as a record of contact.

The mango tree lowered a sound branch in the next wind. The vine accepted it and climbed again. This time, when seedlings asked how it reached the wall, it named sunlight, rain, its own steady growth, and the tree that bore its weight.

Achievement may contain effort without being made of effort alone. Support does not erase the climber's work, and gratitude does not require pretending the climber did nothing. Wisdom begins by seeing the whole structure that makes a rise possible.

questions.stem: What lesson does the fable teach?
choices: Achievement can reflect genuine effort while also depending on support that deserves recognition.
Ambition has value only when a person refuses every form of help.
Receiving support means the supported person's effort was not real.
Success is secure whenever it reaches a position high above others.
questions.explanation: The vine truly grows but misreads the tree's structural support until the fall reveals their dependence.

questions.stem: Why are the spiral marks important to the vine's change?
choices: They prove that the gardeners intentionally damaged the vine.
They make its rise visible as a history of contact with the tree rather than unsupported ascent.
They show the vine how to grow roots without water.
They reveal that the bean plant secretly climbed the mango tree.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph directly contrasts empty air conquered with a path physically wrapped around support.

questions.stem: What does “bore” mean in “the tree that bore its weight”?
choices: became tired of
created a hole through
supported or carried
produced as fruit
questions.explanation: The tree's branch and trunk physically hold the climbing vine, so “bore” means carried.

questions.stem: What causes the vine to fall halfway down?
choices: The mango tree pulls up its roots.
The bean plant removes its frame.
A dry season stops all sunlight.
Gardeners cut a cracked branch supporting it.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph identifies pruning of a cracked supporting branch as the immediate cause.

lesson.strategy: Track what changes in the vine's account, not whether it grew. At first it names only ambition; after the fall and the spiral marks, it keeps its own effort in the story while adding the supports beneath it.

signals.means: The word “alone” reveals the vine's central error about causation.
The bean avoids replacing self-credit with the opposite falsehood that effort did not matter.
The vine reinterprets its path as visible evidence of dependence.

cut away selected plant growth

skillTips.vocabulary: Choose the past-tense meaning of “bear” that matches a branch holding weight.
skillTips.detail: The fall follows the gardeners' removal of the cracked branch around which the vine grew.

passages.title: The Donkey Between Equal Meals
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine a hungry donkey standing exactly between two equal piles of hay. The piles look and smell the same. The donkey has no reason to prefer the left pile or the right one. If action requires a stronger reason, will it remain still and hungry forever?

This puzzle is often called Buridan's donkey, although the exact story was shaped over time by later writers. It turns an abstract problem into a simple scene. Can a decision happen when reasons are balanced?

A real donkey might move randomly, follow a tiny unnoticed difference, or simply choose. Human choices also use habits and chance when reasons tie. The puzzle does not predict animal behavior. It asks whether choosing must always mean identifying one option as better before acting.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Real donkeys always refuse food when two piles are visible.
The donkey puzzle asks how choice is possible when the available reasons for two options seem exactly equal.
A choice counts only when chance and habit play no role.
Buridan personally proved the behavior of every hungry animal.
questions.explanation: The equal hay turns a broad question about reason and action into one clear thought experiment.

questions.stem: Why does the passage mention tiny unnoticed differences?
choices: They would make both piles disappear.
They prove the donkey is not hungry.
They could break the apparent tie in an actual animal's situation.
They make random movement impossible.
questions.explanation: A real choice may be influenced by details missing from the perfectly balanced imaginary setup.

questions.stem: What does “abstract” mean here?
choices: easy for an animal to smell
placed at an equal distance
written by an unknown person
concerned with a general idea rather than a concrete object
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a general problem about choice with the visible scene of donkey and hay.

questions.stem: Where is the donkey standing?
choices: exactly between two hay piles
behind one empty basket
beside a running stream
inside a locked stable
questions.explanation: The opening sentence places the animal exactly between the equal meals.

lesson.strategy: Hold the imagined conditions fixed: equal distance, equal hay, and no preferred side. Then separate the philosophical question from a prediction about how an actual animal would behave.

signals.means: The setup removes an ordinary basis for selecting one pile.
The central question concerns action under an apparent tie.
The example tests a concept rather than reporting animal behavior.

vocab.inContext: like or choose one option more than another
focused on an idea instead of a particular physical thing
equal in weight or strength

skillTips.main-idea: State the question about tied reasons, not a claim that real animals always freeze.
skillTips.inference: A tiny difference would supply a reason missing from the perfectly equal setup.
skillTips.vocabulary: The concrete donkey scene is introduced as a way to picture an “abstract” question.
skillTips.detail: The donkey's precise position is part of what makes the imagined options equal.

passages.title: Why Unfinished Tasks Stay With Us
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A server takes several meal orders without writing them down, yet remembers each one until it is delivered. Later, the finished orders become harder to recall. An unfinished goal can sometimes remain mentally active because the mind is still tracking what needs to happen next.

This pattern is linked to the Zeigarnik effect, named after psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik. In early research, interrupted activities were sometimes remembered better than completed ones. The broad claim is memorable, but results depend on the task, interruption, motivation, and way memory is tested.

An unfinished task may also return to mind because it lacks closure. That can help someone resume work, or it can become distracting. A practical response is to record a clear next action. Writing “email the revised map to Jo” may reassure the mind more than writing the vague word “project.”

The effect does not mean every incomplete job remains unforgettable. It describes one possible influence on attention and recall, not a rule for all minds.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every unfinished task is remembered perfectly until someone completes it.
Completed meal orders cannot enter long-term memory.
Unfinished goals can remain active in attention and memory, but the effect varies with tasks, people, and conditions.
Writing a vague label always provides more closure than naming a next action.
questions.explanation: The passage introduces the tendency, explains possible value and distraction, and repeatedly limits the claim.

questions.stem: Why might a clear next action reduce distraction?
choices: It guarantees that the task is already completed.
It erases all memory of the larger project.
It makes interruptions impossible in the future.
It records how to resume, giving the unfinished goal more structure and closure.
questions.explanation: The example contrasts a specific resumable action with the vague word “project.”

questions.stem: What does “closure” mean here?
choices: a sense that something has been settled or given an endpoint
a locked restaurant door
a method of testing memory
an unexpected new order
questions.explanation: An incomplete task lacks an ending; a recorded next step may reduce that unresolved feeling.

questions.stem: Who is the effect named after?
choices: Katherine Johnson
Bluma Zeigarnik
Janaki Ammal
Morris K. Jesup
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly names psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik.

lesson.strategy: Follow the passage's cautious modal language: unfinished work “can” remain active and “may” return. Pair the server example with the final limits so a tendency does not become a universal memory law.

signals.means: Completion changes the server's need to keep an order mentally available.
Task design and testing conditions can change whether the pattern appears.
A specific resumption cue may give an open goal useful structure.

vocab.inContext: stopped before an activity was finished
a feeling that something has reached an endpoint
not clear or specific

skillTips.main-idea: Retain the possibility and its limits rather than making every incomplete task unforgettable.
skillTips.inference: A specific next step lowers uncertainty about resuming, even though the larger task remains unfinished.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast between unfinished and completed provides the clue that “closure” means an endpoint.
skillTips.detail: The historical paragraph identifies the psychologist whose surname labels the effect.

passages.title: The Message That Took Three Roads
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When a large message crosses the internet, it can be divided into smaller units called packets. Each packet carries part of the data plus information that helps the destination identify where it belongs. The packets do not need to travel as one unbroken train.

Imagine three packets leaving the same device. One route is busy, so a router sends the first packet north. A second goes east through a faster link. The third follows the first route, then changes direction after equipment stops responding. They may arrive out of order.

At the destination, network rules use identifying and sequence information to reassemble the data. If a required packet is missing, a reliable transport process can request or trigger another copy. The exact mechanisms differ by protocol, and not every kind of network traffic waits for retransmission.

Taking different paths makes a network flexible. Traffic can move around congestion or failure instead of depending on one permanent circuit. It does not make delivery magical or guaranteed: packets can be delayed, lost, or duplicated. The useful achievement is that agreed rules let scattered pieces become one meaningful message again.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every internet message travels as one train along a permanent physical circuit.
Packets lose all identifying information when a router changes their route.
