Different routes guarantee that no packet can ever be delayed or lost.
Network packets may take different routes and arrive out of order, while shared rules identify and reassemble their data.
questions.explanation: The passage follows separated packets through varied paths to rule-based reconstruction and describes the system's limits.

questions.stem: Why is sequence information useful?
choices: It helps the destination restore packet contents to their intended order.
It forces every packet to use exactly the same route.
It prevents equipment from ever stopping.
It changes a busy link into a permanent circuit.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links sequence information directly to reassembling data after out-of-order arrival.

questions.stem: What does “congestion” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a packet's identifying label
too much traffic competing for limited network capacity
a message divided into smaller units
a device that has no destination
questions.explanation: Earlier, a busy route causes redirection; congestion names that crowded network condition.

questions.stem: What happens to the third packet in the example?
choices: It arrives before leaving the device.
It becomes the entire message by itself.
It changes direction after equipment stops responding.
It travels only through the faster eastern link.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes the third packet rerouting after an equipment problem.

lesson.strategy: Follow packet identity rather than imagining a continuous stream. Routes may diverge and arrival order may change, so headers and protocol rules, not shared geography, let the destination rebuild meaning.

signals.means: The message's pieces can take independent routes.
Arrival sequence can differ from the original data sequence.
Flexible routing reduces dependence without eliminating delay, loss, or duplication.

vocab.inContext: small labeled units into which network data is divided
put separated parts back into their intended order
crowding caused by too much traffic for available capacity

skillTips.main-idea: Include both route flexibility and destination reconstruction; they are the two halves of the system.
skillTips.inference: If pieces arrive out of order, sequence labels are what allow the original order to be recovered.
skillTips.vocabulary: The earlier “busy” route provides a concrete network example of congestion.
skillTips.detail: Track the third packet separately: it begins with the first route, then redirects after failure.

passages.title: The Orange Umbrella
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On Monday, an orange umbrella appeared in the lobby of Cedar House. Mina from apartment 6B took it upstairs, certain that it belonged to Mr. Cho, who always carried bright colors. He shook his head but accepted it, promising to ask around.

On Tuesday, Mr. Cho saw the cleaner, Paula, leaving in heavy rain without a coat. He lent her the umbrella. Paula returned it Wednesday morning to the mailroom, where a courier recognized a delivery label still tied beneath the strap. The label named apartment 2A.

Mina felt embarrassed. She had privately complained that 2A's new tenant kept leaving belongings in shared spaces. When she knocked, however, Samir from 2A explained that the umbrella had arrived with groceries he never ordered. He had placed it in the lobby so its owner might recognize it.

The courier checked the partial order number. The umbrella belonged to Ms. Bell in 8C, whose grocery bag had been delivered to Samir by mistake. She had assumed it was lost on the bus. On Thursday, four people stood laughing in the lobby as the umbrella finally reached her. Mina later posted a small lost-and-found card near the mailboxes. The umbrella's route had not exposed one careless neighbor. It had revealed a chain of reasonable guesses, quiet favors, and incomplete information.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: An umbrella's journey corrects Mina's unfair assumption and reveals how neighbors help amid incomplete information.
A courier intentionally sends one umbrella through every apartment in Cedar House.
Mr. Cho keeps an umbrella that Mina knows belongs to Ms. Bell.
A new tenant repeatedly abandons groceries and clothing in the lobby.
questions.explanation: Each transfer follows a reasonable clue, while the final discovery overturns Mina's judgment of Samir.

questions.stem: Why is the delivery label important?
choices: It proves Mr. Cho bought the umbrella for Paula.
It provides a traceable clue that moves the search from a color-based guess toward the actual delivery error.
It lists every person who carried the umbrella.
It shows that Mina ordered groceries for apartment 2A.
questions.explanation: The label identifies 2A, and its partial order number later allows the courier to connect the umbrella to 8C.

questions.stem: What does “partial” mean in the fourth paragraph?
choices: written in orange ink
belonging to several people equally
incomplete but containing some of the original information
impossible for a courier to read
questions.explanation: The number is not complete, but it retains enough information for the courier's check.

questions.stem: Who owns the orange umbrella?
choices: Mr. Cho in apartment 6B
Samir in apartment 2A
Paula the cleaner
Ms. Bell in apartment 8C
questions.explanation: The courier's order check identifies Ms. Bell in 8C as the owner.

lesson.strategy: Follow the evidence attached to the umbrella: color suggests Mr. Cho, the label points to 2A, and the order number resolves the delivery error. Mina's judgment changes as each stronger clue arrives.

signals.means: Mina treats a color association as proof, setting up her first mistaken guess.
The explanation interrupts Mina's private accusation of carelessness.
The conclusion replaces a single culprit with a chain shaped by partial evidence.

vocab.inContext: a person who carries and delivers packages
present only in part rather than complete
accepted an explanation without confirming it

skillTips.main-idea: Connect the corrected assumption with the network of favors; the story is more than an ownership puzzle.
skillTips.inference: The label is stronger than the color guess because it carries data from the umbrella's delivery history.
skillTips.vocabulary: The courier can still use the number, so “partial” means incomplete rather than unreadable.
skillTips.detail: The final ownership is established by the order check, not by who temporarily carries the umbrella.

passages.title: The Treaty Recorded in Wampum
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A wampum belt is made from carefully shaped shell beads woven into patterns. Among several Indigenous nations of northeastern North America, such belts could help record agreements, laws, histories, condolences, and responsibilities. The beads were valuable, but treating a diplomatic belt as jewelry alone misses its political work.

When representatives made an agreement, a knowledgeable speaker could present a belt while reciting the commitments connected to its pattern. The object did not operate like a document that any stranger could decode by sight. Meaning lived in a relationship among design, oral explanation, recognized keepers, and future gatherings where the words were renewed.

European colonists sometimes participated in wampum diplomacy, yet they did not always respect the same protocols or preserve the same understanding. Written copies of treaty language could differ from Indigenous accounts. Later collectors also removed belts from communities and displayed them as art or curiosities, separating them from the people authorized to explain them.

Reading a treaty belt responsibly therefore requires more than matching symbols to a translation chart. Historians consider the belt's materials and pattern, surviving speeches and records, the circumstances of exchange, and knowledge held by the nations involved. Repatriating a belt can restore access and authority, not merely change its storage address. The lasting lesson concerns what counts as a record. A woven object and a spoken renewal can carry law and memory together. If an observer recognizes only alphabetic writing, the agreement may appear silent precisely because the observer has ignored the practices that let it speak.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Any viewer can translate a wampum treaty by matching each bead to one alphabetic letter.
Wampum treaty belts carried diplomatic meaning through patterns, oral explanation, community authority, and repeated acts of remembrance.
Wampum belts served mainly as decorative jewelry exchanged after agreements were complete.
European written copies always preserved the same treaty meaning as Indigenous accounts.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the belt as one part of a living diplomatic record and shows how removal from its practices obscures meaning.

questions.stem: Why might returning a belt restore more than its location?
choices: It makes every shell bead physically new again.
It converts an oral agreement into alphabetic writing.
It can reconnect the object with communities holding the knowledge and authority to interpret it.
It guarantees that all historical disagreements disappear.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph links repatriation with renewed access and authority, while earlier paragraphs explain community-held interpretation.

questions.stem: What does “protocols” mean in the third paragraph?
choices: threads used to weave shell beads
alphabetic copies of a treaty
buildings where collectors store art
recognized procedures and customs governing an exchange
questions.explanation: The context concerns whether participants respected the diplomatic practices that gave the belts meaning.

questions.stem: Who could present a belt while reciting its commitments?
choices: a knowledgeable speaker
any stranger who saw its pattern
only a European collector
a shell-bead merchant with no agreement role
questions.explanation: The second paragraph assigns the presentation and recitation to a knowledgeable speaker.

lesson.strategy: Treat the belt, spoken explanation, keeper, and renewal gathering as one recording system. Removing any element, especially community authority, can make a preserved object look more self-explanatory than it is.

signals.means: Material beauty and value do not exhaust the belt's diplomatic function.

signals.phrase: did not operate like a document
signals.means: The pattern requires authorized oral and social context rather than solitary decoding.

signals.phrase: not merely change its storage address
signals.means: Return can restore interpretive relationships and authority as well as possession.

vocab.inContext: carefully made shell beads used in significant cultural and diplomatic practices
recognized customs and procedures for formal interaction
returning a cultural object to its people or place of origin

skillTips.main-idea: Describe the whole record system, including object, speech, keepers, and renewed relationships.
skillTips.inference: A community's interpretive knowledge explains why repatriation restores authority as well as physical access.
skillTips.vocabulary: The surrounding diplomacy and respect language shows that “protocols” are agreed formal practices.
skillTips.detail: The second paragraph identifies a knowledgeable speaker as the person who joins belt and recitation.

passages.title: How a Mangrove Root Breathes
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Mangrove trees can grow in muddy ground flooded by tides. The mud holds much less oxygen than loose, dry soil. Yet the tree's buried cells still need oxygen for respiration.

Some mangroves send special roots upward from the mud. These roots, called pneumatophores, have small openings that let gases enter when the surface is exposed. Air moves through spongy spaces inside the root toward tissues below.

The roots do not breathe with lungs, and they cannot take in air while every opening is deeply covered. Tides matter because falling water exposes the surface again. Mud should not be packed tightly around these roots, since blocked openings reduce gas exchange.

A mangrove's upward roots solve a boundary problem. The tree stands in waterlogged ground, but part of its root system reaches the air above it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Mangrove roots use lungs to breathe continuously under deep water.
Tides remove every trace of oxygen from the air above mangroves.
Some mangroves grow upward roots that admit air and carry oxygen into tissues buried in waterlogged mud.
Packing mud over root openings improves the tree's gas exchange.
questions.explanation: The passage connects oxygen-poor mud with upward roots, openings, internal spaces, and tidal exposure.

questions.stem: Why does falling water help the special roots?
choices: It changes the roots into leaves.
It packs more mud over each opening.
It stops buried cells from needing oxygen.
It exposes their openings to air again.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that lower tide exposes the root surface for gas exchange.

questions.stem: What does “waterlogged” mean here?
choices: soaked and filled with water
covered in dry leaves
heated by sunlight
hollow from damage
questions.explanation: The opening describes muddy ground flooded by tides, establishing the saturated condition.

questions.stem: What are the upward roots called?
choices: chromosomes
pneumatophores
pneumatics
pectoral fins
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives the name immediately after introducing the special roots.

lesson.strategy: Begin with the oxygen problem below ground, then follow the gas path: exposed openings, spongy inner spaces, and buried tissue. Keep the lung comparison figurative rather than literal.

signals.means: Flooded mud creates the problem the specialized roots must address.
The direction of growth carries part of the root system toward air.
The tidal cycle periodically opens a route for gas exchange.

vocab.inContext: the cellular process that releases usable energy and needs oxygen
specialized upward roots that allow gas exchange
saturated or filled with water

skillTips.main-idea: Link the unusual root direction to the oxygen shortage in flooded mud.
skillTips.inference: When tide level falls, previously covered openings contact air and can admit gases.
skillTips.vocabulary: The flooded-mud description provides the direct clue for “waterlogged.”
skillTips.detail: The technical root name appears in the sentence that introduces their small openings.

passages.title: Why Library Books Have Call Numbers
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A library call number is an address for a book. It usually combines letters, numbers, and sometimes dates or other marks. The code places the book within a classification system rather than merely giving it a unique tag.

Books on related subjects receive nearby positions. Within that subject neighborhood, additional parts of the call number can arrange works by author, title, date, or another rule. Reading each line in the correct order guides a person from a broad shelf area to one exact spot.

Different libraries may use different classification systems, and local collections can adapt the rules. A novel may also be shelved in a separate fiction section instead of among literary studies. The call number works only with the map used by that library.

When a returned book is placed in the wrong location, it can become difficult to find even though the catalog still lists it. Careful shelving restores the address. A call number therefore gives each book both a neighborhood of related ideas and a repeatable home.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A call number is only a unique tag and never indicates a book's subject.
All libraries use one identical classification and shelving arrangement.
Catalogs automatically find books even when they are placed on the wrong shelf.
Call numbers organize books into subject neighborhoods and precise repeatable locations within a library's own system.
questions.explanation: The passage develops both classification and exact placement, while explaining local system differences.

questions.stem: Why can a mis-shelved book be hard to find?
choices: Its physical location no longer matches the address recorded in the catalog.
Its call number disappears from the book cover.
A wrong shelf changes the book's author.
Libraries remove every returned book from the catalog.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph contrasts a still-correct catalog listing with the book's incorrect physical placement.

questions.stem: What does “classification” mean here?
choices: a private message written by an author
a system for grouping and arranging things by shared features
a fee charged for returning a book
a mark showing that a book is damaged
questions.explanation: Related subjects receive nearby positions because the classification system groups them.

questions.stem: What might one part of a call number represent?
choices: the current reader's address
the number of pages read
the author
the book's sale price
questions.explanation: The second paragraph includes author among the possible ordering elements.

lesson.strategy: Use the address comparison at two scales. Classification sends the reader to a subject neighborhood; later letters, numbers, and marks narrow that neighborhood to the item's repeatable shelf position.

signals.means: The opening analogy frames call numbers as tools for physical location.
Classification groups intellectual neighbors before identifying an exact item.
A code must be interpreted inside the library system that assigned it.

vocab.inContext: a system that groups things by shared qualities
a searchable record of the library's materials
able to be followed with the same result again

skillTips.main-idea: Include the subject grouping and the exact shelf location; both functions belong to the address analogy.
skillTips.inference: If the shelf and catalog addresses disagree, a searcher following the catalog goes to the wrong place.
skillTips.vocabulary: Nearby positions for related subjects demonstrate what the classification system does.
skillTips.detail: Author appears in the list of finer ordering rules inside a subject neighborhood.

passages.title: The Road That Looks Wet
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On a hot day, a distant road may appear to hold a shining pool. As a driver approaches, the water seems to retreat. The surface is dry. This common mirage is an image produced when light bends through layers of air at different temperatures.

Sun-warmed pavement heats the air directly above it. That air can be much warmer and less dense than air a little higher. Light from the bright sky travels downward through the changing layers, bending gradually. Near the road, its path may curve upward toward an observer's eyes.

The brain usually treats arriving light as if it traveled along a straight line. Tracing the upward ray backward places its apparent source below, near the road. The result can resemble sky reflected from water, including a wavering patch that changes as hot air moves.

The mirage is real as an optical event, but the apparent pool is not a physical object on the pavement. It does not mark a wet patch that keeps escaping. It reveals how the atmosphere can redirect information before light reaches an observer.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A road mirage occurs when temperature layers bend sky light so an observer sees an apparent pool on dry pavement.
Road heat creates a moving pool that evaporates as a driver approaches.
The brain curves every light ray before it enters the atmosphere.
Cool dense air directly above pavement reflects underground water.
questions.explanation: The passage connects the temperature gradient, curved light path, straight-line interpretation, and false pool.

questions.stem: Why does the apparent water look like part of the sky?
choices: Actual water carries pieces of the sky toward the driver.
Bent sky light reaches the observer from a direction that seems to originate near the road.
The pavement turns blue whenever its temperature rises.
The observer's eyes stop receiving light from above.
questions.explanation: The text explains that light from the bright sky curves upward and is traced backward to a low apparent source.

questions.stem: What does “retreat” mean in the opening paragraph?
choices: become deeper and colder
flow toward the driver
seem to move farther away
turn into solid ice
questions.explanation: As the driver approaches, the illusory patch remains distant rather than being reached.

questions.stem: Which air is described as less dense?
choices: the cooler air higher above
the air inside the driver's vehicle
the air beneath the road surface
the warmer air close to the pavement
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly compares hot low air with cooler air above it.

lesson.strategy: Trace a single ray in sequence: bright sky, downward travel through a temperature gradient, upward bend near the hot road, and straight-line interpretation by the observer's brain.

signals.means: The unreachable appearance is the first clue that the pool is not physical water.
The ray changes direction across layers rather than reflecting from a wet surface.
The brain's backward projection locates an image where no object exists.

vocab.inContext: an optical image caused by light bending through air layers
containing more matter within a given volume
move or appear to move farther away

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the atmospheric bending and the observer's interpretation that places the image near the road.
skillTips.inference: Because the ray began with sky light, its low projected image can resemble a reflection of the sky.
skillTips.vocabulary: The pool stays ahead as the observer approaches, showing that “retreat” means move away.
skillTips.detail: The temperature comparison identifies the thin, warm layer nearest the road as less dense.

passages.title: Tu Youyou Returns to Old Texts
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In a search for treatments against malaria, Chinese pharmaceutical researcher Tu Youyou and her team examined both modern screening results and historical medical writings. One plant, sweet wormwood, appeared in old preparations, but early laboratory extracts gave inconsistent results.

Tu reread a historical instruction that described soaking the plant and wringing out its liquid rather than boiling it. She inferred that high heat might damage the active substance. Her team developed a lower-temperature extraction using solvents, separated portions of the extract, and tested them systematically. This process produced a preparation with much more reliable activity in experimental models.

The work did not consist of simply copying an ancient recipe. A historical clue suggested a variable (temperature) that could be examined through controlled comparison. Nor was it a solitary discovery. Researchers gathered texts, identified plants, performed extractions, ran tests, and refined purification across a larger program.

The active compound, later known as artemisinin, became an important basis for malaria treatment. Its history shows two kinds of respect for evidence. Old knowledge was taken seriously enough to revisit, while each interpretation still had to survive laboratory testing. The productive move was neither to accept tradition automatically nor to dismiss it as unscientific, but to turn a textual detail into a testable question.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Tu Youyou copied one ancient recipe exactly and avoided experimental testing.
Tu Youyou's team transformed a clue from historical practice into controlled extraction tests that helped reveal artemisinin.
Boiling sweet wormwood at higher temperatures made every early extract reliable.
One researcher completed the entire discovery without texts, plant experts, or testing teams.
questions.explanation: The passage centers on the productive link between a textual clue, a temperature hypothesis, systematic work, and team evidence.

questions.stem: Why did the team try a lower-temperature extraction?
choices: The historical text said sweet wormwood grew only in cold climates.
Low temperature removed the need to separate and test extracts.
Tu suspected that high heat was damaging the substance responsible for the plant's activity.
The team wanted to make the plant boil more rapidly.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly connects the soaking instruction with Tu's heat-damage inference.

questions.stem: What does “inconsistent” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: written in an older form of language
too cold to contain any solvent
performed by several team members
not producing the same reliable result across attempts
questions.explanation: The later preparation is described as much more reliable, contrasting with the variable early results.

questions.stem: What was the active compound later called?
choices: artemisinin
cellulose
chlorophyll
quinine bark
questions.explanation: The final paragraph names the compound artemisinin.

lesson.strategy: Follow the evidence conversion: an old instruction suggests that heat is a variable, the team changes extraction conditions, and controlled tests judge the result. This is neither automatic trust nor dismissal.

signals.means: Early extracts did not provide dependable evidence of activity.
The textual contrast supplies the clue that redirects laboratory procedure.
Historical knowledge enters a modern test without being treated as final proof.

vocab.inContext: concentrated materials removed from a plant
reached a reasoned conclusion from a clue
the active antimalarial compound identified from sweet wormwood

skillTips.main-idea: Connect the historical clue to the experimental sequence and acknowledge the larger research team.
skillTips.inference: Soaking instead of boiling makes temperature the plausible difference for the next controlled test.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with later “reliable activity” defines inconsistent results as variable and undependable.
skillTips.detail: The compound's name is introduced in the final paragraph after the extraction process.

passages.title: Matching Students to Schools
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Suppose students rank schools, while each school has limited seats and a stated priority order. Assigning students one by one can create a troubling result: a student prefers another school, and that school would also prefer the student over someone it received. Such a pair has an incentive to abandon the official assignment. In matching theory, an arrangement with no such blocking pair is called stable.

One well-known procedure begins with students applying to their highest-ranked school. Each school tentatively holds applicants up to capacity according to its priorities and rejects the rest. Rejected students apply to their next choices. Schools reconsider their held set when new applications arrive. The cycle ends when no further applications remain, and tentative places become final.

The procedure can produce a stable match under its formal assumptions, but “stable” does not mean everyone gets a first choice or regards the outcome as fair. Priorities may reflect distance, siblings, lotteries, exams, or policy decisions. Changing those rules changes the result. Capacity shortages cannot be solved by rearranging names alone.

Strategy also matters. In the student-proposing version under the standard model, reporting true preferences has a protective property for students. Real enrollment systems, however, may add categories, rounds, or constraints outside the simple model. Administrators must verify what their rules guarantee. Matching mechanisms organize competing preferences transparently; they do not choose society's values. Mathematics can show consequences of a priority structure, but communities still decide which priorities deserve authority and how to support students when desired seats are scarce.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A stable school match guarantees every student a first choice and equal satisfaction.
Matching mathematics selects the fairest social priorities without public decisions.
School matching procedures can create stable assignments from preferences and priorities, but stability does not settle capacity or fairness questions.
Schools using tentative holds never reconsider applicants after the first round.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the procedure and stability, then separates mathematical properties from policy values and scarcity.

questions.stem: Why can a stable outcome still disappoint many students?
choices: Stable procedures ignore every school's capacity.
A blocking pair requires both sides to prefer their assigned match.
Students are forbidden to rank more than one school.
Stability prevents blocking pairs but cannot create additional seats or guarantee first choices.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph distinguishes the technical definition from satisfaction and notes that rearrangement cannot eliminate shortages.

questions.stem: What does “tentatively” mean in the procedure?
choices: provisionally, with the possibility of later change
secretly, without recording applicants
permanently after the first application
randomly, without using priorities
questions.explanation: Schools can reconsider the held set when new applications arrive, so the early holds are not final.

questions.stem: When does the application cycle end?
choices: after every student receives a first choice
when no further applications remain
when schools remove their capacity limits
after priorities are chosen by mathematics
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly gives the stopping condition before tentative seats become final.

lesson.strategy: Separate mechanism, guarantee, and value judgment. The rounds describe how assignments form; stability rules out one kind of mutually preferred switch; later paragraphs identify goals the guarantee does not cover.

signals.means: A mutually preferred alternative pair exposes instability in the assignment.
A school keeps current candidates provisionally while later applications remain possible.
The author draws a boundary between technical stability and broader fairness or satisfaction.

vocab.inContext: having no student-school pair that mutually prefers one another to the assignment
for now, subject to later revision
rules or limits that restrict possible outcomes

skillTips.main-idea: Include what stability guarantees and what it cannot decide, especially scarcity and fairness.
skillTips.inference: No assignment rule can give everyone a scarce first-choice seat that does not physically exist.
skillTips.vocabulary: The later reconsideration of held applicants proves that “tentatively” means provisionally.
skillTips.detail: The procedure's stopping rule comes at the end of the application-round paragraph.

passages.title: The Kindness of Clear Instructions
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A sign above a return slot said, “Process materials appropriately.” Regular staff knew this meant placing books inside and leaving donated magazines in a blue box. Visitors did not. Some waited in line to ask; others guessed and felt foolish when corrected.

The library replaced the sign: “Returns: books in this slot. Donations: magazines in the blue box.” The new words were longer, but the task became easier. They named the objects and actions that people needed.

Clear instructions are a form of kindness because they protect time and dignity. Vague language shifts hidden knowledge onto the reader, then treats confusion as failure. Clarity does not require a childish tone or endless detail. It requires noticing what a first-time user cannot already know and making the next action visible.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Shorter instructions are always clearer than longer ones.
Visitors should learn every library rule before approaching a return slot.
A childish tone is necessary whenever a sign explains two actions.
Clear, specific instructions respect people's time and dignity by making hidden expectations visible.
questions.explanation: The sign revision names the needed actions, and the conclusion frames that clarity as practical respect.

questions.stem: Why is the second sign easier to follow?
choices: It connects each kind of material with a specific destination.
It uses fewer words than the original sign.
It assumes every visitor knows staff vocabulary.
It removes the blue donation box.
questions.explanation: The revised sign explicitly pairs books with the slot and magazines with the box.

questions.stem: What does “vague” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: written in blue
not clear or specific
unusually polite
too large to read
questions.explanation: The first sign hides the needed actions, illustrating language that lacks specificity.

questions.stem: Where should donated magazines go?
choices: inside the book-return slot
on the staff desk
in the blue box
at the end of the waiting line
questions.explanation: Both the explanation and the revised sign identify the blue box.

lesson.strategy: Compare the two signs word for word. The revision succeeds by naming categories and destinations, which reveals why brevity alone is not the essay's measure of respectful communication.

signals.means: Insiders possess background knowledge that the original sign assumes.
Unclear directions can create avoidable embarrassment, not only delay.
The conclusion defines clarity through what a newcomer can actually do.

vocab.inContext: in the correct manner for the situation
a person's sense of worth and deserved respect
lacking clear and specific meaning

skillTips.main-idea: Connect specific language with respect for a first-time user's time and dignity.
skillTips.inference: The direct object-destination pairs remove knowledge that only regular staff previously held.
skillTips.vocabulary: The confusing first sign is the passage's example of “vague” language.
skillTips.detail: The revised wording sends donations of magazines to the blue box.

passages.title: The Crab Who Measured the Tide
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A crab drew a line in the sand beside its burrow. “The sea may come this far,” it announced, “but no farther.” At low tide, the line looked official.

The water returned. One wave stopped below the mark, and the crab praised its measurement. The next crossed it. The crab rebuilt the line higher and ordered the sea to obey. Soon foam washed over the burrow.

An oyster called from a rock, “Your mark can record where water went. It cannot command where water goes.” The crab disliked this answer because the line had taken all morning.

At the next low tide, the crab tried again. This time it marked several past water levels and moved loose food above the highest one. The sea still ignored every line, but the crab's plan no longer depended on obedience. A measure became useful when it helped the crab adapt to the tide instead of pretending to rule it.

questions.stem: What lesson does the fable teach?
choices: Measurements help us adapt to forces we cannot control, but drawing a boundary does not command reality.
A carefully drawn line can force the sea to remain at low tide.
Past observations are useless because conditions can change.
Plans work best when they require nature to obey one prediction.
questions.explanation: The crab fails when treating a mark as an order and succeeds when using several observations to relocate food.

questions.stem: Why does the crab dislike the oyster's answer?
choices: The oyster erased every water-level mark.
It has invested effort in the line and does not want to admit the line lacks control.
The crab cannot understand what a measurement records.
The sea has promised to follow the oyster instead.
questions.explanation: The story links the crab's resistance to the entire morning spent making the line.

questions.stem: What does “record” mean in the oyster's statement?
choices: issue an order that must be followed
sing a sound into a shell
preserve information about what happened
erase a mark from wet sand
questions.explanation: The oyster contrasts documenting a past water level with controlling a future one.

questions.stem: What does the crab move above the highest mark?
choices: the oyster's rock
its entire sandy beach
a line of foam
loose food
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that loose food is moved to a safer height.

lesson.strategy: Compare the crab's two uses of a line. First it treats one mark as authority over the sea; later it treats several marks as evidence for a plan that can tolerate changing water.

signals.means: Appearance gives the crab false confidence that a mark carries authority.
The oyster separates description of the past from control of the future.
The revised plan works with the tide's uncertainty instead of denying it.

vocab.inContext: a hole or tunnel used by an animal as shelter
preserve information for later use
change a plan or behavior to fit conditions

skillTips.main-idea: Turn the tide-line contrast into a general lesson about evidence, planning, and limited control.
skillTips.inference: The morning's effort makes admitting the line's weakness emotionally harder for the crab.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with “command” shows that “record” means document rather than control.
skillTips.detail: The crab protects loose food after making several marks at the next low tide.

passages.title: The Person Who Woke With Another Memory
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine that Arun and Bela enter a machine. The next morning, Arun's body wakes with Bela's memories, plans, habits, and affection for her friends. Bela's body wakes with Arun's corresponding mental life. If only one person can claim each past, who is now Arun?

One answer follows the body. It says physical continuity matters because the same living organism persists through the machine. Another follows memory and personality: the person in Bela's body remembers making Arun's promises and can explain why he made them.

Each answer faces pressure. Memory can be incomplete or mistaken, yet ordinary identity survives forgetting. Bodies also change continually, though usually not in one dramatic exchange. A third view may emphasize connected psychological life without requiring a perfect list of memories, while another may combine bodily and mental continuity.

The case becomes harder if both new people claim Arun's past or if a copy preserves it too. Identity seems expected to give one continuing person, but information can be duplicated. The thought experiment does not describe an available machine. It removes familiar alignment between body and memory so readers can see which kind of continuity their judgments rely on.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A real machine has proved that identity always moves with a person's memories.
A memory-swap thought experiment tests whether personal identity follows bodily, psychological, or combined continuity.
Forgetting one event immediately turns someone into a different person.
Bodies remain physically unchanged throughout an ordinary human life.
questions.explanation: The passage separates normally aligned kinds of continuity and presents strengths and problems for several accounts.

questions.stem: Why does the copying variation create a problem?
choices: A copied memory must be completely false.
Two bodies cannot exist in the same room.
The same psychological history could point to more than one future claimant, while identity is usually treated as one-to-one.
Physical continuity disappears whenever information is stored.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly contrasts duplicable information with the expectation of one continuing person.

questions.stem: What does “continuity” mean in this passage?
choices: a complete absence of bodily change
a machine's ability to copy data
agreement among all philosophers
an unbroken connection across time
questions.explanation: The views ask what persistent connection (from organism, memory, or psychology) links past and future person.

questions.stem: What enters the imagined machine?
choices: Arun and Bela
Mara and Sol
Mina and Samir
Lina and Jo
questions.explanation: The opening sentence names Arun and Bela as the two participants.

lesson.strategy: Make a continuity map with separate rows for body, memory, personality, and relationships. The swap sends those rows in different directions, revealing which one each answer treats as identity-bearing.

signals.means: Ordinary identity is assumed to connect one past individual with one later individual.
The passage shifts from biological persistence to psychological evidence.
Body and memory normally travel together, hiding the distinction the case exposes.

vocab.inContext: continues to exist through time
an unbroken connection between stages
copied so that more than one version exists

skillTips.main-idea: Name the rival kinds of continuity rather than choosing an answer the passage leaves open.
skillTips.inference: Copying allows two later people to share one earlier history, challenging a one-person continuation rule.
skillTips.vocabulary: Every theory seeks a connection linking the person before and after, defining continuity.
skillTips.detail: The first sentence gives both names before describing what wakes in each body.

passages.title: How We Guess What Others Believe
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
After a neighborhood meeting, Elena supports turning a parking space into a bench and assumes most residents agree. Her friends do, and the speakers she remembers were favorable. A later anonymous survey shows the community almost evenly divided.

People sometimes overestimate how widely others share their opinions, preferences, or habits. Psychologists call this tendency the false-consensus effect. One's own view is immediately available, and similar people often gather. Public comments may also come from an unrepresentative group. These inputs make agreement easier to imagine than disagreement.

The effect does not mean every estimate is wrong. Some norms are widespread, and people can know their communities well. The problem arises when confidence exceeds the evidence. Elena's friends and vivid memories are a narrow sample.

Better estimation begins by asking who is missing. A private survey may reach people unwilling to speak at meetings. A chosen sample can reveal views outside one's circle. Questions need neutral wording, because asking whether residents “support a welcoming bench” frames the choice differently from asking whether they “oppose removing parking.” Learning that others disagree need not make anyone abandon a position. It changes a factual belief about distribution, not necessarily a value judgment. The useful correction is humility about how many allies an opinion has, paired with curiosity about reasons that familiar conversations did not reveal.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The false-consensus effect means a popular opinion is always morally wrong.
Anonymous surveys guarantee a perfectly accurate result regardless of wording or sample.
People may overestimate agreement by relying on familiar, visible voices, while broader and neutrally gathered evidence can improve the estimate.
Discovering disagreement requires a person to give up the original position.
questions.explanation: The passage explains biased inputs, qualifies the tendency, and offers sampling and wording checks without dictating values.

questions.stem: Why are Elena's friends a narrow source of evidence?
choices: Friends are unable to express opinions about public spaces.
The neighborhood survey excludes every person Elena knows.
A bench can be used only by people outside her social circle.
Friends may resemble one another and fail to represent the full range of residents.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph notes that similar people gather, and the third calls her friends a narrow sample.

questions.stem: What does “distribution” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: how opinions are spread across a group
delivery of survey forms to houses
the location of benches and parking spaces
the strength of one person's value judgment
questions.explanation: The factual belief being corrected concerns how many people hold each view.

questions.stem: What result does the anonymous survey find?
choices: Every resident favors the bench.
The community is almost evenly divided.
Most residents refuse to answer.
Only Elena's friends oppose parking.
questions.explanation: The opening example reports an almost even division, contrary to Elena's assumption.

lesson.strategy: Track evidence quality rather than debating the bench. Elena's view, friends, and memorable speakers form one visible cluster; the survey and sampling discussion ask whether that cluster represents the whole population.

signals.means: Elena turns nearby agreement into a claim about the wider group.

signals.phrase: does not mean every estimate is wrong
signals.means: The passage describes a bias tendency rather than universal error.
Better estimation looks for voices absent from the familiar sample.

vocab.inContext: general agreement within a group
not accurately reflecting the larger group
the way views are spread across people

skillTips.main-idea: Include the biased evidence sources and the corrective role of broader, neutrally collected information.
skillTips.inference: Friend groups often share traits, so their agreement cannot automatically describe all residents.
skillTips.vocabulary: The nearby phrase “how many allies” shows that distribution concerns how opinions are spread.
skillTips.detail: The survey result is given at the end of the opening neighborhood example.

passages.title: The Tiny Clock Inside a Computer
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A computer must coordinate countless changes in its circuits. Many processors use a clock signal produced from an electronic oscillator. The signal rises and falls in a regular rhythm, creating reference moments when parts of the processor advance their work. Its frequency is measured in cycles per second.

A processor described as three gigahertz receives about three billion clock cycles each second. That number does not mean it completes exactly three billion useful instructions. Some instructions require several stages, while modern designs may begin or finish parts of multiple instructions during one cycle. Waiting for memory can also leave execution units without the data they need.

Clock frequency is therefore only one contributor to performance. The amount of work completed per cycle, number of processing cores, cache design, memory speed, cooling, software, and task type all matter. A newer processor at a lower frequency can sometimes finish a job faster than an older one with a higher number.

Raising frequency can increase heat and energy use. A processor may reduce its speed when temperature or power limits are reached. Designers balance frequency with efficiency and parallel work rather than turning one dial upward without consequence. The clock is less like a worker doing every job and more like a conductor supplying shared timing cues. Even that comparison has limits, because different parts can use related clocks or operate asynchronously. Still, the image captures the clock's central role: it coordinates when events may advance, while the architecture determines how much useful work those events accomplish.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Each clock cycle always completes exactly one useful instruction on every processor.
Increasing clock frequency reduces both heat and energy use in all computers.
A processor's architecture has no effect once its oscillator begins running.
A processor clock coordinates circuit activity, but clock frequency alone does not determine computer performance.
questions.explanation: The passage explains timing, distinguishes cycles from work, lists other performance factors, and describes frequency costs.

questions.stem: How can a lower-frequency processor sometimes finish sooner?
choices: It may accomplish more work per cycle or benefit from better cores, memory, cache, software, or design.
A lower frequency always creates more cycles each second.
Its clock completes every instruction without using memory.
Cooling converts each clock cycle into three instructions.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explicitly places frequency among several factors and notes that architecture can overcome a lower rate.

questions.stem: What does “frequency” mean in this passage?
choices: the temperature at which a processor slows
the number of clock cycles occurring each second
the number of files stored in memory
the amount of useful work in one instruction
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph defines clock frequency in cycles per second.

questions.stem: What may a processor do when power or temperature limits are reached?
choices: erase its clock signal permanently
double every memory value
reduce its speed
add physical processing cores
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph directly states that the processor may lower speed under those limits.

lesson.strategy: Separate timing opportunities from completed work. The clock provides cycles; architecture and workload decide what fits into them; heat, power, and memory can prevent a high advertised rate from becoming equal performance.

signals.means: Clock edges provide shared timing points for coordinated circuit changes.
The gigahertz number must not be equated directly with completed instructions.
Frequency joins architecture, memory, software, and other performance factors.

vocab.inContext: an electronic system that produces a repeating signal
the number of repeated cycles in one second
without relying on one shared timing rhythm

skillTips.main-idea: State the clock's coordination role and the limit of using gigahertz as a complete performance measure.
skillTips.inference: A design that does more per cycle can outweigh another design's greater number of cycles.
skillTips.vocabulary: The passage directly measures frequency as cycles per second, before giving the gigahertz example.
skillTips.detail: The heat-and-power paragraph identifies speed reduction as the processor's protective response.

passages.title: The Bowl on the Windowsill
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
After Sora brought soup to her new neighbor, the bowl did not return for several days. She worried that the gesture had felt intrusive. Then she found the clean bowl on her windowsill. Inside it grew a small basil plant.

Sora pinched three leaves for dinner. The next morning, she left the bowl outside with two fresh rolls. It returned holding paper flowers folded from a grocery receipt. Soon the bowl traveled back and forth with a lemon, a borrowed pencil, and short notes about the weather.

Weeks passed before Sora and her neighbor, Mr. Imani, met on the stairs. Both began to apologize for being shy, then laughed. The bowl had already carried the difficult first conversation in smaller pieces. They took it downstairs together and filled it with soup for the building's night guard.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: A returned soup bowl becomes a gentle exchange that helps two shy neighbors build a connection and share kindness.
Sora becomes angry because her neighbor keeps the bowl for several days.
Mr. Imani uses a basil plant to avoid ever meeting Sora.
A night guard asks the neighbors to stop leaving objects outside.
questions.explanation: The bowl carries a series of reciprocal gifts before the neighbors meet and extend the practice to another person.

questions.stem: Why do Sora and Mr. Imani laugh on the stairs?
choices: They learn that neither person likes soup.
They discover that both were shy even though their bowl exchange had already connected them.
The paper flowers have blown into the stairwell.
The night guard has hidden the bowl.
questions.explanation: Their matching apologies reveal a shared worry that the quiet exchange had already overcome.

questions.stem: What does “intrusive” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: too small to hold soup
likely to grow quickly
entering another person's space in an unwelcome way
carefully folded from paper
questions.explanation: Sora worries that an unsolicited neighborly gesture may have crossed a boundary.

questions.stem: What is growing in the returned bowl?
choices: a lemon tree
paper flowers
three rolls
a basil plant
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the clean bowl returns with a small basil plant inside.

lesson.strategy: Follow what the bowl carries in both directions. Each small response answers the previous gift, so the object becomes a low-pressure conversation before the neighbors exchange spoken words.

signals.means: The delay leads Sora to fear that her kindness was unwelcome.
Repeated reciprocal gifts gradually build the relationship.
The final metaphor explains how objects performed parts of a difficult first conversation.

vocab.inContext: unwelcome because it enters someone's personal space
removed a small amount with the fingers
express regret for something that may have caused discomfort

skillTips.main-idea: Trace the exchange from Sora's uncertainty through mutual gifts to kindness shared with the guard.
skillTips.inference: Their laughter follows the realization that both felt the same shyness despite an already successful connection.
skillTips.vocabulary: Sora's fear that a gift crossed a neighbor's boundary explains “intrusive.”
skillTips.detail: The first returned object contains basil; paper flowers arrive during a later exchange.

passages.title: The Roads Without Wheels
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The Inca road system crossed deserts, valleys, and high Andes mountains. Travelers moved on foot, and pack llamas carried loads. The routes did not depend on carts, which would have struggled on steep stairs and narrow paths.

Builders fitted stone paving where it helped, cut steps into slopes, and made drainage channels. Rope suspension bridges crossed deep gorges. Rest stations placed along important routes offered supplies and shelter.

Relay runners called chasquis carried messages from one station to the next. Each runner covered part of the journey, allowing information to move far faster than one person traveling the whole distance. Armies and officials also used the network, while communities maintained sections through organized labor.

The roads show that transport is shaped by terrain and purpose. A wheel can be useful, but it is not the only basis for an effective network.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The Inca road system depended mainly on carts crossing wide paved plains.
The Inca built a far-reaching road system suited to steep terrain, foot travel, llamas, and relay communication.
Every traveler ran the full distance between two Inca cities without stopping.
Rope bridges were used only as shelters beside desert roads.
questions.explanation: The passage links road features and relay stations with the terrain and forms of travel the network served.

questions.stem: Why were stairs and narrow paths workable in this system?
choices: The routes existed only inside flat cities.
Every stair could be removed before an army arrived.
People and pack llamas could use them without requiring wheeled carts.
Chasquis carried the carts across each gorge.
questions.explanation: The opening contrasts foot and llama travel with carts that would struggle on steep, narrow routes.

questions.stem: What does “relay” mean in the runner example?
choices: a bridge woven from plant fibers
a paved place for storing carts
a message sent without any traveler
a system in which people take turns carrying something through stages
questions.explanation: Each chasqui covers one part and transfers the message onward, defining a staged relay.

questions.stem: What crossed deep gorges?
choices: rope suspension bridges
wooden carts
stone aqueducts
underground tunnels
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly identifies rope suspension bridges as the gorge crossings.

lesson.strategy: Match each road feature to a need: steps fit mountain slopes, bridges span gorges, stations support travelers, and relays speed messages. This reveals design adapted to terrain rather than a missing version of another road system.

signals.means: The network served travelers and pack animals without requiring wheeled vehicles.

signals.phrase: from one station to the next
signals.means: The message journey was divided among successive runners.
The conclusion connects design choices to local conditions and needs.

vocab.inContext: deep narrow valleys with steep sides
trained Inca relay runners who carried messages
a staged system in which participants take successive turns

skillTips.main-idea: Connect terrain, road engineering, and the travelers who actually used the network.
skillTips.inference: Stairs are a barrier to carts but remain usable for feet and sure-footed pack animals.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “one station to the next” shows how a relay divides a journey into stages.
skillTips.detail: The gorge-crossing structure is named in the road-construction paragraph.

passages.title: The Albatross Rides the Wind
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An albatross can travel over open ocean for long periods with little flapping. Its long, narrow wings work efficiently as the bird glides, but wing shape alone does not supply endless energy. The moving air above waves helps sustain the journey.

Wind close to the sea is slowed by friction with the surface. Air somewhat higher moves faster. An albatross repeatedly crosses this difference in wind speed. It climbs and turns through faster air, then descends toward the slower layer, adjusting its direction through the cycle. This technique is called dynamic soaring.

Each circuit lets the bird exchange speed, height, and energy from the wind gradient. The path may look like smooth arcs rather than a straight line. Waves can also shape the air and provide shelter from stronger wind near their lower side.

The bird still flaps during takeoff, landing, weak winds, or changes that demand it. Dynamic soaring is not effortless floating. It is active control of wings and route, allowing an albatross to draw useful motion from a layered atmosphere.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Albatrosses gain endless energy from wing shape without using moving air.
Dynamic soaring keeps a bird in one straight line at one constant height.
Albatrosses reduce flapping by repeatedly gliding across layers of different wind speed and controlling a curved flight path.
Ocean waves stop all wind near the sea and force birds to land.
questions.explanation: The explanation centers on the wind gradient, repeated crossings, and active adjustment rather than passive floating.

questions.stem: Why does the albatross repeatedly change height?
choices: Its wings work only when they touch the sea.
Changing height makes the wind layers disappear.
It must avoid every wave by flying directly upward.
Crossing faster and slower air lets it gain and exchange energy during the glide.
questions.explanation: The second and third paragraphs connect the climbing-descending circuit with extracting useful motion from the gradient.

questions.stem: What does “gradient” mean in this passage?
choices: a gradual change in wind speed across height
a straight route across the ocean
a feather that creates friction
a sudden stop in all moving air
questions.explanation: The passage describes slower air near the surface and faster air above, which forms the gradient.

questions.stem: When may an albatross still flap?
choices: only while asleep
during takeoff
whenever it crosses slower air
after every smooth arc
questions.explanation: The final paragraph lists takeoff among situations in which flapping is still needed.

lesson.strategy: Visualize the flight as a loop through two air layers. Track how the bird crosses the wind-speed difference, changes direction, and trades speed with height; this prevents “little flapping” from becoming “no work.”

signals.means: The observation calls for an energy source other than continuous powered wingbeats.
Dynamic soaring depends on cycling through the wind-speed difference.
The bird must actively control wings and direction even while gliding.

vocab.inContext: resistance that slows air moving close to the sea
a gradual difference across distance or height
a route that curves around and repeats

skillTips.main-idea: Name the layered wind and repeated controlled glide, not just the bird's long wings.
skillTips.inference: Changing height matters because wind speed differs between the surface layer and the air above.
skillTips.vocabulary: The slower-to-faster change with height is the passage's concrete example of a gradient.
skillTips.detail: The final paragraph separates takeoff and other special conditions from long gliding travel.

passages.title: Why Time Zone Borders Bend
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
If time zones followed geometry alone, the world could be divided into neat bands based on longitude. Since Earth turns once each day, neighboring bands would differ by regular amounts. Real time-zone maps are far less tidy. Borders bend around countries, regions, islands, and trading partners.

Clock time is a social tool as well as an astronomical measurement. A region may choose to share a time with the city where residents work, shop, or catch trains, even if a straight longitude line suggests another zone. Governments may keep one time across a broad territory to simplify administration. Neighboring areas can choose differently because their daily connections point in different directions.

Daylight creates another tradeoff. Moving clocks shifts how much sunlight falls before or after common work and school hours; it does not create more daylight. A choice that makes winter mornings later may make summer evenings feel longer. Seasonal clock changes add another policy layer in some places.

These decisions can change, so a time-zone database needs updates rather than relying forever on a drawn map. The crooked borders are not failures of geography. They record attempts to coordinate sunlight, travel, government, commerce, and ordinary routines, needs that rarely line up along one clean meridian.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Time zones follow perfectly straight longitude bands that never change.
Changing a clock creates additional hours of sunlight for a region.
Every neighboring region chooses the same time because trade has no effect.
Time-zone borders bend because societies coordinate clocks with geography, travel, government, commerce, daylight, and daily routines.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph adds a social or practical factor that makes the geometric model insufficient.

questions.stem: Why might a region choose the time used by a distant city?
choices: Residents may have strong work, shopping, or transport connections with that city.
Longitude stops affecting sunlight whenever a train runs.
A shared clock makes the two places physically closer.
The distant city controls how fast Earth rotates.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names commuting, commerce, and train connections as reasons to coordinate clock time.

questions.stem: What does “meridian” mean in the final sentence?
choices: a seasonal change to clock hands
an imaginary north-south line of longitude
a border checkpoint between countries
the period between sunrise and noon
questions.explanation: The passage begins with longitude bands and ends by contrasting social borders with a clean meridian.

questions.stem: What must a time-zone database receive when decisions change?
choices: additional sunlight
new lines of latitude
updates
a faster clock motor
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly says databases need updates because time-zone decisions can change.

lesson.strategy: Contrast the clean longitude model with the needs layered onto it. Each bend becomes evidence of a coordination choice involving people and institutions, while the daylight paragraph identifies the tradeoffs clocks cannot erase.

signals.means: The idealized map uses regular longitude bands without social boundaries.
Clock time serves shared coordination in addition to tracking the Sun.
A clock change redistributes labeled hours rather than altering daylight itself.

vocab.inContext: position east or west measured by imaginary lines on Earth
organized management of a government or large territory
an imaginary line running between Earth's poles

skillTips.main-idea: Combine geographic and social factors; the central point is why actual borders depart from a simple model.
skillTips.inference: Shared daily activity can make matching another city's clock more useful than following the nearest geometric band.
skillTips.vocabulary: The opening discussion of longitude supplies the clue that a meridian is a north-south reference line.
skillTips.detail: The database requirement appears in the conclusion, where changing decisions make static maps unreliable.

passages.title: How DNA Fits Inside a Cell
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A eukaryotic cell's DNA contains an enormous molecular chain relative to the space that holds it. Fitting that chain into a nucleus cannot be like stuffing loose thread into a pocket. Random tangling would obstruct copying, repair, and the controlled use of genes. Cells instead organize DNA through several nested levels of packaging.

The double helix wraps around groups of proteins called histones, forming units known as nucleosomes. A string of nucleosomes folds and interacts with additional proteins to create chromatin. Loops of chromatin attach to organizing structures and occupy regions within the nucleus. The arrangement is dynamic: sections can become more accessible or more compact as cellular needs change.

Before many cells divide, DNA is copied and the chromatin condenses further into visible chromosomes. Compaction helps the duplicated material move without becoming hopelessly entangled. After division, much of it relaxes again. A chromosome is therefore not always a rigid X-shaped object; that familiar form represents one especially condensed stage.

Packaging also influences access. Proteins that read or copy DNA must reach particular sequences, so chemical marks and remodeling systems help open or close local regions. Compact does not mean silent forever, and open does not mean active at every moment. The organization is orderly without resembling a single perfect spool. Chromatin bends, loops, and shifts within a crowded nucleus. Its success lies in balancing contradictory needs: DNA must be compressed yet reachable, protected yet changeable, and separated during division without losing the information encoded along its length.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Cells package DNA through dynamic layers of proteins, nucleosomes, chromatin, loops, and chromosomes while preserving controlled access.
DNA fits inside a nucleus by tangling randomly like loose thread in a pocket.
Every chromosome remains in a rigid X shape throughout the cell's life.
Once chromatin becomes compact, no protein can ever reach its DNA.
questions.explanation: The passage traces nested packaging and repeatedly emphasizes the balance between compaction, movement, and access.

questions.stem: Why does chromatin condense further before cell division?
choices: Condensation permanently turns every gene off.
Greater compaction helps copied DNA move and separate with less entanglement.
Histones must leave the nucleus before DNA is copied.
The cell needs to make each DNA sequence longer.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links the extra condensed form with moving duplicated material safely during division.

questions.stem: What does “dynamic” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: perfectly still once nucleosomes form
moving out of the cell every moment
able to change its organization in response to conditions
made only during one stage of division
questions.explanation: The colon explains that sections can become more accessible or compact as needs change.

questions.stem: What proteins does DNA wrap around first?
choices: enzymes in cell walls
collagen fibers
antibodies
histones
questions.explanation: The second paragraph identifies histone groups as the proteins around which the double helix wraps.

lesson.strategy: Follow the hierarchy from double helix to histones, nucleosomes, chromatin, loops, and condensed chromosomes. At each level, ask how packaging serves both physical fit and selective access.

signals.means: DNA organization uses several structures within larger structures rather than one fold.
The highly condensed division form is temporary rather than the chromosome's constant appearance.
The conclusion frames packaging as a balance between compression and accessibility.

vocab.inContext: DNA-and-histone units that form an early level of packaging
DNA together with the proteins that organize it
becomes more tightly packed

skillTips.main-idea: Summarize both the packaging hierarchy and its changing accessibility; size reduction alone is incomplete.
skillTips.inference: A compact ordered form reduces the chance that duplicated DNA strands interfere while they are moved apart.
skillTips.vocabulary: The sentence after “dynamic” gives its definition through changing compactness and access.
skillTips.detail: At the first named packaging step, the double helix wraps around histone proteins.

passages.title: Alma Thomas Finds Her Colors
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Alma Thomas taught art in Washington, D.C., schools for many years. She also painted, studied museums, and watched the garden outside her window. After retiring from teaching, she devoted more time to her own art.

Thomas built many paintings from short strokes of bright color separated by small spaces. Garden leaves, flowers, changing light, and images of space exploration helped spark her ideas. She did not copy those sights exactly. Color and rhythm became subjects of their own.

Her career grew through long attention rather than one sudden beginning. Teaching, looking, experimenting, and painting all fed the work she made later. Thomas showed that careful observation can lead beyond a literal picture and into a new visual language.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Alma Thomas stopped studying art when she began teaching in Washington.
Alma Thomas transformed years of teaching and close observation into abstract paintings built from vivid color and rhythm.
Her paintings copied every garden leaf and spacecraft image exactly.
Thomas discovered color only after she left museums behind.
questions.explanation: The passage connects her long preparation and observed sources with a distinctive nonliteral painting practice.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say Thomas did not copy the garden exactly?
choices: She could see only black-and-white images.
The garden was removed before she began painting.
Observed sights inspired her, but she transformed them into abstract arrangements of color.
Her students forbade her from drawing flowers.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph contrasts sources such as leaves with color and rhythm becoming subjects themselves.

questions.stem: What does “literal” mean in the last sentence?
choices: made from written words
painted very quickly
displayed outside
showing a subject just as it appears
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a direct picture with Thomas's new abstract visual language.

questions.stem: What appeared outside Thomas's window?
choices: a garden
a railway
an ocean
a factory
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies the garden she watched.

lesson.strategy: Track the sources and the transformation separately. Gardens and space imagery provide observations; short bright strokes, spaces, and rhythm show how Thomas turned them into an abstract language.

signals.means: More studio time followed a long teaching career rather than replacing an empty past.
The observed source is transformed instead of reproduced literally.
Her later recognition grew from years of looking, learning, and practice.

vocab.inContext: leaving a long-term job at the end of a career
a repeated visual pattern that creates movement
representing something directly as it appears

skillTips.main-idea: Link Thomas's long preparation with the colorful abstract form that grew from observation.
skillTips.inference: Short strokes and spaces preserve the energy of garden sights without making a literal garden picture.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with a “new visual language” shows that literal means directly representational.
skillTips.detail: The object outside the window is named in the first paragraph among her sources of study.

passages.title: The Fee Hidden in Changing Banks
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A bank may advertise an account with no switching fee. Moving an account can still carry costs that never appear as one charge. During the transition, a customer must compare terms, complete forms, learn a new app, and transfer automatic payments.

Time and attention are scarce resources. If a person worries that a salary deposit or rent payment could be misdirected, staying may feel safer. Familiar staff, a nearby branch, saved payees, or an old record system can also have value. Economists call such burdens switching costs.

Switching costs do not prove that staying is wise, and they do not make every advertised offer misleading. They explain why a small price difference may not cause an immediate move. A useful comparison includes money, time, risk, and lost convenience. The best choice depends on the person's needs and the account's actual terms.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A bank without a switching fee has no costs of any kind.
Every customer should remain with the first bank used.
Changing banks can involve time, effort, risk, and lost convenience even when no explicit switching fee appears.
A small price difference always causes people to move accounts immediately.
questions.explanation: The passage lists nonprice burdens and explains how they influence choices without recommending one bank.

questions.stem: Why might automatic payments make a customer hesitate?
choices: Automatic payments make every new account illegal.
Banks charge the same visible fee for each saved payee.
A new app cannot record any salary deposit.
A transfer mistake could disrupt an important payment during the change.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names concern about misdirected salary or rent as a source of perceived risk.

questions.stem: What does “scarce” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: limited and therefore worth conserving
hidden inside an account
identical at every bank
free from all risk
questions.explanation: Time and attention are described as resources a customer cannot spend without limit.

questions.stem: Which familiar feature may have value?
choices: an unknown account term
a nearby branch
a missing rent payment
a new switching fee
questions.explanation: The passage includes a nearby branch among conveniences that can make an existing account valuable.

lesson.strategy: Look beyond the advertised price and sort costs into money, time, effort, risk, and convenience. The last paragraph keeps this framework descriptive rather than turning it into financial advice.

signals.means: Several real burdens may exist without a labeled fee.
Possible payment disruption can influence behavior even before any mistake occurs.
Switching costs explain hesitation without deciding which account is better.

vocab.inContext: available in limited amounts
people or organizations designated to receive payments
burdens involved in moving from one provider to another

skillTips.main-idea: Include the invisible nonprice burdens and avoid turning the explanation into a recommendation to stay.
skillTips.inference: A customer may protect essential transfers by delaying a change that introduces uncertainty.
skillTips.vocabulary: Calling time and attention “resources” shows that scarce means limited.
skillTips.detail: The familiar-convenience list includes staff, branch location, saved payees, and records.

passages.title: The Pleasure of Knowing One Street Well
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Travel is often measured by distance: more streets, more districts, more cities. Yet one familiar block can offer another kind of discovery. Walk it repeatedly, and the place stops being a row of fixed buildings. A repair begins behind papered windows. A tree changes its shadow. Handwritten notices reveal which problems neighbors are trying to solve.

Repetition makes small differences visible. The observer remembers yesterday's empty planter and notices today's herbs. A new sound at dusk stands out because the usual sounds are known. Even mistakes become instructive: what seemed like an abandoned shop may open only before dawn.

Knowing one street well does not make it representative of an entire city. Intimacy can narrow attention if affection turns every local habit into a universal rule. The point is not to replace broad travel with a tiny territory.

The pleasure lies in exchanging novelty for resolution. A hurried visitor collects striking first impressions; a returning walker sees causes, rhythms, repairs, and consequences. One mode widens the map. The other deepens it. A rich sense of place needs both, but depth begins by giving ordinary change enough time to appear.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Knowing one block allows an observer to generalize safely about every city.
Travel has value only when a person visits the greatest possible distance.
A familiar street becomes unchanging once its usual sounds are known.
Repeated attention to one street reveals gradual changes and relationships that broad, hurried travel can miss.
