choices: a written list of interpreter names
a level or style of language suited to a social setting
a machine that records every word
the delay between two speakers
questions.explanation: Respect, formality, and audience are parts of the language style the interpreter must preserve.

questions.stem: When does a speaker pause for the interpreter?
choices: during every simultaneous interpretation
only when a window opens
during consecutive interpreting
whenever tone is unimportant
questions.explanation: The third paragraph contrasts consecutive pauses with simultaneous overlap.

lesson.strategy: Group the interpreter's listening targets: propositional meaning, relationships, purpose, tone, and register. Then compare consecutive and simultaneous modes without confusing their timing with accuracy standards.

signals.means: Word substitution cannot reliably carry syntax, idiom, or contextual meaning.
The utterance's purpose goes beyond its grammatical question form.
Anticipation remains constrained by language structure and context.

vocab.inContext: expresses meaning in another form or language
following in sequence, with turns rather than overlap
language style appropriate to a situation or audience

skillTips.main-idea: Summarize meaning and intent transfer, not vocabulary replacement or speed alone.
skillTips.inference: The window example proves that translating literal grammar without social function can misrepresent the speaker.
skillTips.vocabulary: References to tone, respect, and audience support register as a socially suited style.
skillTips.detail: The mode with speaker pauses is named before the description of overlapping simultaneous work.

passages.title: How Wings Bend the Air
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A wing moving through air produces lift through shape, angle, speed, and airflow. No slogan captures it. Pressure differences around the wing and downward change in the air's momentum describe the same interaction, not rival tricks.

The wing's curved and angled surfaces guide airflow. Air moves faster over some regions and pressure varies around the surface. The wing also turns a mass of air downward. By Newton's laws, the air exerts an opposing force on the wing. Total pressure across the surface produces a force with an upward component.

Angle of attack, the angle between a wing and the oncoming airflow, matters. Increasing it can raise lift up to a point. If the angle becomes too large, smooth flow separates extensively from the surface and lift can drop; this condition is a stall. A stall concerns airflow and angle, not simply an engine stopping.

Speed and air density also matter, while wing area and shape determine how forces are distributed. Aircraft can fly upside down when their wings and angle redirect air appropriately, which shows why “air on top must travel an equal-time longer path” is not a reliable universal explanation. Lift is therefore a linked result: the wing organizes pressure and redirects air, while the air pushes back. Different mathematical approaches highlight different parts, but a complete account must agree on the same forces and motion.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Wing lift results from shape, angle, speed, pressure distribution, and downward-deflected airflow acting as one physical interaction.
Lift comes only from air particles meeting again after equal travel times above and below a wing.
A stall occurs whenever an aircraft's engine stops, regardless of airflow angle.
Pressure explanations and momentum explanations describe unrelated competing forces.
questions.explanation: The passage connects multiple variables and reconciles pressure and momentum views while rejecting oversimplified slogans.

questions.stem: Why does upside-down flight challenge the equal-time story?
choices: Gravity reverses whenever an aircraft rolls upside down.
A suitable wing angle can still redirect air and create lift without requiring the proposed top-path rule.
Upside-down wings no longer interact with surrounding air.
Air density becomes zero above an inverted aircraft.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph uses inverted flight to show that angle and redirection, not an invented equal-arrival requirement, are central.

questions.stem: What does “separates” mean in the stall paragraph?
choices: divides the aircraft into two parts
sorts air by chemical composition
breaks away from following the wing's surface smoothly
moves equally above and below the wing
questions.explanation: At excessive angle, airflow no longer stays attached to the surface and lift can fall.

questions.stem: What can happen when angle of attack becomes too large?
choices: Air stops having momentum.
The wing's area doubles.
Pressure becomes identical everywhere.
Lift can drop as airflow separates.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph describes extensive flow separation and reduced lift at excessive angle.

lesson.strategy: Tie each description to the same force exchange. The wing shapes pressure and turns air downward; the air's response pushes the wing. Then use the stall and inverted-flight cases to test simplistic rules.

signals.means: Pressure and momentum are compatible views of the same wing-air interaction.
Increasing angle has a limit beyond which flow behavior changes.
The equal-time longer-path slogan fails important flight cases.

vocab.inContext: a quantity of motion depending on mass and velocity
loss of lift associated with extensive airflow separation
spread across an area rather than concentrated at one point

skillTips.main-idea: Integrate pressure and redirected airflow with the wing's angle, shape, and speed.
skillTips.inference: Inverted flight remains possible because angle and air redirection can create the necessary force orientation.
skillTips.vocabulary: The phrase “from the surface” clarifies that separating airflow is breaking away from smooth attachment.
skillTips.detail: The angle-of-attack paragraph states that lift may drop once flow separates extensively.

passages.title: James Baldwin Learns From Distance
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1948, writer James Baldwin left the United States for Paris. He was young, poor, and carrying an unfinished novel. Distance did not free him from American questions about race, identity, family, or power. It changed the position from which he could examine them.

In the United States, Baldwin had often been forced to respond immediately to the categories and dangers placed around him as a Black gay man. France contained prejudice and exclusions of its own, and expatriate life was not simple refuge. Still, living abroad loosened some familiar pressures and brought him into contact with people from varied nations and colonial histories.

From Europe, Baldwin could see that leaving a country does not remove one's formation by it. His essays examined both intimate experience and public myths: how a nation tells stories about innocence, and what those stories require people to forget. Distance became a method of comparison rather than an escape from responsibility.

His novel Go Tell It on the Mountain drew on a Harlem childhood and religious family life even as he completed it abroad. Later work moved among the United States, France, Switzerland, and Turkey, but location alone did not determine insight. Baldwin's persistent revision, conversation, reading, and attention did the work. The lesson is not that every writer must travel. Freedom to leave is unequal, and an outsider can misunderstand a place. Baldwin's route shows how a changed vantage point can interrupt assumptions. Sometimes distance makes the familiar visible, provided the observer remains accountable to what distance cannot erase.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: James Baldwin left the United States and stopped writing about American life.
Living abroad gave James Baldwin a comparative vantage point for examining American identity and responsibility without erasing his connection to them.
Paris removed every form of prejudice and gave Baldwin effortless artistic success.
Travel location alone produced Baldwin's insight without revision, reading, or conversation.
questions.explanation: The passage treats distance as a change in perspective, repeatedly qualifying escape narratives and geographic determinism.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention prejudice and exclusion in France?
choices: It shows that Baldwin never made contact with people outside the United States.
It proves his American experiences no longer influenced him.
It prevents Baldwin's move from being portrayed as entry into a perfect refuge.
It explains why he abandoned his unfinished novel.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph acknowledges new room for reflection while refusing to idealize expatriate life.

questions.stem: What does “vantage point” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a permanent escape from responsibility
a payment made to complete a novel
a category imposed by a government
a position from which something can be viewed or understood
questions.explanation: The essay's repeated distance and comparison language makes the phrase a perspective for seeing familiar assumptions.

questions.stem: Which novel did Baldwin complete while abroad?
choices: Go Tell It on the Mountain
The Great Gatsby
Invisible Cities
The Color Room
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph names the novel and its connection to Baldwin's Harlem childhood.

lesson.strategy: Track what distance changes and what it does not. It changes comparison and immediate pressure; it does not erase formation, responsibility, prejudice, or the labor through which Baldwin produced insight.

signals.means: The move alters perspective rather than removing the questions Baldwin carries.
France offered difference without becoming a prejudice-free haven.
Distance supports comparative responsibility instead of avoidance.

vocab.inContext: a person living outside the country of origin
a position that shapes what can be seen or understood
responsible for answering to facts, effects, or commitments

skillTips.main-idea: Frame travel as a comparative method and retain the connection to American questions and writing labor.
skillTips.inference: Naming France's problems blocks the false inference that geographical departure automatically creates freedom.
skillTips.vocabulary: The passage repeatedly describes position and perspective, defining vantage point.
skillTips.detail: The fourth paragraph names the novel completed abroad and its autobiographical sources.

passages.title: Why a Shop Counts Unsold Shoes
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At closing time, a shoe shop counts pairs still on its shelves. These unsold goods are inventory. They tie up money and storage space, but they also let a customer find a needed size today.

Too little inventory creates empty shelves and missed sales. Too much can leave the shop paying for crowded storage or reducing prices on styles that no longer sell. The owner must also track sizes, because ten pairs are not useful if none fit the customer.

Counting helps the shop decide what to reorder and what to stop buying. The goal is not an empty stockroom or a full one. It is a useful balance between availability and the costs of waiting goods.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A successful shop always keeps its stockroom completely empty.
Ten pairs of any size can meet every customer's need.
A shop tracks inventory to balance having useful shoes available against the money and space held in unsold stock.
Unsold shoes cost no money or space until someone buys them.
questions.explanation: The passage describes both shortage and excess, making balance the inventory goal.

questions.stem: Why can ten pairs still be unhelpful?
choices: The shop is forbidden to count more than nine.
Every pair becomes damaged at closing time.
Inventory includes storage shelves but not shoes.
The available sizes may not fit the customer.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph warns that total quantity does not reveal whether the needed size is present.

questions.stem: What does “inventory” mean here?
choices: goods a business has available or stored for sale
the money paid by one customer
a list of closing-time workers
a discount on old styles
questions.explanation: The opening defines the unsold shoes on shelves as inventory.

questions.stem: What may happen when a style no longer sells?
choices: Every customer must buy it.
The shop may reduce its price.
Its size becomes larger.
It leaves the inventory automatically.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names price reduction as one possible cost of excess outdated stock.

lesson.strategy: Keep the two inventory risks balanced: shortages lose immediate sales, while excess absorbs money and space. The size example shows why useful composition matters beyond the total count.

signals.means: Funds spent on waiting goods cannot be used elsewhere immediately.
The passage begins its explicit comparison of shortage and excess.
The conclusion rejects minimizing inventory as the only goal.

vocab.inContext: goods kept available or stored for sale
place another request for stock
the state of being present and ready for use

skillTips.main-idea: Express the balance between customer availability and the costs of unsold goods.
skillTips.inference: Inventory must match demand by size, not merely contain a large total number of pairs.
skillTips.vocabulary: The first two sentences directly identify unsold shelf goods as inventory.
skillTips.detail: The excess-stock paragraph explains that an old style may require a price reduction.

passages.title: Against Saving the Best for Later
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A fine cup remains wrapped in a cupboard because its owner is saving it for guests. A soft notebook waits for an important idea. Good soap sits unopened until an occasion feels special enough. Protection can quietly prevent an object from doing the work that made it valuable.

Using a cherished thing brings risk. Cups chip, pages collect mistakes, and soap disappears. Yet wear can also record a useful life and the ordinary moments around it. The alternative is not perfect preservation: paper yellows, styles change, and owners move.

This is not an argument to treat every keepsake carelessly. Some objects carry history, scarcity, or meaning that justifies conservation. The question is whether protection serves the object or fear controls the owner. If an ordinary good thing was made to be used, a normal Tuesday may already be occasion enough.

questions.stem: What is the essay's main idea?
choices: Every historical keepsake should be used until it breaks.
Objects remain perfectly preserved whenever they stay inside a cupboard.
Only guests deserve to use cups, notebooks, and fine soap.
Protecting valued objects can defeat their purpose, so ordinary useful things should sometimes be enjoyed before a perfect occasion arrives.
questions.explanation: The essay contrasts intended use with endless postponement while keeping an exception for meaningful conservation.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention yellowing paper?
choices: Even an unused object can change, so storage does not offer perfect preservation.
Yellow paper makes every idea important.
Notebooks are meant to be stored beside soap.
Owners can prevent aging by waiting for guests.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists natural change as a cost of the supposedly safe alternative.

questions.stem: What does “cherished” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: damaged beyond use
deeply valued and cared about
common and unwanted
recently purchased for guests
questions.explanation: The objects are protected because their owners value them highly.

questions.stem: What item waits for an important idea?
choices: a fine cup
good soap
a soft notebook
yellow paper
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says the notebook remains unused while awaiting an important idea.

lesson.strategy: Track the essay's distinction between care and postponement. The everyday examples show purpose lost through waiting, while the keepsake paragraph preserves a reasoned exception for conservation.

signals.means: The cup's protection also blocks the use for which it exists.
Storage reduces some damage but cannot stop time and change.
The author limits the claim before asking what protection actually serves.

vocab.inContext: held with deep affection or value
an object preserved because it carries personal memories
care intended to protect something from loss or damage

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the critique of endless waiting and the exception for significant objects.
skillTips.inference: Yellowing demonstrates that nonuse has costs and cannot freeze an object permanently.
skillTips.vocabulary: The care and protection surrounding the objects show that cherished means deeply valued.
skillTips.detail: The first paragraph pairs the notebook specifically with an idea that never feels important enough.

passages.title: The Camel's Empty Bell
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A caravan gave its loudest bell to the camel that carried medicine, maps, and water. A young camel admired the sound. Before the next journey, he traded his blanket for an even larger bell and hung it proudly around his neck.

“Make way for the important camel,” he called as the caravan loaded. He accepted no bundles because they might hide the polished brass. All morning, his bell rang at the front while the other camels carried the tents and grain.

At the noon stop, a guide heard the grand bell and asked for a map. The young camel had none. A thirsty traveler came next, followed by a cook seeking flour. The bell announced him clearly, but it could supply nothing.

That evening, the camel moved behind an older animal carrying water. “Your bell is smaller,” he said. “It needs only to tell people where the water is,” she replied. The young camel removed his bell and accepted two grain sacks. On the next journey, he still walked proudly, but his pride came from arriving with a useful load. A symbol can point toward important work; it cannot perform the work it symbolizes.

questions.stem: What lesson does the fable teach?
choices: Visible symbols of importance have value only when they connect to real responsibility and useful work.
The loudest bell automatically makes its wearer the most useful traveler.
Important work should be hidden so no one can find needed supplies.
A camel cannot feel pride while carrying an ordinary load.
questions.explanation: The empty camel attracts requests it cannot meet, while the smaller bell works by identifying actual water.

questions.stem: Why does the young camel refuse bundles at first?
choices: The guide has forbidden him to carry grain.
He wants his large polished bell to remain visible.
He believes every bundle contains a map.
The caravan has already reached its destination.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says bundles might hide the bell he uses to display importance.

questions.stem: What does “symbolizes” mean in the final sentence?
choices: physically carries
trades for a blanket
represents or stands for
makes a louder sound than
questions.explanation: The bell points toward useful work but cannot do that work, so it symbolizes importance.

questions.stem: What does the camel carry on the next journey?
choices: medicine and maps
a polished blanket
only the large bell
two grain sacks
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that he removes the bell and accepts two sacks of grain.

lesson.strategy: Contrast announcement with capacity. The bell tells others where something useful should be, but the repeated requests reveal an empty role; the final load changes the basis of the camel's pride.

signals.means: The camel chooses visible status over the responsibility the status implies.
Requests test the bell's promise against the camel's actual load.
The older camel's smaller symbol supports a real practical function.

vocab.inContext: a group traveling together across a long route
made the presence of someone or something known
represents an idea or role

skillTips.main-idea: Turn the empty bell and useful load into a general distinction between status signs and responsibility.
skillTips.inference: The camel protects the bell's visibility because he wants observers to see the appearance of importance.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast between pointing to work and performing it defines “symbolizes.”
skillTips.detail: After removing the oversized bell, the young camel takes two grain sacks.

passages.title: Would a Perfect Copy Still Be You?
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine a transporter that scans Leila, destroys the original, and builds a version on Mars. The Mars person remembers entering the machine, recognizes Leila's friends, and continues her plans. Did Leila travel, or did she die while a successor appeared?

If identity follows psychological continuity, the Mars person has a strong claim: memory, character, intention, and causal connection all continue. If identity requires one continuing organism, the destruction breaks the chain. The two accounts normally agree because bodies and mental lives travel together; the machine pulls them apart.

Now change one feature. Suppose the machine produces the Mars person without destroying the original Leila on Earth. Both people remember a childhood, but they immediately begin different lives. They cannot both be numerically identical to one person if identity is one-to-one.

The duplication case pressures the claim that memory alone carries identity. A defender might say psychological continuity matters for survival even when strict identity branches. Another might insist that only bodily continuation avoids the problem. The language of “copy” already favors one answer, so neutral reasoning must examine what the machine does before naming its product. No available transporter works this way. The case removes familiar cues and tests what people value in continued existence: material persistence, connected consciousness, uniqueness, or some combination. It may not yield one verdict, but it makes hidden criteria visible.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A functioning Mars transporter has proved that identity follows memory alone.
A transporter thought experiment tests whether personal identity depends on bodily continuity, psychological continuity, uniqueness, or a combination.
Both duplicates can be numerically identical to one earlier person while living separately.
Calling the Mars person a copy neutrally resolves the philosophical question.
questions.explanation: The passage compares continuity theories, adds duplication pressure, and warns that ordinary labels can prejudge the case.

questions.stem: Why does leaving the original Leila alive make the puzzle harder?
choices: The original immediately loses every childhood memory.
Mars can support only one person at a time.
Two later people share one psychological past, challenging identity as a unique one-to-one relation.
Bodily continuity becomes identical for both people.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explains that shared history branches into distinct lives, while identity normally selects one continuer.

questions.stem: What does “successor” mean in the opening paragraph?
choices: a machine that performs the body scan
an organism that remains on Earth
a memory erased during transport
someone who follows and continues a prior person's role or history
questions.explanation: The word describes the newly built person who takes up Leila's memories and plans if she did not literally travel.

questions.stem: Which feature is changed in the second version?
choices: The original Leila is not destroyed.
The Mars person receives no memories.
The transporter moves to Earth.
Leila has never met her friends.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explicitly changes destruction: the machine produces another person while the original remains.

lesson.strategy: Track each candidate relation separately: same organism, connected psychology, and unique continuation. The duplication variation holds memory constant while breaking uniqueness, making the theories diverge.

signals.means: The case grants physical and psychological similarity before asking about identity.
The transporter separates bodily from mental continuity, which normally align.
Keeping the original alive isolates duplication as the pressure on memory-based identity.

vocab.inContext: a later person or thing that takes over a prior role
an unbroken or causally connected passage through time
a final judgment about a disputed question

skillTips.main-idea: Name the competing identity criteria and leave the thought experiment's verdict open.
skillTips.inference: One past branching into two futures conflicts with the idea that numerical identity links exactly one person across time.
skillTips.vocabulary: The Mars person continues Leila's plans after her possible death, making that person a successor.
skillTips.detail: The revised case changes whether the Earth body is destroyed, not the copied memories.

passages.title: The Future We Picture Too Brightly
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
People often expect good outcomes for themselves: finishing sooner than peers, avoiding setbacks, or succeeding at a difficult change. This tendency is called optimism bias. It can appear when a person understands general statistics yet believes personal circumstances are unusually favorable.

Optimism can support action. A new shop, demanding course, or creative project requires effort before success is certain. Expecting progress may strengthen persistence, attract cooperation, and help someone recover after failure. A detached forecast is not the only useful mental state.

The same expectation can distort preparation. Someone who underrates delay may leave no schedule buffer. A driver who treats collisions as events that happen to others may neglect precautions. The problem is not hope but confidence that stops looking for contrary evidence.

Researchers distinguish unrealistic optimism from informed confidence. Experience, skill, and resources can improve an individual's prospects. The test is whether a belief updates when evidence changes and whether similar past cases are considered. A favorable estimate supported by data is not automatically a bias. Group patterns also do not diagnose one person's thought from a prediction. Some people expect worse outcomes, and the same person can be optimistic in one domain and cautious in another. Context, control, emotion, and framing all matter. A practical response is not compulsory pessimism. It is to let hope choose the destination while evidence checks the route. A plan can include ambition and a fallback, confidence and a margin for delay. Optimism is most useful when it energizes preparation instead of replacing it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Optimism bias means every hopeful prediction is irrational and harmful.
General statistics determine each person's future without regard to skill or resources.
Optimism can motivate persistence but becomes a bias when favorable expectations resist relevant evidence and weaken preparation.
The best correction is to expect the worst outcome in every domain.
questions.explanation: The passage balances motivational benefits, planning risks, evidence-based confidence, variation, and a calibrated response.

questions.stem: Why is a schedule buffer used as an example?
choices: Buffers ensure every project finishes earlier than expected.
A schedule cannot contain both confidence and preparation.
Delays occur only to people who know general statistics.
Underestimating delay can leave a plan unable to absorb predictable setbacks.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph shows how an overly bright forecast changes a concrete preparation decision.

questions.stem: What does “detached” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: emotionally removed and neutral
separated from all available evidence
guaranteed to be inaccurate
unwilling to begin a project
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a cool forecast with the motivational role that hopeful expectation can play.

questions.stem: What quality distinguishes informed confidence from bias?
choices: It predicts success in every area.
It updates when relevant evidence changes.
It ignores outcomes from similar cases.
It eliminates all emotional influence.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph explicitly makes responsiveness to changing evidence part of the test.

lesson.strategy: Track the function and accuracy of optimism separately. A belief may energize action, yet its factual quality depends on evidence, updates, and comparison cases; the conclusion combines motivation with safeguards.

signals.means: The passage grants optimism a motivational role before describing its risks.
A helpful mindset can also distort preparation when applied without calibration.
The proposed correction preserves hope while adding evidence and fallback plans.

vocab.inContext: a systematic tendency that can tilt judgment
emotionally removed or neutral
chances or possibilities of future success

skillTips.main-idea: Include optimism's possible benefit, its evidence-related risk, and the calibrated response.
skillTips.inference: A buffer is useful precisely when a forecast may omit ordinary setbacks and uncertainty.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast with motivational expectation shows detached as emotionally removed rather than uninformed.
skillTips.detail: The evidence test asks whether the belief updates when new relevant information arrives.

passages.title: The Tap That Pays
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
During a contactless payment, a card or phone comes very close to a reader at the checkout counter. The two devices use a short-range radio method called near-field communication. The small range helps make the intended interaction clear to both devices.

The card does not simply shout an account number across the room. Payment systems exchange structured messages, and a transaction can include a changing security value. A phone may first require a face, fingerprint, or passcode.

The reader sends the request onward through payment networks for approval by the card issuer. A successful tap is therefore not money jumping between two objects. It is a brief local conversation that begins a larger checked process.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A contactless card broadcasts payment details across an entire room.
Money moves directly between two objects without any network check.
Every contactless payment requires the same fingerprint reader.
A contactless tap uses short-range radio messages to begin a larger payment authorization process.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the local radio exchange, possible device checks, and onward authorization.

questions.stem: Why is short range useful?
choices: It helps identify which nearby card or phone is intended to interact with the reader.
It lets the card avoid all structured messages.
It sends the request to every shop at once.
It makes approval unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph connects close distance with clarity about the intended interaction.

questions.stem: What does “structured” mean here?
choices: spoken loudly
organized according to defined rules
made of physical coins
visible across a room
questions.explanation: Payment messages must follow an expected format so the devices and network can process them.

questions.stem: What may a phone require first?
choices: a paper map
a louder radio
a face, fingerprint, or passcode
a new account number
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists these ways a phone may verify its user.

lesson.strategy: Follow the transaction outward: nearby device to reader, then reader through a larger network. Keep proximity, user verification, message security, and final approval as distinct parts.

signals.means: Near-field communication is designed for a small interaction range.
The passage rejects the picture of uncontrolled room-wide broadcasting.
The local tap begins rather than completes the full authorization path.

vocab.inContext: working through close wireless communication rather than inserted contact
organized under defined rules
authorization for a requested action to proceed

skillTips.main-idea: Describe the tap as the local start of a networked process, not direct movement of money.
skillTips.inference: A reader can more confidently associate a close device with the customer's intended tap.
skillTips.vocabulary: The network must interpret each message, so structured means organized by shared rules.
skillTips.detail: The phone-verification list contains face, fingerprint, and passcode.

passages.title: A Seat by the Fountain
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every Thursday, Hana placed her bag on the bench beside the fountain. She was saving the seat for her cousin, who had promised to meet her after work. For three weeks, the cousin's shift ran late, but Hana kept waiting.

Across the path, Mr. León sat alone on a low wall. He had recently moved nearby and came to hear people talk, though he knew no one. When rain began, the wall became wet. He looked at the empty half of Hana's bench and remained standing.

Hana moved her bag aside. “You can sit here until my cousin comes,” she said. Mr. León smiled and thanked her. They talked about the neighborhood until the rain stopped. The next Thursday, Hana saved no seat, yet both places beside her filled: one by Mr. León and one, at last, by her cousin.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Hana releases a long-reserved seat and turns waiting for one connection into room for two.
Hana stops visiting the fountain because her cousin works late.
Mr. León takes Hana's bag so he can keep the whole bench.
Rain prevents Hana's cousin from ever reaching the fountain.
questions.explanation: Moving the bag welcomes Mr. León, and the ending brings both the new acquaintance and cousin together.

questions.stem: Why does Mr. León remain standing at first?
choices: He dislikes hearing people talk near the fountain.
Hana's bag makes the empty half appear reserved for someone else.
The bench is wetter than the low wall.
He is waiting to take Hana's cousin's shift.
questions.explanation: The story pairs his look at the apparently saved place with his choice not to sit.

questions.stem: What does “shift” mean in the first paragraph?
choices: a movement of a bag
a change in rainfall
a scheduled period of work
a place beside a fountain
questions.explanation: The cousin's work period runs late, preventing the planned meeting.

questions.stem: Who finally arrives on the last Thursday?
choices: Hana's manager
a bench painter
Mr. León's cousin
Hana's cousin
questions.explanation: The final sentence says Mr. León takes one place and Hana's cousin takes the other.

lesson.strategy: Track the meaning of the empty seat. It begins as loyalty to an absent person, becomes a barrier to someone present, and finally supports both relationships once Hana stops reserving it rigidly.

signals.means: Hana's repeated loyalty also keeps the neighboring place unavailable.
Mr. León respects the claim communicated by the bag.
The ending replaces guarded space with openness to whoever arrives.

vocab.inContext: gave a clear assurance about a future action
a scheduled block of time at work
a structure that sends water upward into a basin or pool

skillTips.main-idea: Connect Hana's waiting, the moved bag, and the ending in which openness adds rather than replaces a relationship.
skillTips.inference: The bag signals a claim on the seat, so Mr. León avoids taking it without invitation.
skillTips.vocabulary: The cousin is delayed at work, which defines shift as a scheduled work period.
skillTips.detail: At the ending, the long-awaited person is Hana's cousin.

passages.title: Finding Islands Without a Compass
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Polynesian navigators crossed Pacific areas before modern compasses or satellite positioning. They did not travel by intuition alone. Navigation joined observation with trained memory of routes, seasons, and natural signs.

Stars provided directions as they rose and set at known points on the horizon. Navigators could hold a course by following one star, then change to another as the sky turned. During daylight or cloud, ocean swells offered persistent patterns shaped by distant winds. Local waves might change while a deeper swell continued.

Bird behavior, cloud forms, reflected light, and drifting material could suggest nearby land, but no single sign guaranteed an island. A navigator judged several clues together and knew which birds traveled far offshore. Near an unseen island, swells might bend or reflect in ways an experienced observer recognized.

Knowledge was taught through practice, oral instruction, and mental models rather than through one universal chart. Different island communities developed traditions suited to their routes and waters. Voyaging canoes, crews, food planning, and weather judgment were as essential as direction finding. The accomplishment was neither accidental wandering nor a mysterious power outside learning. It was a disciplined system whose instruments included sky, sea, living behavior, vessel, and human memory.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Polynesian voyagers found islands by following one bird that always guaranteed nearby land.
Polynesian wayfinding combined trained memory with stars, swells, living signs, vessels, and judgment to navigate the Pacific.
Ocean navigation depended on a single universal paper chart shared by every island community.
The voyages were accidental wanderings guided without learning or repeated observation.
questions.explanation: The passage presents an integrated learned system, cautions against single clues, and includes crew and vessel preparation.

questions.stem: Why might a navigator change from one star to another?
choices: Every star points toward a different island each hour.
Clouds make ocean swells stop moving.
The sky's rotation causes the first guide star to move from a useful position.
The canoe can travel only while two stars overlap.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says navigators follow one star and switch as the sky turns.

questions.stem: What does “persistent” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: visible only beside an island
created by one passing canoe
impossible to remember
continuing steadily despite shorter local changes
questions.explanation: The deeper swell is contrasted with local waves that can change, showing that it continues.

questions.stem: What could stars provide?
choices: directions from their rising and setting points
fresh food for the crew
a guarantee of clear weather
a paper chart of each route
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly connects horizon positions of stars with direction.

lesson.strategy: Build a layered navigation toolkit: celestial direction, enduring swell patterns, near-land clues, remembered relationships, and voyage preparation. Reject any answer that depends on one infallible sign.

signals.means: The passage frames wayfinding as learned observation rather than unexplained instinct.
Landfall judgments combined evidence with knowledge of each sign's limits.

signals.phrase: rather than through one universal chart
signals.means: Navigation traditions varied with communities, routes, and waters.

vocab.inContext: broad continuing waves produced by distant weather
continuing steadily over time
people trained to determine and follow a route

skillTips.main-idea: Describe the integrated learned system and avoid reducing it to stars, birds, or intuition alone.
skillTips.inference: As Earth turns, a star's position changes, so a sequence of known stars can maintain direction.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast between changing local waves and the continuing deep swell defines persistent.
skillTips.detail: The horizon points where stars rise and set are identified as directional information.

passages.title: The Mantis Shrimp's Extra Colors
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Mantis shrimp have unusually complex eyes. Different species vary, but some possess many classes of photoreceptors, including receptors sensitive to ultraviolet light and to properties of polarization. Humans, by comparison, build most color vision from three classes of cone cells. It is tempting to conclude that the shrimp sees every color with extraordinary precision.

More receptor classes do not automatically mean finer color discrimination. In laboratory tasks, some mantis shrimp distinguish certain neighboring colors less precisely than humans do. Their visual system may classify wavelengths through relatively direct receptor channels instead of making extensive comparisons among a few overlapping signals.

That arrangement could favor speed. A quick category response may help an animal identify signals or objects without spending neural processing on tiny differences. This is a proposed functional interpretation, not a complete translation of the animal's subjective experience.

The eyes add other complexity. Each sits on a movable stalk, and specialized regions can sample different parts of a scene. Polarization sensitivity may support communication or detection in underwater environments. Those abilities should not be collapsed into a single ranking of “better vision.” Comparing species requires specifying the task. Humans may separate nearby hues well; a mantis shrimp may detect ultraviolet or polarization information that humans miss. Receptor count describes available channels, not a universal score for how richly or accurately an animal sees.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Mantis shrimp distinguish every neighboring color more precisely than humans.
Three human cone types detect all ultraviolet and polarization information.
Mantis shrimp have many specialized visual channels, but receptor count alone does not mean universally sharper color vision.
A single score can rank every visual task across different species.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts receptor diversity with discrimination results and explains task-specific strengths.

questions.stem: Why might direct color categories benefit a mantis shrimp?
choices: They guarantee an exact match to human subjective color experience.
They make movable eye stalks unnecessary.
They eliminate all need for photoreceptors.
They may support rapid recognition without extensive neural comparison among signals.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph offers speed as a cautious functional interpretation of more direct channels.

questions.stem: What does “discrimination” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: the ability to tell similar stimuli apart
unfair treatment of another species
movement of an eye stalk
detection of all underwater objects
questions.explanation: The laboratory task asks whether the animal distinguishes neighboring colors precisely.

questions.stem: Which kind of light can some receptors detect?
choices: sound waves
ultraviolet light
infrared heat only
radio transmissions
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph names ultraviolet sensitivity among mantis shrimp receptor classes.

lesson.strategy: Separate sensory dimensions before comparing species. Count receptor classes, measure nearby-color discrimination, and note ultraviolet or polarization detection as different tests; no one measure settles overall vision.

signals.means: The receptor count invites an intuitive conclusion that later evidence qualifies.
An anatomical quantity cannot substitute for measured performance on a task.
Meaningful comparison requires naming the exact visual ability being tested.

vocab.inContext: light-sensitive cells that begin visual processing
ability to distinguish one stimulus from another
the orientation pattern of light waves

skillTips.main-idea: Keep receptor diversity and task performance separate; avoid calling one species' vision simply better.
skillTips.inference: Direct category channels could trade fine comparison for faster identification.
skillTips.vocabulary: Neighboring colors are the items being told apart, defining discrimination in context.
skillTips.detail: Ultraviolet is explicitly named alongside polarization in the opening receptor description.

passages.title: The Journey of a Lost Wallet
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A wallet found on a bus contains clues and private information. A transit employee may see identification, bank and library cards, receipts, and cash. The goal is to preserve the contents and find a safe route back to the owner without exposing details.

Transit agencies log found property with a time, route, location, and description. A record creates a chain of custody: later staff can tell where the wallet came from, who handled it, and where it was stored. Cash may be counted by two workers or sealed under local procedure.

Identification can support a match, but posting a photograph online risks revealing an address, signature, account fragment, or document number. A public directory may point to someone with a similar name. A message should disclose little and direct the possible owner to an official claim process. Claim questions test knowledge without publishing answers. Staff might ask for the wallet's color, an unusual item inside, the bus route, or approximate cash. No single clue is perfect, so several consistent details are stronger than one guess. Sensitive documents may instead go to the issuing authority under agency rules.

The owner must also act. Reporting missing cards can limit unauthorized use, and giving the likely route and time helps staff search records. These are precautions, not a guarantee. A wallet's return depends less on detective drama than on disciplined handling. Each step narrows access while preserving enough information to verify a claim. Privacy and recovery are not opposing goals; careful process lets them support each other.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Publishing every identification card online is the fastest safe way to find an owner.
One matching first name guarantees that a wallet belongs to a claimant.
A chain of custody matters only when a wallet contains no cash or documents.
A lost wallet is most safely returned through documented handling, privacy protection, official contact, and verification using several clues.
questions.explanation: The passage follows the item from logging through contact and claim while balancing information use with privacy.

questions.stem: Why are several claim details stronger than one?
choices: Consistent independent clues reduce the chance that a guess or namesake is mistaken for the owner.
Every owner forgets the wallet's color and bus route.
Multiple clues allow staff to post more private documents.
Cash amounts are always identical across lost wallets.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph notes that no single clue is perfect, so agreement across details improves confidence.

questions.stem: What does “custody” mean in “chain of custody”?
choices: legal ownership of every wallet found
responsibility for possessing and safeguarding the item
a public list of card numbers
permission to spend found cash
questions.explanation: The record tracks who handled and stored the wallet, showing custody as responsible control.

questions.stem: Which transit detail should be recorded?
choices: the driver's favorite destination
every passenger's bank balance
the route where the wallet was found
the owner's future travel plans
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists time, route, location, and description in the found-property record.

lesson.strategy: Follow the wallet as an object with controlled handoffs. At each stage, ask what information helps recovery, what information creates exposure, and how an official record preserves both accountability and verification.

signals.means: The wallet's clues can help identification while creating risk if shared broadly.
Logging connects each handoff so responsibility does not disappear.
Initial contact should invite verification without revealing claim answers.

vocab.inContext: responsible possession and safeguarding of an item
a small incomplete part of a larger number or item
not given official permission

skillTips.main-idea: Combine recovery, documentation, and privacy; the passage rejects solving one by sacrificing another.
skillTips.inference: Independent matching details make a coincidental guess or same-name contact less likely to pass verification.
skillTips.vocabulary: The log follows handlers and storage locations, defining custody as responsible possession.
skillTips.detail: Route appears in the list of facts recorded when transit staff log found property.

passages.title: How Dew Finds the Grass
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
After a clear night, grass may sparkle with water even when no rain fell. The water is dew. It forms when a surface cools enough for water vapor in nearby air to condense.

Grass loses heat toward the night sky and can become cooler than the air above it. Air touching the blades cools too. When it reaches the dew point, some invisible vapor becomes liquid droplets on the surface.

Dew does not fall from the sky like light rain. It forms directly on cool objects. Wind and clouds can reduce cooling, while humidity affects how soon condensation begins.

The drops reveal water that was already present as vapor. Cooling changed its form, not its identity.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Dew forms when grass cools nearby air to the dew point and water vapor condenses into liquid drops.
Dew is a kind of light rain that falls only on grass.
Grass creates new water whenever clouds cover the night sky.
Water vapor disappears permanently when a surface cools.
questions.explanation: The passage traces surface cooling, air cooling, dew point, and condensation.

questions.stem: Why can grass become cooler than nearby air?
choices: It absorbs heat from every water drop.
It loses heat toward the clear night sky.
Wind always freezes each blade.
Its color creates water vapor.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph identifies heat loss toward the sky as the source of surface cooling.

questions.stem: What does “condense” mean here?
choices: fall as frozen snow
create water from nothing
change from gas into liquid
warm above the dew point
questions.explanation: Invisible vapor becomes visible liquid droplets when condensation occurs.

questions.stem: What can reduce nighttime surface cooling?
choices: clear sky
grass blades
water vapor
clouds
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says wind and clouds can reduce cooling.

lesson.strategy: Follow the state change rather than imagining falling water: the surface loses heat, nearby air cools to a threshold, and existing vapor becomes liquid directly on the grass.

signals.means: The opening rules out precipitation as the source of the droplets.

Condensation changes the vapor's state rather than creating new matter.
