Posted prices reduce the effort and uncertainty of routine exchange by making an offer visible to strangers.
A market can function only when sellers refuse to discuss quality, service, or discounts.
questions.explanation: The passage treats a posted offer as shared infrastructure that lowers negotiation effort while preserving choice and exceptions.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe a posted price as shared infrastructure?
choices: It forces every seller to offer the same product.
It proves that the lowest figure always marks the best value.
It replaces all conversation between buyers and sellers.
It gives unknown buyers and workers a common starting offer without repeated negotiation.
questions.explanation: The seller posts before knowing who will enter, and buyers and workers can then act from the same visible offer.

questions.stem: What is a “transaction cost” in the first paragraph?
choices: The effort, uncertainty, and delay involved in reaching an exchange
The lowest possible price printed on a tag
The physical weight of goods at a market stall
A discount offered only for buying one item
questions.explanation: The phrase is immediately defined through the attention, uncertainty, and delay required to reach an agreement.

questions.stem: What does a visible posted price fail to prove?
choices: That the seller has stated an offer
That the price is fair
That buyers can see a number
That a routine exchange is possible
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explicitly warns that visibility does not prove fairness.

lesson.strategy: Treat the price tag as information infrastructure, then separate its real benefit (lower search and negotiation effort) from claims it cannot establish about fairness or quality.

signals.means: This preserves a genuine benefit of bargaining before introducing its cost.
This limits what buyers may conclude from a visible number.
This redirects the economic conclusion from price level to coordination effort.

vocab.inContext: negotiating the terms or price of an exchange
effort and delay required to arrange an exchange
unusual cases that still require individual discussion

skillTips.main-idea: Center the gist on reduced coordination effort, not on a promise of low or fair prices.
skillTips.inference: Infrastructure serves many unknown users; connect that feature to the offer posted before buyers arrive.
skillTips.vocabulary: The colon after transaction cost supplies its three-part definition in context.
skillTips.detail: Locate the fairness warning before considering later examples of changing an offer.

passages.title: The Useful Second Saying
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
I used to hear repetition as a small failure of conversation. If a clerk repeated my booking code, or a dispatcher read an address back, I wondered why the first saying had not been enough. Efficient speech, I assumed, moved forward.

At a ferry office, I once gave a dock number over a poor connection. The clerk answered with the number I meant, or so I thought. Only when she read it back digit by digit did I hear the reversal: forty-two had become twenty-four. No one had been careless. Two short sounds had crossed static and expectation.

Read-back changes communication from delivery into a loop. One person sends; the other returns a compact version; the first confirms or repairs it. The repeated message is not redundant in the useless sense. It tests whether two minds now hold the same actionable detail. The method matters most when a tiny difference (a time, platform, quantity, or name) can redirect everything that follows.

There is a cost. Repeating every sentence would bury conversation under its own echo, and a ritual response can become empty if nobody listens. Good confirmation is selective. It returns the detail whose error would matter and leaves room for correction without blame. I no longer hear the second saying as proof that the first speaker failed. I hear a bridge being inspected before weight crosses it. A few repeated words can save two strangers from building careful plans on different versions of the same fact.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Efficient communication requires people to repeat every sentence they hear.
A message is reliable whenever both speakers are certain they listened carefully.
Read-back is useful only when a ferry office has a poor telephone connection.
Selective read-back helps people detect important message errors before later plans depend on them.
questions.explanation: The reversed dock number reveals the value of returning a crucial detail, while the final paragraph limits confirmation to errors that matter.

questions.stem: Why does the narrator compare read-back to inspecting a bridge?
choices: Both checks test a connection before later actions place weight on it.
Both require strangers to repeat every part of a conversation.
A ferry bridge can translate one dock number into another.
A bridge is useful only after someone makes a careless mistake.
questions.explanation: The image compares confirming a message before building plans on it with checking a structure before it carries weight.

questions.stem: What does “selective” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: Applied to every sentence without exception
Chosen for the important details that need checking
Spoken too softly for anyone to hear
Designed to assign blame for an error
questions.explanation: The essay rejects repeating everything and says good confirmation returns the detail whose error would matter.

questions.stem: Which number was changed during the poor connection?
choices: Twelve became twenty.
Forty became fourteen.
Forty-two became twenty-four.
Twenty-two became forty-four.
questions.explanation: The ferry-office episode states that forty-two had been heard as twenty-four.

lesson.strategy: Use the reversed dock number to model the read-back loop: send, return the critical detail, then confirm or repair it before another decision depends on the message.

signals.phrase: Only when she read it back
signals.means: This identifies the confirmation step that exposes the reversed number.
This introduces the limit that prevents confirmation from becoming constant echo.

signals.phrase: I no longer hear the second saying
signals.means: This marks the narrator's changed judgment about purposeful repetition.

vocab.inContext: an error in which the order of the dock-number parts changed
specific enough to guide a later decision or action
limited to the important details that warrant checking

skillTips.main-idea: Include the error-detection benefit and the essay's limit that only consequential details deserve read-back.
skillTips.inference: Connect the inspected bridge with plans that will later rely on the accuracy of a message.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast selective confirmation with the rejected idea of repeating every sentence.
skillTips.detail: Track the order of the two number words before and after the ferry-office read-back.

passages.title: The Jay and the Bridge Bell
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A bell hung beside a bridge in a valley where fog came often. Travelers rang once before crossing, so anyone on the far side knew to wait.

A jay laughed that the bell knew only one note. He offered to sing a different tune for every kind of traveler. The bell agreed to rest. That morning, a goat heard a quick song and thought it meant hurry. A mule heard the same song and thought it meant stop. They met in the middle and had to back away.

By evening, the jay was tired and the bridge was empty. He asked the bell to return. One plain ring carried across the fog, and the travelers moved in turn. The jay still sang beside the bridge, but never again called a clear shared signal dull.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: A simple signal works when everyone shares its meaning, while clever variety can cause confusion.
A bridge is safest when no traveler ever crosses it.
Every animal naturally understands every song in the same way.
The bell needed many tunes because one ring was too hard to hear.
questions.explanation: The goat and mule misread the jay's changing songs, while the bell's one agreed signal restores orderly crossing.

questions.stem: Why did the goat and mule meet in the middle?
choices: The bell told both animals to hurry.
They gave different meanings to the jay's same song.
The bridge had moved during the fog.
They had agreed to meet before crossing.
questions.explanation: One animal understood hurry and the other understood stop, showing that the jay's tune had no shared meaning.

questions.stem: What does “signal” mean in the final sentence?
choices: A kind of mountain bird
A heavy part of a bridge
A sign or sound that carries a message
A tune meant only for the singer
questions.explanation: The bell's ring tells unseen travelers when to wait, so it is a sound carrying an agreed message.

questions.stem: How many times did travelers ring the bell before crossing?
choices: Four times
Twice
Until the fog lifted
Once
questions.explanation: The opening states that travelers rang once before crossing.

lesson.strategy: Compare the result of the bell's one agreed ring with the jay's many unagreed tunes; the crossing outcomes reveal what makes a public signal useful.

signals.means: This setting makes a sound signal especially important for unseen travelers.
This begins the test of the jay's more elaborate system.
This marks the jay's lasting lesson after the failed experiment.

vocab.inContext: a structure that carries travelers across a gap
people or animals moving from one place to another
a sign or sound with a shared message

skillTips.main-idea: Judge each communication system by whether it lets both sides act safely together.
skillTips.inference: Opposite reactions to one tune show that the animals lacked an agreed meaning.
skillTips.vocabulary: The bell's ring performs the message-carrying job that defines signal.
skillTips.detail: The number of rings appears in the rule stated before the jay interferes.

passages.title: Where a Sign's Meaning Lives
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Imagine that Niko paints a blue circle on a gate and decides it means meet here at noon. Has he created a sign? For himself, perhaps. The mark can remind him of his plan. To a stranger, however, it is only a blue circle.

A public sign needs more than a maker's private intention. Other people must have a way to learn what the mark asks them to notice or do. They might receive an explanation, see the sign used repeatedly, or infer its meaning from its place. Once the rule is shared, the simple circle can coordinate people who never meet its painter.

This does not mean a shape has no qualities of its own. A bright circle may be easy to see, while a tiny gray mark may be missed. Visibility helps a sign succeed, but visibility is not meaning. Meaning lives in a practice that connects the mark with an idea or action. The sign works when that connection can travel from one mind to another.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every visible shape carries one natural public instruction.
A public sign gains meaning through a learnable shared practice, not only through its maker's private intention.
A sign can coordinate people only if they meet its painter in person.
Small gray marks always communicate better than bright circles.
questions.explanation: The blue circle remains private until others can learn the connection between the mark and an intended idea or action.

questions.stem: Why is the blue circle only a circle to a stranger at first?
choices: The stranger cannot see bright colors.
Niko painted the mark too close to noon.
The stranger has not learned the rule connecting the mark with the meeting plan.
Blue circles cannot be used as reminders.
questions.explanation: Niko's private decision supplies no public route to the meaning; the stranger needs explanation, repeated use, or context.

questions.stem: What does “infer” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: Paint a sign a brighter color
Forget a rule after seeing it
Meet the original painter
Work out a meaning from clues
questions.explanation: The sign's location is offered as evidence from which another person might work out what it means.

questions.stem: How might people learn what the mark means?
choices: Through explanation, repeated use, or its location
Only by changing the circle into a square
By making the mark small and gray
Only by meeting Niko at noon
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists explanation, repeated use, and inference from place as three routes to shared meaning.

lesson.strategy: Test the blue circle from two viewpoints: Niko has a private reminder, but strangers gain a public sign only when the mark-to-action connection becomes learnable.

signals.means: This grants the mark a private use while leaving its public status unsettled.
This states the condition that turns the circle into a coordinating sign.
This distinguishes noticing a mark from understanding what it signifies.

vocab.inContext: the private purpose a maker has in mind
work out a conclusion from available clues
a shared way of connecting a mark with meaning

skillTips.main-idea: Distinguish a private reminder from a public sign whose rule other people can learn.
skillTips.inference: Ask what knowledge Niko possesses that the stranger initially lacks.
skillTips.vocabulary: The mark's location provides clues, which makes work out the fitting meaning of infer.
skillTips.detail: The three learning routes appear together before the rule becomes shared.

passages.title: The Hand Beside the Sentence
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
During conversation, a person's hands may carry information that speech leaves vague. Someone saying the path bends over there might trace a curve in the air. A speaker describing two shelves may hold one hand above the other. The gestures do not merely decorate the words; they can show direction, shape, timing, or emphasis.

Listeners usually combine both channels. If a speaker points left while naming the red door, the motion helps select one object from the scene. If the hands show a narrow gap while the sentence says through here, they add a size that the words omit. This coordination is especially useful when the topic is spatial or hard to describe quickly.

Gestures are not a universal dictionary. The same movement can have different social meanings in different places, and some conversational styles use more visible motion than others. Context matters: a point beside a real street sign is easier to interpret than the same point in an empty room.

The useful question is not whether hands or words communicate better. Human communication is often distributed across voice, face, hands, and surroundings. Understanding improves when a listener notices how those parts support or qualify one another.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Hand movements have one fixed meaning that is understood in every place.
Listeners should ignore surroundings whenever a speaker points toward an object.
Gestures, speech, and context can work together as connected parts of human communication.
Spoken words cannot describe direction, shape, timing, or emphasis.
questions.explanation: Examples throughout the passage show hands adding information to speech, with context shaping how the combined message is understood.

questions.stem: Why does pointing left help when the speaker names a red door?
choices: It proves that all red doors are on the left.
It replaces the need to see any part of the scene.
It gives the movement the same meaning in every culture.
It links the spoken description to a particular object in the shared scene.
questions.explanation: The passage says the motion selects one object from the scene, so gesture narrows the reference of the spoken words.

questions.stem: What does “distributed” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: Spread across several sources or channels
Hidden entirely inside spoken words
Limited to movements of one hand
Given the same meaning in every culture
questions.explanation: The sentence immediately spreads communication across voice, face, hands, and surroundings.

questions.stem: What can gestures show according to the first paragraph?
choices: Only the color of a door
Direction, shape, timing, or emphasis
A complete universal dictionary
Only information already stated clearly
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives that exact four-part list after explaining that gestures do more than decorate speech.

lesson.strategy: Read each example as a two-channel message: identify what the words supply, what the hands add, and how the surrounding scene narrows the combined meaning.

signals.phrase: do not merely decorate the words
signals.means: This rejects the idea that gestures are only ornamental movement.
This introduces the setting's role in making a movement interpretable.
This reframes the conclusion away from a competition between hands and words.

vocab.inContext: meaningful movements that accompany communication
relating to position, distance, shape, or direction
spread across several channels rather than kept in one

skillTips.main-idea: Select the gist that integrates speech, bodily movement, and context without making gestures universal.
skillTips.inference: A point gains precision because speaker and listener can both connect it to the visible scene.
skillTips.vocabulary: The list after distributed names the several places where communication is spread.
skillTips.detail: The first paragraph ends by listing four kinds of information a gesture may show.

passages.title: The Number Behind a Written Character
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A computer does not store a written character as ink or shape. It stores numbers. Trouble arose when different systems assigned the same number to different characters, or different numbers to the same character. Text created on one machine could arrive on another as nonsense because sender and receiver were using different code books.

Unicode provides a shared system for identifying characters used in writing. Each encoded character receives a code point, a number written in a standard form. A Latin letter, an Arabic letter, and a mathematical sign can therefore keep their identities as text moves among compatible devices and programs. An encoding such as UTF-8 specifies how those code points become bytes for storage or transmission.

The code point does not dictate the exact mark a reader sees. A font supplies a glyph, the visual form, so one character can appear in many typefaces. Some visible units also require more than one code point, and software must apply rules for combining and arranging them.

This infrastructure coordinates machines; it does not translate sentences or guarantee that every device has a suitable font. Even so, it separates a character's identity from one local machine's drawing of it. That distinction lets the same underlying text survive changes of software, screen, and typeface.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Unicode translates the meaning of every sentence into every human language.
A code point controls the exact shape, size, and typeface of each printed mark.
Different devices can share text only when they are built with identical screens and fonts.
Unicode gives written characters shared numerical identities that help text remain consistent across compatible systems.
questions.explanation: The passage explains shared code points, distinguishes them from glyphs, and shows how character identity can persist across software and displays.

questions.stem: Why could older text appear as nonsense on another machine?
choices: The two systems could interpret the stored numbers with different character assignments.
Every font translated the sentence into a new language.
Computers stored only ink and had no numbers.
UTF-8 required every character to use one visual shape.
questions.explanation: The opening says different systems could assign incompatible characters to the same numbers, causing the receiver to interpret the data differently.

questions.stem: What is a “glyph” in this passage?
choices: A sentence translated by Unicode
The visual form used to display a character
A device that sends radio signals
A number reserved for storing a whole paragraph
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly identifies a glyph as the visual form supplied by a font.

questions.stem: What does an encoding such as UTF-8 specify?
choices: Which sentences should be translated
Which font every reader must install
How code points become bytes for storage or transmission
How ink should be placed on a printed page
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that UTF-8 specifies how code points are represented as bytes.

lesson.strategy: Keep three layers separate: a code point identifies a character, an encoding represents it as bytes, and a font renders a glyph that readers can see.

signals.means: This introduces the incompatibility that a shared character system addresses.
This states the result of assigning shared code points across systems.
This marks the important benefit that remains after the system's limits.

vocab.inContext: a standard number identifying an encoded character
a visible shape that represents a character
the sending of encoded information between systems

skillTips.main-idea: Focus on portable character identity, while excluding translation and exact visual appearance.
skillTips.inference: The nonsense follows when receiver and sender attach different characters to the same stored number.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast the abstract code point with the glyph that a font makes visible.
skillTips.detail: Locate UTF-8 in the code-point paragraph and identify its byte-conversion role.

passages.title: The Names Under the Signs
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Nara was hired to replace signs in a covered market above the harbor. Old boards named aisles after vanished landmarks: Fig Steps, Copper Fountain, and East Gate. Her directory used tidy numbers. Aisle One began at the north door, Aisle Two crossed the center, and visitors needed no local history to understand them.

On installation morning, confusion spread faster than the ladders moved. A fish seller sent ice to Copper Fountain, but the delivery cart stopped at Aisle Three. A visitor followed Aisle Two twice and returned to Nara's desk. The numbers were clear, yet nobody used them when speaking.

Nara walked the market with Oren, its oldest porter. He showed her a blue tile where the fountain had stood and three worn steps that once led to the fig stalls. The old names were not accurate descriptions. They were coordinates held in hundreds of memories.

Before noon, Nara turned the boards over. She kept the large aisle numbers, then painted each familiar name beneath its number and added a simple symbol from the surviving landmark. Oren began every direction with the new number and ended with the old name. Vendors copied him. By closing time, the ice cart reached Aisle Three, also called Copper Fountain, without circling. Nara had expected to choose between a clean system and a messy one. Instead, she built a bridge between them. The market did not need one perfect language for place. It needed signs that allowed newcomers and regulars to confirm they meant the same corner.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Nara solves the market's wayfinding problem by linking a clear numbered system with familiar local names and landmarks.
Oren removes every new sign so only longtime workers can find the aisles.
The market closes because a delivery cart cannot carry ice above the harbor.
Nara proves that old place names are always accurate descriptions of present buildings.
questions.explanation: After the number-only plan fails, Nara combines numbers, remembered names, and symbols so both newcomers and regulars can coordinate.

questions.stem: Why did the number-only signs cause confusion even though they were clear?
choices: The numbers were too small for Nara to paint.
People still gave spoken directions through old names stored in shared memory.
Oren had secretly moved every aisle before installation.
Visitors refused to enter any market near a harbor.
questions.explanation: Sellers and visitors continued to use Copper Fountain and other remembered coordinates, so the new visual system did not match spoken directions.

questions.stem: What does “coordinates” mean in the third paragraph?
choices: Paint colors chosen for every sign
People hired to carry market goods
Reference points used to identify locations
Rules that remove all old names
questions.explanation: Although the named objects were gone, people used their names as reference points for finding market locations.

questions.stem: What surviving traces did Oren show Nara?
choices: A painted clock and a north door
A working fountain and new fig trees
A ladder and an ice cart
A blue tile and three worn steps
questions.explanation: Oren points out the blue tile from the fountain and the worn steps from the former fig stalls.

lesson.strategy: Track the mismatch between visual labels and spoken directions, then notice how Nara's revision preserves the accessible numbers while connecting them to communal memory.

signals.phrase: yet nobody used them when speaking
signals.means: This exposes the gap between the new directory and daily market language.

signals.phrase: Before noon, Nara turned the boards over
signals.means: This marks the moment Nara revises her failed number-only plan.

signals.phrase: Instead, she built a bridge between them
signals.means: This states the story's resolution: integration rather than choosing one system.

vocab.inContext: an organized guide to places within the market
shared reference points for locating a place
remaining after most of an older landmark has disappeared

skillTips.main-idea: Describe the failed replacement and the successful hybrid system, not merely the act of repainting signs.
skillTips.inference: Clear labels still fail when they do not connect with the names people actually say and remember.
skillTips.vocabulary: The vanished landmarks still locate stalls in memory, revealing the reference-point sense of coordinates.
skillTips.detail: Find the physical remnants during Nara and Oren's walk, before she reverses the boards.

passages.title: When Ships Read Flags
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before radio, ships could send messages with flags. Bright colors and bold shapes were visible across water. A sailor raised one flag or a group of flags, and another crew used a codebook to read the signal.

At first, fleets and trading groups used different codes. A pattern understood by one crew might mean nothing to another. During the nineteenth century, published systems helped more ships share fixed meanings. Later international codes made communication across languages easier. Some signals stood for letters, while others carried a whole message about a ship's needs or actions.

Flags still had limits. Fog could hide them, darkness made them hard to see, and each crew needed the same code. Yet in clear daylight, a few pieces of cloth turned distance into a readable space between strangers at sea.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Signal flags worked in all weather without any shared code.
Shared flag codes helped ships communicate across distance and language before radio, though visibility limited them.
Nineteenth-century sailors stopped using shapes and colors on flags.
Every group of ships understood all flag patterns from the beginning.
questions.explanation: The passage follows flag signaling from separate codes toward shared systems and closes by naming fog and darkness as limits.

questions.stem: Why did crews need the same codebook?
choices: A codebook made fog disappear from the sea.
The book supplied brighter cloth for every flag.
Shared definitions let both crews interpret a pattern in the same way.
The book replaced the need to raise any signal.
questions.explanation: The passage notes that a pattern could mean nothing to a crew using a different code, so common definitions were essential.

questions.stem: What are “fleets” in the second paragraph?
choices: Books that explain flag patterns
Bright colors used at night
Messages about a ship's actions
Groups of ships
questions.explanation: The sentence pairs fleets with trading groups that used their own systems, indicating organized groups of ships.

questions.stem: What could make signal flags difficult to see?
choices: Fog and darkness
A shared codebook
Clear daylight
Bold shapes
questions.explanation: The final paragraph identifies fog and darkness as conditions that hid or obscured flags.

lesson.strategy: Follow the history from separate flag codes to shared published meanings, then keep the system's communication benefit paired with its limits in fog and darkness.

signals.means: This introduces the earlier period of separate signaling systems.

signals.phrase: while others carried a whole message
signals.means: This contrasts letter flags with signals that expressed a complete meaning.
This returns to the system's usefulness after naming visibility limits.

vocab.inContext: a guide that gives agreed meanings for signals
organized groups of ships
a visible pattern that communicates a message

skillTips.main-idea: Include the shared code, cross-language use, and weather limits in the historical gist.
skillTips.inference: If crews use different definitions, the same pattern cannot coordinate their actions.
skillTips.vocabulary: The pairing with trading groups supports the groups-of-ships meaning of fleets.
skillTips.detail: Look in the final paragraph for the two conditions that reduce visibility.

passages.title: One Voice in a Penguin Crowd
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
King penguins gather in large, noisy colonies on subantarctic islands. Parents leave to find food at sea, then return to chicks surrounded by many other birds. They cannot rely on a fixed nest as a street address. To reunite, parent and chick call and listen.

Each call carries an individual vocal signature. Its pattern changes in pitch and rhythm in a way the correct listener can recognize. Repeated parts help the signature remain useful even when other calls cover part of it. Experiments using recorded and altered calls have shown that chicks respond to important patterns in their own parent's voice.

The call does more than announce that an adult penguin is present. It identifies one caller inside a moving crowd. A chick may answer and move toward the sound, helping the pair close the distance. In this colony, a route home is not marked on the ground. It travels through the air as a learned pattern of sound.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: King penguins find family members only by returning to one fixed nest.
Every adult penguin in a colony makes an identical call.
King penguins use recognizable vocal patterns to reunite parents and chicks within noisy moving colonies.
Recorded-call experiments show that chicks avoid their own parent's voice.
questions.explanation: The passage connects individual vocal signatures, recognition experiments, and movement toward a caller within the colony.

questions.stem: Why are repeated parts of a call useful in a noisy colony?
choices: They make every penguin sound exactly alike.
They create a fixed nest on the ground.
They prevent parents from leaving for the sea.
They leave recognizable information even when other sounds cover part of the call.
questions.explanation: The text directly links repetition with preserving the vocal signature when other calls mask part of it.

questions.stem: What is a vocal “signature” here?
choices: A distinctive sound pattern that identifies one caller
A mark scratched beside a penguin nest
A route drawn between an island and the sea
A sound shared without variation by the whole colony
questions.explanation: The call's signature varies by individual and lets the correct listener recognize a particular parent.

questions.stem: What can king penguins not use as a street address?
choices: A repeated part of a call
A fixed nest
A parent's pitch pattern
A subantarctic island
questions.explanation: The opening says they cannot rely on a fixed nest as a street address.

lesson.strategy: Follow the reunion problem from crowd noise and no fixed nest to the solution: an individually recognizable, repeated vocal pattern that parent and chick can answer.

signals.means: This begins the reunion task after adults have been away feeding.

signals.phrase: even when other calls cover part of it
signals.means: This explains why repeated call information helps amid colony noise.
This distinguishes individual identity from a general notice of presence.

vocab.inContext: large groups of penguins gathered in breeding areas
a distinctive pattern that identifies one caller
changed for use in a recognition experiment

skillTips.main-idea: Join the noisy-colony problem with the individual-call solution and the resulting reunion.
skillTips.inference: Repetition provides another chance to hear identifying information when noise masks part of a call.
skillTips.vocabulary: The next sentences connect signature with pitch, rhythm, and recognition of one caller.
skillTips.detail: The opening contrasts vocal navigation with the fixed nest the birds cannot rely upon.

passages.title: Glass Armor on an Iron Pot
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An enameled iron pot combines materials that behave differently on their own. The metal body gives the vessel strength and stores heat. Its colored surface is vitreous enamel: a thin layer of glass fused to the iron at high temperature. It is not ordinary paint dried on top.

During firing, powdered glass softens and bonds to the prepared metal substrate. After cooling, the enamel forms a hard, nonporous surface that resists water and many food acids. The iron supports that brittle glass, while the glass separates the iron from moisture and food. Each material supplies something the other lacks.

The partnership has limits. Metal and glass expand by different amounts when heated, so makers adjust the enamel mixture and firing process to keep the layers joined. A hard impact can still chip the coating. A chip may expose iron that can rust when moisture reaches it, even while the surrounding enamel remains sound. The damaged spot reveals how the pot was built: toughness does not come from one perfect substance, but from a carefully managed boundary between two.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: An enameled pot is made entirely from glass so that it can avoid storing heat.
The color of enamel is the main reason an iron pot remains strong under impact.
Any small chip instantly destroys both the glass coating and the iron beneath it.
An enameled pot gains useful qualities by bonding a glass surface to a strong iron body.
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly contrasts the jobs of iron and enamel, then explains that the bonded boundary lets the pot benefit from both materials.

questions.stem: Why is glass used as a coating instead of as the entire pot?
choices: The iron supplies structural strength that the brittle glass surface lacks.
The glass cannot become hard unless food is placed beneath it.
A glass vessel would absorb moisture through a porous surface.
Iron is needed only to give powdered enamel a darker color.
questions.explanation: The text calls enamel brittle and says the iron supports it, so the metal body provides strength that a thin glass layer cannot provide alone.

questions.stem: What does “vitreous” mean in the description of the enamel?
choices: Able to bend repeatedly without changing shape
Made from or resembling glass
Covered with a removable coat of paint
Formed only from untreated iron
questions.explanation: The passage immediately defines vitreous enamel as a thin layer of glass fused to iron, establishing the word's glasslike meaning.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what can happen when the enamel chips?
choices: The entire pot changes into a porous material.
The remaining enamel separates from food acids at once.
Moisture can reach the exposed iron and allow rust to form.
The iron stops storing heat throughout the whole vessel.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph specifically states that a chip may expose iron, which can rust when moisture reaches that spot.

lesson.strategy: Read the pot as a two-material system. Make one column for what iron contributes and another for what enamel contributes, then use the chip example to test why their boundary matters.

signals.means: Introduces the manufacturing stage when the glass coating bonds to metal.
Shifts from the bonding process to the finished surface's properties.
Signals that the useful composite can still be damaged by mismatched behavior or impact.

vocab.inContext: made from glass or having a glasslike character
not containing open pores that readily admit liquid
the underlying iron surface to which enamel bonds

skillTips.main-idea: State both halves of the design: iron provides the body, while fused glass provides the working surface.
skillTips.inference: When the author pairs strength with brittleness, infer why neither material performs every job alone.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the definition after the colon to connect “vitreous” directly with the glass layer.
skillTips.detail: Look in the limits paragraph for the exact chain from impact to exposed iron to possible rust.

passages.title: Why Salt Makes an Ice Bath Colder
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A bowl containing only ice and liquid water tends toward a balance near water's normal freezing point. Add salt, and that balance changes. The salt dissolves into sodium and chloride ions, creating brine whose freezing point is lower than that of pure water. Liquid can therefore remain beside ice at a temperature below zero degrees Celsius.

Salt first needs a film of water in which to dissolve. As a result, some ice melts to make more brine. Melting requires energy because molecules in liquid water have more freedom of motion than molecules locked in ice. That energy comes from the mixture and anything exchanging heat with it, so the bath becomes colder. Salt does not act as a packet of cold; it changes which phase is favored, and the resulting melting absorbs thermal energy.

Concentration matters. More dissolved particles can lower the freezing point across a useful range, but the effect is not unlimited. Eventually no more salt dissolves, while incoming heat and melting ice keep changing the mixture. Hand-cranked freezers used this behavior by placing an ice-and-salt bath around a separate container. Heat moved from the inner mixture into the colder brine as the crank turned it. The device did not make winter from salt alone. It arranged dissolution, melting, and heat transfer so that an ice bath could settle at a colder equilibrium.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point, causing ice to melt and absorb energy so an ice bath can become colder.
Salt contains stored cold that it releases as soon as it touches dry ice.
An ice bath stays at exactly zero degrees Celsius regardless of what dissolves in it.
Hand-cranked freezers worked by mixing salt directly into every food they cooled.
questions.explanation: The text connects freezing-point change, melting, energy absorption, and the colder brine; that full chain is the passage's central explanation.

questions.stem: Why does the temperature fall after some of the ice begins to melt?
choices: The salt blocks all heat from entering the bowl forever.
Melting draws thermal energy from the mixture and nearby material.
The ice releases new salt ions as its crystal structure opens.
The liquid stops exchanging energy with everything around it.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says melting requires energy and that this energy comes from the mixture and objects exchanging heat with it.

questions.stem: In this passage, what is “brine”?
choices: A layer of pure ice with no liquid water
Energy stored inside a hand crank
Water containing dissolved salt
A container that prevents all heat transfer
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says salt dissolves into ions and creates brine, so brine is the resulting saltwater solution.

questions.stem: How did historic hand-cranked freezers use the ice-and-salt mixture?
choices: They burned the brine beneath an open bowl.
They froze the crank before attaching it to the container.
They replaced the inner mixture entirely with salt.
They placed colder brine around a separate inner container.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that an ice-and-salt bath surrounded a separate container and received heat from the mixture inside.

lesson.strategy: Follow the causal chain in order: salt dissolves, the freezing point falls, ice melts, and melting absorbs energy. Keep cause and temperature change separate at each link.

signals.means: Marks the intervention that changes the ice-water balance.
Introduces the melting that follows formation of lower-freezing brine.
Signals a limit and explains why the cooling effect cannot increase forever.

vocab.inContext: liquid water containing dissolved salt ions
relating to heat energy in the mixture
a balance among ice, liquid, salt, and temperature

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the lowered freezing point and the energy absorbed by melting; either fact alone is incomplete.
skillTips.inference: Trace where the energy required for melting comes from to explain why the surroundings cool.
skillTips.vocabulary: The clause before “brine” names dissolved ions, providing the local definition of the solution.
skillTips.detail: For the historical application, identify what surrounded the inner container and where its heat moved.

passages.title: Mary Engle Pennington Tracks the Cold
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Mary Engle Pennington treated refrigeration as a continuous journey rather than a single cold room. Born in 1872, she studied chemistry and biology at the University of Pennsylvania. Women then received certificates rather than bachelor's degrees there, but she earned a doctorate in 1895. After running a clinical laboratory in Philadelphia, she joined the United States Department of Agriculture in 1905 as a bacteriological chemist.

Following the 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act, Pennington became chief of the new Food Research Laboratory. Her team studied perishable foods and compared temperature conditions with bacterial growth and visible deterioration. Their work showed why foods needed steady cold, not cooling at isolated moments. Pennington followed the practical problem through storage, handling, transportation, and distribution. A well-cooled warehouse could not protect an egg that warmed elsewhere on its route.

The work joined laboratory evidence to ordinary equipment and routines. She examined containers and transport conditions and insisted that freshness claims be measured. She did not invent the refrigerator or build the cold chain alone. Engineers, drivers, warehouse workers, inspectors, and many others maintained its continuity.

After leaving federal service in 1919, Pennington continued work on food preservation and later on frozen foods. Her lasting contribution was a way of seeing. Cold was not a treatment applied once; it was a condition that every transfer had to preserve. By making the gaps between facilities part of the scientific question, she helped turn refrigeration from a collection of cold places into a connected system.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Pennington became known mainly for inventing the first household refrigerator by herself.
Mary Engle Pennington used scientific evidence to show that reliable refrigeration depends on continuous care across an entire food journey.
The Food Research Laboratory studied only the appearance of food and avoided temperature measurements.
Cold storage succeeded once warehouses became cool, regardless of later transport or handling.
questions.explanation: The biography follows Pennington from laboratory research to storage, transport, and distribution, emphasizing continuity across every transfer.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe refrigeration as a chain?
choices: Every refrigerated container was physically attached to the next one.
Pennington studied only metal links used inside early iceboxes.
A warm stage anywhere along the route could undermine cooling at other stages.
Food could remain cold only when it traveled by one particular company.
questions.explanation: The warehouse-and-egg example shows that success at one location is insufficient if the food warms during another part of its journey.

questions.stem: What does “perishable” mean as used in the passage?
choices: Made entirely from metal containers
Required by a federal employment rule
Able to remain unchanged at any temperature
Likely to spoil or deteriorate without suitable handling
questions.explanation: The laboratory compared temperature with bacterial growth and deterioration in perishable foods, showing that such foods can spoil.

questions.stem: What position did Pennington take in 1905?
choices: She joined the Department of Agriculture as a bacteriological chemist.
She became director of a household refrigerator factory.
She began driving refrigerated deliveries between warehouses.
She left scientific work to manage a university degree program.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly states that Pennington joined the Department of Agriculture in 1905 as a bacteriological chemist.

lesson.strategy: Build a timeline of Pennington's roles, then draw the route followed by refrigerated food. Connect her career events to the larger insight that every handoff can affect continuity.

signals.means: Moves the biography from Pennington's private work into federal research.

signals.phrase: Following the 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act
signals.means: Links a legal change to her leadership of the new laboratory.
Marks the later phase in which her preservation work continued elsewhere.

vocab.inContext: concerned with bacteria and their study
liable to deteriorate without suitable conditions
unbroken maintenance of cold through every stage

skillTips.main-idea: Join the biographical facts to Pennington's systems insight; the passage is about both a career and a continuous cold route.
skillTips.inference: Use the warming egg example to explain why one excellent facility cannot compensate for every weak handoff.
skillTips.vocabulary: Connect “perishable” with the nearby measurements of bacterial growth and visible deterioration.
skillTips.detail: Return to the opening timeline when a question asks for Pennington's position in a particular year.

passages.title: A Price That Comes Back
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A market sells soup in sturdy glass jars. The label lists two amounts: the soup price and a small deposit for the jar. A buyer pays both amounts. When the jar comes back, the market returns the deposit.

This system changes the cost of keeping the container. A customer who returns it pays only for the soup. Someone who keeps or loses it leaves money to help cover a replacement. The system still has costs. Jars must be washed, inspected, carried, and stored.

An easy return counter matters because time can be a price too. The deposit is therefore not a fine or a discount. It is money held temporarily. It connects one person's choice with the reusable jar's next trip.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A soup market earns most of its money by losing reusable jars.
Glass jars have no costs after a customer brings them back.
A refundable deposit encourages jar returns and helps cover containers that do not return.
A deposit is a permanent fine added to every bowl of soup.
questions.explanation: The text shows that returners receive their money back, while money from unreturned jars can help pay for replacements.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say an easy return counter matters?
choices: It makes every glass jar impossible to lose.
It changes soup into a less costly product.
It removes the need to inspect returned containers.
A difficult return would make customers pay with extra time and effort.
questions.explanation: The passage calls time another kind of price, so a convenient counter lowers the nonmoney burden of returning a jar.

questions.stem: What is a “deposit” in this passage?
choices: Money held until a reusable jar is returned
The full cost of making the soup
A payment for washing someone else's dishes
A discount that only applies to lost jars
questions.explanation: The buyer pays the deposit with the purchase and receives it back when the jar returns, so the money is held temporarily.

questions.stem: What does the market do when a jar comes back?
choices: It charges the soup price a second time.
It returns the customer's deposit.
It gives the customer a permanent fine.
It throws the sturdy jar away.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly says that the market returns the deposit when the jar comes back.

lesson.strategy: Track the same money through two outcomes: a returned jar and a missing jar. Then separate the soup's price from the temporary payment tied to the container.

signals.means: Introduces the action that causes the deposit to be returned.
Adds the work required even when jars are reused.
Clarifies that a deposit is not a permanent charge.

vocab.inContext: a payment returned when the jar comes back
a new jar needed when another does not return
for a limited time rather than forever

skillTips.main-idea: Explain what happens to the deposit in both outcomes, not merely that the jar can be reused.
skillTips.inference: Treat time as a cost when reasoning about why the place of return changes customer behavior.
skillTips.vocabulary: Follow the deposit from payment to refund to understand what the market is holding.
skillTips.detail: The return action and its result appear together in the final sentence of the first paragraph.

passages.title: The Empty Square Beside the Stove
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The most useful part of our kitchen counter is the part we try to fill. A clear square beside the stove looks wasted when jars, appliances, and decorations all compete for room. Then a hot pot needs to land, groceries need sorting, or two cooks must pass a bowl without balancing it on the sink.

I have come to see emptiness as equipment. It asks for little beyond restraint, yet it gives each task a stable beginning and ending. In a shared kitchen, clear space is also a courtesy to the person whose next plan we cannot predict. Filling every surface spends that capacity before the need arrives.

The point is not that every counter should look bare. Useful tools deserve homes within reach. The distinction is between unused and available. A packed surface displays what is already owned; a deliberate gap offers possibility. The empty square performs no task by itself. It lets the next pair of hands begin without first moving someone else's world.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Kitchen decorations should always be moved into the sink before cooking.
Only hot pots deserve a permanent place on a shared counter.
A counter is useful only when every tool remains visible on it.
Deliberately open counter space is useful capacity that supports tasks and other people.
questions.explanation: The essay gives several uses for the clear square and reframes its emptiness as available capacity and courtesy.

questions.stem: Why does the writer call emptiness “equipment”?
choices: The open area enables work even though it is not a physical tool.
The square contains a hidden appliance beneath the counter.
An empty surface requires more repairs than a filled surface.
The writer wants every kitchen to remove all useful objects.
questions.explanation: The clear area receives pots, groceries, and shared work, so its availability performs a practical function like equipment.

questions.stem: What does “restraint” mean in this essay?
choices: Adding more shelves whenever an object appears
Choosing not to fill the available space
Balancing a bowl on the edge of a sink
Hiding all kitchen tools beyond reach
questions.explanation: The empty square stays useful only when people resist filling it, so restraint means holding back from occupying the space.

questions.stem: Which need does the writer name for the clear square?
choices: Displaying every jar owned by the household
Keeping decorations close to the stove
Giving a hot pot a place to land
Preventing groceries from entering the kitchen
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph lists a hot pot needing to land as one reason the clear counter space becomes useful.

lesson.strategy: Notice how the essay reverses the meaning of “empty.” Gather each task the clear square enables, then explain why availability can be a useful feature rather than a lack.

signals.means: Turns an apparently wasted area into space needed for a real task.
Expands the argument from personal convenience to courtesy for others.
Introduces the essay's key contrast between unused and available.

vocab.inContext: the choice not to occupy every open surface
room available for work that has not happened yet
kept open by intention rather than by accident

skillTips.main-idea: Use the repeated examples to show that the gap is practical space, not merely a style preference.
skillTips.inference: Ask what the empty square allows people to do before deciding why the writer calls it equipment.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast restraint with the nearby image of jars and appliances competing to fill the counter.
skillTips.detail: The first paragraph supplies concrete kitchen actions; later paragraphs interpret what those actions mean.

passages.title: The Bell and the Iron Hammer
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At the door of a hill-town kitchen hung a brass Bell. A maple Mallet struck it before each shared meal, making a clear note that crossed the market. Across the courtyard, an Iron Hammer set hinges and straightened bent hooks. The Bell admired the sparks around the Hammer and began to despise its quiet partner.

Before winter supper, the Bell asked for the strongest blow in town. The Hammer warned that strength required fit, but the Bell called caution envy. On the first blow, sound rolled over the roofs. On the second blow, the Bell's thin rim folded inward. What followed was not grander music but a dull buzz, and half the diners missed the call.

A tinker spent two days easing the brass back into shape. A faint crease remained. At the next meal, the Mallet sounded the Bell gently, and a clear note reached the last house. Later, when the kitchen gate sagged, the Hammer reset its hinge with three exact blows. The Bell finally understood that neither tool was weak; each was strong where material and task could receive it. From then on, the Bell asked not for the hardest strike, but for a fitted one.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: A tool serves well when its force fits the material and task, rather than when it is simply the strongest.
Every public bell should be struck with an iron hammer to reach distant houses.
A maple mallet can repair any hinge more exactly than a metal tool.
Visible sparks prove that one tool is useful for every kind of work.
questions.explanation: The iron hammer damages the bell but repairs the hinge, while the mallet gives the bell a clear note, showing that fitness depends on the task.

questions.stem: Why did half the diners miss the supper call?
choices: The tinker moved the kitchen beyond the last house.
The damaged bell produced a dull buzz instead of its clear signal.
The maple mallet refused to strike before winter.
The iron hammer repaired the gate during the meal.
questions.explanation: After the rim folds, the passage replaces the bell's carrying note with a dull buzz and then says half the diners missed the call.

questions.stem: What does “fitted” mean in the final sentence?
choices: Louder than any sound heard before
Decorated to look like another tool
Well matched to the object and purpose
Too weak to produce a useful result
questions.explanation: The ending contrasts a fitted strike with the hardest strike, so fitted means suited to the bell's material and job.

questions.stem: What remained after the tinker reshaped the bell?
choices: A broken maple handle
A loose kitchen hinge
A layer of sparks on the rim
A faint crease in the brass
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly states that a faint crease remained after the tinker eased the brass back into shape.

lesson.strategy: Compare each tool in two moments: striking the bell and repairing the gate. The reversal shows that strength is not a fixed ranking; it depends on material and purpose.

signals.means: Sets up the Bell's test of the stronger tool.
Marks the moment when excess force changes pride into damage.
Shows the repaired bell succeeding again with the matched mallet.

vocab.inContext: the metal from which the kitchen bell is made
resentment the Bell wrongly attributes to the Hammer
matched in force to a particular material and job

skillTips.main-idea: Use both outcomes (the bent bell and repaired hinge) to express the fable's lesson about appropriate force.
skillTips.inference: Connect the changed sound after the folded rim with the diners' failure to recognize the call.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast between “hardest” and “fitted” defines the final word through the story's two tools.
skillTips.detail: After the tinker works, separate what was restored from the small mark that could not be removed.

passages.title: The Shared Thermostat Has No Neutral Number
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A meeting room contains one thermostat and twelve bodies. One person sits beneath a vent in a coat; another loosens a collar beside a window. At first glance, setting one temperature looks equal. Yet the same air can place different burdens on different people. Is there a fair number?

The group could vote. Majority rule gives a clear result, but the same minority might lose every day. A fixed rule offers predictability, yet predictable discomfort is discomfort. Giving control to whoever reports the greatest need sounds responsive, but people describe sensation differently, and the loudest voice is not necessarily the strongest claim.

The puzzle reveals that a number does not become impartial merely because it appears on a machine. Fairness may also depend on the procedure around the dial: whether preferences can be voiced without embarrassment, whether seats or layers can change, and whether yesterday's decision can be revised. Such accommodations do not erase conflict. Heating and cooling use shared energy, and one adjustment can affect the entire room.

In the end, philosophy cannot supply a magic temperature. It can distinguish equality of setting from equality of consideration. A fair process gives reasons that others may question and leaves a path for correction when effects differ from expectations. The thermostat governs machinery. The community still decides whose experience counts and how disagreement will be carried.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The fairest room always gives permanent thermostat control to the loudest speaker.
A shared temperature becomes fair through how differing needs are considered, not through one automatically neutral number.
Equal treatment requires every person to feel the same physical sensation.
Philosophy can calculate a perfect temperature without hearing from anyone in the room.
questions.explanation: The passage tests several rules and concludes that fairness lies in reasons, voice, accommodation, and revision rather than a magic setting.

questions.stem: Why is a number on the thermostat not automatically impartial?
choices: The thermostat displays a different number to every person.
No temperature can be measured in a sunny room.
One setting can affect people differently and can reflect an unfair decision process.
A printed number always changes when a group votes.
questions.explanation: The opening shows different burdens under the same air, while later paragraphs show that the rule for choosing the number also matters.

questions.stem: What does “impartial” mean in this passage?
choices: Easy to revise after every minute
Expensive to maintain with shared energy
Based only on the position of a vent
Not unfairly favoring one person or group
questions.explanation: The discussion asks whether the setting and procedure treat competing experiences fairly, so impartial means not favoring a side unfairly.

questions.stem: What problem does the passage identify with majority rule?
choices: The same minority could lose the temperature vote every day.
It prevents the thermostat from displaying any number.
It requires the room to have more than one sunny window.
The majority must always wear coats beneath the vent.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that majority rule is clear but may leave the same minority losing on every occasion.

lesson.strategy: List each proposed decision rule and the objection that follows it. Then separate equal settings from equal consideration to identify the philosophical question beneath the thermostat.

signals.means: Introduces an appealing idea of equality that the passage will complicate.
Moves from practical options to the deeper issue of impartiality.
Signals the conclusion about fair procedure rather than a magic number.

vocab.inContext: the quality of knowing the setting in advance
not unfairly favoring one person's claim
adjustments that respond to differing needs

skillTips.main-idea: Do not choose one thermostat rule as the gist; summarize why the passage values a revisable, reasoned process.
skillTips.inference: Pair the same numerical setting with the two people in the opening to see why equal input can yield unequal burden.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the fairness question surrounding the machine to infer what “impartial” must exclude.
skillTips.detail: Each proposed rule is followed immediately by its weakness; keep the objection attached to the correct rule.

passages.title: When a Mug Becomes Yours
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At a swap table, a mug may seem worth little until it is placed in your hand and called yours. Asked what you would pay to acquire an identical mug, you might name an amount. Asked what you would accept to give up the mug you possess, you might demand more. Researchers call this ownership-linked gap the endowment effect.

One explanation begins with a reference point. Before ownership, not acquiring the mug is ordinary. Afterward, surrender can feel like a loss, which may weigh more than a comparable gain. Possession may also redirect attention. A seller pictures tomorrow's coffee, the familiar handle, and future use, while a buyer notices alternatives. These accounts can operate together.

But the result is not a law. Procedures, expectations, market experience, and an object's meaning can reduce the gap. People who trade certain goods routinely may treat them as inventory rather than as personal belongings. A poorly designed exchange can confuse reluctance to trade with uncertainty about a fair price. The effect therefore does not prove that ownership automatically transforms every value.

In a shared cupboard, the same shift can complicate clearing a crowded shelf. The owner of an unused pan imagines a future meal; the organizer sees present demand and scarce space. Naming the endowment effect does not decide who is right. It reveals that possession can move the viewpoint before discussion begins. A careful decision can separate memory, likely future use, and replacement cost from the bare fact that an object has crossed an ownership boundary.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every owner demands the same high price for every object in every market.
A shared cupboard should discard all pans that have not been used recently.
Ownership can change how people value an object, but context and competing explanations limit this endowment effect.
The endowment effect proves that memories have no proper place in decisions about belongings.
questions.explanation: The passage explains several ownership-based mechanisms, then qualifies them with procedural, contextual, and practical limits.

questions.stem: Why might experienced traders show a smaller ownership-linked gap?
choices: They cannot tell whether an object belongs to them.
They always value every item at no cost.
They are required to forget all possible future uses.
They may view goods as inventory meant for exchange rather than as personal possessions.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph contrasts routine inventory with personal belongings, implying that an exchange frame can weaken attachment to present ownership.

questions.stem: What is an “endowment” in the phrase “endowment effect”?
choices: Something a person currently possesses
A price chosen by an outside organizer
A defect hidden inside a used object
A rule that forces every owner to sell
questions.explanation: The entire effect begins when the mug is given to someone and becomes that person's possession, making endowment refer to what is owned.

questions.stem: What does the seller picture that the buyer may not?
choices: A rule banning mugs from the swap table
Tomorrow's coffee and the familiar handle
A laboratory with no objects to exchange
A guarantee that the mug will rise in price
questions.explanation: The second paragraph specifically says the seller pictures tomorrow's coffee, the familiar handle, and possible future use.

lesson.strategy: Compare buyer and owner viewpoints before reading the qualifications. Then sort the explanations (loss, attention, and context) so the effect is not mistaken for an automatic rule.

signals.means: Introduces the reference-point account of the ownership gap.

signals.phrase: But the result is not a law
signals.means: Signals limits on when and how strongly the effect appears.
Applies the psychological idea to an ordinary resource decision.

vocab.inContext: an object already placed in someone's possession
the starting state against which a change feels like gain or loss
goods held for routine exchange rather than personal use

skillTips.main-idea: Balance the ownership effect with the passage's explicit warning that procedures and expectations can alter it.
skillTips.inference: Contrast personal belongings with inventory to reason about how an experienced trader frames the same object.
skillTips.vocabulary: Trace the word “endowment” back to the moment the mug is placed in a person's hand and called theirs.
skillTips.detail: The attention explanation lists the seller's imagined uses in the middle of the second paragraph.

passages.title: How an Induction Cooktop Heats a Pan
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An induction cooktop can warm a pan without a glowing burner. Beneath the glass, a coil carries a rapidly changing electric current. The current creates a changing magnetic field.

When a compatible metal pan sits above the coil, the field induces electric currents inside the pan. Electrical resistance changes their energy into heat. As a result, the pan itself becomes the heater, and food warms by contact with it. The glass can still grow hot because the pan sends heat back into it. The cooktop does not heat the pan mainly by warming the glass first.

Not every pot responds strongly to the field. Its material and construction matter. When the pan is removed, the induced currents stop. The technology transfers energy into a suitable vessel instead of using a flame or a hot coil on the surface.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: An induction cooktop first heats its glass until every kind of pot becomes hot.
A hidden flame beneath the glass warms food without touching a pan.
All pots respond equally because their material does not affect induction.
An induction cooktop uses a changing magnetic field to create heating currents inside compatible cookware.
questions.explanation: The passage follows energy from the coil's magnetic field into electric currents and resistance heating within a suitable pan.

questions.stem: Why can the glass surface become hot during cooking?
choices: The heated pan can transfer some of its heat back to the glass.
The glass contains the only electrical resistance in the system.
A flame touches the top of the glass around the pan.
Every magnetic field is made from stored heat.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the glass can grow hot because the pan, already heated by induction, sends heat back into it.

questions.stem: What does “induces” mean in the passage?
choices: Measures the pan's weight
Causes electric currents to arise
Blocks all energy from moving
Paints the coil beneath the glass
questions.explanation: The changing field produces currents inside the pan, so induces means causes those currents to arise.

questions.stem: Where is the cooktop's coil located?
choices: Inside the food
Around the pan's handle
Beneath the glass surface
Above a visible flame
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly locates the coil beneath the glass.

lesson.strategy: Trace the energy path through four parts: coil, magnetic field, pan currents, and heat. This sequence explains why the cookware, rather than the glass, is heated first.

signals.means: Locates the hidden coil that begins the energy transfer.
Connects electrical resistance to the pan becoming hot.
Shows what happens when compatible cookware leaves the field.

vocab.inContext: the wire component carrying changing current below the glass
the electrical property that turns current energy into heat
made to respond suitably to the magnetic field

skillTips.main-idea: Name both the changing magnetic field and the currents created inside suitable cookware.
skillTips.inference: Separate the pan's first source of heat from the heat it later sends back into the glass.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read the subject and result around “induces” to see that the field causes currents inside the pan.
skillTips.detail: The opening locates the coil before the passage explains what that coil produces.

passages.title: The Purple Tile
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Only one tile in the repair box was purple. Every other tile in West Market underpass was white. Nia set the bright square into an empty patch and aligned the grout, but she left thinking the repair looked like a mistake.

The next afternoon, a fruit seller told a delivery driver to turn left at the purple tile. By Friday, a violinist was meeting a student there, and two children counted their steps from it to the stairs. The mismatch did what the uniform wall could not: it gave the long corridor an address.

When the white tiles arrived, Nia returned with her tools. Her supervisor asked whether a sound tile should become rubble merely to hide a useful difference. Nia studied the clean purple square, then used the new tile on another damaged patch. She sealed the purple grout and marked the landmark on the maintenance map. She had thought a good repair had to disappear. This one finished its work by becoming easy to find.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Nia learns that a visible repair can gain an unexpected public use instead of needing to disappear.
The underpass must be rebuilt because people cannot follow directions near white walls.
A fruit seller secretly damages tiles so delivery drivers will stop nearby.
The supervisor orders Nia to replace every white tile with a purple one.
questions.explanation: Nia first sees the purple patch as a mistake, then keeps it after observing that people use it as a shared landmark.

questions.stem: Why does Nia decide not to replace the purple tile?
choices: She has lost every tool needed to remove it.
It is sound, useful as a landmark, and need not become waste.
The white tiles have all turned purple during delivery.
She wants the corridor to remain damaged.
questions.explanation: The supervisor calls the tile sound, people rely on its location, and Nia chooses to use the new white tile on another damaged place.

questions.stem: What does “uniform” mean in the phrase “uniform wall”?
choices: Covered with written directions
Unsafe for people to walk beside
The same in appearance throughout
Made from several bright colors
questions.explanation: Every other tile is white, so the uniform wall is visually the same until the single purple square provides a point of difference.

questions.stem: How does the fruit seller use the purple tile?
choices: The seller removes it from the wall.
The seller paints it white.
The seller counts it as damaged stock.
The seller uses it when giving a driver directions.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the fruit seller tells a delivery driver to turn left at the purple tile.

lesson.strategy: Track how the purple tile's meaning changes for Nia: mistake, observed landmark, and accepted repair. The public's actions provide the evidence for her final choice.

signals.means: Begins the evidence that other people see value in the visible patch.
Shows that use of the tile as a meeting point has spread.
Creates the final choice between replacing and preserving the purple tile.

vocab.inContext: the public corridor where Nia repairs the wall
visually the same across the white tiled wall
a recognizable point people use to locate places

skillTips.main-idea: Center the gist on Nia's changed judgment and the practical use that causes it.
skillTips.inference: Combine the tile's sound condition with the directions and meetings that now depend on its color.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast the single purple square with all the white tiles to define “uniform.”
skillTips.detail: The fruit seller's direction appears at the start of the paragraph describing public uses.

passages.title: Winter Stored for Summer
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before mechanical refrigeration, winter cold could be harvested as a material. In many cold regions, workers first cleared snow from frozen ponds and lakes. They scored the ice into a grid, cut blocks with saws, and guided the heavy pieces toward shore with poles and hooks. Ice cutting was skilled seasonal labor, not a gift that moved itself.

Inside the icehouse, blocks were packed into a large, close stack. Thick walls, earth, dry straw, or sawdust slowed heat moving in from summer air. Loose insulating material often filled space near the walls and covered the top. Drainage carried meltwater away so it did not pool around the remaining blocks. Some ice was always lost, but careful packing preserved much of the store for later use.

Later, commercial networks carried natural ice by wagon, ship, and rail. Homes and businesses used delivered blocks in insulated iceboxes, which required regular attention as the ice melted. Mechanical ice making and electric refrigerators eventually displaced much of this trade. The old system shows that stored cold was never merely a substance. It joined winter labor, building design, waste material, transport, and repeated delivery so that part of one season could serve another.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Natural ice reached summer without insulation, labor, transport, or loss.
Before mechanical refrigeration, people built coordinated systems to harvest, insulate, store, and deliver winter ice.
Electric refrigerators were used to cut blocks from frozen ponds.
Icehouses created cold by burning straw and sawdust beneath their floors.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph covers one part of the system (harvesting, insulated storage, and distribution) before the conclusion joins them.

questions.stem: Why were blocks packed into one large, close stack?
choices: A close stack made every block melt at once.
Workers wanted summer air to reach more ice surfaces.
Compact packing reduced exposure to incoming heat and helped preserve the store.
The stack allowed meltwater to remain around the blocks.
questions.explanation: The paragraph pairs close stacking with insulation that slows heat, so compact storage helped limit melting rather than encourage it.

questions.stem: What does “insulated” mean in the description of iceboxes?
choices: Painted to resemble a winter pond
Connected directly to an electric freezer
Built to collect warm rainwater
Protected by material that slows heat transfer
questions.explanation: Earlier, the passage describes walls, earth, straw, and sawdust slowing summer heat, which establishes what insulated boxes do.

questions.stem: Which materials were used to slow heat entering an icehouse?
choices: Earth, dry straw, and sawdust
Fresh leaves and liquid water
Thin glass and exposed iron
Salt, cloth, and open windows
questions.explanation: The storage paragraph names thick walls, earth, dry straw, and sawdust as barriers that slowed summer heat.

lesson.strategy: Organize the history as a cold supply chain: harvest, store, transport, and use. At each stage, identify the labor or material that kept winter ice available later.

signals.means: Begins the ordered labor required before blocks could be cut.
Moves from harvesting ice to preserving it through warmer months.
Shifts from storage to the wider distribution of natural ice.

vocab.inContext: collected from winter ice as a useful seasonal material
a way for melted water to leave the stored blocks
protected with material that slows heat movement

skillTips.main-idea: Include the whole system rather than reducing the history to the act of sawing ice from a pond.
skillTips.inference: Connect close packing to the passage's repeated goal of slowing incoming heat and limiting melt.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the listed wall materials and their stated effect to define “insulated.”
skillTips.detail: The second paragraph groups the storage materials together before explaining drainage and loss.

passages.title: The Room Beneath the Snow
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
