passages.title: The Ancient Game That Traveled
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Long ago, people played a board game now called the game of twenty squares. Beautiful boards were found in royal graves at Ur in Mesopotamia. Simpler boards appeared across a much wider region.

Players carried game pieces along rivers and trade roads. The board pattern traveled with them. Local players may have changed rules or made the board from different materials. Most early players left no written instructions.

A later clay tablet gives rules for one version. It helps scholars interpret old boards, but it does not prove that every community played alike. Games move like stories: people learn a pattern, teach it, and adjust it.

The scattered boards record more than free time. They show people sharing ideas across languages and borders. A game can travel without one official rulebook, held in memory by the people who play.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every ancient community followed one official printed rulebook.
Ancient boards show a game spreading between communities that may have adapted its remembered rules.
The game of twenty squares stayed only inside royal graves at Ur.
A clay tablet proves how every early player used each board.
questions.explanation: The passage connects widespread boards with travel, local change, incomplete rules, and cultural exchange.

questions.stem: Why can’t the tablet prove that everyone played alike?
choices: The tablet contains no marks at all.
Players never carried games along trade routes.
It records one version from one time rather than every community’s practice.
All boards were made from one material.
questions.explanation: The text presents the tablet as helpful evidence while explicitly limiting it to a version.

questions.stem: What does “interpret” mean?
choices: destroy an ancient board
write one rule for the future
win a game in a royal grave
use evidence to explain the likely meaning of something
questions.explanation: Scholars use the tablet to make sense of boards whose instructions are missing.

questions.stem: Where were beautiful boards found?
choices: in royal graves at Ur
inside modern schools
beneath a lighthouse
on theater stages
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph names royal graves at Ur as the find location.

lesson.strategy: Separate physical evidence from reconstructed rules. The boards prove that a pattern traveled more securely than they prove exactly how each community played.

signals.means: This expands the game beyond the famous royal examples at Ur.
This limits what one written rules source can establish.
This turns game objects into evidence of communication among communities.

vocab.inContext: an ancient region around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
a flat piece of clay used here for written signs
use evidence to explain possible meaning

skillTips.main-idea: Include travel, local adaptation, and incomplete evidence in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the tablet’s limit by distinguishing one recorded version from many places and eras.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use scholars making sense of boards to define interpret.
skillTips.detail: For the excavation detail, return to the named place in the first paragraph.

passages.title: How a Pitcher Plant Sets a Trap
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Some pitcher plants grow where soil provides little usable nitrogen. Their leaves form deep cups that collect liquid. Bright color, scent, or nectar can attract an insect to the rim.

The rim may become very slippery when wet. An insect loses its grip and falls inside. Downward-pointing hairs and smooth walls make climbing out difficult. Fluid in the pitcher traps the animal, and enzymes or tiny organisms help break its body into nutrients the plant can absorb.

The plant still makes sugars through photosynthesis. Insects supply nutrients, not the plant's main energy. This distinction matters because “meat-eating plant” can create the wrong picture of how it lives.

A pitcher is not perfectly closed to all animals. Some small organisms live safely in its fluid, and certain insects can escape or avoid the rim. The trap is a modified leaf that improves the plant's chances in poor ground. It is effective without being certain.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A pitcher plant gets all of its energy by eating insects.
Every animal that touches a pitcher plant is trapped permanently.
A pitcher plant’s modified leaf attracts and traps some insects, gaining nutrients that scarce soil does not provide.
Pitcher plants grow only where soil contains unlimited nitrogen.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the trap’s structure, nutritional role, exceptions, and habitat advantage.

questions.stem: Why is the “meat-eating plant” picture incomplete?
choices: The pitcher is not made from a leaf.
Insects provide light instead of nutrients.
The plant cannot absorb any material from prey.
The plant still captures sunlight to make sugars through photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph separates the insect nutrients from the plant’s primary energy-making process.

questions.stem: What does “modified” mean here?
choices: changed in form to perform a specialized job
damaged so it no longer functions
made entirely by insects
removed from the plant
questions.explanation: The leaf takes the form of a trapping cup, showing a specialized change in structure.

questions.stem: What can make the rim slippery?
choices: dry soil
water
sugar made in roots
downward light
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the rim may become very slippery when wet.

lesson.strategy: Trace the physical trap from attraction to fall to digestion, then keep nutrients separate from energy. The final exceptions prevent the mechanism from becoming a guarantee.

signals.means: This corrects the idea that captured animals replace photosynthesis.
This introduces organisms that resist, avoid, or live within the trap.
This summarizes effectiveness as probability rather than automatic success.

vocab.inContext: sweet liquid that can attract visiting animals
substances that speed the breakdown of materials
changed into a form suited to a particular function

skillTips.main-idea: Include the altered leaf, capture sequence, and nutrient benefit in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer what the label misses by comparing nutrients with sugar production from light.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the leaf becoming a specialized cup to define modified.
skillTips.detail: For the slippery condition, return to the rim description early in paragraph two.

passages.title: What Happens to a Returned Package
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A return does not simply travel backward. Its label directs it to a seller, warehouse, or return center. Each scan links the parcel with its order and return reason. Workers inspect the item. An unopened product in sound packaging may be restocked. A damaged box can be replaced if the product remains new. Electronics may need testing and removal of personal data. Clothing may be checked for wear, stains, and missing tags.

Not every usable item returns to inventory. Some are sold as open-box goods, sent to an outlet, repaired, donated, or grouped for a secondary market. Products that are unsafe, too costly to process, or impossible to resell may be recycled when facilities exist. Others become waste.

The route depends on value, condition, handling cost, safety rules, and the seller's system. Transport itself also uses labor, packaging, and fuel. A free return label means the customer may not pay a separate fee; it does not mean the return has no cost.

Clear descriptions and packing can prevent some avoidable returns or damage. Once a parcel comes back, records help workers choose the next path. The reverse journey is therefore a sorting process, not the simple undoing of a sale.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every returned package goes directly back onto the same store shelf unopened.
A free return label means transport and inspection use no resources.
All damaged goods must become waste even when repair is practical.
Returned goods follow a recorded inspection and sorting process that weighs condition, safety, value, and handling cost.
questions.explanation: The passage traces routing, inspection, possible destinations, costs, and the role of records.

questions.stem: Why might a working product not return to ordinary inventory?
choices: Its opened condition, processing needs, or sales category may direct it to another channel.
A scan prevents anyone from identifying the original order.
Working products are never allowed in secondary markets.
The return label always requires destruction.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists open-box sale, outlet, repair, donation, and secondary markets for usable items.

questions.stem: What does “restocked” mean?
choices: mailed to the same customer again
placed back into inventory for ordinary sale
erased from all order records
taken apart for raw material
questions.explanation: An unopened, sound product can return to the seller’s normal stock.

questions.stem: What may need to be removed from returned electronics?
choices: every working part
the package label
personal data
all safety rules
questions.explanation: The inspection paragraph names personal data removal for electronic products.

lesson.strategy: Follow the parcel through routing, inspection, classification, and destination. The passage distinguishes a customer-facing free label from the real resources used behind it.

signals.means: This rejects the idea that a return is a sale running backward.
This widens possible routes beyond ordinary restocking.
This separates zero separate customer fee from zero system cost.

vocab.inContext: returned to ordinary inventory so it can be sold again
a channel where goods are resold outside ordinary new inventory
goods a seller currently holds for sale

skillTips.main-idea: Include records, inspection, multiple routes, and real processing costs in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer alternate sales channels from condition and processing differences even when a product works.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast between inspection and normal inventory to define restocked.
skillTips.detail: For electronics, locate the special inspection steps in paragraph two.

passages.title: Reading Time in Ancient Wood
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A living tree takes in atmospheric carbon. It includes a small amount of radioactive carbon-14. After the tree dies, exchange largely stops, and carbon-14 in its wood decays at a known rate. Measuring how much remains can help estimate when the living material stopped exchanging carbon.

The measurement is not a clock with a printed calendar date. Laboratories compare carbon-14 with stable carbon and report an age with uncertainty. Contamination from newer roots, conservation glue, or older carbon can shift a result. Researchers clean samples and choose material tied closely to the event they want to date.

Atmospheric carbon-14 has varied over time. A raw radiocarbon age must therefore be calibrated against records with independently known dates. Tree rings are valuable because their calendar years can be counted and matched across overlapping wood. Other archives extend parts of the calibration record.

Calibration can turn one measured range into an irregular set of possible calendar ranges. Greater numerical precision in the laboratory does not remove every ambiguity in the curve. Archaeological context also matters. A beam cut from an old tree may be reused centuries later, so the wood's age need not equal the building's age. Radiocarbon dating is powerful because physical decay supplies a measurable connection to time. It is careful rather than magical: sampling, chemistry, calibration, context, and uncertainty all shape the final interpretation.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Radiocarbon dating estimates when organic material stopped exchanging carbon, but sampling, calibration, contamination, context, and uncertainty shape the result.
Carbon-14 gives every ancient object one exact printed calendar date without interpretation.
A reused beam must have grown in the same year its final building was constructed.
Atmospheric carbon-14 has remained perfectly constant through time.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the decay basis while emphasizing the steps required to turn measurement into a historical date.

questions.stem: Why might a timber date be older than a building?
choices: Calibration makes carbon-14 appear in stone walls.
Wood from an old tree or earlier structure may have been reused later.
A building continues absorbing carbon after demolition.
Tree rings can never be matched across wood.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph distinguishes when wood grew from when people used it in the current structure.

questions.stem: What does “calibrated” mean here?
choices: cleaned only with conservation glue
converted from wood into atmospheric gas
adjusted by comparison with independently dated records
reported without any uncertainty
questions.explanation: Raw radiocarbon ages are compared with tree-ring and other dated archives to relate them to calendar time.

questions.stem: What independently dated archive is especially valuable?
choices: new roots
conservation glue
reused beams
tree rings
questions.explanation: The third paragraph identifies countable and matchable tree rings as especially valuable.

lesson.strategy: Separate measurement, radiocarbon age, and calendar interpretation. Then test whether the sample’s biological age answers the archaeological question being asked.

signals.phrase: not a clock with a printed calendar date
signals.means: This warns that measurement must be interpreted rather than read as an exact date.
This links changing atmospheric carbon with comparison to dated records.

signals.phrase: so the wood's age need not equal
signals.means: This introduces reuse as a mismatch between sample date and building event.

vocab.inContext: changes radioactively at a statistically known rate
adjusted through comparison with an independent dated standard
unwanted material that can shift a measurement

skillTips.main-idea: Include physical decay and every major interpretive control in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the old-wood effect by separating tree growth from later reuse in a building.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use tree rings with known years to define calibrated as adjusted against a standard.
skillTips.detail: For the named archive, return to the record whose individual years can be counted.

passages.title: Srinivasa Ramanujan's Notebooks
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Srinivasa Ramanujan filled notebooks with formulas in India, often recording results without the detailed proofs expected in university mathematics. Largely self-taught, he explored number theory, infinite series, continued fractions, and other subjects with originality. Yet unusual notation and missing demonstrations made his work difficult for others to assess.

In 1913, Ramanujan wrote to British mathematician G. H. Hardy and included many claims. Hardy recognized that some were known, some appeared wrong or incomplete, and others could only have come from a remarkable mathematical mind. Ramanujan traveled to Cambridge, where the two men collaborated across differences in training, culture, and proof style.

Their partnership was neither a simple rescue nor effortless harmony. Ramanujan brought deep independent insight; Hardy provided access to a research community and insisted on rigorous proof. War, English weather, restricted food, illness, and separation from home burdened Ramanujan. He returned to India in 1919 and died the next year at age thirty-two. Ramanujan published work during his lifetime, but his notebooks continued to generate research. Later mathematicians supplied proofs, corrected statements, connected formulas with new theories, and discovered unexpected applications. A separate collection known as the “lost notebook” came to scholarly attention decades after his death.

Calling the notebooks unfinished does not make them failed work. They preserve both achievement and invitation: compressed statements born from exceptional intuition, waiting for public verification and extension. Their history shows that mathematics grows through individual imagination and communal checking. A beautiful claim can open a field, while proof makes the path available for others to walk.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the biography?
choices: Ramanujan’s notebooks contained complete university-style proofs for every recorded formula.
Ramanujan’s original formulas and later collaboration left notebooks whose verification and extension continue to shape communal mathematics.
Hardy decided that all the claims in Ramanujan’s first letter were already known and correct.
Later mathematicians ignored the notebooks because unfinished work has no value.
questions.explanation: The biography balances individual insight, proof standards, difficult collaboration, and continuing verification.

questions.stem: Why did missing proofs create difficulty for other mathematicians?
choices: The formulas were written only as musical notes.
Proof would have prevented any later application.
They could not readily check why a claim followed or whether it held in all intended cases.
Hardy required every known claim to be wrong.
questions.explanation: The conclusion distinguishes an inspired claim from a verified path others can examine and reuse.

questions.stem: What does “rigorous” mean when describing proof?
choices: briefly written without any supporting steps
based mainly on personal reputation
translated into a different spoken language
carefully reasoned and able to withstand exact checking
questions.explanation: Hardy’s expectation contrasts with unsupported statements, so rigorous means logically thorough and checkable.

questions.stem: When did Ramanujan return to India?
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says he returned in 1919 and died the following year.

lesson.strategy: Keep discovery, proof, and later verification as distinct contributions. Read the cross-cultural partnership without turning either mathematician into the sole source of Ramanujan’s achievement.

signals.means: This qualifies originality with the problem of public assessment.
This rejects a one-sided story and prepares a more balanced account of collaboration.
This interprets unfinished records as discoveries plus work left for a community.

vocab.inContext: the branch of mathematics concerned with properties of numbers
logically thorough and open to exact checking
insight that reaches a promising idea before all formal steps are stated

skillTips.main-idea: Include Ramanujan’s insight, collaboration, proof, hardship, and posthumous influence in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the problem of missing proof from what communal checking requires before a result can be trusted.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast with compressed unsupported statements to define rigorous.
skillTips.detail: For the return date, keep the 1913 letter, 1919 return, and 1920 death in order.

passages.title: The Market Without a Building
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A market does not always have stalls or one address. Suppose fishers announce today's catch by phone. Restaurants reply with prices and amounts. Buyers and sellers are forming a market through shared information.

The market exists because offers can meet. A buyer learns what is available and what it costs. A seller learns who wants the product. Payment and delivery may happen later in different places.

Clear information helps the market work. If only one buyer knows the catch, fishers may have little basis for comparison. If prices arrive too late, fresh fish may spoil.

Rules and trust also matter. People need to know what a kilogram means, when payment is due, and whether a promise will be kept. A building can make meeting easier, but exchange depends on communication, not walls.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every market must keep all goods and buyers inside one physical hall.
A market exists only after fish have spoiled.
A market can form without one building when buyers and sellers share offers, rules, and enough trust to exchange.
Shared price information prevents sellers from comparing offers.
questions.explanation: The passage defines a market through connected exchange rather than a particular building.

questions.stem: Why do fishers benefit from hearing several offers?
choices: They can make every fish remain fresh forever.
They no longer need units or payment rules.
Restaurants stop requesting any amounts.
They gain information for comparing buyers and prices.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links limited buyer knowledge with a weak basis for comparison.

questions.stem: What does “exchange” mean here?
choices: giving goods or services in return for payment or value
building walls around a product
announcing weather without prices
weighing only one kilogram
questions.explanation: The buyers and sellers coordinate price, product, payment, and delivery.

questions.stem: What unit does the passage say people must understand?
choices: a liter
a kilogram
a mile
an hour
questions.explanation: The final paragraph names agreement about what a kilogram means.

lesson.strategy: Identify the essential connections among offers, comparison, payment, delivery, and trust. The physical location is useful but not part of the definition.

signals.means: This names the informational connection that lets exchange become possible.
This shows how unequal information can weaken comparison.
This contrasts the convenience of a building with the core role of communication.

vocab.inContext: a system connecting buyers and sellers for possible exchange
information or reasoning used to support a comparison
trade goods or services for money or other value

skillTips.main-idea: State the main idea through information, rules, trust, and exchange rather than location.
skillTips.inference: Infer comparison value from the different offers fishers can consider.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use payment and delivery between buyer and seller to define exchange.
skillTips.detail: For the shared unit, return to the examples of rules in the final paragraph.

passages.title: The Value of a Beginner's Map
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An expert crosses a building without noticing its missing signs. Years of practice have turned each choice into habit. “The archive is obvious,” she says, forgetting the three unmarked doors between the entrance and its desk.

A beginner sees the building differently. The first confusing turn, hidden elevator, or unexplained abbreviation remains visible. A map drawn from that journey can reveal assumptions that experienced people no longer feel.

Beginner knowledge has limits. A newcomer may not know why a secure door must remain locked or which route floods in winter. An expert understands patterns that one visit cannot show. The best map joins both views.

Ask a newcomer to mark every pause. Ask an experienced user to explain constraints and rare cases. Then test the map with another person who has never seen the route. Expertise supplies depth; fresh attention reveals the missing bridge into that depth. A beginner is not valuable for knowing less, but for still noticing where knowledge first becomes necessary.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: A newcomer always understands a building more completely than every expert.
Experts should draw maps without watching where new users pause.
Locked doors and seasonal flooding have no effect on route design.
A useful map combines beginners’ notice of confusing gaps with experts’ knowledge of constraints and unusual cases.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that the two perspectives correct different blind spots and should be tested together.

questions.stem: Why should another newcomer test the map?
choices: The test can reveal whether revisions actually help someone without prior route knowledge.
The newcomer can remove every secure door.
Testing makes expert knowledge unnecessary.
One new user knows all winter conditions.
questions.explanation: A second fresh user checks whether the combined map bridges the same knowledge gap in practice.

questions.stem: What does “constraints” mean?
choices: decorations added to an archive
conditions or limits a route must respect
habits that make every sign visible
questions a map must hide
questions.explanation: Locked security doors and seasonally flooded routes are examples of limiting conditions.

questions.stem: What does the author ask a newcomer to mark?
choices: every locked door as open
only the final destination
every pause
the expert’s years of work
questions.explanation: The final paragraph directly asks a newcomer to mark every pause.

lesson.strategy: Compare the blind spots of familiarity with the blind spots of one-time observation. The proposed workflow combines and tests both forms of knowledge.

signals.means: This demonstrates how expertise can hide the steps a newcomer needs.
This prevents fresh perspective from being treated as complete understanding.
This states the essay’s synthesis of beginner and expert perspectives.

vocab.inContext: a place or collection that preserves records
ideas treated as given without being stated or checked
conditions that restrict which choices are possible

skillTips.main-idea: Include the complementary strengths and weaknesses of both perspectives in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the purpose of retesting from the need to verify that missing guidance has been repaired.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use secure doors and winter flooding to define constraints as limiting conditions.
skillTips.detail: For the newcomer task, locate the pair of instructions in the conclusion.

passages.title: The Pebble in the Sandal
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A courier felt a pebble enter her sandal at sunrise. She had promised to deliver a letter before noon. “Stopping will waste time,” she said, and walked faster.

The pebble rubbed one spot on her heel. At the next well, a heron advised her to remove it. The courier saw carts passing and refused. “I have already ignored it for an hour. I can ignore it for one more.”

Soon she changed her stride to avoid the sore place. Her knee began to ache. At last she sat beside the road. The pebble took three breaths to shake free, but the blister made every remaining step slow. The heron passed again near noon. “Was the pebble large?” he asked. “No,” said the courier. “Only the delay was.”

She delivered the letter late. On the return journey, a thread loosened from her bag. She stopped, tied it, and continued before the seam could open. The lesson was not to interrupt every journey for every discomfort. It was to notice which small problem was actively becoming a larger one.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: The courier learns that briefly addressing a growing small problem can prevent a much larger delay later.
Every minor discomfort should end a journey permanently.
The pebble is so large that no traveler could remove it.
Walking faster immediately heals the courier’s blister and knee.
questions.explanation: The pebble, altered stride, blister, and later thread show the compounding cost and the qualified lesson.

questions.stem: Why does the courier mention already ignoring the pebble for an hour?
choices: The pebble has disappeared during that hour.
Past delay makes her feel committed to continuing the same choice.
The heron asks her to count every cart.
Noon has already passed before sunrise.
questions.explanation: She treats earlier endurance as a reason for more endurance even as evidence of harm grows.

questions.stem: What does “stride” mean?
choices: a tied thread in a bag
a drink from a well
the pattern or manner of walking steps
the contents of a letter
questions.explanation: She changes how she walks to protect the sore heel, so stride means her walking pattern.

questions.stem: How long does removing the pebble take?
choices: one hour
until noon
the entire return trip
three breaths
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the pebble takes three breaths to shake free.

lesson.strategy: Follow the cost as it compounds from irritation to changed stride to injury and delay. The final thread example distinguishes growing faults from every passing discomfort.

signals.means: This states the belief the later events test.
This shows a small untreated problem beginning to distort other actions.
This qualifies the moral so it does not demand constant interruption.

vocab.inContext: a person who carries and delivers a message or package
the pattern, length, or manner of walking steps
a sore pocket on skin caused here by repeated rubbing

skillTips.main-idea: State the lesson through compounding harm and timely repair, including the final qualification.
skillTips.inference: Infer her reasoning from how prior endurance becomes a reason to keep enduring.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the changed walk and new knee pain to define stride.
skillTips.detail: For removal time, return to the short action contrasted with the long blister delay.

passages.title: When No One Person Caused the Harm
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A thousand visitors each step off a marked trail once. No single footprint destroys the meadow. Together, the shortcuts crush plants, loosen soil, and create a channel for rain. Who caused the damage? One tempting answer is “nobody,” because each contribution was small. Another is “everybody equally.” Both answers miss important structure. The first lets predictable collective harm disappear inside tiny actions. The second ignores differences in knowledge, power, frequency, and alternatives.

A tour company that brings hundreds of visitors may have more ability to prevent damage than one lost hiker. A park agency controls signs and barriers. A repeat visitor knows more than someone misdirected by a poor map. Responsibility can be distributed without being identical.

Collective problems also require more than private guilt. Better trail design, group rules, repair funds, limited access during recovery, and shared information can change the pattern producing harm. Individual restraint matters, but a system can make the responsible choice easier or harder.

No participant needs to intend the damaged meadow for a duty to arise. Foreseeable effects and capacity to respond matter. Yet blame should remain proportional, and some people may have had no reasonable alternative. The useful question is not only “Whose foot made this bare patch?” It is “Which roles and choices sustained the pattern, and who can now help change it?”

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: When each action is small, nobody can have any responsibility for the combined result.
Collective harm can create unequal shared responsibilities based on contribution, knowledge, power, alternatives, and capacity to repair the system.
Every person connected to collective damage deserves exactly the same blame.
Private guilt alone repairs systems that repeatedly produce harmful choices.
questions.explanation: The passage rejects both no responsibility and equal blame, then develops role-sensitive action and repair.

questions.stem: Why may a tour company bear more responsibility than one lost hiker?
choices: Its individual footprints are always physically larger.
The hiker controls all park signs and barriers.
It directs many visits and has greater knowledge and capacity to change the pattern.
Companies cannot contribute money to repair.
questions.explanation: Scale and institutional control give the company more influence over repeated behavior.

questions.stem: What does “proportional” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: divided into exactly equal shares
limited to people with bad intentions
unrelated to available alternatives
matched in degree to relevant contribution and capacity
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly distinguishes responsibility by role, knowledge, power, and reasonable options.

questions.stem: What physical change can repeated shortcuts create?
choices: a channel for rain
a new marked trail overnight
a stronger meadow surface
a building for visitors
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says loosened soil becomes a rain channel.

lesson.strategy: Compare the two rejected extremes, then map responsibility across roles and capacities. The solution shifts attention from isolated blame to the system that repeats the outcome.

signals.means: This rejects no responsibility and equal responsibility as incomplete.
This states that a duty can be shared in unequal degrees.

signals.phrase: also require more than private guilt
signals.means: This moves from personal feeling to structural prevention and repair.

vocab.inContext: produced or addressed by many people acting within a shared pattern
reasonably possible to predict before the outcome
matched in amount or degree to relevant differences

skillTips.main-idea: Include shared causation, unequal roles, system design, and proportionate response in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the company’s greater duty from the number of visits it directs and the controls it possesses.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the stated differences among participants to define proportional as matched in degree.
skillTips.detail: For the landscape result, return to the chain from footprints through loosened soil.

passages.title: Why We Misjudge Future Feelings
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A student awaiting exam results may predict, “If I fail, I will feel terrible for months.” Before a move, another imagines constant happiness. They are affective forecasts: estimates of how future events will shape emotion. People often predict whether an event will feel pleasant or unpleasant. They are less reliable about intensity and duration. One reason is focalism. The event fills attention, while the rest of life (meals, work, weather, jokes, errands, and other relationships) fades from the picture.

Adaptation also matters. Routines form, attention shifts, and people respond to consequences. A new city eventually includes laundry and traffic; a disappointing result leads to conversations and next steps. This does not mean every emotional wound quickly disappears or every joy becomes ordinary. Events differ, and conditions can have persistent effects. Present feelings color prediction. Hunger or excitement can make it hard to imagine another state. Memory may emphasize an experience's peak and ending rather than its duration. Stories teach people which outcomes are supposed to transform a life.

Better forecasting begins by widening the scene. What will an ordinary Tuesday contain after the event? How did people in similar situations actually feel over time? What parts of life will remain unchanged? These questions do not make emotion calculable, but they correct the spotlight around one outcome.

Forecasting errors matter because predictions guide choices. Caution matters when a decision is irreversible or based on one imagined feeling. A future self will encounter the event inside a whole life, not inside the isolated frame the present mind first constructs.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: People cannot predict whether any future event will feel pleasant or unpleasant.
Every disappointment fades quickly and every joy becomes completely ordinary.
People often misjudge future emotion by spotlighting one event and neglecting adaptation, changing states, ordinary life, and evidence from comparable experiences.
Affective forecasting becomes exact whenever a person imagines only the event’s peak.
questions.explanation: The passage explains several error sources, qualifications, corrective questions, and decision relevance.

questions.stem: Why does the author ask about an ordinary Tuesday?
choices: It guarantees the future emotion will be positive.
It removes the event from the person’s future entirely.
It measures emotion without uncertainty.
It restores routine parts of future life that a vivid focal event may hide.
questions.explanation: The question widens attention beyond the spotlighted outcome to the surrounding life.

questions.stem: What does “focalism” mean here?
choices: overconcentrating on one event while neglecting the rest of the context
forgetting whether an event seems pleasant
adapting instantly to every condition
measuring a feeling through a laboratory lens
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines the event filling attention as other future experiences fade.

questions.stem: What two parts of an experience may memory emphasize?
choices: its meals and weather
its peak and ending
its beginning and exact average
its causes and price
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph directly names the peak and ending as features memory may emphasize.

lesson.strategy: Identify each source of forecasting error separately: focalism, adaptation, present state, memory, and social narrative. The suggested questions widen rather than eliminate uncertainty.

signals.phrase: less reliable about intensity and duration
signals.means: This refines the claim after granting some accuracy about emotional direction.
This prevents adaptation from becoming a universal promise that feelings vanish.
This introduces the main correction for an outcome held in isolation.

vocab.inContext: predictions about the direction, strength, or duration of future feelings
giving one event too much attention while neglecting its wider context
not realistically capable of being undone after a choice

skillTips.main-idea: Include major error mechanisms, their limits, corrective evidence, and decision importance in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the ordinary-Tuesday question’s purpose by contrasting whole life with one vivid event.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the event spotlight and fading background to define focalism.
skillTips.detail: For the memory detail, return to the pair of moments named in paragraph four.

passages.title: The Picture Made of Tiny Dots
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A screen picture is built from tiny parts called pixels. Each pixel can shine with a mix of red, green, and blue light. From nearby, the parts may look like colored dots.

Different brightness levels create many colors. Red and green light together can appear yellow. All three shining strongly can appear white. Dark pixels give off little light.

A screen places rows of pixels close together. From a normal viewing distance, the eye joins them into edges, letters, faces, and shadows. More pixels can show finer detail when the screen size and image support them.

A pixel does not know what it depicts. It follows a number telling each color how brightly to shine. Software changes many numbers rapidly to make video move. The complete picture emerges from a grid of small, coordinated lights.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Each pixel contains a complete picture of a face.
Screens create yellow only by using yellow light inside every dot.
A dark pixel shines all three colors as brightly as possible.
A screen coordinates tiny red, green, and blue pixels at different brightness levels to form complete images.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from one pixel’s colored light to the grid and software that produce an image.

questions.stem: Why do the colored dots look like one picture from farther away?
choices: The eye combines closely spaced pixels into larger shapes and details.
Each dot grows physically larger with distance.
Software turns off every color except white.
The screen removes rows of pixels.
questions.explanation: Normal viewing distance makes the tiny coordinated parts merge perceptually into edges and forms.

questions.stem: What does “pixel” mean?
choices: a full moving video
one tiny controllable picture element on a screen
a lens inside the eye
a row of printed letters
questions.explanation: The opening defines pixels as the tiny parts from which a screen picture is built.

questions.stem: Which three light colors does the passage name?
choices: red, yellow, and black
orange, white, and purple
red, green, and blue
green, gray, and brown
questions.explanation: The first paragraph lists red, green, and blue light in each pixel.

lesson.strategy: Move from one pixel to the full grid. Keep emitted screen light separate from mixed paint, and connect changing numerical instructions with motion.

signals.means: This introduces what the individual image elements look like at close range.
This explains when many small lights merge into recognizable forms.
This separates a pixel’s simple instruction from the meaning viewers see.

vocab.inContext: tiny controllable elements that make up a screen image
the amount of light a pixel gives off
an ordered pattern of rows and columns

skillTips.main-idea: State the main idea from colored subparts through coordinated grid and visible image.
skillTips.inference: Infer visual joining by comparing the close-up dots with the normal-distance picture.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the direct opening definition to identify a pixel as one image element.
skillTips.detail: For the component colors, return to the mixture named in the first paragraph.

passages.title: The Paper Crane on the Bus
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Mei folded a paper crane while riding to her first day at a new school. At her stop, she hurried away and left it on the seat. Mr. Alvarez found the crane. On one wing he wrote, “I hope today is gentle.” He passed it to a nurse boarding at the next stop. She added, “Drink some water.” A mechanic wrote, “Ask for help before the bolt breaks.”

The driver placed the crane near the fare box. All day, riders added tiny messages. Some were serious; one simply said, “The moon looked enormous last night.”

After school, Mei boarded the same bus. She recognized the fold and reached for it. The driver asked her to read the wings before taking it home.

Mei had lost a blank crane and found a crowded one. The messages did not remove the hard parts of her day. They made the city feel less empty. She added, “I sat with someone at lunch,” and left the crane for one more trip.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: A lost paper crane gathers small messages from bus riders and helps Mei feel connected in a new city.
Mei’s crane is thrown away before anyone can find it.
Every rider writes the same advice about school.
The messages make every difficult part of Mei’s day disappear.
questions.explanation: The story follows the object’s community journey and Mei’s realistic change in belonging.

questions.stem: Why does Mei leave the crane for another trip?
choices: She no longer recognizes how the crane was folded.
She wants other riders to continue the shared exchange that helped her.
The driver refuses to let her read any message.
She plans to avoid riding the bus again.
questions.explanation: After receiving connection from the messages, Mei contributes her own and extends the practice.

questions.stem: What does “crowded” mean when describing the crane?
choices: packed with bus passengers inside it
folded from heavy cardboard
filled with many written messages
hidden beneath the fare box
questions.explanation: The contrast with a blank crane shows that writing now fills its wings.

questions.stem: What does the mechanic advise?
choices: Drink some water.
Watch the moon tonight.
Sit alone at lunch.
Ask for help before the bolt breaks.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph assigns the bolt message to the mechanic.

lesson.strategy: Follow how each rider changes the same object, then compare the blank and crowded crane. The ending turns Mei from recipient into participant.

signals.means: This compresses the crane’s continuing exchange among many riders.
This keeps connection from becoming a magical solution to every difficulty.
This shows Mei choosing to continue the community ritual.

vocab.inContext: a bird represented here by folded paper
the place where bus riders pay for a trip
filled closely with many messages in this context

skillTips.main-idea: Include the crane’s journey, collected messages, and Mei’s changed sense of connection.
skillTips.inference: Infer Mei’s final choice from the comfort she receives and the new message she contributes.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the blank-versus-written contrast to define crowded figuratively.
skillTips.detail: For the mechanic’s words, distinguish the three named riders and their separate messages.

passages.title: The Canal Across the Isthmus
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A ship traveling between the Atlantic and Pacific once had to round South America to avoid crossing land at Panama. In the 1880s, a French-led canal project attempted a sea-level passage. Disease, terrain, engineering problems, and financial failure ended that effort.

The United States took over construction after Panama separated from Colombia in 1903 and granted the United States control in a canal zone. The politics involved pressure and unequal power, not only engineering. Workers came from many places, especially the Caribbean, and faced dangerous labor, disease, segregation, and unequal pay.

Builders chose a lock canal. A dam formed Gatun Lake, and lock chambers raised ships to the lake and lowered them on the other side. Excavators cut through hills while drainage and mosquito control reduced yellow fever and malaria.

The canal opened in 1914. It shortened sea routes and changed trade and naval planning. It also divided communities and placed a strip across Panama under foreign control. Panama gradually gained greater authority, receiving full control at the end of 1999. The canal's history cannot be reduced to one engineering triumph. It joins technical adaptation, international commerce, disease control, thousands of workers, environmental change, and a long dispute over sovereignty.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The French sea-level canal opened successfully in 1880 without disease or financial trouble.
The Panama Canal combined major engineering and health work with global labor, unequal power, environmental change, and a long struggle over control.
Panama held complete authority over the canal zone from the first day of United States construction.
The canal changed only ship routes and had no effects on workers or communities.
questions.explanation: The passage deliberately integrates technical achievement with labor conditions, politics, environment, and sovereignty.

questions.stem: Why did builders use locks and a lake?
choices: They wanted every ship to travel around South America.
Locks eliminated the need for a dam or excavation.
They adapted the route to inland elevation instead of cutting one sea-level channel through all terrain.
The French project had already completed a working sea-level passage.
questions.explanation: The lock chambers raise vessels to Gatun Lake and lower them, solving the change in height.

questions.stem: What does “sovereignty” mean?
choices: a chamber that raises one ship
a disease carried by mosquitoes
a payment made to excavators
a country’s authority to govern its territory
questions.explanation: The long dispute concerns foreign control of land across Panama and the later transfer of authority.

questions.stem: When did Panama receive full control?
choices: at the end of 1999
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph gives the end of 1999 as the point of full control.

lesson.strategy: Read engineering, labor, health, politics, and sovereignty as interacting strands. The final paragraph warns against letting one triumph erase the conditions that made it possible.

signals.means: This broadens the history from a technical project to power and politics.
This introduces the design adaptation that overcame elevation.
This rejects a single-story interpretation of the canal.

vocab.inContext: a human-made waterway used here by ships
a chamber that raises or lowers vessels between water levels
the authority of a state to govern its territory

skillTips.main-idea: Include technical achievement and the political and human costs in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the lock design’s purpose from ships being raised to a lake and lowered afterward.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the foreign-control dispute to define sovereignty as governing authority.
skillTips.detail: For the transfer date, keep canal opening and later Panamanian control separate.

passages.title: The Narwhal's Sensitive Tusk
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A narwhal's tusk is a tooth, usually a male’s left upper canine, that grows outward in a long spiral. Females can also grow tusks, and rare individuals have two. Its structure raises questions about function. The tusk contains pathways connected with nerves, and tiny channels link its inner tissues with surrounding seawater. Experiments and anatomy suggest that it can provide sensory information about the environment. Changes in salt concentration may produce responses, for example. Researchers still study how narwhals use it.

Sensory ability is probably not the tusk's only significance. Males may cross or rub tusks, and observations connect it with social display and competition. On rare occasions narwhals have been recorded striking fish with tusks. One behavior does not establish a single universal purpose.

The animal lives in Arctic waters, navigating sea ice and finding prey at depth. A sensitive tooth may carry information unlike vision or hearing, but a useful feature can serve several roles. Evolution does not assign labels such as “sensor” and “weapon” as separate tools in a box.

Caution matters because narwhals are difficult to observe for long periods beneath ice. Evidence comes from anatomy, controlled tests, tags, and limited direct behavior. The best account holds these sources together: the tusk is living tissue capable of sensation, strongly shaped by sex and social life, and still not fully explained.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every narwhal has exactly one tusk used only as a weapon.
The tusk is a lifeless horn with no connection to surrounding seawater.
The narwhal tusk is a living, nerve-connected tooth with sensory and social roles that evidence has not yet reduced to one purpose.
One recorded fish strike proves the universal function of all tusks.
questions.explanation: The passage combines anatomy, experiment, behavior, sex differences, and limits of observation.

questions.stem: Why is it difficult to identify one purpose for the tusk?
choices: The tusk contains no living tissue to study.
Researchers have never examined anatomy or behavior.
Every female and male uses two tusks identically.
Several evidence types suggest different roles, and narwhals are hard to observe beneath ice.
questions.explanation: Multiple plausible functions and limited long-term observations prevent a simple universal conclusion.

questions.stem: What does “canine” mean here?
choices: a type of tooth in the upper jaw
an animal related to a dog
a channel carrying seawater
a tag attached to ice
questions.explanation: The opening identifies the tusk as the left upper canine, explicitly making it a tooth.

questions.stem: What environmental change may the tusk detect?
choices: a change in the number of its teeth
a change in salt concentration
a ship lock opening
a forest growing
questions.explanation: The second paragraph uses salt concentration as an example of a possible sensory response.

lesson.strategy: Sort claims by evidence strength: anatomy shows capacity, experiments suggest sensitivity, and field observations suggest behavior. Avoid turning any single clue into one final function.

signals.means: This marks salt response as one instance rather than a complete explanation.

signals.phrase: probably not the tusk's only significance
signals.means: This opens the account from sensory function to additional social roles.
This preserves uncertainty after drawing the evidence together.

vocab.inContext: one type of jaw tooth, elongated into the narwhal’s tusk
the amount of a substance, such as salt, within a mixture
the physical structures and organization of a living body

skillTips.main-idea: Include the tooth’s living structure, multiple roles, and unresolved questions in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer uncertainty from both hard-to-see behavior and evidence supporting more than one function.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the opening apposition to define canine as a type of tooth.
skillTips.detail: For the sensory example, locate the change named after the seawater channels.

passages.title: The Chain of Custody Behind an Artifact
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A museum receives a figure said to come from a temple. Style may suggest age and place, but not travel or lawful removal. Investigators seek provenance: the history of ownership and location. They also examine chain of custody, the handling sequence during a transfer or investigation.

Records might include excavation notes, permits, customs forms, invoices, collection catalogs, photographs, conservation reports, and signed receipts. Dates and descriptions should connect without unexplained gaps. Material analysis can test whether the object fits the account, but scientific consistency does not prove lawful ownership. A strong record makes substitution or recent manufacture harder to hide. It also assigns responsibility for condition. If a crack appears between two inspections, handling records may show where to investigate. Seals and identification numbers connect object and record.

Documentation can still mislead. A false invoice is a record, and an old catalog may repeat an earlier error. Colonial officials sometimes created legal-looking papers for removals that source communities never accepted. “Documented” therefore does not automatically mean legitimate or just. Museums examine how objects entered collections and respond to restitution claims. Claims may involve law, ethics, sacred meaning, coercion, and authenticity. Missing records deserve study, but archives reflect who could preserve paperwork.

A chain of custody protects evidence only when its links are trustworthy and interpreted in context. The goal is not a long paper trail for its own sake. It is an accountable account of what the object is, where it traveled, who made decisions about it, and whose authority those decisions recognized.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A scientific match between material and age proves that every object was removed lawfully.
Any long paper trail automatically makes a museum’s ownership legitimate and just.
Missing records prove one exact story about an artifact’s origin and travel.
Artifact records can support authenticity and accountability, but trustworthy interpretation must also confront gaps, false papers, coercion, and contested ownership.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes provenance and custody, explains their uses, and critically examines their limits and power.

questions.stem: Why might a colonial permit fail to settle an ownership dispute?
choices: The issuing authority may not have had consent recognized by the source community.
A permit prevents anyone from recording an object’s age.
All colonial records were written without dates.
Source communities cannot have sacred relationships with objects.
questions.explanation: The passage notes that legal-looking documents can reflect imposed power rather than accepted authority.

questions.stem: What does “provenance” mean?
choices: the chemical material inside a carving
the history of an object’s ownership and locations
a crack appearing during transport
a seal placed on one package
questions.explanation: The opening directly defines provenance as the history of ownership and location.

questions.stem: What can help connect an object with its documentation?
choices: an unexplained gap
a repeated catalog error
identification numbers
appearance alone
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists seals and identification numbers as linking safeguards.

lesson.strategy: Keep four questions separate: Is the object authentic? Where has it been? Was transfer lawful? Was it just? Records contribute to each question without answering all of them automatically.

signals.phrase: but not travel or lawful removal
signals.means: This establishes why visual style cannot replace object history.

signals.phrase: but scientific consistency does not prove
signals.means: This separates material authenticity from lawful transfer.
This blocks the equation of paperwork with legitimacy or justice.

vocab.inContext: the documented history of an object’s ownership and location
the quality of being what an object is claimed to be
the return of an object to a person or community with a valid claim

skillTips.main-idea: Include the evidentiary value of records and the ethical, legal, and archival limits in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the permit problem by asking whose authority and consent the document represents.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the passage’s direct definition to distinguish provenance from a shorter handling chain.
skillTips.detail: For a linking safeguard, return to the physical and record controls in paragraph three.

passages.title: The Empty Space in a Thermos
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A thermos often has one container inside another. Between their walls is a space with very little matter. This vacuum slows the movement of heat.

Heat can travel when moving particles bump into nearby particles. With almost no air between the walls, there are fewer particles to carry energy by conduction or circulation. The gap does not stop all heat.

Shiny surfaces can reflect some thermal radiation. A tight stopper also matters because an open top would let warm air or vapor move. Each part slows a different route.

A thermos does not create cold or heat. It helps a drink keep its starting temperature longer by reducing energy transfer. Hot soup gradually cools, and ice water gradually warms. The empty-looking gap is useful because what is missing, most of the air, leaves heat fewer paths to follow.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A thermos slows several routes of heat transfer through a vacuum gap, reflective surfaces, and a tight stopper.
A thermos creates new heat to keep every drink warm forever.
The vacuum contains extra air that rapidly carries energy.
Only the color of the outside wall affects temperature.
questions.explanation: The passage assigns different heat-transfer limits to the gap, surfaces, and stopper.

questions.stem: Why does the vacuum slow heat transfer?
choices: It adds moving warm air between the walls.
It contains very few particles to pass energy through the gap.
It makes the drink begin at a new temperature.
It removes the need for a stopper.
questions.explanation: Conduction and circulation require matter, and the vacuum greatly reduces that matter.

questions.stem: What does “vacuum” mean here?
choices: a machine that cleans the bottle
a shiny outer paint
a space containing very little matter
a stream of warm vapor
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly defines the space between the walls.

questions.stem: What helps prevent air or vapor leaving through the top?
choices: the outer label
ice water
a colored straw
a tight stopper
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explains why the stopper matters at the opening.

lesson.strategy: Match each design feature with a heat route: sparse particles, reflected radiation, and blocked air movement. The thermos slows change rather than generating a temperature.

signals.means: This limits the claim after explaining the vacuum’s benefit.
This adds the top opening to the wall-based design.
This corrects the idea that insulation produces heat or cold.

vocab.inContext: a space containing extremely little matter
heat transfer through direct interaction of nearby particles
energy carried by electromagnetic waves

skillTips.main-idea: Include the three design features and their shared job in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the vacuum’s effect from the particle collisions required to pass heat.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the direct opening definition to identify vacuum.
skillTips.detail: For the top opening, locate the component discussed with moving air and vapor.

passages.title: Augusta Savage Makes a Place for Artists
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Augusta Savage shaped clay as a child in Florida, despite a father who first opposed her art. She moved to New York and studied sculpture at Cooper Union. Her skill earned attention, but racism closed opportunities, including a summer program in France.

Savage continued creating portrait sculptures of Black leaders and children. She also taught. During the Harlem Renaissance, her studio became a place where young artists could learn even when money was scarce. She later directed the Harlem Community Art Center.

For the 1939 New York World's Fair, Savage created a large sculpture inspired by Black music. It was commonly called The Harp. Like many temporary fair works, it was destroyed after the event because funds were not available to cast or store it permanently.

Much of Savage's art has been lost, but her influence survives through students and institutions. She did more than seek a place in the art world. She made places where other artists could enter, practice, and be seen.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the biography?
choices: Augusta Savage stopped making art after a program in France rejected her.
Augusta Savage created important sculpture while building teaching spaces and opportunities for other Black artists.
The Harp remains permanently stored at the World’s Fair site.
Savage refused to teach students who could not pay much money.
questions.explanation: The biography balances Savage’s own work with the institutions and access she created for others.

questions.stem: Why was The Harp destroyed?
choices: Savage decided that music should never inspire sculpture.
Cooper Union required every graduate work to be destroyed.
It was temporary, and funds were unavailable to preserve it permanently.
Students damaged it during a class.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph connects temporary fair construction with missing funds for casting or storage.

questions.stem: What does “influence” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a tool used for shaping clay
a ticket to a summer program
the size of one sculpture
an effect on later people and institutions
questions.explanation: Her teaching and organizing continue to affect art through students and institutions.

questions.stem: What center did Savage direct?
choices: the Harlem Community Art Center
the Panama Canal Zone
the Royal Game Center
the Lighthouse Archive
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly names the Harlem Community Art Center.

lesson.strategy: Follow two connected legacies: objects Savage made and conditions she made for others. Lost artwork does not erase influence carried through people and institutions.

signals.means: This identifies structural barriers despite Savage’s demonstrated skill.
This turns from Savage’s own sculpture to her role in developing artists.
This widens her legacy from personal entry to creating entry for others.

vocab.inContext: art made by shaping or assembling material in three dimensions
intended to last for a limited time
an effect that helps shape later people, choices, or institutions

skillTips.main-idea: Include both Savage’s sculpture and her community-building work in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the loss of The Harp from its temporary construction and the cost of preserving it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use students and institutions that continue her work to define influence.
skillTips.detail: For the organization, return to the named center in paragraph two.

passages.title: The Farmer's Choice Before Rain
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A farmer must choose seed before knowing how much rain the season will bring. One variety may thrive when wet but fail in drought. Another yields less but survives with little water. Choosing only the highest possible harvest ignores risk. Choosing only the toughest seed may sacrifice income in ordinary years. The farmer weighs expected return, the outcomes and their likelihoods, alongside the household's ability to survive a poor result.

Several strategies can reduce exposure. Planting more than one variety spreads weather risk. Saving cash or grain creates a buffer. Irrigation can reduce dependence on rain where water and equipment are available. Insurance may exchange a known premium for payment after a covered loss, though cost, trust, and claim rules matter.

No method removes uncertainty. A diverse field can still face a region-wide disaster, and a drought-tolerant seed can meet flood. Information from forecasts, soil, past seasons, and local experience can improve a choice without making it certain.

The economically best decision is not always the seed with the highest average yield. A family unable to absorb one disastrous year may reasonably value resilience more. The choice depends on probabilities, consequences, resources, and which risks can be shared or recovered from.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The seed with the highest possible harvest is always the best choice for every farmer.
Planting several varieties removes all risk from weather.
Seed choices under uncertain rain balance expected return with resilience, household capacity, information, and ways to share risk.
Insurance guarantees payment after any kind of crop loss.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the return-risk tradeoff, several tools, remaining uncertainty, and differing ability to bear loss.

questions.stem: Why might a farmer choose a lower-yielding variety?
choices: It produces the highest harvest in every possible season.
It makes forecasts and soil irrelevant.
It guarantees that floods never occur.
Its drought survival may protect the household from a result it cannot afford to bear.
questions.explanation: The conclusion connects resilience with a family’s limited capacity to absorb disaster.

questions.stem: What does “buffer” mean here?
choices: a reserve that reduces the impact of a loss
a forecast that guarantees rain
a seed that grows only in floods
a fee paid after a claim
questions.explanation: Saved cash or grain provides support when a bad outcome reduces current harvest.

questions.stem: What strategy spreads weather risk across crops?
choices: choosing only the highest possible yield
planting more than one variety
ignoring past seasons
spending all saved grain
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly describes crop variety as a way to spread risk.

lesson.strategy: Separate maximum outcome, average expectation, and ability to survive a bad outcome. Then evaluate each risk tool by both what it reduces and what uncertainty remains.

signals.means: This identifies what is missing from a choice based only on the best possible harvest.

signals.phrase: though cost, trust, and claim rules matter
signals.means: This qualifies insurance rather than presenting it as automatic protection.
This limits what improved information can do under uncertainty.

vocab.inContext: an average of possible outcomes weighted by their likelihoods
a reserve that softens the effect of a bad outcome
the capacity to continue and recover after difficulty

skillTips.main-idea: Include return, risk, household capacity, coping tools, and uncertainty in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the lower-yield choice from the severe consequence of one drought for a vulnerable household.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use saved cash or grain after a poor harvest to define buffer.
skillTips.detail: For diversification, locate the first strategy in paragraph three.

passages.title: The Quiet Pride of Maintenance
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A bridge repair earns a photograph. Routine inspection rarely does. An inspector finding a loose connection leaves no wreck, only an ordinary day. Prevention makes its own evidence disappear. This invisibility shapes what communities reward. New buildings offer ribbons to cut and names to place on walls. Drain cleaning, record updates, alarm tests, or new seals look unambitious. Yet neglected systems do not remain still. Water enters, knowledge becomes outdated, and small faults combine.

Maintenance is not merely repeating the past. A repairer learns where a design wears, which users struggle, and what conditions have changed. A patch may preserve the current system, while accumulated observations may justify redesign. Care includes knowing when restoration is no longer enough.

There are bad forms of maintenance. An institution can preserve an unfair rule simply because it is familiar. Workers can be asked to keep a failing system alive without time, authority, or safe equipment. Praising devotion must not excuse poor design or hidden exploitation.

The quiet pride worth defending is disciplined attention to continuity. It values the person who records a crack, the crew that clears a culvert before rain, and the librarian who migrates an aging digital archive. Their work protects possibilities other people expect to find tomorrow. Its success often looks like nothing happened, which is precisely why it requires deliberate notice.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Maintenance means keeping every old rule and design unchanged forever.
Prevention is unimportant because successful work leaves no wreck to photograph.
Workers should maintain failing systems even without authority or safe equipment.
Maintenance deserves recognition for preserving future possibilities, while its observations should guide redesign and never excuse unfair or unsafe systems.
questions.explanation: The essay values preventive continuity but qualifies it through learning, redesign, justice, and worker conditions.

questions.stem: Why does the author say prevention makes its evidence disappear?
choices: When maintenance succeeds, the failure that would demonstrate its value never occurs.
Inspectors erase every record after finding a fault.
New buildings prevent people from taking photographs.
A loose connection becomes more visible after collapse.
questions.explanation: The ordinary day produced by prevention lacks the dramatic counterfactual accident.

questions.stem: What does “culvert” mean in context?
choices: a ribbon used at a new building
a channel that carries water beneath a road or path
an unfair institutional rule
a file stored in a digital archive
questions.explanation: Crews clear it before rain as part of drainage maintenance, indicating a water channel.

questions.stem: What does the librarian maintain?
choices: a bridge beam
a storm drain
an aging digital archive
a fire alarm
questions.explanation: The final paragraph names migrating an aging digital archive as the librarian’s work.

lesson.strategy: Track the paradox that successful prevention leaves no disaster as proof. Then follow how maintenance produces knowledge for repair, redesign, and ethical limits.

signals.means: This introduces the active deterioration hidden by a lack of dramatic change.
This reframes maintenance as observation and adaptation rather than stasis.
This prevents praise for devotion from justifying harmful conditions.

vocab.inContext: ongoing work that preserves function and prevents deterioration
returning something toward an earlier working condition
a channel carrying water beneath a road, track, or path

skillTips.inference: Infer disappearing evidence by imagining the accident that successful inspection prevents.

passages.title: The Tortoise's Shortcut
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A tortoise carried herbs along a path curving around silver moss. The curve added nine minutes. Late one morning, he crossed the moss directly. His feet left a dark line, but he reached the healer early. “A useful shortcut,” he decided. He used it again. A rabbit saw the new track and followed. Goats widened it, then carts cut the corner. Rain entered the broken moss. Water gathered in the footprints, loosened soil, and flowed onto the stone path. Soon the curve was buried under mud. Travelers now spent twenty minutes pulling wheels and cleaning their feet.

The village council blamed the goats. The goats blamed the first visible cart rut. The tortoise said nothing until a child asked why one narrow track began beneath the shape of a tortoise shell. “I saved nine minutes twice,” he admitted, “and gave the road a habit.”

Repair took many mornings. People moved water through a lined channel, closed the damaged ground, and carried pieces of moss only under a gardener's guidance. The tortoise volunteered for every trip. He did not pretend his two crossings caused each later choice, but he had made the harmful route look available.

When the moss recovered, the council added a proper side path on durable ground. The lesson was not that every shortcut is selfish. Some remove pointless delay. The question is where saved effort goes: a shortcut may reduce the user's cost by placing a larger cost on land, workers, or travelers who come later.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: The tortoise learns that a personal shortcut can export larger costs by making a fragile, harmful route appear available to others.
Every shortcut is selfish and should be forbidden even on durable ground.
The goats alone cause all damage because they make the widest footprints.
The moss recovers immediately without labor, drainage, or a new route.
questions.explanation: The fable traces one time saving into imitation and shared cost, then qualifies the lesson with better shortcuts.

questions.stem: Why does the tortoise say he gave the road a habit?
choices: He taught the stone path how to move by itself.
His first track invited repeated use that turned one action into a damaging pattern.
His shell physically created every later cart rut.
The villagers had always crossed the moss before him.
questions.explanation: The visible line made the route seem available, allowing others’ choices to compound the harm.

questions.stem: What does “durable” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: covered in newly damaged moss
slower than every existing path
able to withstand repeated use without failing quickly
hidden from all travelers
questions.explanation: The new path is placed on ground that can bear traffic without repeating the fragile-moss damage.

questions.stem: How much time did the original shortcut save per trip?
choices: twenty minutes
two mornings
one minute
nine minutes
questions.explanation: The opening says the curve added nine minutes, which the direct crossing avoided.

lesson.strategy: Trace costs across people and time: one traveler saves minutes, imitation damages moss, and later travelers and repairers pay more. The new path distinguishes redesign from simple prohibition.

signals.means: This explains the immediate reward that hides the developing cost.
This metaphor names how a visible individual act becomes a repeated social pattern.
This assigns initiating responsibility without making the tortoise the sole cause of every choice.

vocab.inContext: a route intended to reduce travel distance or time
a burden or resource use created by a choice
able to withstand wear and continue functioning

skillTips.main-idea: Include personal benefit, imitation, shifted costs, repair, and the qualified view of shortcuts.
skillTips.inference: Infer the road-habit metaphor by following how one visible track invites many later users.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast between fragile moss and the new path to define durable.
skillTips.detail: For time saved, return to the extra duration of the original curved route.

passages.title: A Good Act or a Good Character?
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Milo returns a lost wallet. Was the act good because its result helped the owner? Was it good because Milo followed a rule? Or does it show that Milo is an honest person?

The last question is about character. A character trait is a habit of choosing and feeling across many situations. One returned wallet is evidence, but it may not reveal a whole life.

A person might do one helpful act to win praise. Another might act kindly most days but fail when afraid. We can still judge each action while also asking what habits it builds.

Good character is not a label earned once. Honesty grows through repeated choices, reflection after failure, and repair. An act matters for what it does now and for the kind of person it helps someone become.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: One helpful act proves that a person will behave perfectly forever.
A good action can be judged now while also serving as evidence and practice for an evolving character.
Character has no connection with repeated choices or habits.
Only the final result of an act can ever matter.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes act judgment from patterns of character and explains how the two connect.

questions.stem: Why might one returned wallet not reveal a whole character?
choices: The wallet has no owner who can be helped.
Honesty can happen only when someone is afraid.
A lasting trait depends on patterns across many situations and motives.
A single act never has any value.
questions.explanation: The passage defines character as a habit across situations, not one isolated event.

questions.stem: What does “trait” mean?
choices: an object found inside a wallet
a prize for one action
a rule that never changes
a lasting quality or tendency in a person
questions.explanation: Honesty is presented as a repeated tendency, making it a character trait.

questions.stem: What item does Milo return?
choices: a lost wallet
a borrowed book
a paper crane
a broken chair
questions.explanation: The opening example begins with Milo returning a lost wallet.
